<meta>The following text continues the correspondence of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, a celebrated Renaissance philosopher. These letters reflect his interpersonal relationships and his intense dedication to his studies.</meta>

...you were the first to call me to this duty, especially with such a letter that has so captivated and delighted me that I cannot remember being more pleased by any reading for many days now. It is full of eloquence, full of grace, full of love and benevolence. Perhaps you expected me to say it was full of my own praises. Indeed, I was going to say this as well—for I am not so iron-hearted, or if you prefer the term, so much of a philosopher <note>original: "adeo sum philosophus"</note>, that I am not delighted by the praises of friends. If those praises are true, they recommend me to myself; if they are false, they recommend to me the writer's love and goodwill. 

Therefore, I will easily obtain permission from my philosophy to read your letters both frequently and with pleasure, even the parts where they praise me. But it is not so easy for me to appear sufficiently civil, or at least not ungrateful, in returning this literary favor. For an imperious mistress <note>Pico is likely personifying "Philosophy" or his intense study schedule as a demanding mistress.</note> so distracts me, so demands her daily task, and finally so occupies me entirely that hardly anything of myself is left even for me. But such is your kindness that you will take even bad letters in good part when I write them, and take my silence well when I am quiet. Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano, the renowned humanist poet and Pico's close friend.</note>, our mutual delight, sends his greetings. Farewell.

## **Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Troilo Malvezzi, greetings.**

<gloss>l</gloss> Your little book on lots <note>original: "de sortibus." This likely refers to a treatise on divination or the "casting of lots" to determine fate.</note> has given me as much pleasure as is usually felt by one who has drawn the best lot. I give you great thanks for making me a sharer in your labors <note>original: "lucubrationum," literally meaning work done by lamplight at night.</note>, especially such as these. In them, both the subtlety of argument and a multifaceted, varied knowledge of things are easily apparent. One of these deserves praise for talent, the other for diligence. I will give you my trifles <note>original: "nugas nostras," a common humanist humble-brag for their own writings.</note>, which you desire, very soon. For it is uncertain whether it is more unworthy that you—a very busy <term>jurisconsult [a professional legal expert]</term>—should be detained by reading them, or that a very dear friend should be kept in suspense for so long by his desire for them. Farewell and love me. Florence, May 29, 1492.

## **Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Taddeo Ugolini, greetings.**

<gloss>g</gloss> Your letter was most welcome to me, full of love, faith, and charity—not only because you remembered me, but because in it you friendly advise me that I should remember myself. By this, I mean I should remember my good studies and the expectation I must uphold. Indeed, conscious of my own weakness, I would not dare to promise anything even mediocre about myself. 

But He from whom every good comes, the most merciful Father of Lights <note>A biblical reference to James 1:17.</note>, just as He has previously given the means by which men might hope for something from us, so He will give in the future, so that we may not hold this well-conceived opinion in vain. I am hurrying to Rome where we shall make a trial of our studies, even at some risk <note>Pico had famously proposed 900 theses for public debate in Rome in 1486, which led to a papal ban and significant personal danger.</note>. If we achieve anything, it is God's gift; to Him be the praise and thanks. If we fail in anything, it is our own weakness; let it be attributed to us. For the rest, I am yours, as one who, because of the integrity of your life and character, would hardly yield the first place in loving you even to our Hieronymo <note>Almost certainly a reference to Girolamo Savonarola, the influential Dominican friar who was a close spiritual mentor to Pico.</note>. Farewell, from Fratta.

<meta>This page begins a correspondence from the famed Italian Renaissance philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to the Venetian humanist Tommaso Medio.</meta>

->Giovanni Pico della Mirandola sends greetings to Tommaso Medio.<-

**N**ever do I remember being more delighted than recently, while I was reading your *Epyrota* <note>original: "epyrotam"; The *Epyrota* was a Latin comedy written by Tommaso Medio in 1483, modeled after the ancient Roman plays of Plautus and Terence.</note>. It is undoubtedly a most witty little story, challenging even the ancient comedies with both the festive nature of its subject matter and the erudition of its style. For what should I say of these modern plays? <note>Pico is likely referring to contemporary "sacred representations" or less refined humanist plays.</note> They are clearly inept and humorless, which easily demonstrates the lack of eloquence in their authors. 

It was certainly worthy of being dedicated by name to Ermolao Barbaro <note>Ermolao Barbaro (1454–1493) was a preeminent Venetian scholar and diplomat, known for his work on Aristotle and Pliny.</note>—I know not whether he is more your friend or mine. To him alone, I believe all men of letters owe as much as they scarcely owe even to antiquity itself. In not depriving me of this work, you have acted in accordance with your benevolence toward me, which has been most clearly proven before now. 

And there is nothing in my possession of such value that, if I were to send it to you in return, I would consider the favor to be fully repaid. I am now waiting with open mouth <note>original: "expectans inhio"; a vivid Latin idiom for eager anticipation.</note> for the new comedy which you promise me. Nor is there anything I desire more than that, except for one thing: your arrival here to visit us. Had it not been that I must depart from here in ten days—as I believe you have learned from our <unclear>mutual friend</unclear>—I certainly would have obtained a visit from you by urgent request. For it is...

...as you were seeking. I have no doubt that you understood. They will be sent as soon as I have returned to my own library; I came here for the present specifically to explore the collections of others. Nor is there any reason for me to regret the journey, as I have found so many things here—both Greek and Latin—pertaining to the <term>liberal arts</term> <note>original: "humaniores litteras," referring to the study of classical literature, history, and moral philosophy that defined Renaissance Humanism.</note> and to learned philosophy. Indeed, on this very day that I was sending this letter, a fragment of Apuleius <note>Lucius Apuleius Madaurensis (c. 124 – c. 170 AD), a Roman philosopher and prose writer best known for his novel "The Golden Ass."</note> titled *On Interpretation* <note>original: "de interpretatione"</note> fell into my hands; it is a scholarly work, and one that is clearly recognized as being the work of Apuleius...

<meta>This page continues a letter from Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to the humanist scholar Hermolao Barbaro, discussing the restoration of classical texts and the philosophical harmony between Plato and Aristotle. It then begins a new letter to the poet Battista Mantuanus.</meta>

...but it is mutilated and defective. I would like to know from you whether it is considered complete there, as far as you know; although, once you have published your own works, which you currently have <term>under the anvil<note>original: "sub incude"; a Latin idiom meaning a work is still being forged or refined.</note></term>, there will no longer be any reason for us to miss Apuleius. Regarding my own studies, I have nothing to write to you except that I am constantly occupied with "Hermolao" <note>He refers to Barbaro's own writings.</note> and that I spend the greatest part of my nights keeping watch over your work on Themistius <note>Hermolao Barbaro was famous for his Latin translations of the Greek philosopher Themistius.</note>. I have recently turned away from Aristotle toward the Academy <note>The Academy refers to the school of Plato.</note>. But I go not as a deserter—as that famous man <note>A reference to Seneca (Epistle 2.5), who said he visited other schools of thought not as a defector, but as an explorer.</note> says—but as an explorer.

I seem, however, to recognize two things in Plato (I will tell you, Hermolao, what I feel): that Homeric faculty of eloquence that raises itself above the level of prose speech, and, if one looks more deeply into them, a complete communion of meaning with Aristotle. Thus, if you look at the words, nothing is more conflicting; if you look at the matter, nothing is more harmonious. If it should ever be granted—which is the summit of my prayers—to philosophize with you for a few days, we shall discuss these things more extensively in person and put this opinion of mine to some test. Farewell, glory of our age.

Florence, December 6, 1484.

...I was with a cheerful and open countenance <note>original: "hilari & porrecta fronte" - a Latin idiom meaning to be open and sincere</note> [sending] those letters of mine, inept indeed and disorganized, but a most serious testimony of my faith toward you and of a will truly most devoted to you. By which I wish one thing especially to be indicated to you: that there is nothing I desire more than that some occasion be given to me through which I might clearly leave with you a witness of my faith, piety, and respect toward you. For if you ever make a trial of us in these matters, you will recognize me to be as superior among those devoted to you as you wonderfully excel the other prelates of your order in virtue, learning, and holiness.

->**Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Baldassare Migliavacca, greetings.**<- <note>The letter "S" stands for "Salutem," a standard Latin greeting. The "x" mark to the right is likely a filing mark made by a contemporary secretary.</note>

You will be angry, and indeed not unjustly, at a response from me to your letters [coming] much <margin>m</margin> later than perhaps you desired and your letters themselves deservedly required; hear in a few words why this happened. A man truly honest but previously unknown to me was about to go to you around the same days I received yours; he said he was doing business in Milan. I considered it an opportune departure, by which it would happen that through a faithful messenger—and what I especially hoped for—my letters would be delivered to you without delay. But I struck the south wind <note>original: "austrum perculi" - a nautical metaphor meaning a plan was frustrated or went off course</note>: for since he had postponed his departure by a month through putting it off day after day, he finally left: but while I was completely unaware. Truly, since I had become more negligent in the hope of a certain messenger, a forgetfulness of letters had almost crept up on me. Now at last, when your letter to me fell into my hands, it immediately roused me as if I were sleeping and reminded me of the time passed without duty. I grieved (I call God to witness) no small amount, and even now I grieve; nor would I wish these things said to excuse myself, but rather to accuse myself: I will easily allow myself to be condemned for negligence, and if you prefer, for a punishment to be called by you. Now to your letters. I received no small pleasure both from the letters themselves and from the Greek books, of which you so liberally and so kindly gave me the use. [This was] not so much because the use of them contributed greatly to my studies, but because we have laid the foundations of a perpetual bond to be between us. This one thing I value more than the entire library of either Sunandius <note>This name is likely a corruption or specific reference to a collector; it may refer to a contemporary library or an ancient one, possibly a misreading of "Suidas" or "Symmachus"</note> or Ptolemy. For I am so far from neglecting the friendships of learned men that nothing is more a matter of concern or dearer to my heart. Moreover, I know what place you claim for yourself among learned men: since indeed your letter was to me the most evident proof of your learning, erudition, and humanity. Therefore, if I did not love you very much, I would have surely forgotten myself and would act far differently than I am accustomed. I love you, therefore, uniquely, although I have never seen you; I love you so from my soul that there are few I love more from my soul; such that something might finally be added to our familiarity, but nothing could be added to my love. And if there is anything that can be added, it would be through your arrival here. This you promised of your own accord in your letters, and we seek it so ardently as we impatiently desire it. If you could provide me with John the Grammarian <note>Also known as John Philoponus, a 6th-century Alexandrian scholar whose commentaries on Aristotle were highly sought after during the Renaissance</note> on the *Physics* and *Metaphysics* of Aristotle, you will have bound me to you in perpetual obligation. For I do not have them with me, and I am in great expectation of them. Farewell.

**Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Giacomo of Feltre, Greetings.** <note>The Latin abbreviation "S." stands for "Salutem," a standard opening wishing the recipient health and prosperity.</note>

Your letters, if ever they did before, have now delighted me most highly; from them, I have learned that your opinion of me is such that a better one could not even be imagined in a wish. One thing alone disturbed me: since you noted nothing <note>The Latin *notaueris* suggests a lack of critical feedback or corrections in the recipient's previous reply.</note> in what I wrote to you, you have raised a suspicion that you did not consider the works worthy of any remark at all. For I would have believed that most things had truly pleased you only if you had indicated that at least some things had displeased you. Thus it happens that I do not sufficiently trust your testimony—otherwise most highly esteemed—in my own case. For you love all our works just as we do; and since, out of the innate kindness of your nature, you uplift everyone, this happens to you especially regarding my affairs, since everything that is in me has flowed from your own fountain. Indeed, I do not cease, nor shall I ever stop, emulating you and following in your footsteps. Would that I might one day catch up to you! But I grieve that the distance between our locations prevents me from hearing you in person as you weightily treat the most profound topics of philosophy, as is your house's custom. And even if those same things you say could be sent through your letters—which I would most dearly wish to obtain from you—the **living** <note>The text likely concludes with "living voice" (*viva vox*), a common Renaissance concept suggesting that spoken teaching is more powerful than the written word.</note> [voice] nevertheless possesses something...

<meta>This page contains two letters from the philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to the humanist scholar Angelo Poliziano. The correspondence centers on the exchange of literary works for critique and Pico's request to suppress his earlier, immature poetry.</meta>

<margin>c</margin>
# Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Angelo, Sends Greetings.

Since I have organized my slight muses <note>original: "tenues musas meas" — a humble way of referring to his poetry</note>, with which I played about my loves while my age allowed, into five little books: I am sending the first of them to you, intending to send the rest if, in this one case, I find you to be a friend and not a flatterer. For they come to you on the condition that they be corrected and "beaten" <note>a metaphor for rigorous editing</note>: that they pay the penalty for their errors with both the fingernail and with obelisks <note>original: "ungue & obeliscis" — refers to the critical marks used by ancient scholars to denote errors or deletions</note>. Therefore, show yourself a fair judge to them, not an unfair one—that is, be severe, not indulgent. For what is greater unfairness than to deceive a friend who expects everything of you? I am not of such a delicate nature that I loathe the erasures of another; I do not seem so handsome to myself that I would either ignore or blame a censor. 

Indeed, perhaps neither you nor anyone would believe how much these works of mine fail to satisfy me; even in those which please me more, I fear lest I be as that man Suffenus <note>A character from the poet Catullus, used as a symbol of a delusional, bad poet</note> says. Surely we are all deceived and do not see the knapsack that is on our back <note>A reference to Aesop’s fable: we carry a bag of our own faults on our back where we can't see them, while others' faults are in a bag in front</note>. Therefore, do not deny your effort in this honest and noble matter to a man who is most friendly to you—especially one who entreats it with such great zeal and from his very soul. But if I were the kind of person who could return the favor to you in such a matter, I would not keep silent about that Greek saying: that Lysippus was accustomed to use the work of Apelles, and Apelles that of Lysippus, in turn <note>original: "Lisippum apellis & apellem lisippi" — Lysippus was a famous sculptor and Apelles a famous painter; the anecdote suggests mutual professional critique</note>. Farewell.

<margin>c</margin>
# Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Angelo Poliziano, Sends Greetings.

When I was in Florence in previous years, I left four love elegies with you which, as often happens, I had composed almost as a boy for the sake of exercising my talent. They were indeed tasteless, unlearned, and slight, clearly displaying the author’s age and ignorance. You, however, approved of them—not because of the merit of the work, but out of your own kindness and indulgence. And for that very reason, to show your faith in what you approved, you asked for copies; surely you were not unaware that such things are sharp incentives for the minds of youths toward virtue, so that, enticed by the desire for praise, they might soon strive to taste more deeply the "little glory" <note>original: "gloriolam"</note> they have sipped. For just as strengths lie flat and freeze in desperation, so there is no one who doubts they are raised up and inflamed by hope. 

But now the protection of age is removed, and those errors which were previously signed off on will now be turned into a fault against me, if I, now more mature in years, have not either cleaned them up better or deleted them. Therefore, whatever poems of mine are with you, if you love me, either send them back to me, or tear them up, or commit them to the fire. All those, more carefully worked, and many others which I tossed off in my leisure after I left there, will shortly be entrusted to your "file" <note>original: "limæ" — a common metaphor for the polishing or refining of a literary work</note>. In the meantime, let those which cannot live without harm to a friend be condemned by the "death sentence" <note>original: "capitali damnentur calculo" — literally "the capital pebble," referring to the black pebble used in ancient voting to signal a death sentence or condemnation</note>. 

Furthermore, I would entirely wish for you to send me your *Epictetus* and those things from Homer which you have translated up to this day; likewise what you composed about Giuliano de' Medici in the mother tongue <note>original: "sermone patrio" — referring to Italian (Tuscan) rather than Latin</note> and whatever else you have composed in the Latin tongue. I ask this of you as urgently as possible, for I desire it most impatiently. Nor is there any reason for you to refuse because they might not yet be brought "to the navel" <note>original: "ad umbilicum" — an ancient idiom for finishing a book, referring to the cylinder at the end of a scroll</note>; for I already announce and promise you that all these things will remain secret with me, if that be your wish. Farewell.

<meta>This page captures the opening of a letter from the brilliant young philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to his mentor, Marsilio Ficino, the head of the Platonic Academy in Florence. It establishes the central Renaissance theme of human dignity and the "cultivation of the soul."</meta>

->Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Marsilio Ficino, Greetings.<-

It has always been my judgment, most learned Marsilio, that there is no matter upon which we should work more intensely than ensuring that we do not, through sloth or laziness, in any way fall away from the nobility of the soul. According to the testimony of Trismegistus <note>original: "trimegiſto"; referring to Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary figure who Renaissance scholars believed was an ancient Egyptian sage and contemporary of Moses</note>, it is this nobility that makes us considered next in rank after Jove <note>original: "Iouē"; Pico uses the Roman name for Jupiter to refer to God or the supreme divine power</note>. 

This has always been my primary goal: to acquire, from whatever source I could, the cultivation of my soul and the study of the liberal arts. While this purpose has been constant within me since my childhood, your encouragements when I was with you in years past stirred and inflamed me so greatly that never have I devoted myself more ardently to "letters" <note>The "literae humaniores" or the humanities, encompassing literature, history, and philosophy</note> than from that day until this. 

For three years now, Marsilio, I have been occupied among the Peripatetics <note>term: Peripatetics — Followers of Aristotle's philosophy. At this time, Aristotelianism was the dominant academic framework in universities</note>, and I have omitted nothing that was within my power to study...

<meta>This page continues a correspondence between the Italian humanists Ermolao Barbaro and Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. The previous text likely contained Barbaro's initial thoughts on the nature of friendship and the necessity of letter-writing.</meta>

...they feel they must write so that this might be paid as if it were a debt to friendship. Indeed, this whole business of writing and sending letters belongs to a friendship that is weak and rather cold: one that does not stand firm on its own strength, but seeks support from elsewhere to stay upright. But for a friendship that has already taken deep root in the very recesses of the soul: why, I ask, does it need the crutches of letters? 

I will therefore give my letter to Hermolaus the barbarian <note>original: "Hermolae barbaro." This is a playful pun on his own name, Ermolao Barbaro, suggesting he is "barbarous" or perhaps referring to the messenger</note> to bring to you, so that I might entice your letters, which I most greatly desire. You, in turn, will return yours as abundantly as possible so they are not longed for by me in vain. For just as it is the mark of a weak soul to use letters like props <note>original: "tibicines," literally "flute-players" used as architectural supports or "buttresses"</note> for friendship lest it falter, so it is the mark of singular generosity and benevolence to show oneself easy and beneficial to friends. 

Farewell. And send me Ptolemy’s *Harmonics* <note>original: "musicam Ptolomei." Claudius Ptolemy's 2nd-century work on the mathematical theory of music</note> if it is not an inconvenience to you; it will be here for only a few days. For what should I not boldly ask of you, to whom I have long since vowed and dedicated all my own things?

### Giovanni Pico della Mirandola sends greetings to Hermolaus.

I have never either pleased myself more or owed more abundantly than at this time, when I have called forth from you letters so sweet, so erudite, and so very like yourself by means of a single letter of mine. If both your absence from Padua while I was there and my two-year longing for your company were the reason why you wrote this to me, whatever that reason might be, it cannot fail to be pleasant to me now. Your single letter has so abundantly not only fulfilled but even surpassed my every wish. 

For I shall remain silent about the elegance, charm, erudition, and sweetness of the letter—the reading of which demands a return of favor in full measure—how much do you believe it means to me that you give yourself to me as a friend so lovingly, so kindly, and so truly from the heart? And, since I would not dare to hope for anything greater, that you so liberally promise your effort in honoring me in every way? Indeed, I would not blush to confess frankly, even in person, that this kind of service is not merely to be received by me, but even actively sought. 

For not even the Stoics themselves, as you know, approve of *apatheia* <term>freedom from passion; a state of being unaffected by emotions</term>; nor among these which the Greeks call *pathe* <term>affections or passions</term> can any be more praiseworthy or more honorable than this one: if indeed that which is called the "desire for name and glory" is numbered among them. Truly, this can be provided to me more richly by no one than by yourself, in whom all the virtues, as if individually, compete to claim the palm of victory for themselves. And I certainly have no one to whom I would more willingly owe a debt. 

Therefore, this promise of yours is as pleasing and desirable to me as it is an honor, in which I rejoice most greatly for this reason: that it gives proof of a certain extraordinary love and a most affectionate will toward me. I have at last what I have desired for a long time before this; so now I truly triumph. I have, I say, Hermolaus Barbarus—the delight of the Latin language and the distinguished storehouse of all the noble arts—not only well-disposed toward me, but as a most intimate friend. 

You likewise have Giovanni Pico della Mirandola so devoted to you, so studious of your interests, that no one could be more devoted or more studious. In mutual duties toward you—since he can provide nothing either great or worthy of Hermolaus—he will indeed be unequal; but if you look at his spirit, he will certainly be either equal or superior. Farewell.

<meta>This page continues the correspondence of the Italian Renaissance philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494). The previous pages likely established his relationships with fellow humanists in Florence and Padua. This section features a letter regarding his work "Heptaplus" and a deeply personal letter to a mentor, likely Marsilio Ficino, emphasizing the harmony between philosophy and religion.</meta>

**Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, etc.**

Nothing was sweeter to me while you were here with us than your company; likewise, nothing was more useful, such is the sweetness of your character and such is your learning. See then how sweet and how welcome you were to me while I enjoyed your presence, since now, while you are absent, nothing is sweeter to me than the memory of you. But indeed, if the seat of friendship is the soul, and if we are primarily our souls—as Plato and Aristotle write—there is no reason why any distance of place or long intervals of time should be able to create a separation between us. I was thinking, however, whether I might be able to achieve being with you in some other way, and nothing else came to mind except that my late-night study <note>original: "lucubratio" — a term for scholarly work produced by candlelight, implying intense dedication.</note> on the sevenfold narration of the six days of Genesis <note>This refers to Pico's work "Heptaplus" (1489), a mystical and philosophical commentary on the creation story in the Bible.</note> should come to you. For if we give birth to books as if they were our children, and the greatest part of the father is in the son, I too shall come to you in that which I have begotten. Receive, therefore, my little son as he comes to you, as you used to receive me, cheerfully and gladly. He will please you, I know, because you love me. I know also that he will displease you, likewise because you love me. For it is the nature of such devotion to look closely into the errors of those we love so that we may correct them, and, having looked into them, to indulge them lightly so that we do not cause distress.

**Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to M.F.** <note>The abbreviation likely refers to Marsilio Ficino, the influential Neoplatonic philosopher who was a mentor to Pico.</note>

<margin>f</margin> Greetings, most beloved father! Here is the Apollonius <note>Likely referring to the biography of the ancient mystic Apollonius of Tyana.</note> for you. If I did not owe him to your virtue and your services toward me, I would certainly owe him because of this letter in which you demand him with such great love and such great kindness. For it is a mark of the highest love to call me to that place where you have already arrived: namely, to the purification of the soul, which is true happiness. And it is a mark of the highest kindness to encourage me as if I were an equal, though you could give laws to me as if to a son. 

But would that it might happen one day in some retreat that we might be able to philosophize together piously. You will see that in my eyes, nothing comes before the joining of piety with wisdom. You will see that I am most firmly convinced that there is no wisdom which should erase the image of eternal wisdom within us, making us like the foolish beasts. I have my guardian angel as a witness that I daily add as much to the "profit" of my studies as I emerge from them more prepared and stronger for the struggle of purifying the soul. This multifaceted handling of disciplines, and whatever literature can promise us, colors the skin and makes us appear more beautiful, as if with a painted face. But we cannot hope for a healthy, firm, and robust mind from anywhere else but from integrity of life, from character, and finally from divine religion. Therefore, you compel one who is already willing (so to speak) to be even more willing. But help me also with your sacred prayers, so that I may be able to achieve both what I myself desired and what you so greatly wish me to desire. Farewell, most loving father, whom I love uniquely and hold dearer than my own eyes. Florence, January 13, 1490. I await all your news. My Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), a brilliant poet and scholar in the Medici circle.</note>, the delight of all literature, sends his greetings to you.

**Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Ermolao Barbaro, Greetings.**

I remember when I was deliberating which of the schools of Italy I should choose as my primary seat for the study of philosophy, and while many things called me to Padua, I sought that place more willingly so that my love for you, which I had long nourished in my soul, might [grow] through mutual company...

<meta>This page continues the author's personal reflection on his time in Padua and his introduction to a prominent scholar, likely Ermolao Barbaro, whose reputation preceded their meeting.</meta>

It was clear: I was in Padua for two years, and yet—who would believe it?—I neither saw Hermolaus <note>referring to Ermolao Barbaro (1454–1493), a famous Venetian scholar and diplomat</note> nor knew him except by his reputation from long before. Thus it often happens that while we neglect a presented opportunity through a certain lazy procrastination, it slips from our hands as if it were coated in oil. 

I have deeply regretted this matter and continue to regret it, all the more because, while I previously knew your reputation for learning in all things only by rumor, I have now recognized it with these very eyes and these ears. This happened while I heard the "Roman Themistius" <note>Themistius was an ancient Greek philosopher; the author here uses the title to praise the recipient's skill in translating or explaining philosophy</note> discussing the nature of the soul, the first beginnings of all things, and the science of reasoning <term>logic or dialectics</term> with your very own voice. 

Good God, what a depth of learning! What a wealth of expression! What clarity! What purity of speech! O most distinguished man, O living image of antiquity! It was my frequent prayer that the writings of Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BCE), an ancient Roman scholar known as "the most learned of the Romans"</note> on things divine and human might someday come back to life, so that there might be someone from whom we could learn the principles of physics <note>original: "physicas rationes," referring to natural philosophy or the study of the physical world</note> in the Latin language. 

Truly, you—reflecting both him and all the most esteemed authors—have shown yourself to us in such a way that nothing remains for us to desire, except that by translating other Greek works you may produce even greater praise for yourself and more abundantly...

But it is far from being the case that moving from the contemplative

<meta>This page continues a correspondence regarding personal matters, literary advice, and the behavior of a wayward acquaintance. The author remains in Perugia, maintaining his network with the Borromeo family.</meta>

...is lacking in literary matters. In Rome and wherever else in the world I may be, those princes will have someone to command—someone whom they can turn at their whim like a "hand-driven millstone," as Plautus <note>original: "trusatilem molā"; a reference to the grueling labor of slaves in Roman comedy</note> says.

What you write regarding the matter of a wife, I do not think was said rashly or without cause. But I am Davus, not Oedipus <note>A common Latin idiom meaning "I am a simple man, not a solver of riddles"</note>—nor, if I were, would I wish to be. Whatever that matter is, if it seems right to you, explain it more broadly; if not, then be Harpocrates <note>The Greco-Roman god of silence and secrets</note>. And as circumstances unfold, I shall take counsel. There is no reason for you to long for my "Tuscan rhythms" <note>original: "Rhythmos meos ethrușcos"; referring to his Italian poetry, likely in the style of Petrarch</note>. For some time now, I have sent a farewell to amorous games, as I am meditating on other things.

But I wish to warn you of this: your "Laura," if you were intending to publish her, suppress her for a few days more. For perhaps very soon our people will read things about love—mark my words—that they have not yet read. And you will be able to make many notes which will be of great use to your own work.

Concerning Alibrana—although he is not worthy of me speaking about him—I would nevertheless say this: that man, despite having been well-treated, has returned poor gratitude to his master. Nor is there any reason why he should cast or deflect the blame for his flight onto anyone else but himself, since he owes almost as much to my own household staff—which he cannot deny—as he does to me. But as you know, this is not the first time he has either broken faith or made a fool of his master. I know what he said against me and about me even after he fled. But the elephant does not care about the gnat <note>A proverbial expression meaning a great man ignores the pestering of the insignificant</note>. I am willing to pardon whatever that frivolous man has sinned before now for your sake; but let him not abuse my patience in the future, lest I be forced to eventually treat him exactly as he has undeservedly treated me.

As for your friend whose love affair ended badly: in excusing him to our friend Florianus, you acted out of duty. Indeed, he has examples from history, from the poets, and even from philosophy itself with which to clear himself of the mark of a crime. He has the precedents of great men like David and especially Solomon to protect him—to say nothing of Aristotle. Even Aristotle, while he was desperately in love with certain courtesans, remembered none of his own moral precepts; he even performed sacred rites for a beloved woman as if to Eleusinian Ceres <note>Aristotle was famously accused of offering sacrifices to his concubine, Pythias, as if she were a goddess</note>. 

But your friend does not merely embrace or love these defenses and "ramparts" for his deed; rather, he hates, rejects, and refuses them. He laments his loss; he does not plead against his guilt. He grieves that he sinned; he does not defend it. And to me, for this reason alone he seems worthy of being excused by others: because he does not excuse himself. 

Nothing is weaker than man, and nothing is more powerful than love. Even the invincible and unshaken mind of Saint Jerome, while it clung entirely to heaven, felt itself present among the dances of girls <note>Referring to Jerome's famous letter describing his lustful visions while living as a hermit in the desert</note>. What plague could infest a man that love will not eventually tame? If love could do this in the desert, with limbs dashed against the ground and amidst weeks of fasting, what will it not be able to do among downy feathers, in the shade, and in every abundance of delights?

Add to this that he has now fallen for the first time, being otherwise unaccustomed to and ignorant of such a ruin. He who has suffered shipwreck only once has the right to complain to Neptune. If he strikes the same stone a second time, let no one stretch out a hand to him; let no one pity him. But now, he cannot rightly *not* be excused, since he so repents of the deed that he does not even think himself worthy of the favor of an excuse. 

But this is enough of this, since your friend desires that the memory of such a deed not only be recorded in some way in writing, but that his subsequent life should cause it to be utterly blotted out.

Farewell. Christopher was not present when I received your letter. Recommend me in no ordinary way to your lord and to the entire Borromeo family, whom I have always loved and now love very much.

At Perugia, the 15th of October, in the year of grace 1491.

# Giovanni Pico of Mirandola sends many greetings to his nephew, Gianfrancesco.

Your letters were most welcome to me. This is not only because I had heard nothing from you for a long time, but also because they signaled things to me in which I took wonderful delight: for I do not doubt that these same things are pleasing to you and most pleasing to God. You also should have no doubt that if you continue on the path you have begun, your reward will be "great in heaven." <note>original: "mercedem tuam copiosam in celis esse futuram"; a reference to Matthew 5:12.</note> I have not yet sufficiently determined whether I must go to Rome or not. And as far as I can gather by conjecture, I believe it is more likely that I will have to go there; you know the reason. <note>Pico was likely referring to his ongoing legal and theological disputes with the Church authorities regarding his "900 Theses."</note> As soon as I have certainty on this, I will immediately inform you, lest if you happen to come here (which I would otherwise greatly desire) you either do not find me here, or you would have to return home immediately upon my departure.

In the meantime, you can remain at home, unless you feel otherwise. But you should also remember that you have a wife, to whom you owe your body no less than you owe your soul to God. Her desire must be satisfied in some part: and you must consider what she, by her physical nature or her age, either desires or could desire; and what, out of modesty or virtue, she does not ask for. For why should I be ashamed to write these things which the Apostle Paul also writes? <note>Pico refers to 1 Corinthians 7:3-4, where Paul discusses the reciprocal physical duties of husbands and wives.</note> There is almost no matter in which I suspect you could be more mistaken. Indeed, our men are very often deceived, thinking that their wives are bound and devoted to them, but that they owe nothing to their wives: or that they can, concerning themselves, decide whatever they please by their own will. Finally, you cannot be entirely your own master once you have submitted yourself to the laws of marriage and chosen to belong to a wife; nonetheless, you can belong entirely to God, whose favor you earn even while, in order to obey His law, you obey yourself less even in those things which belong to God. <note>Pico is arguing that fulfilling marital duties is itself an act of religious obedience.</note> But I have spoken with you about these things in person at other times. 

As soon as the air turns like spring—that is, during the first days of Lent—when I have extricated myself from these bundles of Greek books, <note>Pico was a legendary polyglot and book collector; he is likely referring to his intense study of newly acquired manuscripts.</note> I will immediately come to Ferrara. In the meantime, devote yourself to sacred literature: and especially to the reading of the Gospel, which repeatedly brings the soul back to God; for the world and the devil never cease, day and night, to lead the soul away from Him with allurements and deceits. Farewell, half of my soul, and pray to God for me. As soon as I have decided anything regarding my departure toward Rome, I will let you know. Florence, 27 November 1492.

# Giovanni Pico of Mirandola sends greetings to his friend, Jacopo Antiquari.

Among the pleasures I used to take most from the company of Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), one of the greatest poets and scholars of the Italian Renaissance and a close friend of Pico.</note> when I was in Florence—a man who, in my opinion, is the most learned of all in our age—it was no small joy that, whenever he received your serious and elegant letters, he would immediately give them to me to read. I was vehemently delighted by them, both by a certain singular wisdom by which you are commended by the most prudent men even in handling great affairs and business, and by the refinement and sobriety of your speech. Furthermore, since you made honorable mention of me in several of them, not only did your letters please me, but in them I also found pleasure in myself—that is to say, yielding to the testimony of such a great man...

...since you call out into the public my follies and the trifles that flowed from me in my younger years—for they are all quite foolish and unlearned, even if one judges them most kindly—they certainly are not the things that can sustain the opinion those men have perhaps already conceived of me through your speech. ->Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to R. C. C. S.<-

<margin>m</margin> Our Matthew, a most dutiful man, both spoke much health to me in your words and most clearly declared with what love and benevolence you pursue me. He promised, moreover, in your name, your zeal and your effort, if ever it should happen that I use them. Would that I were equal to this duty, most kind father! For I have always both desired and hoped to be received into your trust and to be numbered among your own. But to have you coming to meet me voluntarily, so kindly, with such friendly and liberal promises—and, if I may say so, calling me to your friendship—has surpassed both my hope and my every prayer. For what or how great a thing is it to be invited by him from whom it would have been enough not to be excluded? Which thing you have done; even if it is not worthy of me, it is yet worthy of you. For I could have been not admitted on account of my merits. I could not, because of your kindness, even not be called. For which reason, how much I rejoice for myself, or how much I owe you, in what way may I explain, when I cannot even conceive of it? Certainly, I owe you so much more for this because you owe me nothing in return (not in any part). For those things are not too grand or too many which Matthew and the rest of my friends have reported, estimating me out of goodwill rather than judgment. But whatever or however great I am, allow me also to be among all those who worship and admire your virtues—to say nothing of the rest—through which it is possible to see in you both what surpasses antiquity and what cannot be surpassed by posterity. I might say this deservedly, since in you nothing is lacking that might be placed in honor, or prudence, or learning. This one thing ought to be desired by all: that through you, at last, according to Plato’s wish <note>Referring to Plato's famous argument in the *Republic* that the ideal state occurs only when "philosophers become kings or kings become philosophers."</note>, the highest power might be joined with the highest wisdom. 

But these things are from God; from you, meanwhile, I seek and ask this: that you provide me an occasion, not of returning thanks—for there is no place for that either through your greatness or through my smallness—but of testifying my mind toward you, and testifying my faith and respect. You will experience John Pico as a man devoted and dedicated to you beyond all opinion, concerning whom you cannot promise yourself more; but you can use all those things, whatever they may be, which are in him. When you yourself use them, you will bring something of your own splendor to them, and they will become great when they begin to be yours, which while they are mine cannot be great. Farewell.

<meta>This page contains a series of personal letters from the philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to various humanist colleagues. It follows the typical Renaissance format of collected epistles, intended both as private correspondence and as examples of elegant Latin style for a wider audience.</meta>

->Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to his friend Alessandro Cortese, Greetings.<-

Your letter was most welcome to me. You did not send it, as you think, as a stranger to a stranger, but as a friend—and indeed an old friend—to a friend; or rather, as one well-known to another who knows him well. For you have known me for some time, as you write, and you deemed me worthy of your love. I, likewise, have heard of your learning and virtue, both from many others and very often from our friend Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494) was a brilliant poet and scholar, and one of Pico's closest intellectual allies.</note>. Who would not trust his judgment? He created in me a faith in your integrity, just as he can create in you a faith in my long-standing goodwill toward you. 

Although that goodwill was already very great, know that your letter has added such heaps to it as few could even conceive in their minds. What is sweeter than that letter? What more scholarly? How learned it is! How lovely! And you subscribe most generously to our friend Poliziano, who speaks of me more as a friend than with strict truth <note>Pico is using "humanist modesty" here, suggesting Poliziano's high praise of his genius is biased by their friendship.</note>. Truly, nothing more pleasing could have come to me from you, nor anything more honorable than your opinion of me. For all these things I give you the greatest possible thanks, and I confess that whatever I am or have, I owe to my Alessandro. I am sending you the letter you requested, the one I wrote to Lorenzo de' Medici <note>Lorenzo "the Magnificent" de' Medici, the ruler of Florence and a major patron of the philosophers in Pico's circle.</note>.

->Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Domenico Benivieni, Greetings.<-

Greetings, my Domenico, chosen for the Lord's portion <note>original: "ī domini fortem"</note>. Your letter was pleasing to me. It was even more pleasing to learn—both in person from your brother <note>Girolamo Benivieni, a poet whose work Pico famously commented upon.</note> while he was here, and by letter from our friend Pierantonio—that you are in stronger physical condition and have a better stomach. If you care for us all, if you care for scholarship <note>The Latin "litterae" (letters) refers to the whole world of classical learning and philosophy.</note>, then take care of your health. 

I have always been and am now anxious about it, not only because I love you (and I love you intensely), but because I love the scholarship which I believe and certainly know is at risk along with you. If your brother reported any of my goodwill toward you, have the fullest faith in it; if he said anything regarding my praises, believe him as little as he loves me much. As for our little commentary <note>This likely refers to Pico's "Commentary on a Poem of Love," an exploration of Platonic philosophy.</note>, there is nothing for you to admire. We wanted to be at leisure and do nothing at all; we did this while relaxing our minds rather than exerting them. It is entirely a prelude to the commentaries we are contemplating on Plato’s *Symposium*. 

There will be something in those for you at least to love and praise, you who love and praise everything of ours. Regarding the Council and the "Questions," <note>Pico is referring to his "900 Theses," which he intended to defend at a great council in Rome to prove the harmony of all philosophies.</note> I think your brother has already told you why I wrote that I am working for you. This I will do most gladly once I understand that you have been restored to your former and desired health from that physical weakness you have suffered until now. I pray and wish for this for you with the same spirit with which you pray and wish for the salvation of my soul. Farewell. From Fratta, November 10, 1486.

->Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Andrea Corneo, Greetings.<-

Even if I have sent letters to you either rarely or never, I have thought about you and your affairs either often or always. But I do not wish to "sell you hope," <note>A classical idiom meaning to make empty promises or give false encouragement.</note> nor will I write to you about what I am doing for your benefit until I can write about what I have accomplished. But if it should never happen, due to either your misfortune or mine, I would prefer you believe that I have done nothing rather than that I have worked on your behalf in vain...

### ->Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Battista Guarini, his teacher, Greetings.<-

Why do you knit your brow? Is it because I have addressed you as "teacher" against your instructions and therefore perhaps wrongly? If you are not my teacher, I am not rightfully bound by your instructions; if you are my teacher, I rightly call you teacher. But why do you reject a student whom you praise so much? These things conflict with each other, unless perhaps one is a matter of love and the other of judgment; and while you proclaim his praises out of benevolence, you fear his errors out of conscience—lest, perhaps, they bring shame upon you—things which you might be able to acknowledge as a praiser, but perhaps not as a teacher. But I beg you, receive me into this partnership of learning on this condition: that I may admit you into a partnership of our little glory, if there shall be any. I would bear the blows <note>likely referring to the "blows" of critical academic correction</note> alone.

But why do I delay the heat of my joy with cold jokes? Joy which I conceived from your letters and from your so grave and honorable praise. Now at last my ***Heptaplus*** <note>Pico's famous work, a seven-fold mystical explanation of the creation story in Genesis</note> smiles upon me. Now it is pleasing to me, since under your public praise, as if under the **shield of Pallas** <note>The Aegis of Athena/Minerva, representing divine protection and wisdom</note>, it now shows itself invulnerable to rivals. You urge me toward other writings of this kind, which you would do in vain if you had not made me far stronger for writing than I was before, by signing such a full endorsement for me and instilling sparks of good hope. For I trust myself so much by your judgment that I have undertaken the burden of explaining the whole Old Testament. Though I am entirely unequal to it, I shall nevertheless carry it far more strongly than usual. Regarding the books, perhaps I could satisfy you better if I had an index of those books which are with you, since many could serve your purpose, which you nevertheless might not need. Your aforementioned virtue has made you most highly recommended to **Lorenzo de' Medici**. Nor is there ever a mention between us of the learned men of this age without **Guarini** being frequently on our lips, especially when our friend **Poliziano** <note>Angelo Poliziano, the leading humanist poet and scholar of the Medici circle</note> joins in (and he always joins in), who attributes so much to you that...

**Giovanni Pico della Mirandola sends greetings to Antonio Pizzamano.**

<margin>n</margin> Nothing in my whole life has been more pleasant to me than those letters I recently received from you, so full of love, duty, and kindness. Indeed, may I be happy—and I do not deceive you—unless perhaps that day was even more pleasant when you and your friend Grimani <note>Domenico Grimani (1461–1523), a Venetian nobleman who later became a Cardinal and a famed collector of books and art.</note> (I know not whether to call him yours or mine more) visited me as friends and greeted me with such honor. For although you took on a persona, as if you were not who you truly were, but presented yourselves to me through some witty fiction of names, your most delightful character, singular learning, lovely gravity, noble modesty, honest face, and most charming speech nevertheless revealed the open and true Grimani and Pizzamano to me. Therefore, even if I could be deceived by the naming itself, I could not be cheated of the pleasure I owed to you. You were able to hide your names, but you could not hide your virtue, which betrays itself by its own brilliance and does not know how to stay hidden. 

That serious treatment of physical matters, those sharp and intricate arguments, those most refined judgments—whom else could they announce to me but your very selves? I congratulated myself silently as I listened to you, thinking how much more fertile our age had become, producing not just one Grimani or one Pizzamano, as I had thought, but two Grimanis and two Pizzamanis. However, when our friend Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), the preeminent Renaissance humanist and poet, who was a close companion of Pico.</note> indicated to me who you actually were, I began to congratulate my own judgment no less than my era; for I seemed to have recognized in you all those qualities which I had understood to be in "those" men (that is, yourselves) by the most consistent testimony of everyone. 

But see how your praises lead me astray and draw me away from your letter. And yet, that letter calls me to the same place even against my will; but I will restrain myself, lest I seem to want to repay your praises with a "mutual service," for you have heaped so many upon me. Whether these come from an inclination of the heart or from your judgment, I do not know which brings me greater honor or pleasure. I owe very much to that spirit of yours toward me, my dear Pizzamano. But please, you must also do the same if ever a test of me arises—that is, regarding my goodwill toward you. You will find a man so loving and studious of your virtue that I will not yield even to your friend Grimani in the first rank of loving you. Farewell. July 9, 1489.

<meta>This page begins a letter of spiritual counsel from the famous Renaissance philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to his nephew. It establishes a theme of finding joy in persecution, a common trope in humanist and early Christian correspondence.</meta>

**Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Gianfrancesco Pico, his nephew, sends greetings.**

**F**elix—you are happy, my son <note>Pico addresses his nephew as "son" to show spiritual mentorship and affection.</note>, when God grants you not only that you live well, but that while living well, you are spoken ill of by evil men—and especially for the very reason that you live well.
It is an equal praise to be praised by those who are praiseworthy and to be disapproved of by those who are wicked. But I do not call you happy for that reason alone, because this slander is glorious for you; but because the Lord Jesus, who is truthful—or rather Truth itself—affirms that our reward will be abundant in heaven when men speak evil of us and speak every kind of evil against us, lying for his sake.
This is an apostolic dignity <note>original: "Apostolica dignitas," referring to the honor of sharing in the suffering or status of the original Apostles.</note>, if you did not know: to be considered worthy of being defamed by the impious for the sake of the name of the Gospel. <meta>This page continues a moral and spiritual exhortation, likely following a passage encouraging the reader to remain steadfast despite social pressure or worldly criticism.</meta>

Let them gape, bark, and howl; you must continue the journey you have begun without fear. Consider, from their wickedness and misery, how much you yourself owe to God. For He has illuminated the one sitting in the shadow of death <note>A reference to Luke 1:79, describing those without divine guidance.</note> and has associated you with the children of light—having moved you away from the company of those who, wandering here and there in the thickest darkness without a guide, revel like madmen. Let that sweetest voice of the Lord sound in your ears always: "Let the dead bury their own dead; you, follow me." <note>original: "sine mortuos fepellire mortuos fuos/tu me fequere" — Matthew 8:22.</note> For they are truly dead who do not live for God; in this span of temporary death, they most laboriously acquire eternal death for themselves.

If you were to ask these people where they are heading, or to what end they direct their studies, works, and cares—or what final goal they have set for themselves, in the attainment of which they might be happy—they will either have nothing at all to answer, or they will speak words that contradict and fight against one another, like the ravings of madmen. For they do not even know what they are doing. Instead, like those swimming in rivers, they are carried along by the force of ill-acquired habit as if by the rush of a torrent. Because their own wickedness blinds them, and because Satan goads them toward evil, they rush headlong into every crime—blind leaders of the blind <note>A reference to Matthew 15:14.</note>—until unforeseen death seizes them and it is said to them: "Friend, this night they will demand your soul from you; but these things you have prepared, whose will they be?" <note>original: "Amice hac nocte repetent animam tuam a te/hæc autem quæ parafti cuius erunt" — A reference to the Parable of the Rich Fool in Luke 12:20.</note> 

Then, they will envy those whom they once looked down upon and praise those whom they once mocked. They will wish to imitate those whom they cannot, the very people they preferred to persecute when they were still able to follow them. Therefore, my dearest son, stop up your ears with wax <note>A classical allusion to Odysseus protecting his crew from the Sirens’ song.</note> and hold as nothing whatever men might say or feel about you. Look only to the judgment of God, who will render to each according to his works <note>A common scriptural theme, notably in Romans 2:6.</note> when He is revealed from heaven with the angels of His power, taking vengeance in a flame of fire upon those who did not know God, nor obeyed His gospel. As the Apostle says, they will pay the penalty of eternal destruction <note>original: "interitu æternas" — 2 Thessalonians 1:9.</note> from the face of the Lord and from the glory of His power, when He comes to be glorified among His saints and to be marveled at by all who have believed. 

It is written: "Do not fear those who can kill the body, but rather Him who can send the soul into Gehenna." <note>original: "nolite timere qui corpus poffunt occidere; Sed qui animam poteft mittere in gehēnam" — Matthew 10:28. "Gehenna" refers to a place of spiritual punishment or hell.</note> How much less should you fear those who can harm neither your body nor your soul? If they disparage you now for living according to reason, they would disparage you no less if you abandoned virtue and were overwhelmed by vice—not because vice displeases them, but because the vice of disparagement always pleases them. 

Flee, if your salvation is dear to your heart! Flee their company as much as you can, and returning to yourself, pray often in secret to the most merciful Father, crying out with the Prophet: "To you, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul; my God, in you I trust, I shall not be ashamed, even if my enemies mock me; for indeed all who hope in you shall not be confounded." <note>original: "Ad te domine leuaui animam meam..." — Psalm 25:1-3.</note> Let those who act wickedly without cause be confounded. "Show me your ways, O Lord, and teach me your paths; lead me in your truth and teach me, for you are God my Savior, and in you I will hope all day long." <note>original: "uias tuas domine demonftra mihi..." — Psalm 25:4-5.</note>

Likewise, make sure you reflect that death is always imminent. Realize that our life is but a point <term>point (punctum): a Stoic and medieval concept describing the infinitesimal smallness of human life compared to eternity</term>, or even less than a point. Consider how evil is that ancient enemy <note>The Devil.</note> who promises us the kingdoms of the world so that he may snatch from us the kingdom of heaven. Consider how false are those pleasures that embrace us only to strangle us; how deceitful are the honors that lift us up only to cast us down afterward; how lethal are those riches which poison us even as they feed us. How brief, uncertain, shadowy, false, and imaginary is everything that combines all these things together...

<meta>This page concludes a letter of spiritual counsel, likely written by or to the circle of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, and transitions into one of Pico’s most famous devotional poems. The letter emphasizes the preference for heavenly "homelands" over earthly desires.</meta>

...even if things flow to us according to our wishes, [earthly goods] can provide little. Great are the things promised and prepared for those who, looking past the present, long for that homeland whose King is Divinity, whose Law is Charity, whose Measure is Eternity. Occupy your mind with these and similar thoughts, which rouse the sleeper, set the lukewarm aflame, strengthen the wavering, and grant the wings of divine love to those reaching for heaven. Thus, when you come to us—which we all await with great longing—we may see you not only as the person we want, but in the spiritual state we desire for you. Farewell. And love God, whom you once began to fear. Bigus <note>original: "Bigus"; likely Lodovico Bigi Pittorio (c. 1452–1525), a Latin poet from Ferrara and friend of Pico della Mirandola</note> sends his greetings. Ferrara, July 2nd, 1482.

->**Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's <term>Prayer of Supplication</term> to God.**<-
<note>original: "Deprecatoria"; a specific type of prayer intended to turn away divine wrath or seek mercy.</note>

Gracious God, who must be revered in highest majesty,
You truly possess one divine power in a triple divinity.
Above the flaming walls of the high heavens,
The blessed crowd of the angelic choir serves you fervently.
Your almighty right hand once created this
Immense work, visible to our eyes.
You who turn the ethers, who guide the world with a nod,
By whose command the sent lightning falls:
Spare the wretched, I pray; wash away our filth, I pray,
Lest the just punishment of your fury drive us.
For if our debts were weighed in an equal balance,
And the rule of your judgment were severe,
Who could bear the terrifying whip of the living
Avenger? Or who could have endured his heavy blows?
The very Fabric of the World <note>original: "Machina"; the "Machine of the World," a common Renaissance term for the structure of the cosmos</note> would not withstand your angry right hand—
The Fabric that is not meant to perish until the final day.
What mind is not condemned by the origin of the first sin?
Or what soul is not made guilty by its own crime?
But surely you are that very one whose nature it is always to spare,
Who holds justice and mercy in equal measure.
You who pay out rewards far greater than our merits deserve,
Just as you grant punishments lighter than the sins committed.
For your mercy is greater than our faults,
And to give to those who are unworthy is a deed more worthy of God.
And yet they are worthy enough, if he deigns to love them—
He who makes worthy those whom he found unworthy.
Therefore, I pray, look with a peaceful and pitying face upon your own,
Whether you prefer to call them servants or, rather, defendants:
Truly defendants, if you look upon the crimes of our lives...

The text reflects the Renaissance Neoplatonic focus on the soul's ascent to a divine "homeland."</summary>

<meta>This page appears to be the conclusion of a neo-Latin poem or devotional work, likely from the early modern period. The tone is one of penitence and a plea for divine grace, transitioning from a reflection on human sin to a hope for salvation.</meta>

Crimes are the work of a mind far too ungrateful:
But if you instead look upon your gifts within us—
Gifts ennobled by the most excellent of goods—
We ourselves are those whom nature once made your servants,
But whom holy grace soon made your own children.
Yet, alas, the indulgence of such a great destiny weighs upon us wretches:
Those whom grace made children, guilt has made defendants.
Guilt made us defendants, but let grace conquer guilt,
So that your honor may increase through our crime:
For whether your wisdom or your power might otherwise
Be able to make its riches known to the world,
The glory of your goodness shines greater in our errors,
And that love shines forth to be loved above all others:
The love which was able to lead the Lord down from high heaven,
And to lift the limbs of the highest God onto the cross:
So that the blood and water from your side might wash away
The filth evilly contracted from our ancestral seed. <note>original: "patrio de semine". This refers to the concept of Original Sin inherited from Adam.</note>
Thus your love and piety, most merciful king,
Allows evils to provide the material for such great goods. <note>This reflects the theological concept of "O Felix Culpa" (O Happy Fault), suggesting that human sin was "blessed" because it led to the greater mercy of the Redemption.</note>
O love, o piety, so well-provided for our affairs!
O goodness, made the servant of your own servant!
O love, o piety, so poorly known in our current age!
O goodness, now nearly conquered by our evils:
Grant, I pray, that there may be an ardor in our hearts
Equal to this great love which always burns:
Grant that I may cast off the yoke and lay down the empire of Satan,
Whom I repent having served for so many years.
Grant, I pray, that the fires of a mad mind be extinguished,
And that your love may live within our breast:
So that when the spirit, having finished the duty of mortal life,
Shall be led before its Lord,
Having obtained the happy fate of the promised kingdom,
It may feel you to be not a Master, but a Father.

FINIS

# Various testimonies of the life, teaching, and commentaries of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. Collected from various places; though many [testimonies] of these most celebrated men, as well as others, have been omitted.

## Two letters from Brother Battista Mantovano, a most learned and eloquent Carmelite theologian, to Giovanni Francesco Pico della Mirandola, Count of Concordia etc., concerning the death of Giovanni Pico, his uncle. <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494) was one of the most famous philosophers of the Renaissance. This letter is written to his nephew, Gianfrancesco Pico, who was also a scholar.</note>

<margin>i</margin> Illustrious lord. Having recently heard of the death of Giovanni Pico, your uncle—a most famous and learned man—I was so dismayed in spirit that neither my feet nor my mind could sufficiently perform their duty. I was nearly moved to complain against both God and nature: that they have taken such a great light from the world so quickly, such an ornament of Italy, such a glory of our age. It is as if they envied the earthly <term>commonwealth</term> <note>original: "rei pu." abbreviated from "rei publicae," referring here to the collective community of scholars and the state.</note> of its blessings and, having no regard for us, they have cut him down. They have cut him down, I say, while he was still growing, while he was flourishing, and while he was nourishing everyone with the most abundant fertility of his genius. But remembering the sentiment of Paul where he says, "the judgments of God are a great deep," <note>original: "iudicia dei abissus multa" - Although the author attributes this to St. Paul, the phrase "Thy judgments are a great deep" is found in Psalm 36:6.</note> I restrained myself, lest I speak poorly of God and His works with impious rashness...

<meta>This page continues a correspondence with Giovanni Francesco Pico della Mirandola (1469–1533), the nephew of the famous philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. The writer is responding to a long-awaited letter and recounts a visionary dream about the deceased elder Pico.</meta>

->Illustrious Count Giovanni Francesco,<-

The very honorable delay of your response had made me believe that my letters had been lost on the road; and while I was determined for that reason to send you new ones—and had indeed already begun to write them—your most longed-for, most refined, and most delightful letters arrived. On the following night, I believe because I had been thinking of you during the day, a vision of your late uncle appeared to me as I slept, just before dawn <note>In the Renaissance, dreams occurring "at dawn" were traditionally believed to be prophetic or "true" visions.</note> at the time when true dreams are usually seen. He seemed to come to me and discuss many things regarding the nature of angels, and the species, names, and duties of aerial, terrestrial, and even aquatic spirits, to the greatest pleasure of us both. And when I asked him why he stuttered (for he appeared to be a stutterer), he replied that it was a sign of the imperfect and unfinished speech which he had begun long ago concerning the nature of things and philosophy. I seemed to be inflamed with a desire to inquire about many occult matters which are wondrous and unknown to us mortals; and I know not how, but the first thing that occurred to me was whether amulets and corals, and other things of that kind which are tied around the necks of infants, were of any use. He replied that there was sometimes some power in these things, and that this pertained to <term>natural magic</term> <note>Natural Magic: Unlike "black magic," this was considered a legitimate branch of science that used the inherent properties of plants, stones, and stars to produce effects.</note>. But he said that for the most part, they were condemned customs and superstitions. Having said these things, he vanished. Upon waking, I thought long and hard about what we had discussed in the dream, because the words seemed to have some weight rather than being empty. I write this to you not because I place any faith in dreams—for that is foreign both to my profession and my nature—but because I cannot marvel enough at how it happens that those who sleep can dispute, teach, learn, and do many things that are impossible or certainly difficult for those who are awake. Our soul certainly possesses something of the divine. And if we lived holily and piously, and our minds were not spun around by so many tangles of business, we would have great commerce with the separated spirits. But enough of these matters.

As for your wish to write the life of your uncle, I both praise it and urge and beseech you to do it more promptly. For this duty is most fitting for you, and must be undertaken by you for many reasons: for you excel greatly in style and eloquence, which is a singular gift of nature, industry, and God. Likewise, since you are his kinsman and closely related by blood to such a wonderful man, it follows that you cannot help but share in his glory. Nor should you allow your most illustrious family to lose any part of such great ornament and splendor. Added to this is the fact that his life ought to be better known to no one than to you, whom you had long ago proposed to imitate—and indeed most wisely, for he was an outstanding example of sanctity and religion, in whom the light of all wisdom appeared. I will say to you, therefore, what Christ said to the apostles: "Gather the fragments, so they are not lost" <note>original: "colligite fragmenta ne pereant"; a quote from the Gospel of John 6:12 regarding the miracle of the loaves and fishes, here used to mean preserving the intellectual remains of the deceased.</note>. And this must be done all the more studiously because it will be more profitable for us who survive and for future posterity. Without a doubt, although I see that he is more to be congratulated because, after such a short voyage, he gathered so much spiritual wealth and arrived so happily in port, I cannot help but grieve with you over the loss of such a great man. The death of Giorgio Merula <note>Giorgio Merula (c. 1430–1494) was an Italian humanist and classical scholar.</note>, first my fellow student and later my teacher (for we served together under Gregorio Tifernate), filled me with sadness; but he was already elderly and, with old age weighing him down, was already failing and had fulfilled his duty. Of the two, Hermolaus and Poliziano <note>Hermolao Barbaro and Angelo Poliziano, two of the most famous humanists of the 15th century, both died in the early 1490s, near the time of Pico della Mirandola.</note>...

<meta>This letter continues the mourning period following the death of the philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola in late 1494. The author, the famous poet Baptista Mantuanus, is writing to Pico's nephew or a close associate regarding the preservation of Pico's intellectual legacy.</meta>

The lamentable death of illustrious men has brought a heavy sorrow of the heart <note>original: "cordolium" — an expressive term for deep, heartfelt grief</note> both to me and to all learned people. But this wound has sunk even deeper: in the person of our Pico, the world of letters has suffered a far greater loss. The fields of eloquence mourn; the studies of the mathematical arts have collapsed. All philosophy, as well as the highest speculations of metaphysics and the most profound theology—which he had already begun to expand and illuminate—will henceforth fall silent.

But I restrain myself now, lest I indulge more than is right in this just grief. Our care must rather be to ensure that we strive to become like him, both in the study and practice of the sciences and in the integrity of his character and his devotion. Thus, enriched by a similar spiritual pursuit <term>negotiatione: literally "business" or "commerce," but here used to describe the exchange of ideas and the soul's labor</term>, we may one day arrive where he now rejoices to have arrived.

I will come as soon as I am able, so that I may see and venerate those immortal remnants of his divine genius <note>referring to Pico's unpublished manuscripts and notebooks</note> which are currently in your possession. Meanwhile, devote yourself to the task of writing his biography, and continue to hold me in your affection. Farewell. 

To your Lordship, to whom I commend myself. At Mantua, on the 3rd day of January, 1495.

Brother Baptista of Mantua, Carmelite. <note>Baptista Mantuanus (1447–1516) was a prolific Neo-Latin poet whose works were so highly regarded they were often taught alongside Virgil.</note>
