### Ermolao Barbaro to Roberto Salviati, sends greetings. <note>original: "S. D." for "Salutem Dicit."</note>

You are mistaken, Salviati, if you suspect there was any reason other than my busy schedule why I have sent you such a bare response. This is a common and much-tossed-about excuse for silence, but by Hercules, it is so true that unless you accept it, you would seem to be ungrateful for my love, loyalty, and devotion toward you. All your letters are always most welcome to me, but those especially so in which my friend Mirandola <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), the famous polymath and philosopher.</note> is named and mentioned. There is nothing more wonderful <note>original: "mirius," a pun on Pico's name, Mirandula.</note> in literature than that man alone; there is no one whom I would rather see praised, honored, and lifted to the heavens.

There is no one from whose praise I can less easily depart. In this matter I am perhaps excessive, yet I seem so to no one; his merit is so great and so boundless that there is no longer any room for either ambition or flattery. I have read his *Apologia* <note>Pico's defense of his "900 Theses," which had been condemned by the Church.</note>, and in it—why does he grant me so much, who deserve so little? Why does he announce me with such an honorable preface, as if I were more than an ordinary witness, not to say a Gregory <note>Likely referring to Saint Gregory the Great, an ultimate authority in the Church.</note>? Especially in that work, than which nothing is more subtle, more forceful, or more acute—though my full judgment on it I shall defer until I have read the whole thing through.

As for your desire to know what I am doing: what else can I say but that I am studying? Public duties <note>Barbaro was serving as a Venetian ambassador at the time.</note> certainly take away something from my intensity—or rather from my studies, not my intensity. For I press on more sharply and demand my task more severely; what this greater business has taken from my persistence, I make up for with diligence. The more my business has increased, the more greed and eagerness for study it has struck into me. Thus, all those leisure hours which a private man would give to his health, I distribute among public affairs; so that what I lose for one reason, I gather back by another means.

I believe I have written to you elsewhere, or said to those who might have told you, that the <term>Organon</term> <note>The collected logical works of Aristotle.</note>—for that is what the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note> usually call Logic—as well as the eight books of *Physics* <note>original: "auscultatione physica"</note> and his three books on *Rhetoric*, have long since been translated by me into Latin. My work on Dioscorides <note>Pedanius Dioscorides, an ancient Greek physician and botanist. Barbaro's translation and commentary was a major scientific achievement of the era.</note> is now finished; I am currently putting the finishing touches on it. The dowry for my daughter is ready; she will be settled very soon <note>Barbaro is likely using "daughter" as a metaphor for his book/work being ready for publication.</note>. Then, relieved of that burden, I shall devote myself entirely to Aristotle. Unless God calls me elsewhere, within about two years of the publication of Dioscorides, he [Aristotle] will come forth complete, at least in the logic, along with the commentaries which I have already finished on the *Posterior Analytics*. After...

Every day I experience more truly than the common saying that "to embrace everything is to embrace nothing." Farewell from Milan. October 21, 1488. <note>original: "xii. Kal. Nouembris. ### Ermolao Barbaro to Giovanni Pico, greetings.

Your *Hexameron* <note>original: "e Xameron." Barbaro is referring to Pico's "Heptaplus," a mystical explanation of the seven days of creation</note> was delivered to us three days ago through the efforts of Salviati. I read it so greedily that I drank it all down on the very first day, and not without a total sense of inspiration. Three things in it wonderfully delight me: first, that your speech both teaches and moves. This is something that the ancient theologians in Sacred Scripture—and even the Pythagoreans and Platonists in natural philosophy—are known to have observed, while more recent scholars <note>A reference to the "modern" Scholastic philosophers, whom the Humanists often criticized for being dry</note> sweat only over the teaching. 

Second, that in such a great abundance of material and such freedom to plunder from others, you have such pure and innocent hands; in this style of writing, you seem to have followed yourself and no one else. This is not common among either the ancients or the moderns, but is peculiar and your own. In this matter (I shall open my mind to you), I am so affected that since those who came before did not say the things you have said, they seem to me to have said almost nothing at all. 

Third, I see that you have been initiated into the sacred mysteries not so much of Aristotle as of Plato and his schools; you have brought full draughts from there into this late-night study. I will not mention how many excellent points from Plotinus <note>A major Neoplatonist philosopher</note> you have touched upon elegantly and in passing; it seems as if you have not just read, but mastered, nearly everything contained in his fifty-four volumes arranged into six "nines" <note>The Enneads</note> by Porphyry. Nor can I pass over how you carry yourself as a middle ground between the new and old theologians: you do not hate the simple majesty of the former, nor are you carried away by the ambitious subtlety of the latter. Thus it happens that while you wish to imitate one group, you are able to do so for the other; you have gathered the best of both kinds. We hope you will do the same in your explanation of the Davidic poems <note>The Psalms</note>. Farewell. Venice, September 4, 1489. <note>original: "pridie nonas Septē. Mcccclxxxix."</note>

### Ermolao Barbaro to Giovanni Pico of Mirandola, greetings.

Greetings, <note>original: "f Alue," a typo for "Salve"</note> most kind Mirandola. I truly speak of you so willingly everywhere that I do nothing with greater pleasure; not only because nothing (as Plato says) is more pleasant to hear than the truth, but also because, as Palemo says, it is much more pleasant to speak truths than to hear them. It happens with no effort—as found in Aeschylus, Menander, and Euripides <note>Famous Greek playwrights</note>—that truth often comes forth even when not sought; it is expressed even by the most unwilling man, not through questioning, but by its own force.

That is a form of tyranny: which you, following your own sincerity, interpret as humanity and kindness. ### Ermolao Barbaro, Venetian orator and Patriarch of Aquileia, sends greetings to Giovanni Pico.

It is well; it is fitting. Since you love me much, you congratulate me much on the Patriarchate of Aquileia <note>Barbaro was appointed Patriarch of Aquileia in 1491, a prestigious but controversial appointment given his status as a Venetian citizen.</note>. You even attribute much greater things to me and predict more for me than I could either hope for, were I most ambitious, or deserve, were I most modest. I know your piety toward me; I see how much you value me. I recognize the force of your love; I have found nothing more certain. Would that at some time it may be permitted to me to live with you, to philosophize about nature, about God, and about holy conduct. How much I desire this, and how much of an addition I judge it would be to my prosperity if this should happen, I can neither express, nor would I wish to in this particular place even if I could. I pray, if you have ever judged me worthy of your benevolence, let me be counted in that same number—and in an even better place if possible—in your estimation. Ermolao is now a priest; may you cherish more closely and hold more dear as a soldier of Christ the man you loved as a secular person of the world. As for you and your most illustrious virtues, I am as unable to stop proclaiming them, admiring them, and extolling them as you are unable to stop increasing them. If I flatter you or lie to you, may I be an object of contempt to all learned men; wonder regarding you and your affairs has long possessed me.

Now there is amazement and an ecstasy of knowledge. You will read these things patiently; your heart will not be puffed up, nor will you have arrogant eyes. For why should you be pleased with yourself, you who know that these good things you possess are not your own? They are not from your own private savings, but are granted from elsewhere and belong to the Lord. Forgive me. The north wind of truth and the west wind of charity have seized me and carried me away. Farewell.

->Rome, on the day before the Calends of April [March 31], 1491.<-

->From a letter of Hermolao Barbaro <note>A prominent Venetian humanist and diplomat (1454–1493)</note> to Giovanni Pico.<-

Your genius is distinguished and clearly divine, Pico: since, although those things which you write are excellent, you nevertheless express and shape the ideas of others—which are the worst—so that they seem to be yours, which are the best. For I consider it to be worth more to lower oneself and descend than to strive for lofty heights. For as the latter may be more honorable, the former is certainly more laborious and of greater effort. Hence, whether you believe our writings to be such that you spend effort in imitating them, or you do this for the sake of obliging me: in both ways I owe you very much. I shall return the favor someday; I do not want to say when I am able (for I shall never be able), but when you yourself or your family think I can. For so great is the goodness and humanity of your whole family that you are accustomed to credit a benefit where none exists as if it were a benefit. Therefore, I will have acted for my own benefit if I leave to you both the manner and the time of demanding back the favor, so that in the settling of accounts, every false reasoning and deception <note>original: "paralogismus et impostura"</note> may proceed not from me but entirely from you.

But those things which you wrote about the plan of your studies and wished to communicate with me have affected me with the greatest pleasure. I congratulated this age for a man of such great learning that he knows almost nothing [he doesn't know]; yet of such great care that he seems to know nothing at all. I see you are an excellent poet, a most eminent orator. I notice that you, previously an Aristotelian philosopher, have now also become a Platonic one <note>A reference to Pico's attempt to synthesize the two major schools of Greek philosophy</note>. I see that Greek letters—which alone could have been found lacking in you, and without which you would have been nothing in the future—you have not only learned but mastered. And that with such ease and speed that you yourself no longer remember, nor can you persuade others, that you were ever ignorant of Greek letters. This is something I declare regarding my friend Girolamo Donà <note>original: "Hieronymo donato", a Venetian humanist and diplomat</note> no less gladly than truly. I would urge you toward these letters so that you might hold them as plainly and familiarly as Latin, but you do not need spurs... and so forth.

This is rather a gift of some celestial nature than something produced by any lower force. ...[the worlds] rotate not with a simple and uniform motion, but with a triple and threefold motion; yet who is unaware that all these things fall within our senses? But the same man <note>referring to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</note> gave me the third world to be traversed in such a way that, with all the senses lulled to sleep (for these hinder rather than help such an inspection), it is traveled by the mind alone. For by the mind alone are these vast spaces traversed. And I would surely have looked upon and seen through it, but its vision—like an owl blinking at the sun's rays—could not withstand such great splendor. Therefore, whatever was hidden from me or escaped our eyes in this kind of pilgrimage—or more truly, this return to the homeland—the fault is easily found not in the guide himself, but in the one to whom it was being shown. For the divine genius of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola both promises and provides a demonstration of everything.

What is there then, my dear Robert, that I should not confess I owe you, having been enriched by such a great gift from you? As soon as I began to taste it, such greed was at once excited in me, and such a love of feasting from the sweetness of this food, that impatient of all delay, I committed nothing to be chewed by the jaws, but like a most greedy bullock, I devoured it all whole. But when, through continuous reading, I had completed the whole thing, and like that same beast, I brought back to my mouth what had been gathered in my stomach to ruminate more carefully, then indeed a wonderful sweetness appeared; then a stupor such as never before came upon me. 

But you will say: "Did you not admire the man's learning before?" I did admire that he was so engaged in all disciplines that he seemed to excel in each one. No topic of dispute escaped him in physics or mathematics; and in metaphysics and every kind of theology—whether you seek that which was awakened by Mercury <note>original: "a mercurio excitata"; this refers to the Hermetic tradition, an ancient system of philosophy and magic</note> and brought to perfection by Plato, or our own Christian theology, the most excellent and truest of all—these centuries of ours, and even several before them, have seen nothing more learned than him. 

But lest you perhaps think (a fault which many of us have labored under) that he separated eloquence from wisdom, does he not describe everything with the greatest weight, abundance, and moreover, elegance, so that he can now rightly be numbered among those ancient orators? These things, then, I admired about him until now, so that I thought nothing could be added to such an invention. But having seen his <term>Heptaplus</term> <note>Pico's famous work providing a seven-fold explanation of the six days of Creation in Genesis.</note>, I began to admire it even more than those previous things. 

Therefore, I would believe it happened neither rashly nor by some chance, but by God’s command, that this divine man emerged distinguished by these three names. For "John" <note>original: "Ioannes"; the author is playing on the Hebrew etymology of the name</note> is interpreted as "the grace of the Lord," or "he in whom there is grace," or "he to whom a gift has been made by God." Who would not see that he could not have attained the learning he reached without the special and greatest grace of God? In the "Woodpecker" <note>original: "Picus"; the Latin word for woodpecker, which was Pico's family name</note>, however, we know there is such hardness of beak and strength of head that you can find no wood so bony (if I may say so) or so stony that this bird does not bore through it, and skillfully carves out a hiding place in it where he may retreat and build his nest. In the same way, then, nothing in all the disciplines is so difficult for human intellect to know that he has not, by hammering at even its hardest parts, penetrated it, nested there, hatched his young, and brought them forth. Since, indeed, everything in that man is to be wondered at, who would not think he should be called "Mirandola" <note>The author puns on the name "Mirandola" and the Latin "mirandus," meaning wonderful or admirable.</note>? 

Therefore, as I congratulate you, who enjoy his constant friendship, so I grieve for myself; for myself, I say, who consider myself unhappy in this, since because of many and necessary...

Farewell. November 22nd. <note>original: "x. Kalen. Decembris," the 10th day before the Kalends of December.</note>

## Alexander Cortesi to his Pico, Greetings.

I have taken no greater pleasure in my whole life than I did recently from your letters; and although I had believed everything highest of you, you have nevertheless (I confess) surpassed my opinion. Indeed, you have surpassed it so much that I now think the boundaries of your glory, though they are spread far and wide, are yet narrow compared to your merit. 

Let us speak more openly and far from flattery, from which illustrious minds have always recoiled. What is there in you that is not extraordinary? What is not worthy of admiration? Individual traits could honor anyone, yet in you they have all been brought together equally; in you alone (if I may say so), you have stolen away all the Graces <note>original: "veneres," referring to the charms or qualities of Venus/the Graces.</note>. And although your ancestors reached a height where none but their own descendants could easily arrive, you however have turned out so great that you seem to return a greater honor to them than you received. 

While old age brings authority to others, youth exalts your dignity; and what others achieve by time, you have surpassed by invincible virtue. In my judgment, you are placed beyond all risk of genius <note>meaning his talent is so certain it is no longer a matter of luck or "the roll of the dice"</note>, and I would seek out Greek praises for you—whom it is right to praise, though it is not permitted to see you at this time. 

Let all talented men forgive me: they are all surpassed by Pico alone. Nature's kindness has so cherished him that it must seem a marvel even to her that such a wealth of all praises has been gathered into one man. Why do you blush? Or do you think I am false? Indeed, I will yield if you attribute this to love, which is painted blind. But I have witnesses in my Politiano <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), a renowned Renaissance humanist and friend of Pico.</note>, who is deceived only regarding me; he is a most reliable witness, even if he daily (as I hear) increases his riches of gold no less than of speech. For that I congratulate him as much as I thank him—would that he might possess the horn of plenty <note>original: "copiæ cornu," the cornucopia</note>, since he is not unmindful of hospitality...

### Filippo Beroaldo to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, Greetings.

I was staying with Mino Rossi—a man most polished in literary studies and a great ornament of our local senate—and I was reading the plays of Plautus, which overflow with the most sophisticated wit. Just then, your letter was brought to me. It was exceedingly literate, polished, and refined. Immediately setting aside the charm of the comic poet, I began to read your most delightful writings with great haste. Good gods! What grace, what erudition, and what majesty we recognized within them. A great reputation had preceded Giovanni Pico, but the man himself was found to be even greater. Your writings echo nothing trite, nothing trivial. 

Your facts match your words, and your words match your facts perfectly <note>original: "ad amussim," a technical term referring to a carpenter’s rule, implying precision</note>. You speak Latin purely. You use an eloquence that is both splendid and magnificent. Your style is full of pleasantness and clarity; you possess a most copious supply of the best words. Your thoughts are frequent and well-rounded. You express the feelings of your mind so clearly and so elegantly that the immortal gods seem to have given to you alone what they have granted to very few: namely, the ability to think the best things and to say the best things. You achieve this no less in verse than in prose. 

Livy and Homer write, almost as if by divine inspiration, that the gods do not grant all gifts to one person. This is why we often read that some have flourished by excelling in eloquence, and others by being gifted with erudition; but very few have stood out as being both eloquent and learned at the same time. For this reason, the two summits of the Roman language are cited: Terentius Varro and Marcus Cicero. From the former, a mastery of *facts* was sought; from the latter, a mastery of *words*. One is called "most learned in every respect" by Terentiano, the other is called "most eloquent" by everyone. 

Virgil—as Seneca so aptly says—was abandoned by that felicity of genius when he wrote in prose. Cicero wrote poems with no beauty and no charm, for the Muses were, frankly, unwilling and resistant. But you are both most learned and most eloquent. You excel in prose and in verse. You write things worth reading, and you know how to write what should be written. You can rightly be called a foster-child of the Muses; for you have not, like many, drunk only one or two cups of the Muses' wine, but like a second Apuleius <note>a reference to the 2nd-century author of *The Golden Ass*, famous for his wide-ranging knowledge</note>, you have drained every cup. Above all, you have drunk from that clear and nectar-like cup of philosophy, which very few touch even with the tips of their lips, and which they hardly greet from the threshold. 

O, what great fertility of mind! O, most blessed abundance of immortal genius, which has forged such virtues in Pico della Mirandola while he is still a boy, still a youth! It has poured into him such varied disciplines and implanted such great gifts of soul. He who is a mere recruit in age is a veteran in erudition. Proceed, most learned man, as you have begun. See to it that as your years increase, your knowledge grows, your genius matures, and your memory becomes more vigorous and reliable. You, who in your youth are the glory of our age and an example of virtue—what will you be in your old age? Papinian is called by Spartianus a "refuge of the law" and a "treasury of legal learning." You shall be called by us the "refuge of the liberal disciplines." Whenever something hidden in literature...

In inner things you will find a treasure; or rather, to speak more truly, you are already now a treasure yourself. Everything, even the most profound depths of literature, is at your fingertips; everything is ready and presents itself to you. That **circle of learning** <note>original: *orbis doctrinae*; this refers to the "encyclopedia" or the interconnected body of all knowledge that a Renaissance humanist was expected to master</note> which is praised by the learned seems to be in your service. Both Greek and Latin letters serve as your handmaidens. You are permitted to nourish your intellect now with this reflection, now with that; for one is the seasoning of the other. And just as various and alternating seeds restore and refresh the earth, so the changing of studies revives and delights the mind.

You are permitted to gladden your spirit with the sweeter studies of poetry if it ever grows weary from the more austere <term>dogmas</term> <note>In this context, *dogmatibus* refers to the formal principles or established tenets of philosophical schools.</note> of philosophy. You, finally, stand at the citadel and peak of the noble disciplines, while we toil with effort on the very first slope. You have climbed the narrow path of virtue with a steady, certain stride <note>original: *gradatoris gradu*</note>; we attempt to climb with the crawling pace of a tortoise or an ant, and we labor on rough paths, repeatedly slipping, repeatedly nodding and stumbling. I write what I feel.

Battista Guarini to the most learned prince Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, greetings.

<margin>n</margin> I do not yet concede that the dispute should be settled in your favor. For I can easily turn those clever traps of yours back upon you <note>original: αντιστρεφοντα (antistrephonta), a rhetorical term for an argument that can be flipped against the opponent</note>. If I am your teacher, why do you not obey me? If I am not, why do you call me teacher? Nor do I refuse this name because I look down on you as a disciple—for I assert that you are *my* teacher—but because I both venerate and praise your learning. In this learning, I am aware that you have advanced not through my natural talent, nor by the marks of a crossing pen <note>original: "transuersi calami," referring to the act of striking out errors</note>, nor by little wax marks, nor finally by the dagger or asterisk <note>original: "obelisco... asterisco," classical symbols used by editors to mark passages as doubtful or noteworthy</note>. 

But it seems we have stumbled into a new kind of legal case, while you strive to claim for me that status of "teacher" which I am trying to grant to you. What rhetorical case ever had a plaintiff or a defendant of this kind? My dear Pico, I will never "stretch out the grass" to you in this battle <note>original: "herbam porrigere," a Roman idiom meaning to admit defeat</note> unless we first settle the matter gracefully, so that since you will not yield otherwise, each of us may be judged to be both teacher and disciple to the other.

But jokes aside, let us discuss serious things. You may rightly take pleasure in yourself and your *Heptaplus* <note>Pico’s famous seven-fold commentary on the creation story in Genesis</note>. You have won all the votes of learned men so thoroughly that no stain of envy appears even in the hidden corners. One should hope that the same will be granted to you even more easily in your other writings, especially when practice is added—which is usually the best master in writing. 

As for what concerns me, I rejoice greatly that I am spoken of by Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo de' Medici, "The Magnificent," the de facto ruler of Florence and a great patron of the arts</note>, a man already praised and to be praised by everyone everywhere. This is especially true with the added endorsement of Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano, a renowned humanist scholar and poet</note>, whose vast and secret reading in many disciplines I embrace with such admiration—and admire so much that I never cease to commend it. Thus it is that I consider it like a triumph to be placed by him beyond the risks of scholarship. 

As for your request for a list of my books, that would be laborious and useless; it will be enough if you attend to my requests as time permits. For now, I desire Martianus Capella and Seneca’s *Natural Questions*, provided the manuscripts are free of errors. For the copies we have here are so corrupted they would require a prophetess to decipher <note>original: "opera sibyllae indigent," literally "needing the works of a Sibyl"</note>. If I can buy them in printed editions, that would please me more; if not, they shall return to you shortly after I use them. Farewell, my hope and the hope of good learning, and continue to love me. 

Ferrara, the Nones of December [December 5], 1489.

->From a letter of Hermolao to Giovanni Pico.<-

<margin>q</margin> Although I love these letters of yours, which flow naturally and are not affected—letters which do not—I won't say "know no care"—but rather reject it. That is, they do not accept care by design, and they shut out any effort that tries to force its way in. So it is that there are indeed traces of diligence deep within them, but traces that have been suppressed and, in a way, rejected. I am not so skilled that I can peer into your genius and estimate its magnitude and fertility. I seem to see this (and perhaps I am not mistaken): the direction you are taking and where you will arrive shortly. Nothing is more generous than that natural talent of yours, nothing more adaptable; and to put it bluntly, nothing produces more vigorous results—if indeed it should be called "natural talent." For it has produced fruits that should not be looked down upon even by those of mature age or the most practiced learning. Truly, how great is your spirit in poetry, as I hear! What happiness, what strength, and finally, what nobility and splendor in every pursuit, especially in literature.

### From a letter of Hermolao to Giovanni Pico.

I have congratulated this age on a man of such great learning that he knows almost everything; <margin>g</margin> and of such great care <note>Latin: *cura*. In this context, it refers to scholarly diligence or the meticulous refinement of one's work.</note> that he seems to know nothing at all <note>This is a classic humanist compliment: Pico’s learning is so deep and his modesty so great that he appears to have the "Socratic" wisdom of claiming to know nothing, despite knowing everything.</note>. I see that you are already an excellent poet and a most eminent orator, or will be shortly. I notice that you were first an Aristotelian philosopher, and now you have also become a Platonic one. I see that Greek literature—which alone could have been found wanting in you, and without which you were going to achieve nothing—you have not just learned, but have drunk deep; and with such ease and speed that you yourself do not remember, nor can you persuade others, that you were ever once ignorant of Greek letters. This is something I proclaim about my friend Girolamo Donato <note>A Venetian diplomat and fellow humanist scholar.</note> no less gladly than truly. I would urge you, and the rest.

### From a letter of Jacopo Antiquari to Angelo Poliziano.

Do not, therefore, let the offspring of your long labor <note>Latin: *longi incubatus foetura*—literally the "brood of a long incubation," a metaphor for the "birth" of a book after years of study.</note> waste us away in expectation. But having received Pico as a guarantor for the security of your name—Pico, whose whole life is full of glories—I hope with all my prayers to be received by him into the flock of your friends. I always adore his footsteps. Whatever is born at home from your "fattened flock" <note>Latin: *altilium cohorte*. Antiquari is playfully comparing Poliziano's refined literary works to a flock of prized, well-fed birds ready to be presented.</note> that is worth seeing, reading, and learning by heart, you should send out, intending to hold all those in your trust who are said to possess some image of virtue or harmony. Farewell.

### Angelo Poliziano to his friend Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, greetings. <note>The "S." stands for *Salutem*, the standard Latin epistolary greeting.</note>

I have burned almost always (perhaps too immodestly), yet I have always burned with a desire for perpetual fame, such that surviving glory was compared to nothing else. <margin>a</margin> But since what I was writing promised hardly any longevity for my name, you appeared, Pico, who could provide what I could not: namely, by dedicating your commentary *On the One and the Being* <note>Latin: *De Ente et Uno*, one of Pico’s most famous works, attempting to reconcile Plato and Aristotle.</note> (for so you title it), in which you call back the streams running through the Lyceum <term>Lyceum: The school of Aristotle</term> and the Academy <term>Academy: The school of Plato</term> to a single head. And since philosophy is more "one" than "twin," you also join it to our theology. Why then should I seek the grass of Glaucus <note>In Greek mythology, the fisherman Glaucus became immortal after eating a magical herb. Poliziano is saying he no longer needs magical means for immortality because Pico's dedication of a book to him grants him eternal fame.</note> now that I am to live forever through you? But it is with you that posterity will one day tell that there once was a Poliziano—

<meta>This page contains a letter from the philosopher Marsilio Ficino to the French official Germain de Ganay, reporting on the death of the famous scholar Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. It follows the previous correspondence regarding the intellectual climate in Florence during the French invasion.</meta>

->**Marsilio Ficino of Florence to Germain de Ganay, President in Paris, sends greetings.** <note>original: "S.D." (Salutem Dicit), a standard Latin greeting meaning "He says health/greetings."</note><-

You wish to be made more certain regarding the death of **Pico della Mirandola** <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494) was a brilliant young nobleman and philosopher who sought to reconcile all schools of thought.</note>, which seems to you as yet uncertain; you wish, surely, **Germain**, to grieve more heavily. For since you have until now grieved heavily over this ambiguous loss, once you are made more certain, I think you will soon grieve most heavily of all. Perhaps it was better to mourn a doubtful loss than to be tortured by a certain one. Alas, what do you ask, my most longed-for Germain? Indeed, I myself would still prefer to be in doubt. I cannot make you more certain at this present time without tears. On that day this past November when **Charles**, the great King of the French, entered our city of Florence <note>Charles VIII entered Florence on November 17, 1494, during his invasion of Italy.</note>, our **Mirandola** deserted us. He affected the learned world with almost as much grief as the King, meanwhile, affected the city with joy. Thus the provident **spirit of the place** <note>original: "loci genius," a protective spirit or atmosphere</note> and of the people compensated for the groans of the learned with the joy of the public; and in place of an extinguished **philosophical divinity**, it meanwhile kindled a royal light. Lest, perhaps, Florence should seem too dark on 그날 that day, the light of Mirandola was extinguished on earth and returned to heaven. For **Pico** migrated from this shadow of life with such cheerful security that he seemed, without a doubt, to be returning from a kind of exile to his heavenly fatherland.

You desire, furthermore, to know what **Pico** once composed, or what he was composing just now. He wrote the *Six Days of Creation* <note>original: "Exameron," also known as the "Heptaplus."</note>, the *Apology*, and *On Being and the One*, as well as several letters. Whatever he had once composed concerning love while his youth was still burning, he later condemned with a more mature judgment and wished to be utterly destroyed; it cannot be published without doing him an injustice. Indeed, I know the final will of this pious man. For in age, **Pico** was a son to me; in familiarity, a brother; and in love, truly a **second self**. <note>original: "alter ego"</note> He was laboring daily on three things: the harmony of **Aristotle** with **Plato**, commentaries on the sacred scriptures, and the *Refutations of the Astrologers*. All these were disputed with as much eloquence as subtlety. But as much as they were brilliant in style, they were sketched in such new and obscure characters <note>This refers to Pico's notoriously difficult handwriting and perhaps his use of shorthand or esoteric symbols.</note> that they could scarcely be read by him. Therefore, they have not yet been finished or revised by him, nor can they be transcribed by others, unless perhaps they possess the gift of prophecy. For if by chance they could be, we would not long for our **Pico** so much as if he were absent, nor would we ever suspect him to be extinguished. But his pious nephew, **Gianfrancesco**, who is powerful in letters and intellect, strives daily to rescue them from the shadows into the light, and is writing the life and deeds of his uncle.

Receive, finally, this epigram of ours regarding him:
"The high priests very rarely grant the more secret mysteries to the eyes, and immediately hide them away; thus God showed to mortals the divine philosopher **Giovanni Pico della Mirandola**, mature in the thirtieth year of his age."

So that the rest of the loss to letters made this autumn in Florence may be known to you: our **Angelo Poliziano** <note>Poliziano (1454–1494) was a renowned poet and classical scholar.</note>, most learned in the Latin and Greek languages, had for some time [been working on] seven *Miscellanies*, and *Silvae*, and certain *Declamations*, and several letters; all were composed with both sharpness and elegance. He also noted down many things daily that were necessary for elegance in uncertain characters, just like **Pico**; so that in both cases, a most heavy loss to letters has occurred.

The 23rd day of March, 1494. <note>In the Florentine calendar, the new year began on March 25th; therefore, by modern reckoning, this letter was written in 1495.</note>

Marsilio Ficino of Florence to Gianfrancesco Pico, Count of Mirandola and Concordia, sends greetings.
<note>original: "Marfilius Ficinus Florentinus Ioanni Francifco Mirādulæ Cōcordiæ comiti. S. D." Gianfrancesco was the nephew of the famous philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.</note>

I sent a brief letter to France regarding the death and the praises of Pico after your departure. "The priests of the more secret mysteries rarely grant them to our eyes, and they hide them away again immediately. In the same way, God showed the divine philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to mortals, fully mature in his thirtieth year."
<note>Pico della Mirandola died tragically young at age 31, a loss felt deeply by the intellectual community of the Renaissance.</note>

Let the epitaph end there. God seems to have given all the most abundant goods of soul, body, and fortune to Giovanni Pico—if only He had granted a longer span of life. But it is not right to blame Providence in this matter. For if God, in the shortest amount of time, had already led him to the summit beyond the powers of nature, perhaps it was not possible to progress to anything better. The shifting nature of the world does not allow one to remain in the same state, yet a perfected virtue does not permit one to slide back into a worse state. 

But you yourself have written of these and other such things better and more extensively in your *Life of Pico*, not so much to make him famous—for who can add light to the sun?—but rather to clear the clouds and bring his hidden works, which are most worthy of light, into the clear. Therefore, mortals will wonderfully commend your great devotion to your uncle, and God will judge it worthy of no small reward.

The first day of November, 1495.

### Twelve rules of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, partly for awakening and partly for directing men in spiritual combat.

**The First Rule:** If the way of virtue seems hard to a man because we must continually fight against the flesh, the devil, and the world, let him remember that whatever life he chooses, even according to the ways of the world, he must suffer many adversities, sorrows, inconveniences, and labors.

**The Second Rule:** Let him remember that in the affairs of the world, one fights for a longer time, more laboriously, and with less fruit; in those affairs, labor is the end of labor, and at last, there is eternal pain.

**The Third Rule:** Let him remember that it is foolish to believe that heaven can be reached except through this kind of fight, just as Christ, our head, did not ascend into heaven except by the cross; nor should the condition of the servant be better than the condition of the lord.
<note>original: "caput noſtrum chriſtus" — "Christ our head." A common metaphor for the relationship between the Church (the body) and Christ.</note>

**The Fourth Rule:** Let him remember that this fight should not only be endured with difficulty, but even desired—even if no reward were to come to us from it—simply so that we may be conformed to Christ, our God and our Lord. Whenever you resist any temptation or do violence to any of your senses, think of which part of the cross of Christ you are being made to resemble. For example, when you resist gluttony and afflict your sense of taste, remember that He was given gall and vinegar to drink. When your hands...
<note>original: "felle potatum & aceto" — Referring to the biblical account of the Crucifixion where Christ is offered bitter liquids.</note>

<meta>This page continues the theological commentary on the nature of divine service and the opening verses of Psalm 16 (Psalm 15 in the Latin Vulgate). It shifts from the benefits of God to the psychological and spiritual necessity of humility in prayer.</meta>

...He has bestowed many benefits upon you; and these three things are in God: because in His service, nothing new is received that is not good for us, both regarding the soul and regarding the body. For to serve Him is nothing other than to strive toward Him—that is, toward the <term>highest good|the 'summum bonum', or the ultimate source of all happiness and perfection</term>. Likewise, He Himself is the best, the most beautiful, and the wisest; He possesses all the qualities that usually move us to love someone and to serve them freely. He has bestowed the greatest benefits upon us, since He created us from nothing and redeemed us from hell through the blood of His Son.

->**PRESERVE me, O Lord.** <note>original: "CONSERVA me domine." This is the opening phrase of Psalm 16.</note><-

If anyone who is perfect wishes to recognize his own status, he faces one danger: that he might become proud of his own virtue. Therefore David, speaking in the persona of the just man about his status, begins with this word: "Preserve me." When rightly considered, this removes every occasion for pride. For whoever can acquire something by his own power can also preserve it for himself by his own power. Therefore, he who asks to be preserved by God in a state of virtue signifies by this that he did not acquire that virtue by himself from the beginning. Furthermore, he who remembers that he attained virtue not by his own power, but by the power of God, cannot be proud of it, but is rather humbled before God according to that saying of <term>the Apostle|referring to Saint Paul</term>: *What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?* <note>original: "Quid habes quod non accepisti?..." from 1 Corinthians 4:7.</note> There are, therefore, two phrases that we ought always to have in our mouths: one is "Have mercy on me, O God," <note>original: "miserere mei deus."</note> for when we remember our sins; the other is "Preserve me, O God," for when we remember our virtues.

->**BECAUSE I have hoped in Thee.** <note>original: "QVONIAM speraui in te."</note><-

This is the one thing that causes us to obtain from God what we seek: namely, when we hope that we shall obtain it. And if we observe these two conditions—that we never ask anything from God except those things which are <term>salutary|beneficial for our eternal salvation</term>, and that we ask for what we seek ardently with a firm hope that God may hear us—our prayers will never be in vain. Therefore, when we do not obtain something, it is either because it is harmful to us—for we do not know what we should ask for, as Christ says—and Jesus said: *Whatever you ask in my name shall be given to you.* <note>Referencing John 14:13.</note> For this name "Jesus" means "Savior"; and therefore, nothing is asked in the name of Jesus except that which pertains to the salvation of the one asking. Or, He does not hear us because, even if we ask for good things, we do not ask well—that is, we ask with little hope. For he who hopes timidly asks coldly; therefore James said: *Let him ask in faith, nothing wavering.* <note>original: "postulet autem in fide nihil haesitans," from James 1:6.</note>

->**I HAVE SAID to the Lord: You are my God.** <note>original: "DIXI domino deus meus es tu."</note><-

After he has fortified himself against pride, he begins to describe his status. The entire status of the just man consists in this phrase: "I have said to the Lord: You are my God." Although this phrase seems common to almost everyone, there are few who can truly say it. For a person holds as "God" that which he holds as his highest good. We consider that to be our highest good which, if we possess it alone even if all other things are lacking, we think ourselves happy; and which, if it alone is missing even if we have all other goods, we think ourselves miserable. Thus the miser says to his money: "You are my God"; because even if he lacks honor, health, virtue, and friends, as long as he has money, he is content. But if he has all those other goods we mentioned and money is lacking, he considers himself unhappy.

It defines true prayer as asking with hope for one's salvation and defines "God" as whatever a person treasures as their ultimate source of happiness.</summary>

--- Page 48 ---
<meta>This page continues a line-by-line commentary on a Psalm (specifically Psalm 16, known in the Vulgate as Psalm 15). The previous context likely established the speaker's devotion to God; this page explores why God alone is the "supreme good" and contrasts the joy of the saints in heaven with the "infirmities" or idols of the wicked.</meta>

Likewise, the glutton says to his excess, the incontinent man to his lust, and the ambitious man to power or glory: "You are my God." See, therefore, how few can truly say: "I have said to the Lord, you are my God" <note>original: "Dixi domino deus meus es tu"</note>; because only he can do this for whom God alone is enough. This person is so devoted that even if all the kingdoms of the world, all heavenly things, and all earthly goods were offered to him, he would not offend God even once to obtain them. In this saying, therefore, consists the whole state of the righteous man.

->**BECAUSE you have no need of my goods.**<-

He gives the reason for his proposition: namely, why he says to the Lord alone: "You are my God." The reason is that only God does not need our goods. For there is no creature that does not need other creatures—even those more imperfect than itself—as philosophers and theologians prove. This is because if those lesser things did not exist, these greater things would not exist; for if one part of the universe is destroyed, the whole universe is destroyed, and when the whole is destroyed, all its parts are destroyed. All creatures are parts of one single universe. Of this universe, God himself is not a part, but the beginning <term>First Principle; the independent source from which all existence flows</term>, depending on nothing. For God gained nothing from the fact that he created the world, and he would lose nothing if the whole world were annihilated. Therefore, God alone has no need of our goods.

We ought to blush to hold anything as a god which requires our goods, as every creature does. Furthermore, we should not take anything as God—that is, as the highest good <term>summum bonum; the ultimate or supreme good</term>—except that in which the complete, highest good resides. Yet in no creature is the "complete good" found. Therefore, to the Lord alone we must say: "You are my God."

->**TO THE SAINTS who are in his land.**<-

After God, we must especially love those who are most closely joined to God, such as the angels and the blessed in the fatherland <note>The "fatherland" (patria) refers to the heavenly home of the soul</note>. Therefore, after he said to the Lord: "You are my God," he adds that God...

->**HAS REVEALED THE WONDERS of his will.**<-

That is, he has made his love and his desires wonderful toward the saints who are in his land; that is, in the heavenly fatherland which is called the "land of God" and the "land of the living." And truly, if we consider how great the happiness of that fatherland is, how great the misery of this world is, and how great the goodness and charity of those citizens are, we will always desire to depart from here so that we may dwell there. 

When we meditate on these and similar things, we must always take care that our meditations are not fruitless. Instead, from every meditation we should always acquire some virtue. Specifically, from this meditation on the goodness of that higher fatherland, we should acquire the virtue of not only bearing death bravely and patiently when our hour comes, or if we must face it for the faith of Christ <note>Latin: "per fide xpi" (Christi)</note>, but even seeking it willingly. We should desire to depart from this valley of miseries so that we may reign with God and his saints in that happy fatherland. Therefore, when the righteous man has described his own state—that he is entirely focused on God—and looks down from on high upon the state of evil men, he says:

->**THEIR infirmities ARE MULTIPLIED.**<-

By "infirmities" <note>original: "infirmitates"</note> he understands "idols," and so the Hebrew text has it. For just as a good man has one God whom he worships, so the wicked have many gods and idols; because they serve many pleasures, many vain desires, and diverse passions. Therefore, they seek many pleasures...

<meta>This page continues a line-by-line theological commentary on the Psalms, specifically moving through the verses of Psalm 16 (Psalm 15 in the Latin Vulgate numbering). The text contrasts the restless, circular path of the wicked with the steady, inherited portion of the righteous man who chooses God over idols.</meta>

...because they find nothing to quiet them: and therefore "they walk in the circle of the wicked" <note>original: "in circuitu impii ambulant" – the OCR reads "imperii" (empire), but this is a standard reference to Psalm 12:8. It suggests the wicked are trapped in a repetitive, restless cycle of desire.</note>: and he added afterwards, "they shouted": because, namely, they rush headlong and thoughtlessly after their desires. From this we are taught that we ourselves should run toward virtues no less quickly than they run toward vice; nor should we serve our Lord less diligently than they serve their lord, the devil. The righteous man, however, considering the state of the wicked, firmly resolves—as we always ought to do—by no means wishing to follow them; and he says:

**I WILL NOT gather their assembly of blood: nor will I be mindful of their names.**

Now he speaks "of blood": both because idolaters were accustomed to perform their ceremonies around the collected blood of victims; and because the entire life of the wicked, having abandoned reason, follows the sensuality which is located in the blood <note>In medieval and ancient thought, the blood was often considered the "seat" of the physical passions and animal soul.</note>. Moreover, he said that he not only refuses to sacrifice to idols, but even to name them: showing by this (insofar as it can be said and done) that a perfect man must not only abstain from illicit pleasures but even from licit ones, so that he may be more completely carried into heaven, and may more purely devote himself to the contemplation of divine things. And because someone might believe it to be foolishness to deprive oneself of all pleasure, he adds:

**THE LORD is the portion of my inheritance.**

As if he were to say: do not wonder if I leave all other things to possess God, in whom all other good things are finally possessed. This ought to be the voice of every good Christian: "The Lord is the portion of my inheritance"; because we Christians, to whom God Himself is promised as an inheritance, ought to be ashamed to desire anything besides Him. And because it might seem to some to be a matter of presumption to dare to promise these things to oneself, he adds the same:

**YOU ARE HE who restores my inheritance to me.**

As if he says: Lord my God, I know well that since I am nothing in respect to You, I cannot by my own strength ascend to possess You. But You are the one who draws me to You through Your grace: and You are the one who will give Yourself to me to be possessed. Then let the righteous man consider how great this happiness is, that God has fallen to him as an inheritance; he adds:

**THE MEASURING LINES have fallen for me in excellent places.**

For in ancient times, portions and lots <term>lots: the practice of "casting lots" or using measuring cords to divide land among heirs</term> were divided by lines; and since there are many who, although they are called to this happiness—as all Christians are—nevertheless make nothing of it, and often exchange it for a trivial pleasure; therefore he adds:

**MY INHERITANCE is excellent to me.**

As if he says: just as it is excellent in itself, so I reckon it excellent: and everything else in respect to it—as Paul used to say—I reckon as dung <note>original: "sicut stercora" – a reference to Philippians 3:8, where the Apostle Paul counts all worldly things as loss or rubbish compared to Christ.</note>. But since having this light of the intellect, so that a man recognizes the happiness given to him, is a gift of God, he therefore adds:

**I WILL BLESS the Lord who has granted understanding.**

But since a man often judges according to reason that he should serve God, but sensuality and the flesh resist, a man is only then perfect when not only his soul but also his flesh is moved toward God, according to that saying: "My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God" <note>original: "Cor meũ & caro mea exultauerũt in deũ uiuũ" – a quote from Psalm 84:2</note>: therefore he adds:

AND even into the night my kidneys have rebuked me. <note>original: "ET VSQue ad noctem increpuerunt me renes mei." Psalm 16:7. In biblical and medieval thought, the "kidneys" or "reins" were considered the seat of a person's innermost desires and conscience.</note>

That is, the kidneys themselves—in which there is usually the greatest inclination toward <term>concupiscence</term> <note>A theological term for the tendency of human nature toward sin or worldly desires.</note>—do not only incline me toward evil but rather rebuke me: that is, they pull me back even into the night. This means they go so far as to even voluntarily afflict their own body. For affliction is often signified by the night. He then shows what the root of such deprivation is, and says:

I SET God always before my sight. <note>original: "PROvidebam deum ſemper in conſpectu meo." Psalm 16:8.</note>

For if anyone always had God before their eyes as a rule for all their actions—and in all their actions sought neither their own utility, nor glory, nor pleasure, but only to please God—they would quickly become perfect. And because one who acts this way always prospers in all things, he therefore says:

HE is at my right hand, so that I may not be moved. <note>original: "IPSE a dextris eſt mihi ne commouear."</note>

He then shows how great is the happiness of a just man: namely, that he will be happy forever both in soul and in body; therefore he adds because of these things:

MY heart has rejoiced. <note>original: "LAETandum eſt cor meum." Psalm 16:9.</note>

That is, my soul is joyful, knowing that after death heaven is prepared for it.

AND my FLESH shall rest in hope. <note>original: "ET CARO mea requieſcet in ſpe."</note>

That is, although the flesh itself does not rejoice as if it were to receive its state immediately after death, it nevertheless rests in burial with this hope: that it will rise again on the day of judgment with its soul, immortal and most splendid. And he declares all of this in the following verse; for because he had said that the soul rejoiced, he adds the reason:

BECAUSE you will not abandon my soul in hell. <note>original: "QVIA non derelinquet animam in inferno." Psalm 16:10. In this context, "hell" or "inferno" refers to the dwelling place of the dead.</note>

And because he had said that the flesh was resting in hope, he adds the reason, saying:

NOR will you ALLOW your holy one to see corruption. <note>original: "NEC DAbis ſanctum tuum uidere corruptionem."</note>

Because whatever was corruptible shall rise incorruptible. And because Christ was the first who entered paradise and opened life to us, and was the first who rose again, and his resurrection is the cause of our resurrection; therefore these things which we have said about the resurrection are understood principally regarding Christ, as <term>Peter the Apostle</term> <note>A reference to the Book of Acts 2:25-31, where Peter cites this Psalm to prove the Resurrection of Jesus.</note> declared; and secondarily they can be understood regarding us, insofar as we are members of Christ, who alone did not see corruption, because his body was not decayed in the tomb. Since, therefore, the way of living well leads us to the perpetual life of the soul and body, he therefore adds:

YOU have made known to me the paths of life. <note>original: "NOTAS mihi feciſti uias uitæ." Psalm 16:11.</note>

And because the whole happiness of this life consists in the clear <term>vision</term> <note>The "Beatific Vision," or the ultimate direct self-communication of God to the individual.</note> and enjoyment of God, he therefore adds:

YOU will FILL me with joy with your face. <note>original: "ADIMPLEbis me lætitia cum uultu tuo."</note>

And because happiness will endure for eternity, he therefore adds:

DELIGHTS at your right hand even until the end. <note>original: "DELECTAtiones in dextera tua uſq; in finem."</note>

Now, he says "at your right hand" because our happiness is completed in the vision and enjoyment of the humanity of Christ, who sits at the right hand of majesty on high, according to that saying of John:

This is the whole reward: that we may see God and the one whom you sent, Jesus Christ. <note>original: "Hæc ē tota merces ut uideamus deū & quē miſiſti ieſum xp̄m." A paraphrase of John 17:3.</note>

<meta>This page appears to be a prefatory letter or dedication, likely from the scholar Junianus Maius to a recipient named Robert. It discusses a work of great intellectual depth, almost certainly referring to the "900 Theses" or the "Oration on the Dignity of Man" by the young prodigy Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, given the themes of reconciling Moses with philosophy.</meta>

For when first this work—so hidden <note>original: *reconditū*, meaning obscure or deep</note> and removed from the knowledge of many—came into my hands, I began to read it with great care. It not only brought me pleasure mixed with admiration, but it also raised my contemplating mind to such a height of sublimity that I have never seen or heard anything more wonderful or more clearly explained <note>original: *enucleatius*, literally "having the kernel removed from the husk," meaning a clear and thorough explanation</note>. 

Indeed, his genius stands above the sharpest wits of others; he is skilled in an incredible investigation of the sciences <term>sciences: in this context, the *liberal arts* or the systematic branches of Renaissance knowledge</term>, and already possesses a knowledge of all things beyond what is believable. This is especially remarkable at his age, for having just barely passed his youth <note>original: *pubertatem egreſſus*; the subject, likely Pico della Mirandola, was a famous child prodigy who shocked the church with his vast knowledge at age 23</note>, he has attained such a command of subjects that even the most learned and elderly have not been permitted to reach. 

Therefore, I shall never hesitate to call him the sacred dwelling of all the fine arts and sciences, and the miracle of our age. This is especially true when I read more closely the work's hidden meanings—the progressions of nature devised by only a few men, the revealed secrets of nature and of God, and finally the hidden riches of the Supreme Creator <term>Supreme Creator: God, often referred to by Humanists as the *Summus Opifex* or Great Architect of the universe</term> now brought into the light. I know of nothing more wonderful I have ever heard, nor anything more profound I have ever read.

Since a peace has now been entered between the philosophers and Moses <note>A reference to the "Perennial Philosophy," the Renaissance idea that ancient Greek philosophy (like Plato) and the Hebrew Bible (Moses) share a single divine truth</note>—who previously wove the creation of things by different paths—and certain joined covenants of nature and God are understood without controversy. But I reserve the deeper repetition and more wordy explanation of this for another time. 

I come now to you, my Robert—a truly distinguished man—whom I love uniquely because of your writings. Though they may be few, they show such a specimen of your virtue that they promise a future harvest of genius no less great than the pleasing hope of blossoms they offer now. Know then your friend Junianus—and if you send me any of your writings hereafter—know him to be no less a herald of your accomplishments than a lover of yourself for that very reason. 

Victorius <note>likely a mutual friend or intermediary between the two scholars</note> proclaims the excellence of your genius and your learned refinement in these letters, so that I am provoked to desire and proclaim the same. One thing, however, I ask: that as Victorius invited me to love you with his charming encouragements, you do not cease to welcome and embrace me with your own kindness. By this, you will stir my laziness so that I may write to you more often—provided you do not despise my efforts. And if, based on the words of our Victorius, you do not set my friendship aside, you will call me to you by a bond of intimacy to serve you in every duty. For there is nothing I would rather do than to engage with noble and learned men in mutual love and the exchange of letters.

<meta>This page continues a series of laudatory testimonials regarding Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), likely following excerpts from Angelo Poliziano. It concludes with the printer's colophon for the 1496 Bologna edition of Pico’s minor works.</meta>

...the work of nature, from which philosophy, now meditating on how to speak in Latin, will, I believe, receive its highest pinnacle.

### Likewise, from the ninety-fourth chapter of the same work.

Sometime ago, Pico della Mirandola—this man who can never be praised enough—and I, in our leisure hours, ran through the ancient commentators of the Old Testament <note>original: "instrumenti sacri veteris," a common Renaissance term for the Hebrew Bible</note>, especially the Greeks: Diodorus, Philo, Gennadius, Aquila, Origen, Basil, Didymus, Isidore, Apollinaris, Severianus, and many others of that kind. Pico, just as he does with all the opinions of the Latin writers, most diligently compares these with the views of the Jewish and Chaldean <note>original: "chaldeorum," referring here to Aramaic or Syriac translations/commentaries like the Targums</note> interpreters, sifting and weighing everything. From this, truth might be drawn out, obscurity removed, faith strengthened, or impiety refuted.

### From the book *On Ecclesiastical Writers* by John, Abbot of Sponheim.
<note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), a celebrated German abbot, scholar, and occultist.</note>

Giovanni Pico, an Italian by birth, Count of Mirandola and Lord of Concordia: a man most devoted to the study of all good literature. Just as he is of noble blood, so he is most noble by his truly divine intellect. He is surrounded by a great retinue of all kinds of arts; a man worthy and most deserving, whose perfection the Muses might follow. He is the most learned philosopher of our age and a most sharp debater. He wrote several things in a most elegant style, which our age will both approve of and especially admire; by these, he has rendered the memory of his name and glory everlasting, as is only fitting.

### From the *Compendium of Revelations* by the most learned and holy man, Brother Girolamo Savonarola of Ferrara, of the Order of Preachers.
<note>Savonarola (1452–1498) was the fiery Dominican reformer of Florence and a close friend of Pico in his final years.</note>

Count Giovanni of Mirandola, a man unique in our times for his genius and multifaceted learning.

### From the second commentary on Propertius by the most learned and eloquent man, Filippo Beroaldo of Bologna:
#### regarding that verse, "Not so many Achaemenid..." and so on.
<note>Propertius was a Roman elegiac poet; Beroaldo was a leading humanist scholar at the University of Bologna.</note>

I read the word *Susa* <note>an ancient city in Persia</note> written instead of *Etruscan* in a manuscript belonging to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. He is a man worthy of the memory of the ages; endowed with manifold disciplines, he adorns the glory of our age. To him can be applied what Terentianus wrote about Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, widely considered ancient Rome's greatest scholar</note>: Pico is a most learned man in every respect. He loves you, Minemus <note>likely the person Beroaldo is addressing</note>, not only as an educated man loves an educated one, or a noble loves a noble, but he loves you vehemently. He speaks honorifically of you and thinks the best of you. After his more serious studies, he is accustomed to rest in the reading of Propertius as if in a most pleasant inn; and he agreed with me when I read this passage thus, and showed me that in his own manuscript, *Susa* was written, not *Etruscan*, and so forth.

These minor works of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, Count of Concordia, were diligently printed by Benedictus Hectoris of Bologna. He applied all his skill and diligence so that he might not stray from the original manuscript <note>original: "archetypo"</note>. Printed at Bologna in the Year of Salvation 1496, on the 20th day of March.

--- Page 67 ---
<meta>This is the opening page of the "Life of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola," written by his nephew, Gianfrancesco Pico. It serves as a formal dedication to Ludovico Maria Sforza, the Duke of Milan, establishing the author's intent to preserve his uncle's legacy as both a family duty and a moral example for others.</meta>

->**Giovanni Francesco Pico della Mirandola to Ludovico Maria Sforza Visconti, called "the Englishman," <note>original: "Anglo"; the Sforza family claimed a legendary descent from the royal house of Britain</note> Duke of Milan. Greetings.**<-

Most illustrious Prince, among those who have handed down the lives of famous men written for the study of posterity, some have done so with the aim that the names of those to whom they were bound—either by the ties of blood or by the education they received—should not fade away through devouring antiquity, but be rescued entirely from the injustice of oblivion. This was the kind of devotion that Pliny <note>Pliny the Younger</note> showed to his uncle <note>Pliny the Elder</note>, and that Porphyry showed to his teacher, Plotinus. 

Others, however, have achieved this same goal in a more auspicious way: namely, not so much to provide for the eternal memory of the dead as to provide a guide for the lives of those who remain. For this reason, we find that Jerome wrote of Hilarion, Athanasius of Anthony, Sulpicius Severus of Martin, and Paulinus of Ambrose. They committed to paper their tireless studies, their most disciplined conduct, and their most distinguished works. Through these writings, the glory of God has spread throughout the world, and people are even now stirred to live well and blessedly by both their teaching and their example. Drawn by these precedents, I believed I would be doing something worthwhile if...

<summary>In this dedicatory preface, Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola addresses the Duke of Milan, explaining that he is writing the biography of his uncle to preserve his memory and provide a moral model for others, following the tradition of Great Roman and Christian biographers.</summary>

<meta>This page begins the biography of the famous Renaissance philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, written by his nephew Gianfrancesco Pico. It establishes the author's intent for objectivity despite their family ties and details Pico's noble genealogy and the supernatural omen attending his birth.</meta>

->### THE LIFE OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA, A MAN MOST ACCOMPLISHED IN EVERY BRANCH OF KNOWLEDGE, PUBLISHED BY GIANFRANCESCO, SON OF THE ILLUSTRIOUS PRINCE GALEOTTI PICO<-

[Rectangular stamp: ROYAL LIBRARY OF MUNICH] Having begun to write the life of my uncle, Giovanni Pico, I consider it first necessary to declare to my readers—lest they suspect that, because I am either his brother’s son or his pupil, I might say anything merely to please him in the manner of a flatterer—that nothing here is granted to friendship, nothing to family, and nothing is repaid with fictional praise in exchange for the very great favors he truly bestowed upon me. Indeed, my narrative is as far removed from adulation as was the necessity of flattering him; and I have taken great care that readers do not judge me to have lied or to have been excessive in my praises. If I had committed to writing everything I had begun to learn about him, there might perhaps have been a danger that his own lofty virtues, or those who defend them, could accuse me of being too sparing in my account. This can be seen by this very evidence: many of the most learned men of our age, including some of the highest rank, have produced highly polished writings which not only offer the richest testimony to the things we are about to say, but—both while he enjoyed this earthly light <note>original: "hac luce", a common Latin metaphor for life</note> and after he exchanged it for a better one—they excelled me in their public praises of his character and learning. I have ordered some of these to be appended at the end of this book, after his own commentaries, so that a firmer faith might be placed in witnesses who are not of his own kin. 

<margin>Paternal lineage</margin>
<margin><note>original: "picus pnepos cōstantinj"</note> Pico, the great-grandson of Constantine</margin>
Leaving aside his paternal lineage (though it is recorded in memory that his origins began with the Emperor Constantine <note>A legendary claim common among noble families of the era to assert ancient Roman legitimacy.</note> through a great-grandson named Pico, from whom the surname of the entire family is said to be derived), we shall begin with the very time of his birth. For he perhaps brought no less honor to his family than he received from it; and I have thought it right to reveal the unique gifts of his mind, and the rest of the course of his whole life and death, which I have either drawn from my own ears and eyes or received from most reliable witnesses. 

<margin>Mother Julia</margin>
<margin>Gianfrancesco the father</margin>
<margin>Galeotto and Antonio Maria, the brothers</margin>
Setting aside his family tree and the famous deeds of his ancestors, his birth is to be recorded in the year 1463 from the birth of the Virgin <note>February 24, 1463</note>, while Pope Pius II <note>Enea Silvio Piccolomini, a famous humanist pope.</note> presided over the Church and Frederick III held the reins of the Roman Empire. His mother, Julia, of the noble Boiardo family, gave birth to him as her final child for his father, Gianfrancesco. She had already borne Galeotto the elder (from whom I was born) and Antonio Maria, as well as two sisters. 

<margin>Sisters</margin>
<margin>Alberto Pio</margin>
<margin>Prodigy</margin>
One of these sisters, having married Leonello, gave birth to Alberto Pio <note>Alberto Pio (1475–1531) became a noted diplomat and defender of the Church.</note>, one of the princes of Carpi, and is now the consort of Prince Rodolfo Gonzaga. The other, having formerly been married to Pino Ordelaffi, the prince of Forlì, granted a second marriage to the Count of Monteagano after her husband's death. A significant prodigy appeared just before his birth: a circular flame was seen to stand above the chamber of the mother as she was giving birth, and it soon vanished—perhaps suggesting to us that he who was being brought forth among mortals at that same hour would be most like a circular figure <note>In Renaissance philosophy, the circle was the symbol of perfection and the divine intellect.</note> in the perfection of his intellect...

and with the excellence of his name to be celebrated everywhere across the globe: his mind was always destined to seek heavenly things like a fire. His ignited eloquence, in harmony with his fiery mind, would one day celebrate with all its might our God, who is a "consuming fire" <note>original: "ignis comburens"; a reference to Hebrews 12:29.</note>. But we read that, immediately after he vanished from the sight of men, unusual signs either preceded or followed the births of the most learned and holy men. These signs, as if setting their infancy apart from the company of others by divine will, indicated they were born for the greatest deeds. Thus, to omit others, a swarm of bees brushed across the mouth of the great Ambrose <note>Saint Ambrose (c. 340–397), whose legendary eloquence was said to have been predicted by bees landing on his lips as an infant.</note>; it entered therein, then exiting and flying very high, it hid itself among the clouds and escaped the sight of his father and the others present. Paulinus <note>Paulinus of Milan, the biographer of St. Ambrose.</note>, making much of this omen in his writings, argued that the bees indicated to us honeycombs that would announce heavenly gifts and raise the minds of men from the earth to heaven. 

Furthermore, he was of distinguished and noble form: of a tall and lofty stature, with soft skin. His face was beautiful throughout, his white complexion interspersed with a becoming blush. He had bluish-gray and watchful eyes, and golden, natural hair. His teeth were also white and even. Under his mother’s authority, he was brought to teachers and disciplines where he cultivated the study of the humanities <term>Humanities: The "studia humanitatis," the Renaissance curriculum of grammar, rhetoric, poetry, history, and moral philosophy.</term> with such an ardent spirit that, in a short time, he was rightly placed among the leading poets and orators of that age. In learning, he was indeed most rapid, endowed with such a ready wit that he could recite poems heard only once from a reader in both direct and reverse order, to the great admiration of everyone. He retained them with a most tenacious memory, which usually happens to others in the opposite way. For it often happens by nature that those who have a quick wit do not excel much in memory; whereas those who perceive with labor turn out to be more tenacious of what they have grasped. 

When he reached his fourteenth year, by the command of his mother—who vehemently desired him to be initiated into sacred matters—he moved to Bologna for the sake of learning Canon Law <term>Canon Law: The body of laws and regulations governing the Church.</term>. After he had tasted this for two years, seeing that it relied on mere traditions, he turned elsewhere. Yet he did not leave without a harvest of good fruit: for even as a boy, and a tender one at that, he compiled a certain epitome or brief summary from the letters of the supreme pontiffs which they call "Decretals" <note>original: "decretales"; papal letters that formulate church law.</note>. In this work, he concluded all the opinions of those sanctions with as much conciseness as possible—a work not insignificant even for accomplished professors. 

But as a curious explorer of the secrets of nature, leaving these worn paths, he dedicated himself entirely to the contemplation of the intellect and to philosophy, both human and divine. For the sake of attaining this, he traveled through the literary gymnasiums not only of Italy but also of the regions of France, most scrupulously seeking out the celebrated teachers of that time in the manner of Plato and Apollonius <note>Apollonius of Tyana, a Greek Neopythagorean philosopher known for his extensive travels.</note>. He expended such untiring effort in those studies that he was, and was considered to be, an accomplished theologian and philosopher while still beardless. He had already spent seven years among them when, being desirous of human praise and glory—for he was not yet warmed by divine love, as will become clear—he migrated to Rome, and there showed...
