...desiring to show how much envy would await him hereafter from his inferiors: he proposed **nine hundred** <margin>Nine hundred</margin> questions regarding logic, mathematics, and natural and divine matters. These were drawn not only from Latin archives, but also excerpted from Greek <margin>conclusions to be debated at Rome</margin> book-chests; they were even unearthed from the mysteries of the Hebrews, the secrets of the Chaldeans <note>The "Chaldeans" here refers to ancient Babylonian or Mesopotamian sages, often associated with astrology and magic in the Renaissance.</note>, and tracked down from the Arabs. Likewise, he included many things from the ancient and obscure philosophy of **Pythagoras**, **Hermes Trismegistus**, and **Orpheus**. He wove into these questions many things regarding the **Kabbalah** <note>Original: Cabala. A form of Jewish mysticism that Pico believed could prove the divinity of Christ.</note>—that is, the secret reception of Hebrew doctrines—which Origen <margin>Origen</margin> and Hilary <margin>Hilary</margin> <note>Origen and Hilary of Poitiers were early Church Fathers.</note> among our own authors particularly mention. He also included many points regarding **natural magic**, which he taught was separated by no small distance from impious and wicked magic; and he proved this most elegantly by the testimony of many. Nor were there lacking seventy-two new physical and metaphysical dogmas—his own inventions and reflections—adapted to elucidate any philosophical questions. To these, he added a new method of philosophizing through numbers. 

He posted all of these at once in public places so they might be more easily known, promising that he would pay the expenses of those who traveled to Rome from remote lands for the sake of debating him. But because of the jealousy of detractors (which, like fire, always seeks the heights), he was never able to ensure that a day for the debate was appointed. For this reason, he stayed in Rome for a year, during which time those fault-finders did not dare to attack him openly or in a free examination. Instead, they tried to mock him with tricks and "rabbit-holes" <note>Metaphor for secret tunnels or underhanded subterfuge.</note> and to undermine him with hidden weapons, corrupted by a pestilential envy (as most people believed). It was thought that they had provoked this spite for one reason or another because many who had long devoted themselves to literary business—perhaps out of ambition or greed—thought it would be a mark against them <margin>Envy [unclear] with</margin> if that young man, abounding in his ancestors' wealth and great learning—like a lush, fertile field—did not fear to test his doctrine and genius in the premier city of the world regarding natural and divine matters, and many things that had not been accessible to our people for several centuries.

And when they realized they could achieve nothing against his doctrine by honest means, they brought forth the tortures of calumny, shouting out that thirteen of the nine hundred questions were suspect regarding the true faith. To these critics some joined themselves who—perhaps out of zeal for the faith and under the pretext of religion—attacked those questions as they were unfamiliar to their ears, doing so piously perhaps, but with little erudition. However, not a few celebrated doctors of theology had previously approved these same questions as pious and pure, and had signed their names to them. Among their number was counted **Bonfrancesco**, Bishop of Reggio <margin>Bonfrancesco Bishop of Reggio</margin>, a man of every kind of learning, sharpest judgment, and famous for his gravity of character, who was acting as legate in Rome at that time to the Pope on behalf of the Duke of Ferrara. Against him, however, those "babblers" <note>Original: Blaterones. A derogatory term for those who talk much but say little of substance.</note> attempted nothing, since they realized his reputation could not be undermined by them.

<meta>This page continues a biographical account of a scholar, likely Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, focusing on his views on rhetoric, his philosophical works, and his efforts to harmonize the teachings of Plato and Aristotle.</meta>

<margin>The eloquence of the Old Law</margin>
<margin>Augustine</margin>
<margin>Septimius <note>Referring to Tertullian, whose full name was Quintus Septimius Florens Tertullianus.</note></margin>
<margin>Eusebius</margin>
<margin>Cassiodorus</margin>

He used to say that eloquence excelled in the writings of all; specifically citing the works of Cicero himself and of Demosthenes, the primary masters of speaking (as he called them). He did so not because those works were, so to speak, "singed by curling irons" <note>original: "calamistris inustæ"; a metaphor for overly artificial or superficial rhetorical flourishes</note>, or smeared everywhere with coral-colored dyes and crowded with artificial curls; but because they smelled and tasted of a true and solid eloquence, supported by genuine thoughts and true art. They were, to put it briefly, not deliberately stuffed with the "wealth of the Egyptians" <note>original: "egyptiorum opibus"; a common theological metaphor for using pagan wisdom and rhetoric to serve Christian purposes</note>. Furthermore, he proclaimed that all the utterances of the Old Law <note>The Old Testament</note> were full of the most consummate knowledge and wisdom. Even if others—most notably Augustine in his book *On Christian Doctrine*—have brilliantly shown this, and Septimius Tertullian, Eusebius Pamphili, and Cassiodorus all affirm that the ancient grammarians, rhetoricians, orators, and philosophers drank the streams of their own eloquence and learning from the fountains of the Divine Scriptures, he nonetheless pursued this theme with countless other reasons. It is worth the effort to see a part of these in the introductions to his very famous *Heptaplus* <note>original: "heptapli"; Pico's work providing a seven-fold interpretation of the six days of Genesis</note> and in the very preface of the *Second Exposition*.

<margin>A little book on Being and the One</margin>
<margin>Note</margin>

Among so many constant studies of the Divine Law, in the second year after the publication of the *Heptaplus*, he completed a small work titled *On Being and the One* <note>original: "de ente & uno"</note>, divided into ten chapters. It was brief in size but great in its power, filled on all sides with the deepest doctrines of the philosophers <term>phōrū: philosophers</term> and theological meanings. In this work, he showed that "Being" is not superior to the "One," but that they correspond to each other and are equal in scope. He reviewed the controversy held on this matter by the followers of Plato and Aristotle, asserting that those Academics who contended for the opposite had not grasped Plato's true doctrine. He was prepared to demonstrate that there was no lack of a total agreement of meaning between Aristotle and Plato regarding the "One" and "Being"—just as with other matters—even if their words seemed to disagree.

<margin>Antonio of Faenza</margin>
<margin>Some Platonic matters</margin>

In the final chapter of the work, he turned the entire disputation toward the instruction of life and the improvement of morals, with no less ingenuity than piety. Against this work, Antonio of Faenza <note>original: "Antonius faventinus"; a contemporary philosopher who challenged Pico’s attempts to harmonize Plato and Aristotle</note>—otherwise an excellent philosopher—brought forth several objections in four letters. Pico himself responded to three of these; to the fourth, however—either because it was not faithfully delivered, or because he thought it could be answered from what he had already written, or for some other reason which must be believed to be just—he made no mention of it that I know of. After he departed this life, I myself took up the task of responding, so that no opportunity would be given to the malevolent to bark falsehoods, or to the unrefined to believe something sinister. I took the greatest care to show that the response had already been largely provided by his own preceding opinions.

We have also seen several Platonic matters organized by him in the vernacular <note>original: "uernaculo sermone"; likely referring to Italian</note>. In these, many things are found that serve to unravel the theology of the ancients, and many hidden thoughts of the wise are revealed through enigmas and riddles. Perhaps, having gained greater leisure, we will attempt to translate these into Latin, lest the towering learning of such a man—though most accessible in these matters—be carried only before the eyes of the common people.

<meta>This page continues the biography or catalog of works of a deceased scholar (likely Giovanni Pico della Mirandola), transitioning from his completed publications to his more ambitious unfinished projects and his polemical works against various groups.</meta>

Thus far we have spoken of the completed works <note>literally "lucubrations," referring to works produced by candlelight or nocturnal study</note> which he had published before his death. These were like messengers and harbingers of the magnificent works he had conceived and was forging. For he had already illuminated the **Old Testament** with the torches of his interpretation, <margin>The Old Testament interpreted</margin> and he was girding himself to perform the same service for the **New Testament**. He did not merely bring forth the meanings that the literal sequence of the text could carry; rather, in those places which were meant to bear three other meanings <note>The "fourfold sense of Scripture": literal, allegorical, moral, and anagogical (spiritual)</note> proper to the divine word, he built upon that foundation. He compared the differing readings of our manuscripts with the Greek and Hebrew originals. 

But this was established most powerfully in his mind—and among all the projects he had conceived in the genre of commentary, this sat the deepest: that he would not simply cite the dogmas of others (as these were already possessed, read, and known), but would instead set forth his own entirely new discoveries and meditations. He intended, by his own powers rather than those of others, to satisfy the souls who hunger for truth to the best of his ability.

After this, being proficient in the Hebrew language, <margin>A treatise on the truth of Jerome’s translation</margin> he published a short book on the **truth of Jerome’s translation** <note>original: "translationis Hieronymi." This refers to the Latin Vulgate bible translation.</note> against the slanders of the Jews. He also wrote a defense of the **Seventy Interpreters** <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> regarding the Psalms against those same critics. Likewise, he wrote a short book on the **true calculation of time** <margin>A treatise on the true calculation of time</margin> <note>original: "supputatione temporum," likely a work on biblical chronology.</note>.

Finally, he had turned his mind to defeating the **seven enemies of the Church**. <margin>Seven enemies of the Christian faith</margin> For whoever obeys neither Christ nor His Church is, by consequence, His enemy. Such a person is either:
1.  **An atheist**, receiving no dogma of belief;
2.  **An idolater**, serving false idols and worshipping demons under these images;
3.  **A Jew**, observing the Mosaic Law according to the ritual of that most lost people;
4.  **A Muslim**, following the unspeakable Muhammad <note>original: "Maomethem"</note> and enslaved to his detestable decrees;
5.  **A hypocrite**, living a Christian life in name only, but not in works or a sincere mind, thereby perverting the Gospel teachings;
6.  **A heretic**, not consenting to the Catholic Church but kicking back with an obstinate heart, or receiving the Gospels with a faith that is not pure but rather adulterated and profaned by various superstitions;
7.  **A sinner**, who, though he may receive the faith with a solid, clear, and constant mind, nevertheless acts contrary to it in his works.

These seven, therefore—who are like the leaders under whom the rest are contained like common soldiers—he had summoned to a struggle, intending to fight them with their own weapons. 

Against the **impious philosophers**—who, depressed by the yoke of no religion and devoted to no deity, worship only natural reasons—he fought with those same reasons. He battled most strongly against the **Jews** using the sayings of the Old Testament and the specific authoritative texts of the Jewish schools. In his struggle with the **Muslims**, he relied upon the **Quran** <note>original: "Alcorano"</note> as his footing. He laid prostrate the **worshippers of idols**, who were entangled in vain superstitions, with many wounds and great force. 

He especially attacked those who worship **divinatory astrology** <note>This refers to Pico della Mirandola’s famous "Disputationes adversus astrologiam divinatricem," which argued that the stars do not control human fate.</note> using both true philosophy and the specific arguments of the astrologers themselves. He had already pursued their delusions in twelve books—and indeed most perfectly executed ones—out of the thirteen destined for this purpose. Finally, he addressed **hydromancy** <note>divination by water</note>, **geomancy** <note>divination by earth/markings</note>, **pyromancy** <note>divination by fire</note>, **haruspicy** <note>divination by inspecting entrails</note>, and other vanities of that kind...

<margin>Mad Orestes</margin>

...exploded these things one by one. But he had intentionally directed his battle-line <note>original: "cuneum," a military formation or wedge</note> against the prognosticating astrologers and had swung his battering ram with all his might [against them], since the other superstitions catch at the supports for their errors from the futile and worthless dogmas of those men—whether they are weighing the moments of a birth <note>original: "geneſeos," referring to the casting of horoscopes based on the moment of birth</note>, or in choosing hours, or reconciling either the hexagonal or trigonal aspects <note>These are "aspects" or specific geometric angles between planets; a "trine" (120°) or "sextile" (60°) was considered harmonious in astrology</note> which they call "benign," and other things of that sort, which not even **mad Orestes** <note>A classical reference to the son of Agamemnon, used here as a proverb for someone completely insane</note> would approach. 

| |

Not content with having utterly overturned all astrology, he wanted to show the astrologers of our time—who are mostly ignorant of the Greek language—that astrology, the vainest of all professions, had been rendered even vainer (if such a thing can be said) by perverse translations. 

<margin>Ptolemy’s Centiloquy translated from Greek into Latin</margin>

While writing against these same men, as if he were doing something else, he translated Ptolemy’s "Fruits"—which are commonly called the <term>Centiloquy: A collection of 100 astrological aphorisms falsely attributed to the astronomer Ptolemy</term>—from the Greek language into Latin, and honored it with a most elegant exposition. In this book, he demonstrates that more errors (so to speak) than words are contained in that common translation, which nevertheless its ignorant practitioners have always guarded in secret like a precious treasure. 

Regarding those who feel wrongly about the faith of Christ and do not obey the command of Mother Church—whom we call by the common name "heretics"—he had attacked them with a new instrument and distinguished reasons in an excellent rebuke. Nearly ninety heresies are publicly known; but he, having scrutinized everything, found two hundred, which he proposed not only to eliminate and drive out one by one, but also to teach from what part of philosophy, not rightly understood, they had drawn or branched out their errors. 

| |

Finally, he had vehemently inveighed against those Christians whose faith is seen without works. He also diligently investigated how it could be that men believe there is a fire established in the very center of the earth, where the bodies of the damned and other things of that kind are to suffer punishments forever—unthinkable torments of both soul and body—and also the immense joys of the life of the Godhead, by which souls joined to bodies are made blessed; and yet they are not obedient to the sayings of the Church which compel them to believe. 

<margin>Note</margin>

Nevertheless, they run riot everywhere, leaning into vices and the piling up of riches, and nothing is feared by them less than punishment, and nothing is sought less than the kingdom of God. Likewise, he tried to apply suitable help according to the quality of the diseases: namely, to cauterize foul and naturally impure diseases with sharp and bitter medicines; but those wounds which were infected with less malice and depravity and desired to be covered by a scar, he cherished with mild and soothing treatments; and for those who had recovered their health but feared a relapse, he prepared the most wholesome potions and famous antidotes. 

| |

Many other works he had begun, from which it could be hoped that the study of philosophy as a whole would flourish again, once errors were eliminated and barbarism exploded. 

<margin>The Concord of Plato and Aristotle</margin>

| |

Among these, the **Concord of Plato and Aristotle**, which he had already begun, was considered the most important...

In him, one can see the strength and power of Thomas <note>original: "Thome"; likely referring to St. Thomas Aquinas</note> and the vastness of Albert <note>original: "Alberti"; likely referring to Albert the Great</note>. However, he had long ago sent word that he wished to avoid these public conflicts; indeed, he had become more and more averse to that duty by the day. He so declined such tasks that when Ercole d'Este, the Duke of Ferrara, asked him most earnestly—both through messengers and in person—to agree to a public debate while the General Chapter of the Dominican friars was being held in Ferrara, he initially resisted complying. Yet, yielding finally to many requests, he deferred to that prince, for whom he felt no small measure of affection. From this, it was debated whether he appeared more skillful or more eloquent, more learned or more kind. Whenever he debated, such a cheerful spirit was evident from his speech that he seemed to be discussing a pleasant and peaceful matter rather than a sharp and difficult one. For this reason, those who hung on his every word were moved to a wonderful love for him.

However, he had a frequent adage: that such a task belonged to the logician, not the philosopher. He also said that those discussions were beneficial which were conducted with a calm mind to track down and investigate the truth in private places, away from spectators. But he believed those which took place in public did the most harm, as they were done to show off learning or to catch the breeze of popular favor and the applause of the unlearned. He judged it almost impossible for the desire for honor—which drives those "roaming" debaters—to not be joined by an inseparable bond to a desire for the shame and confusion of the person with whom one disputes; this he called a lethal wound to the soul and a deadly poison to charity. 

Nothing at all escaped him regarding the little traps and quibbles of the sophists and those <term>Swineshead’s trifles: original "suiseticas quilquilias," referring to the complex logical puzzles of the 14th-century English mathematician Richard Swineshead, known as "The Calculator."</term> which are called "Calculations." These are mathematical commentaries applied to natural philosophy with thoughts that are perhaps too subtle, if not too pedantic. Truly, even if he were learned in them and had read such writings—which perhaps Italy does not fully know (for no corner of literature could be found so pathless or inaccessible that he had not explored it thoroughly by his own light)—he nevertheless seemed to hate and detest them. In my judgment, he realized that their common use served only to bring shame upon colleagues and to weaken the memory of those responding, whereas they contributed nothing or very little to finding the truth, to which he believed tireless effort should be devoted.

But lest I go on too long and detain the reader, I will summarize briefly. One man may have shone in eloquence but was disgraced by ignorance of the secrets of nature; another knew foreign languages but did not master the universal decrees of the philosophers; another read the inventions of the ancients but composed no new doctrines. From another, knowledge of both divine and human things was sought only for the sake of human glory, not for the benefit of the Christian commonwealth. But he, in truth, had embraced all these things with such equal zeal that they seemed to have flowed into him in troops and heaps; nor was he like many who, not excelling in any one thing, merely have a small part in all.

<meta>This page continues the biographical account of a Renaissance philosopher, likely Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, focusing on his spiritual priorities and his famous indifference to worldly wealth.</meta>

In the body we are capable of more than we can either express or know; by loving we profit ourselves more, we labor less, and we obey Him <note>Referring to God.</note> more. Yet we always prefer never to find through knowledge what we seek, rather than to possess through loving that which, without love, would be found in vain. <margin>A saying he frequently had on his lips</margin> **That saying of Saint Francis—*A man knows as much as he practices*—was frequently on his lips.** <note>original: "Tantum scit homo quantum operatur." This is a famous maxim attributed to St. Francis of Assisi, emphasizing that true knowledge is lived, not just thought.</note> Otherwise, generosity was the only area in which he exceeded moderation; indeed, he was so far from applying any care to earthly matters that he was even stained by the blemish of indifference. <margin>Excessive generosity</margin> We find that he was often warned by his friends not to despise riches entirely. They asserted that it brought shame upon him when it became common knowledge—whether true or false—that he provided an opportunity for theft to his stewards. Nevertheless, that mind, which was always intent on contemplating and scrutinizing the designs of all nature, could not easily lower itself to weigh these lowest and most abject matters.

I remember while I was staying with him in Ferrara, a caterer presented a small page seeking approval of expenses. Seeing this, I was struck with wonder and asked him whether he had finally applied his mind to that which he had neglected in times past. My friend replied that he had not only requested it from him, but demanded that he undergo this duty, and that he had done so merely to comply with their customs, yet he held as little actual care for it as he had before. Furthermore, when his chief steward interrupted him to ask that an audit <term>dispunctionem: a formal settling of accounts or balancing of books</term> be made of the money he had handled for many years, so that he might provide for his own peace of mind, and had brought the books before him for that purpose, we heard him reply with these words: "I know that I could have been, and can be, defrauded by you very often. Therefore, there is no need for a release of these expenses. If I owe you, I shall pay the coins immediately; if you owe me, pay it back now if you can, or in the future if the means are not presently available."

<margin>Benevolence toward friends</margin> **He always treated his friends with great indulgence,** whom he used to address with speeches encouraging them to live well. I knew a man who, while relying on his teaching and reputation, spoke with him; when the conversation turned to morals, he was so moved by only two of his words that he abandoned the path of vice and reformed his character. The words were as follows: <margin>Two most wholesome remedies against vices</margin> **"If we held before our eyes the death of Christ suffered for love of us, and likewise by thinking of our own [death], we would beware of vices."** 

He exhibited admirable modesty and courtesy toward those whom he felt should be won over—not because of their power or fortune, but through both love and learning. However, he was accustomed to love those who showed any spark of literary skill, or at least a diligent and fit application to the study of the liberal arts. <margin>Similarity is the cause of love</margin> **For similarity is the cause of love;** and regarding a wise man, as Philostratus <note>Flavius Philostratus (c. 170–250 AD), author of the "Life of Apollonius of Tyana."</note> testifies, Apollonius said: "There is a certain affinity that knowledge also perfects in a man; wherein a man is perfected, he consequently attains goodness beyond other honest men..."

It is not doubted that they are to be loved. However, nothing was more intolerable to him than (to use the words of the poet Horace) "the proud thresholds of powerful citizens." <margin>Horace</margin> <note>original: *superba civium potentiorum limina*. Furthermore, the prince of that city <note>Ercole I d'Este, Duke of Ferrara.</note> loved him wonderfully and was joined to him by a kind of kinship—seeing as I myself was born of the prince's sister, Bianca Maria d'Este. <margin>Bianca Maria d'Este</margin> Nor was it too far from his homeland, since Ferrara is only thirty miles east of Mirandola.

Among these friends, he bound two to himself above all with a literary love: Angelo Poliziano, <margin>Angelo Poliziano</margin> a man most learned in Greek and Latin, filled with the "flowers" of various literatures, and nearly the champion of the Roman tongue; and the other, Marsilio Ficino, <margin>Marsilio Ficino</margin> a Florentine, a man redolent with every kind of literature, but the greatest Platonist among those now living, whose work he used in claiming Academic doctrines for himself. <note>Ficino was the head of the Platonic Academy in Florence and a mentor to Pico.</note>

He was not a great lover of the outward worship of <term>latria</term> <note>Original: *latria*. This is a technical theological term referring to the supreme worship offered to God alone, as opposed to the veneration given to saints.</note>. <margin>Outward worship of latria</margin> I do not speak of those things which the Church commands to be observed (for we saw him practice those before our very eyes), but I mention those ceremonies which some people pursue and promote while neglecting the true worship of God, who is to be worshipped "in spirit and in truth." <margin>True worship of God</margin> But with his internal affections, he followed God with a most fervent love. <margin>Interior worship of latria</margin>

At times that eagerness of soul almost grew faint and fell away; but then, gathering strength with greater effort, I remember how he burned for God because of God. <margin>Fervor of love for God</margin> For instance, when we were walking along long paths in a certain orchard in Ferrara, talking about the love of Christ, he broke out into these words: "Let me tell you this in secret: once I have finished and completed certain of my late-night studies, I will bestow what wealth remains to me upon the poor; and, armed with the crucifix, walking barefoot, I will travel the world through towns and cities preaching Christ." I heard later that he changed this plan, for he decided to join the Order of Preachers <note>The Dominicans, the order of the reformer Savonarola, with whom Pico was close.</note>; in the meantime, he hurried the publication of those works he had conceived and begun. But in the year one thousand four hundred...

...in the year 1494 of our redemption <note>original: "nonagesimo quarto anno redemptionis nostræ"</note>: While he was completing his thirty-second year of age and staying in Florence, he was seized by a most treacherous fever. One such instance occurred after he had received the sacrament of the Eucharist: an image <note>original: "Sigillum"</note> of the crucified Christ was offered to him, so that from it he might draw deep draughts of love in memory of that ineffable Passion suffered for the sake of our salvation. Before he breathed his last, he was able to take up this most powerful defense against any adversity and a most sturdy bulwark against wicked demons. 

<margin>The image of God</margin>
Soon after, an elder asked him whether he firmly believed that this was the true image of the true God and true man—who, as God, was begotten by God the Father before all time and eternity, equal to Him in all things. He was asked if he believed that Christ was conceived in the womb of Mary, ever-virgin, in time, by the Holy Spirit (who is also God, proceeding co-eternally from both the Son and the Father, which three are one); that He endured hunger, thirst, labors, heat, and sleepless nights; and that finally, to wash away our filth contracted from the seed of Adam and to throw wide the great gate of heaven, He had shed His most precious blood both voluntarily and most willingly on the altar of the cross out of the greatest love for the human race. When these and other such points of the Creed were recited, he responded that he not only believed them, but was certain of them.

<margin>Alberto Pio</margin>
<margin>Alexander of Aphrodisias, Themistius, Averroes</margin>

As Alberto tried to make the approaching boundaries of death more bearable, he replied in this way: He said his mind was not calmed by those reasons alone, nor did they ease the agonies of death; rather, he was comforted most of all because an end was now being put to his offenses against his God. He felt that if his life were extended even a little longer, it would only be filled with more frequent offenses against God.

<margin>That the Queen of Heaven came to the sick man by night</margin>
Furthermore, he revealed to several most proven witnesses from the college of preachers <note>The Dominican Order</note>, and to the aforementioned Alberto shortly before his death, that the Queen of Heaven <note>The Virgin Mary</note> had come to him at night. She was fragrant with a wondrous scent and she restored all his limbs, which had been crushed and broken by the fever. She promised that he would not yield entirely to death. He was found lying in his bed with a cheerful and peaceful face while he was ill. Even amidst the stings of death which he endured, he was accustomed to speak as if he saw the heavens opened to him, greeting everyone and promising his help (as is the custom) with the greatest kindness.

But if they considered that sins worthy not of death <note>i.e., venial sins rather than mortal sins</note> but of pardon are to be punished by purgatorial fire, they would not wonder that even the just pay penalties. Likewise, if they were not ignorant that the servant who knows the master's will and did not fulfill it—as Truth <note>A common title for Christ or the Gospel</note> testifies—will be beaten with many stripes, they would not report it as a delusion that this man, who knew God's will and deferred fulfilling it, should suffer punishments, even if he were immune from all other faults. 

On the other hand, I cannot sufficiently marvel at the crude and senseless cunning of those who, while they believe Christ died for men, do not easily believe that the same Christ can speak to those same men. And by a more vehement argument, they believe that mortal men cannot become partakers of the inspirations of the Virgin Mother, or of the blessed angels or spirits of men. It should certainly be noticed by them that all lower things are governed by higher things, as witnessed also by Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A 5th-century mystical theologian whose works were highly influential in the Renaissance</note> in the book *On the Celestial Hierarchy*. He teaches that minds of a lower grade and nature, to whom the care of men is entrusted, are illuminated by higher minds—which in turn drink in the divine mysteries either from the supreme minds or from God himself—and that men inspired by the divine spirit receive those same revelations, which are to be revealed to the multitude of men when it is expedient. This is the sacrosanct law of divinity—as we are taught by the same Dionysius in the book of the *Celestial Hierarchy*—so that through the first things, those following might be raised up to the most majestic light. Without a doubt, they are ignorant of the divine scriptures, insolent...

# HEPTAPLUS BY GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA: ON THE SEVENFOLD EXPOSITION OF THE SIX DAYS OF GENESIS, TO LORENZO DE' MEDICI.

### PREFACE

**M**Y EMULATION OF YOUR STUDIES, Lorenzo de' Medici, moved me to review the secret volumes of Moses. I noticed last winter that whenever you were granted leisure from the affairs of the Republic <note>Latin: *res publica*; the state or public business of Florence</note>, you devoted yourself to that reading more eagerly and willingly than to anything else. Then, a private reason also invited me: for another work of mine—begun long ago under your auspices but growing in your name—in which I attempted to defend the Davidic hymns <note>The Psalms</note> translated by the Seventy interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> (which sound constantly in the Church) not only from every suspicion and slander but also to illuminate them with the light of interpretation, I found absolutely no study more useful, none more fruitful, and none more fitting (or to speak more truly, more necessary) than the study of those books of Moses.

<margin>That the mysteries of all nature are in Moses's Genesis.</margin>
It happened during these days that I was diligent in studying the fabric of the world and those celebrated works of the six days. Great reasons present themselves for us to believe that the secrets of all nature are contained within them. For to pass over the fact that our prophet <note>Moses</note>, filled with God and by the dictation of the heavenly Spirit, received all these things from the teacher of all truth—did not the testimonies of our own people, of his own people, and finally of the Gentiles, hand him down to us as the most skilled in all human wisdom, doctrines, and letters? 

<margin>Moses the most learned by the testimony of all.</margin>
<margin>The legitimate book of Solomon which is called Wisdom.</margin>
There exists among the Hebrews a book by that Solomon surnamed "the Wisest," titled *Wisdom*. This is not the work by Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria</note> which is currently in circulation, but another composed in what they call the more secret language of Jerusalem. In this book, a man who is considered an interpreter of the nature of things confesses that he received all such discipline from the inner sanctuaries of the Mosaic law. Likewise, as far as our own authors are concerned, both Luke <note>In the Acts of the Apostles</note> and Philo are most serious authorities stating that Moses was most highly educated in the entire doctrine of the Egyptians. 

Furthermore, all the Greeks who were considered more "divine"—Pythagoras, Plato, Empedocles, and Democritus—employed Egyptian teachers. There is that famous saying of the philosopher Numenius: <note>original: *non aliud eſſe Platonem q̃ atticum Moſem*</note> "What is Plato but Moses speaking in Attic Greek?" Moreover, Hermippus the Pythagorean testifies that Pythagoras transferred many things from the Mosaic law into his own philosophy. 

<margin>Why Moses appears crude and popular.</margin>
<margin>The custom of the ancients in writing divine things.</margin>
If, meanwhile, Moses appears in his books to be crude and popular rather than a philosopher, a theologian, or a craftsman of some great wisdom, let us recall that it was a celebrated custom of the ancient sages either not to write of divine things at all, or to write of them in a veiled manner. 

<margin>Mysteries</margin>
<margin>Gymnosophists</margin>
<margin>Egyptians</margin>
<margin>Pythagoras</margin>
<margin>Golden Verses</margin>
<margin>Philolaus</margin>
<margin>Pythagoreans</margin>
<margin>Lysis</margin>
<margin>Hipparchus</margin>
Hence they were called "mysteries"—for they are not mysteries if they are not hidden. This was observed by the Indians; by the Ethiopians (who are nicknamed for their nakedness) <note>The "Gymnosophists" or naked philosophers</note>; and by the Egyptians. Those Sphinxes placed before the temples suggested this same secrecy. Taught by them, Pythagoras became a master of silence, nor did he himself commit anything to writing except for a very few things which he commended to his daughter Damo as he was dying. For the *Golden Verses* <note>original: *aurea carmina*</note> that are in circulation are not by Pythagoras, as is commonly believed even by the learned, but by Philolaus...

<margin>The second difficulty</margin>
...for he <note>Likely referring to the author of the text being commented upon, or God as the ultimate author</note> either should have, could have, or wished to help the learned less than the unlearned. The second difficulty is that the interpretation should maintain a consistent tone, being internally coherent and fitting; the entire series should flow as if in a single stroke, returning to that same original meaning from which it first proceeded, as if mindful of its purpose. Nor should we, if perhaps we introduce him here speaking of Ideas <note>original: "de ideis"; referring to the Platonic concept of universal forms or archetypes</note>, want him in the very next clause to deal with the physical elements or with man. 

*This type of exposition is arbitrary and forced. To avoid this, however, in the explanation of this book has seemed to many impossible—not to say difficult—and certainly a laborious task to everyone.*

<margin>How difficult it is to do what is being undertaken</margin>
Such is the complexity, such the ambiguity, such the variety of the entire reading. See how much labor is involved, and how it is not easy to perform what we have conceived in our minds (would that we might achieve it!): that we might begin a new work from the very start, not with merely one, but with a **sevenfold sense** <note>original: "septemplici sensu"; the author is attempting to provide seven distinct layers of interpretation for the same text</note> of a continuous and unmixed exposition.

<meta>This page begins a new section of the work, titled "Another Preface." It establishes the cosmological framework of the three "worlds" that the author will use to interpret the creation story.</meta>

->### ANOTHER PREFACE TO THE WHOLE WORK.<-

**TRES** <note>original: "THREE"</note> Worlds are depicted by antiquity: The highest of all is the super-mundane, which theologians call the angelic and philosophers call the intellectual; Plato says in the *Phaedrus* that no one has sung of this world worthily enough. Next to this is the celestial world, and the last of all is this sublunary <term>sublunary</term><note>The region "under the moon" (the Earth), which ancient science believed was the only place subject to change and decay.</note> world which we inhabit. This is the world of darkness, while that other is the world of light; the heavens are a mixture of both light and darkness. This world is characterized by "waters"—a fluid and unstable substance; that higher world is characterized by the "fire" of the brightness of light and the highness of its station. Heaven, being of a middle nature, is therefore called by the Hebrews **Shamayim** <note>original: *sciamaim*</note>, as if it were made from *fire* <note>original: *es* / *esh*</note> and *water* <note>original: *maim*</note>, because, as we said, it is composed of both. 

Here in our world, there is a constant cycle of life and death; there, in the highest world, is perpetual life and stable activity. In heaven, there is stability of life but a constant change of activities and positions. This world is made of the decaying substance of bodies; that highest world is made of the nature of the divine mind. Heaven is constituted of body, but an incorruptible one, and of mind, though one that is bound to a body. 

The third world is moved by the second; the second is ruled by the first. Furthermore, there are many other differences between them which it is not my intention to list here, where we are merely flowing past the subject rather than flooding it with detail. However, I should not overlook that these three worlds were most clearly symbolized by Moses in the construction of his wonderful Tabernacle. For he divided the Tabernacle into three parts: each of which could not more perfectly represent the three worlds we have mentioned. 

The first part, protected by no roof or shade, was exposed and vulnerable to rain, snow, sun, heat, and cold; it is a very clear image of our sublunary world. It was inhabited not only by men (clean and unclean, sacred and profane) but also by animals of every kind. In it, because of the sacrifices and constant offerings, there was a perpetual cycle of life and death. 

The remaining two parts were both covered and free on all sides from any outside harm, just as both higher worlds—the celestial and the super-celestial—are incapable of suffering harm or insult. Both were also honored with the name of holiness, yet in such a way that the more secret part was called the **Holy of Holies**, while the other was decorated only with the title of **Holy**. This is just as the celestial and angelic worlds are both holy (since above the moon, after the fall of Lucifer, no stain or sin exists or can exist); nevertheless, the angelic world is held to be far holier and more divine than the celestial. 

But why do we pursue these remote similarities? For if the last part of the Tabernacle was common to men and beasts, the second part—which shone entirely with the splendor of gold—was illuminated by a candelabrum <note>The Menorah</note> divided into seven lamps. These, as all Latin, Greek, and Hebrew interpreters say, signify the seven planets. In the third part, the most sacred of all, were the winged **Cherubim**. Do these not place the three worlds before our eyes? This world which both beasts and men inhabit; the celestial world in which the planets flash; and the super-celestial dwelling of the angels. We are also reminded from here of a higher gospel mystery <note>original: *sacramenti*</note>. For since to us, toward the super-celestial... <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence at the bottom of the page.</note>

For all these worlds, bound by the chains of concord, grant to one another not only their natures but also their names, with a mutual generosity. From this principle (if perhaps someone has not yet noticed it) the discipline of the entire **allegorical sense** has flowed. <meta>This page continues the discussion of how the ancient sages and Moses used allegorical language to represent the deep connections between different levels of reality. It follows the argument that one world can represent another because they all share a divine blueprint.</meta>

...to represent [them] unless they were learned in the secret—so to speak—friendships and affinities of the whole of nature. Otherwise, there would be no reason why they would represent this thing by this image rather than another, or vice-versa. But being knowledgeable of all things and driven by that Spirit which not only knows all these things but made them, they very aptly depicted the natures of one world through those things which they knew corresponded to them in the remaining worlds. Therefore, the same knowledge is needed (unless the same Spirit is present) for those who wish to correctly interpret their figures and allegorical meanings. 

However, besides the three worlds we have described <note>Pico previously identified the Angelic, Celestial, and Sublunary (earthly) worlds.</note>, there is a fourth world in which all those things found in the others are also found. <margin>Fourth world / man is the lesser [world]</margin> This is man himself, who, for this reason—as the Catholic doctors <note>Theologians and scholars of the Church.</note> say—is considered in the Gospel under the title of "every creature." <margin>every man</margin> Since the Gospel is to be preached to men, and not to beasts and angels, yet Christ commands that it be preached to "every creature." It is a common saying in the schools that man is a **microcosm** <note>original: "minorem mundum," literally a "lesser world." This was a central idea in Renaissance philosophy: that the human being contains the entire universe in miniature.</note>, in whom is seen a body mixed from the elements, a heavenly spirit, the vegetative soul of plants, the senses of beasts, reason, an angelic mind, and the likeness of God. <margin>How man is the lesser world</margin> 

Therefore, if we establish these four worlds, it is credible that Moses, intending to speak sufficiently about the world, discussed all of these. <margin>About all these worlds</margin> And since a writer portrays nature—if he is skilled in nature, as we believe our Moses was above all others—it is credible that the teaching concerning them was arranged no differently than Almighty God the Creator arranged them in themselves. <margin>Moses treated [these]</margin> This is so that this scripture of Moses might truly be an expressed image of the world, just as we read he was also commanded on the mountain where he learned these things: that he should **"make all things according to the pattern"** <note>A reference to Exodus 25:40, where God instructs Moses to build the Tabernacle according to a divine model.</note> he had seen on the mountain. <margin>Scripture is this image of nature</margin>

First, therefore—which is the greatest point of all—as we have shown that what is in all the worlds is contained in each individual one, Moses, as an emulator of nature, ought not to deal with any one of those worlds without dealing with all of them simultaneously and equally under the same words and the same context. <margin>No part of the work in which he does not treat all worlds together</margin> 

From this, a fourfold exposition of the entire Mosaic reading immediately arises: 
1. First, we explain whatever is written there concerning the angelic and invisible world, making no mention of the others at all. 
2. Second, likewise, everything concerning the celestial world. 
3. Then, concerning this sublunary <note>The world below the moon: the earth and its atmosphere, subject to change and decay.</note> and corruptible world. 
4. Fourth, concerning the nature of man. 

<margin>The root of the fourfold exposition</margin> For if, for instance, the intelligible world is never discussed without the scripture reminding us of the remaining worlds (just as that world contains all subsequent natures within itself), we certainly can—indeed, we must—interpret every small part regarding all of them. 

Again, just as natures, although they are mutually contained within one another in a mixed way, have nevertheless been assigned distinct and proper seats and certain peculiar laws; so also, if in each part of the present work the same sequence of letters treats the fourfold nature, we must believe that in the first part, the first nature is dealt with more specifically, and so on in the same order for the rest. <margin>The root of the fifth exposition</margin> From this, the necessity of a fifth exposition arises. 

It follows that, by the same reasoning that these are distinct, yet because there is no multitude which is not "one," they are bound together by a certain **"discordant concord"** <note>original: "discordi concordia" — the idea that harmony arises from the joining of opposing forces.</note> and are tied together by multiform chains of connections, as it were. <margin>The root of the sixth exposition</margin> Since it is likely that Moses deals with this throughout the whole work, it calls us, even if unwillingly, to a sixth interpretation.

It is fitting that we, after having distributed the orders of the worlds <note>original: "regum," likely a scribal error or variant for "rerum" (things/worlds) given the context of the Heptaplus</note> arranged by God, and having explained their union, difference, covenants, and relationships, should now touch upon some matters in this seventh and "sabbath-like" (if I may call it so) narration. This concerns the happiness of creatures and the return to God—a return which falls to man through the Mosaic and Christian laws, after he was distanced from God by the sin of our first parent. In doing so, we shall report those things which Moses most clearly hid <note>A classic Renaissance idea: that the most profound truths are "hidden in plain sight" within the literal text for those with the eyes to see them.</note> in the present scripture regarding these matters, so that it may become clear that a most distinct prophecy is read here concerning the coming of Christ, the progress of the Church, and the calling of the nations. *That this book may truly be:* if any other is such, a book sealed with seven seals, full of all doctrine and all mysteries. <note>A reference to the Book of Revelation 5:1.</note>

   However, we will not imitate those who, when they occasionally attempted to explain this creation of the world, heaped up here whatever has been disputed among philosophers and theologians regarding God, angels, matter, <margin>Isaac the Persian / Samuel Ophinides</margin> heaven, and the whole of nature. In this, Isaac the Persian and Samuel Ophinides <note>Two medieval Jewish commentators often cited for their overly expansive or "unscientific" commentaries.</note> were particularly at fault. Instead, we shall strive with all our strength to declare only what the Mosaic letter intends, and what the context of the words either indicates or signifies. Nor, if we show that the "firmament" signifies, for instance, the eighth sphere, will we immediately launch into a dispute about how it carries the other spheres along with it, how many signs or images it is distinguished by, or whether it is rotated by a simple motion, or rather two, or more truly three. Or, if in some passage we say the human soul is indicated by a certain word, we will not digress to explain everything written about the soul; rather, we will note only those things about each subject, briefly and even cursorily, <margin>These are written for the learned, not for those unrefined in philosophy</margin> of which the author seems to make express mention. *I said briefly and also cursorily:* because the purpose of this work is not that those who have not learned these things elsewhere should learn them here for the first time, but that they should recognize in the words of the Prophet <note>Referring to Moses as the "Prophet."</note> those things they already know to be true. Having understood how the author here both included and concealed in a few words what they have read digested in the immense volumes of theologians and philosophers, they may hear the Law-giver speaking with his face revealed. But if anyone, perhaps moved by a spirit of "holy rusticity," <note>original: "sanctae rusticitatis"; a phrase used to describe a simple, unlettered faith that is nevertheless holy.</note> does not approve of these mysteries sought from such depths, but prefers a simpler and more accommodating <margin>Paul</margin> explanation of the sacred context, I will bid him first to remember Paul's instruction: that neither the one who eats should despise the one who does not eat, nor should the one who does not eat judge the one who eats. <note>A reference to Romans 14:3, using the metaphor of spiritual "food" or knowledge.</note> <margin>Augustine</margin> Then I will address him not with my own words, but with those of Augustine in his own exposition on Genesis, in this manner: "If you can grasp these things, do so; if you cannot yet grasp them, leave them to those who are stronger. But you, as long as Scripture does not desert your weakness and walks more slowly with you with a motherly gait, shall make progress." <margin>The power of Scripture</margin> For Scripture speaks in such a way that it mocks the proud with its height, terrifies the attentive with its depth, feeds the great with its truth, and nourishes the small with its affability. *But let us return to ourselves and,* starting from this corruptible world which we inhabit, let us provide as much as we can of what we have promised. After all, even in great things, it is enough to have willed them; and, <margin>Pomerius</margin> as Pomerius <note>Likely Julianus Pomerius, a 5th-century priest; this quote emphasizes that the effort itself is a form of success.</note> says, a great effort in great matters is itself progress.

Behold how correctly—not only in its position but in the property of its nature—this <term>firmament|The "sky" or atmosphere that separates the higher, pure regions from the lower, changeable world.</term> separates and distinguishes the superior elements from the inferior ones, like waters from waters. Above it, the elements are pure; below it, they depart from elemental simplicity through a perfect mixture. There, they become mixed, but in an imperfect and intermediate way, so that it may be most truly said to lie between the nature of mixed things and the pure elements.

->### Chapter Four<-

But let us see what Moses further philosophizes. He says, <margin>The waters are gathered into one place and the earth appears</margin> "Let the waters which are under the heaven be gathered into one place, and let the dry land appear." "The dry" is matter, as we have already established, and matter does not appear nor is it perceived unless it is clothed in the outward appearance of forms. But neither does it appear clothed merely in the appearance of a single <term>element|Earth, water, air, or fire in their purest, unmixed states.</term>, because (as we have said and as the philosophers prove) a simple element can neither be seen nor touched, nor can it fall under the notice of any sense at all. 

Therefore, if the earth—which was once invisible—is to come into view, it is necessary that the waters under the heaven (that is, under the middle region of the air) gather into one place. This means they flow together into a common mass of mixture, yet, prescribed by certain laws as if by shores, they coalesce into a single "mixed" form. As we have shown, this happens to the inferior waters, but not to the superior ones, where there is either no mixture at all or only an imperfect one. <margin>The earth sprouts plants</margin> Now, if the <term>vegetative soul|The basic level of "life force" that allows plants to grow and reproduce.</term> immediately follows the formation of this mixture, what else should we expect from our philosopher <note>referring to Moses as a "philosopher" of nature</note> than that, after the gathering of the waters, he should immediately introduce the earth as fertile with herbs, shrubs, and trees?

->### Chapter Five<-

Although from this point it seemed that the next logical step was to move to the animals—whose soul is most closely joined to the vegetative one—nevertheless, since one moves from animals to Man (in whom all discussion of the corruptible world finally ends), Moses instead interspersed some details about those things which occur in the firmament. He describes how the firmament is adorned, just as the earth is adorned by the things produced within it: metals, plants, and living creatures. 

These are those "impressions" which occur in the heights—that is, in the middle region of the air. This region he previously called both "heaven" and "firmament," but here he calls it the "firmament of heaven," so that we may know it is not the "true" heaven <note>The unchanging celestial realm of the stars</note>, but the region that lies beneath it. For this reason, <margin>Ennius</margin> the poet Ennius, in his play *Achilles*, called this the "subject part," because it is situated directly beneath the heavens. 

It is well known—more than requires many proofs—that these "secondary impressions" <note>atmospheric events like meteors or clouds</note> are called "stars" and "constellations" by the philosophers. Therefore, it should not seem difficult for anyone that we explain here what is said about the "stars" in this context. Since the entire diversity of these phenomena is traced back to two primary causes, heat and cold, we shall appropriately refer those things caused by heat to the Sun, and those caused by cold to the Moon. 

These phenomena claim the names of the Sun, Moon, and other stars for themselves not only because they are to the lower heaven what the real stars are to their own (albeit more divine) heaven, or because they show a similar face to men—shining and sparkling alike—but because some of them follow a particular star in the heaven as their prince and leader. For this reason, they are "signs" of those things which the stars (by which they were stirred up) are accustomed to portend for things here below. The proof of this is that they follow the movement of the stars; it is by the stars' power and influence that these phenomena consist of matter gathered from the earth—that is, from a vaporous breath.

According to the author Dionysius and Saint Thomas—the glory of our theology—that mind among the angelic ranks <margin>Dionysius</margin> is supreme which perceives through the fewest possible notions and forms. Whereas lower minds <margin>Saint Thomas</margin> <note>The author refers to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite and Thomas Aquinas, who argued that higher angels possess more universal knowledge requiring fewer specific concepts.</note> understand through various and manifold forms, so too among the scriptures, that one is supreme and holds the peak of all perfection which embraces all things, as if individually, both appropriately and profoundly, in very few words.

->### Chapter One<-

Above the nine spheres of the heavens—that is, the seven planets, the eighth sphere which they call the fixed stars <margin>The Empyrean Heaven</margin>, and the ninth sphere which is grasped by reason rather than by the senses and is the first among moving bodies—it is believed there exists a tenth heaven that remains fixed and quiet, sharing in no motion at all. 

Nor is this believed only by our own writers—most notably the younger <margin>Strabo</margin> Strabo and <margin>Bede</margin> <note>Walafrid Strabo and the Venerable Bede were foundational medieval theologians.</note> Bede—but also by many of the Hebrews, as well as certain philosophers and mathematicians. From these, it is sufficient to cite two: <margin>Abraham the Astrologer</margin> Abraham the Spaniard, a supreme astrologer <note>Likely referring to the Jewish scholar Abraham Ibn Ezra.</note>, and <margin>Isaac the Philosopher</margin> Isaac the philosopher, both of whom attest to this. 

Indeed, this Isaac understands the tenth sphere to be that designated by <margin>Ezekiel on the Empyrean Heaven</margin> Ezekiel as the "Sapphire" in the likeness of a throne; thus, the color of the sapphire signifies the brightness of light, and the likeness of the throne signifies its immobility. 

He <margin>Zechariah</margin> also understands the ten spheres to be symbolized by Zechariah through the golden lampstand, distinguished by seven lamps and a bowl atop it, and then two olive trees above the bowl. Since the seven lamps indicate the seven planets, and the bowl represents the eighth sphere shining with so many lights, he intends the two olive trees to indicate the ninth and tenth spheres. This is because oil flows from the olives to the bowl and the lamps to nourish the light. Therefore, by an analogy of reason, since the light of the heavens we see emanates from and is preserved by those supreme spheres (for he who gives light also preserves it), the former are rightly compared to the olives, and the latter to the lamps and the bowl. 

Truly, if two primary springs of the same water cannot be established, it is necessary that one of those two supreme spheres be the principle of all light. If this is attributed to one, it must certainly be to the first—that is, the tenth—so that it may be, as it were, the <margin>Source and unity of light</margin> unity of lights. Then, the ninth sphere receives that light most closely in the entire essence of its substance. From there <margin>Three degrees of participated light</margin>...

The "waters which are under the heaven" <margin>The waters under the heaven</margin> are the seven stars <note>The "seven stars" refers to the seven classical planets of the ancient world: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, the Sun, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon.</note> which are beneath the firmament, which he called "heaven." I believe a deeper mystery of the ancient Hebrew discipline <note>Referring to the Kabbalistic or esoteric Jewish traditions that the author, likely Pico della Mirandola, sought to integrate with Christian philosophy.</note> lies hidden here. Among their dogmas concerning the heavens, this is <margin>A dogma of the ancient Hebrews regarding the stars</margin> the most important: that Jupiter and Mars are "enclosed" by the Sun, while Venus and Mercury are enclosed by the Moon. Jupiter is hot, Mars is hot, and the Sun is hot; but the heat of Mars is sharp and violent, while that of Jupiter is beneficial. In the Sun, we see that sharp and violent quality of Mars <margin>The affinity of the Sun with Jupiter and Mars</margin> and the beneficial property of Jupiter; that is, we see a certain nature that is mixed from these and tempered in the middle, if I may put it that way. Aries is the "house" of Mars, and Cancer is the "dignity" of Jupiter; the Sun, having attained "exaltation" in Cancer and "dignity" in Aries, shows a manifest kinship with both stars.

Let us come to the Moon, which clearly participates in the "waters" of Mercury; <margin>The affinity of the Moon with Venus and Mercury</margin> and how much affinity it has with Venus is indicated especially by the fact that it is so "exalted" in Taurus (the home of Venus) that it is judged to be nowhere more happy or more beneficial. Therefore, concerning the Empyrean heaven, the ninth sphere (called the firmament), the star of Saturn, and the Sun and Moon—which embrace all the rest—Moses has spoken sufficiently thus far, <margin>Epilogue</margin> reminding us of this inclusion by his very silence.

It remained that after they had spoken of the nature of the stars, they should discuss their works and their office, declaring for what use they were founded and to what duty they were delegated by God. Know, however, that the discussion so far concerns the heaven as a luminous body; nothing has yet been said by the prophet <note>referring to Moses as the author of Genesis</note> regarding its intellect or its moving power. This is the same order that Timaeus <note>The narrator of Plato’s dialogue *Timaeus*, which explains the creation of the universe</note> follows: first fashioning the body, then attaching the soul to the completed body. 

There are two generally manifest operations of the celestial bodies: motion and illumination. Motion is established as two-fold: one is that of the whole world, by which the heaven and the ether are revolved in a perfect circuit through the whole space of the universe in twenty-four hours; the other is the specific motion of the stars, which is manifold and various, among which the principal is the motion of the sun, which circles all the signs of the Zodiac in the space of twelve months. The former makes the day (from which it is called "diurnal"); the latter makes the year. The remaining motions of the stars are completed in various intervals of time. Rightly and briefly, therefore, Moses reminded us of all these when he said the stars were placed in the firmament for **days, years, and seasons**. He added **for signs**, but because this is sufficiently explained by other interpreters, I shall pass over it. 

Furthermore, he expressly indicated the other operation of the stars, which is illumination, when he said those laws were established **so that they might shine in the heaven and illuminate the earth**. Although there are diverse opinions among the ancients regarding what the celestial bodies influence in lower things, the words of Moses fit any of them aptly. For if they influence nothing but light—which Aristotle seems to have intended, if we interpret his words more religiously and not according to our own whim—nothing can be thought more consistent with the Mosaic sayings. If, besides light, they also influence heat (and nothing else, as the Arab Averroës <term>Averroës: Ibn Rushd, a 12th-century Islamic philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle</term> and Abraham the Jew <term>Abraham: Likely Abraham Ibn Ezra, a medieval scholar of astrology and scripture</term> believe), it was enough to have spoken of light, from which these same authors confess heat proceeds. Likewise, if many other and manifold powers are sent down from heaven (as it seemed to Avicenna <term>Avicenna: Ibn Sina, a Persian polymath whose medical and philosophical works were standard texts in Europe</term> and the Babylonians), mention of light alone was not made rashly; for as Avicenna himself writes, light alone is what carries all other powers from heaven to us. In these ministries, therefore, the bodies of the moon, sun, and stars are distributed.

### Chapter Five

It remained that he should mention both the signs which are visible in the Zodiac and those which, although invisible to us, are far more effective in the crystalline heaven <note>The "crystalline heaven" was traditionally considered the 9th sphere in medieval astronomy, located beyond the stars</note> of the eighth and ninth spheres. For nothing has been said of these so far. This, therefore, is the meaning of the **living creatures** <note>original: *animalia*</note> which both the **waters produce** and the **earth produces**: namely, those waters which are above the heavens and the earth which is the firmament itself, as was proven above. For the signs which are seen in those two spheres alone are in the form of animals, such as those noted among us by the Egyptians and Indians; they were able to detect them more easily and correctly than our people, aided by the flatness of the ground and the serenity of the sky. Otherwise, the production of the perishable animals that are here on earth pertains no more to these two elements—earth and water—than to the others, namely fire and air. And because he gave the name "waters" to the crystalline sphere, he consistently called the animals there "fish"; conversely, in the firmament which he calls "earth," he called them "beasts of burden and wild animals."

What is appropriately said regarding the human soul is likewise transferred to the soul of the heaven. <margin>Holy Scripture</margin> Holy Scripture supports our exposition: in which all angelic and rational nature is often designated by the name "man." It is likewise not without mystery that he created that man male and female. <margin>In what way the celestial man is male and female</margin> For it is the prerogative of celestial souls that they perform both duties simultaneously: both contemplating and ruling bodies, without one being an obstacle or hindrance to the other. This was widely used by the ancients, as we observe even in the <term>Orphic hymns</term> <note>A collection of ancient Greek poems dedicated to various deities, often used by Renaissance philosophers to find hidden theological truths.</note>; they designate these two powers in the same substance—one which contemplates and the other which presides over the body—by the names "male" and "female." <margin>Conclusion</margin> These things regarding the celestial world, the divine body, the number of spheres, their nature, properties, and office—and finally, regarding its motive force, its rational substance, and its character—are delivered by the prophet.

<margin>To what extent we should honor the heaven</margin>

For he himself, when asked who he was, being best aware of himself, responded: *I am the beginning who speaks to you.* <note>John 8:25</note> Therefore, let us not reshape the images of stars in metals; but let us reform the image of Him—that is, the Word of God—in our souls. Nor from the heavens, or from the body, or from fortune (which will not provide them), but from the Lord of heaven, the Lord of all good things—to whom all power in heaven and earth has been given—let us seek present goods insofar as they are good, and the true happiness of eternal life.

### THIRD EXPOSITION CONCERNING THE ANGELIC AND INVISIBLE WORLD.
#### PREFACE TO THE THIRD BOOK.

Thus far, we have discussed the mysteries of Moses, revealing them according to the strength of our intellect, concerning the celestial world. Now, however, who will give me wings like a dove—wings silvered and glowing with the paleness of gold—and I shall fly into the super-celestial region where there is true rest, true peace, and true tranquility; a peace, indeed, which this visible and corporeal world cannot give. Unveil my eyes, O spirits beyond this world, and I shall contemplate the miracles of your city, which God has set aside for those who fear Him: that which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor heart conceived. <note>1 Corinthians 2:9</note> While many things concerning this angelic and invisible nature are handed down by the ancient Hebrews—and likewise many by Dionysius— <margin>Dionysius</margin> <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century theologian whose works on the "Celestial Hierarchy" were central to medieval and Renaissance angelology.</note> it was my plan to explain the words of Moses according to the doctrine of both families. But since the things said by the Hebrews, being unusual among the Latins, <margin>Ancient dogmas of the Hebrews</margin> could not be easily understood by our people unless we started "from the twin egg" <note>original: "gemino... ouo"; a Latin idiom meaning to start from the very beginning, or the earliest possible point.</note> (as they say) and recounted most and nearly all the dogmas of the ancient discipline of the Hebrew nation, I thought it best to postpone this until we have written about these things more extensively elsewhere. There, we shall make their opinions known to our countrymen, examining how much they harmonize with Egyptian monuments, how much with Platonic philosophy, and how much with Catholic truth. If they agree with us, we shall bid the Hebrews to stand in the ancient traditions of their fathers; if they disagree, being equipped with Catholic legions, <note>A metaphor for theological arguments and Church authority.</note> we shall make an assault upon them. Finally, whatever we find foreign <margin>Dionysius, Paul, Hierotheus</margin> <note>Hierotheus was the semi-legendary teacher of Dionysius the Areopagite.</note> to the Gospel truth, we shall refute as best we can; whatever is sound and true, we shall transfer from the **synagogue** (as if from an unjust possessor) to ourselves, the legitimate Israelites. Meanwhile, following in the footsteps of Dionysius, or rather of Paul and Hierotheus whom he followed, we will try—despite our weakness—to bring light into the darkness of the Law, where the Spirit of God, the author of the Law, placed his hiding place.

#### Chapter One.

<margin>Unity</margin> Whatever exists after **unity** is number, and number is perfected and completed by unity. Unity alone is entirely simple and perfect by itself; it does not go out of itself, but in indivisible simplicity and solitude, it clings to itself, because it is sufficient to itself, needing nothing, and full of its own riches. <margin>Number</margin> Number, although by its nature it is a multitude, becomes "one" by the benefit of unity, insofar as it is capable of simplicity. However, every number, the further it is removed from unity, always falls into a greater multitude; there is more dissimilarity within it, more parts, and more composition. No number is so <margin>An ascent from mathematics to things divine</margin> close to unity that it is not a multitude; it possesses an accidental unity, being "one" not by nature, but by composition. Let us transfer these things to divine matters in the **Pythagorean manner**. <note>The use of mathematical concepts (like Unity and Number) to explain the nature of God and the soul.</note> God alone—who is from no one and from whom all things are—is the most simple and indivisible essence. Whatever He has, He has from Himself: by the same thing that He is, He knows; by the same He wills; by the same He is good; and by the same He is just. Nor...

...we are able to understand something of what He is, beyond that very **Being** which He is. Other things are not that—that is, **Being** itself—but exist through it. Therefore, an angel is not unity itself; otherwise, he would be God, or there would be many gods, which cannot even be conceived. For what will be "one" if unity itself is not even one? It remains, then, that an angel is a <term>number</term> <note>In this Neoplatonic context, "number" refers to a thing that is composed of parts or multiplicity, unlike God who is absolute simplicity.</note>. And if he is a number, in one part of himself he is a multitude, and in another part he is a "unified multitude." <margin>Angel</margin> Every number is imperfect insofar as it is a multitude, but perfect insofar as it is one. Therefore, whatever is imperfect in an angel we should attribute to the angelic "multitude"—which he has from the fact that he is a "number," that is, a creature—and whatever is perfect we should attribute to the "approaching unity," which he has from the fact that he is joined to God. 

We find a twofold imperfection in the angel: First, because he is not **Being** itself, but only an essence to which "participated being" is added so that he may exist. Second, because he is not "understanding" itself, but it comes to him so that he may understand; although he is, by his own nature, an intellect capable of understanding. This second point depends on the first: for that which does not exist by its own power certainly does not understand by its own power, since nothing can exist where **Being** itself is not present.

Both of these conditions happen to the angel because he is a "multitude." It remains for his release and perfection to come from the "approaching unity" from above. But God is Unity, from whom being, life, and all perfection are derived for the angel. Just as there is a twofold imperfection (which is a twofold multitude), so let us understand a twofold approach of unity so that both may be perfected. The first is that by which there is a raw and formless essence, devoid of life and being. This is the **earth without form and void** <margin>The formless earth</margin> which God also created—lest perhaps you should believe, as some have believed, that only the *formation* of essence belongs to the Creator and not its *creation*. 

At the same time as the earth, He created heaven: that is, the act of that essence and the "participated unity" within the multitude, which is **Being** itself. Thus, the creation of heaven and earth is, as it were, the same act, since they are a coupled embrace of two natures meeting in a similar bond. Not inconsistently with the ancients, we call "heaven" this participation in divinity; even as **Xenophanes** <margin>Xenophanes</margin> <note>A Greek philosopher who famously described God as a single, eternal sphere.</note> called the archetypal world a "sphere," and the **Saracens** <margin>Saracens</margin> <note>A term here referring to Islamic philosophers, such as Avicenna or the Sufi traditions, who often used the geometry of the circle to describe divine emanation.</note>—and indeed our own thinkers—call God a "circle."

### Chapter Three.

We have seen the nature of the angel created by God, and that same nature turned toward God by the spirit of love; then we saw it illuminated and made perfect by the light of intelligible reasons. Let us now see in what order the angelic hosts are distinguished among themselves. We read that a **firmament** was placed **in the midst of the waters**, where three angelic <term>hierarchies</term> <note>The traditional ranking of angels into nine choirs, grouped into three main tiers.</note> (for we shall always call them by this common name) are indicated to us. The first and the last of these are designated by the "waters": the first by those **above the heavens**, and the last by those which are **below the heavens**. The middle hierarchy, dividing the two, is called the **firmament**. If we examine the nature and duties of the three hierarchies, they could not harmonize more perfectly with the doctrine of Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, an early Christian theologian whose work "The Celestial Hierarchy" defined the ranks of angels for the Middle Ages.</note>. The highest hierarchy, as he writes, is devoted solely to contemplation; it is rightly symbolized by the waters that are set **above the heavens**—that is, above all earthly or celestial action concerning the world—and they praise God unceasingly with an eternal sound. The middle order, however, being assigned to celestial duties, could certainly not be more appropriately signified than by the **firmament** (that is, the sky). The final hierarchy, although by nature it is above every physical body and above the heavens, nevertheless cares for those things which are **under the heavens**. Since it is divided into **Principalities**, **Archangels**, and **Angels**, the entire operation of all these is only concerned with the sublunary realm <note>The world below the moon, i.e., the Earthly sphere subject to change and decay.</note>. The Principalities look after republics, kings, and princes (as we learn from the book of Daniel); the Archangels look after mysteries and sacred ceremonies. The Angels attend to private matters, and individual angels are assigned to individual humans. Correcty, then, this host "under the heavens" is symbolized by the **waters under the heavens**. It presides over things that are flowing and fleeting, and it is subject to that higher order which deals with the heavens.
