# FOURTH EXPOSITION ON THE HUMAN WORLD, THAT IS, ON THE NATURE OF MAN.

## Preface to the Fourth Book.

After we have shown that the prophet has sufficiently treated all parts of the world and every nature—celestial, angelic, and corruptible—it remains (if we are mindful of our promise) to interpret the entire reading once again concerning man. This will prove by the facts themselves that there is no discourse in this whole work which does not contain hidden meanings and the highest truths regarding the nature of man, just as it did regarding the three worlds discussed above. Nor shall we perform a less worthwhile task if we are diligent in explaining this fourth exposition than we were in the previous ones. For how useful and necessary self-knowledge is to man (to pass over the Delphic letter <margin>The Delphic Letter</margin> <note>The famous Greek maxim "Know Thyself" inscribed at the Temple of Apollo in Delphi</note>), was so demonstrated by Plato <margin>Plato</margin> in the first *Alcibiades* <margin>Chapter</margin> <note>A Socratic dialogue exploring the nature of the self</note> that he left nothing for those who came after him to attempt to bring as something new on this subject. And indeed, the pursuit of that man is wicked and reckless who, still ignorant of himself and still not knowing whether he can know anything at all, yet so boldly affects knowledge of things that are so far from him. 

Let us return therefore into ourselves, and let us see (as the prophet says) what great things God has done for our soul. Lest, perhaps, if it should be less diligent in recognizing itself, it should hear the Father saying in the *Song of Songs*: "If you know not yourself, O fairest among women, go forth and depart following the tracks of your flocks." <note>A reference to Song of Solomon 1:8, interpreted here as a warning against losing one's human status by remaining ignorant of the soul's divine nature.</note> You see what punishment <margin>The threefold punishment for self-ignorance</margin> awaits us for our ignorance. For there must be a departure from the Father, which departure is followed by disinheritance—and what could be more unhappy than that? Likewise, there must be a going out: certainly out of ourselves. For the mind is not with itself <margin>Above itself</margin> when it does not see itself. But he who goes out from himself <margin>From itself</margin> is torn apart—and what could be more bitter? Third, there must be a going after the tracks of our flocks <margin>After itself</margin>, that is, after the tracks of the brutes <note>Referring to the animalistic or base instincts within the human being</note> that are in us (about which we shall say enough in the exposition)—and what could be more miserable? What more despicable and contemptible than to become the attendants of the beasts over whom nature had appointed us as leaders? Therefore, let us walk not after the tracks of brutes, but after the tracks of Moses, and let us enter into ourselves; let us enter the inner chambers of the soul with the prophet himself opening the way for us, so that in ourselves we may happily recognize both all the worlds and also the Father and our homeland.

<margin>The rational soul</margin>
Before we proceed with a more careful exposition according to the words and order of the prophet <note>The "prophet" refers to Moses, traditionally considered the author of Genesis.</note>, it is necessary to first say a few things about the nature of man and briefly explain certain terms, so that the understanding of the entire meaning may be clearer afterward. It is established that man consists of a body and a **rational soul**. The **rational soul** is called "heaven." For Aristotle calls heaven an "animal" moved by itself, and our soul (as the <margin>Aristotle</margin> Platonists prove) is a substance that moves itself. Heaven is a circle; likewise, the soul is a circle. Indeed, as Plotinus writes, the heaven is a circle precisely because its soul <margin>The Platonists</margin> is a circle. Heaven moves in an orbit; the rational soul, transferring itself from causes to effects and returning again from effects to causes, revolves in a circle of reasoning. If these points had to be explained individually to those who have not <margin>Plotinus</margin> read them elsewhere, we would no longer be interpreters of Moses, but of Aristotle and Plato.

<margin>The Body</margin>
The **body** is called "earth" because it is an earthy and heavy substance. For this reason, Moses writes that man was made from the soil <note>original: "de humo factum"</note>, which gave man his name. <note>"Adam" is etymologically linked to "Adamah," meaning ground or earth.</note> But between the earthly body and the celestial substance of the soul, there was a need for a middle bond that could join together such distant natures. To this duty was assigned that thin and spiritual <margin>The Spirit</margin> "bodylet" <note>The author uses the Latin "corpusculum" to describe a very fine, subtle matter.</note> which both physicians and philosophers call **spirit**. Aristotle writes that this spirit is of a more divine nature than the elements and corresponds to the proportion of the heavens. Here, it is named "light." This name could not be more <margin>Aristotle</margin> fitting to the opinion of philosophers and physicians, whose common consensus is that this substance is extremely bright and rejoices in, is nourished by, and is recreated by nothing more than light. 

Furthermore, just as all the power of the heavens (as Avicenna writes) is <margin>Avicenna</margin> transferred to the earth by the vehicle of light, so all the power of the soul—which we have called "heaven"—and all its power of life (namely, motion and sense) travels and is poured into this earthly body (which we have called "earth") through the mediation of the lucid spirit.

Let us now descend to the words of the prophet. In his writing, we first see "heaven and earth" being created as the extremes: namely, the rational power of our substance and the earthly body. Finally, when "light" is made—that is, when the lucid spirit arrives—they are joined, so that from "evening and morning"—that is, from the nocturnal nature of the body and the morning nature of the soul—one man is formed. And since (as we have shown) all vital and sensory power descends to our "earth" through this light, it is with good reason that the earth was "empty and void" before the birth of light. For the earth could not participate in the benefits of life and motion from its "heaven" except through light as a messenger. Therefore, he immediately added the cause of that emptiness: because, of course, darkness was still upon it, and the light had not yet risen.

If we desire the true meaning of all these things, let us consult nature itself, which our prophet (as we have often said) portrays and represents with perfect precision. We have seen mention made of the three-fold part of human substance: namely, the **rational**, the **mortal body**, and the **middle spirit**. Two parts remain. For between the rational part by which we are men and the middle spirit (which is bodily within us, whether it be thick or thin and spiritual), there is a middle part: the **sensory soul** which we share with the beasts. ### Chapter Six.

Observe how perfectly this agrees with what we have said: that it follows that man was made by God in His own image so that he might rule over the fish, birds, and beasts which both the water and the earth had produced. For man was so established by nature that **reason** should rule over the senses, and that by its law every madness and appetite—both of anger and of lust—should be restrained. But once the image of God was blotted out by the stain of sin, we—miserable and unhappy—began to serve our own "beasts." ### Chapter One.

In speaking of the angelic nature—which is pure intellect—let us first conceive in our minds that spirits are like certain eyes. For what the eye is among physical things, the mind itself is in the spiritual category. Even if the eye possesses some light within the mixture of its own innermost substance, it still requires external light to perform the function of vision, by which it observes the colors and differences of things. It is not, therefore, that the eye is not "sight" by its own nature, even if it only sees by the benefit of light. For the ears—not to mention inanimate objects—and all other parts of the body are illuminated by light, yet they do not see. Therefore, that which is allotted the nature of seeing and is "sight" by the very logic of its essence is that which can see once light is received. 

Let us consider these same things regarding intellects: Intellects are the eyes, and intelligible truth is the light. Since the intelligible intellect itself is internal, it has some light by which it can see itself, but it cannot see other things. Truly, it requires the "forms" and "ideas" of things; using these like certain rays of invisible light, the intelligible truth is undoubtedly perceived. Because of this, we must not say—as we declared through the example of the eye—that they are not intelligent by nature, or that they have been allotted their intellectual property by some accident in the same condition as our own souls. From this comes the opinion of those who think the name "intellect" is unworthy of God. For if we take the intellect as a kind of eye that sees not of itself but by participation in light, and since God is light (for truth is light) and vision is the action by which the eye reaches the light, then God does not need this operation, as He is light itself. He is as much more removed from the ignorance of all things than the angels as the nature of light is further from darkness than the eyes are.

But let us return to the angels. But the common opinion, however it is understood, is sufficient for us regarding this passage. 

Moses reveals all these things we have said to us on the first day. He divides the substance of the angel into "heaven" and "earth"—namely, the nature of "act" and the nature of "potency." The same thing, just as it has different properties, also has different names. Again, insofar as it lacks light and cannot perform its own proper function of understanding by itself, it is symbolized by **"the waters"**: a body capable of receiving light, yet by its own nature not shining at all. ### Chapter Two
The celestial world is closest to this world. Its primary property is that it is the "interval" <note>an intermediary or bridge</note> between both worlds: namely, the intelligible world of which we have just spoken, and this sensible world <term>sensible: the physical world we can see, touch, and feel</term> which we inhabit. We cannot more clearly indicate the essence of any middle nature than by expressing the extremes by which it is enclosed, since a middle nature is tempered by those extremes. Therefore, he opens to us the greatest knowledge concerning the condition of the heaven when he says that the **heaven** is placed as a medium **between the waters and the waters**—that is, between angelic and corruptible <term>corruptible: subject to decay, change, and death</term> substances—not so much by its physical location as by the nature of its essence. Now, we have already said that by "waters" one should understand "forms," which are closest to potentiality (the "earth") and which bring an essence to its perfection. However, just as there is one "earth" of the angels and another of the elements (because the potentiality in each is different), so too is the nature of the "waters"—that is, the forms—different in each place. Between these, the heaven is truly the medium: on one side is the divine life, on the other is physical embodiment; here is incorruptible substance, there is visible substance; here is the firmness of essence, there is the change of location; on one side is whatever is simple and uniform, and on the other is whatever is varied, mixed, and dissimilar. Such was the lot assigned by the disposing providence of the Creator.

### Chapter Three
After these things, he briefly reminds us of the integrity, positioning, and order of the elements through the gathering of the waters into one place and the laws prescribed for the sea, so that it might not overwhelm the earth. For there is nothing that more clearly indicates that there are laws instilled by an intelligent Cause—by which they are governed and held in their places—within the elements (beyond the mere inclination of their heavy, brute nature) than these barriers of the waters. By these, the ocean is restrained; otherwise, its momentum would carry it over the entire circuit of the earth. Just as the fire rests upon the air, the sea—as if warned by the rod of a schoolmaster—draws back its foot and does not put itself further forward than our safety and the life of all living creatures demands. This cannot be attributed to "material necessity" (which would rather incline all elements equally toward the shape of a globe), nor to the "fortuitous collision of atoms" <margin>Epicurus</margin> <note>The author is refuting the materialist philosophy of Epicurus, who argued the world formed by chance.</note> as Epicurus dreams, nor to the "seminal force of nature" <margin>Strato</margin> <note>Strato of Lampsacus, a Greek philosopher who believed nature functioned without divine intervention.</note> as **Strato** says (who was ignorant of any higher purpose), but only to the **Final Cause** <term>Final Cause: the ultimate purpose or "end goal" for which a thing exists</term>.

Hence that saying of Paul: <note>original: *hinc illud Pauli*</note> "I have delivered him to Satan for the destruction of the flesh." <note>1 Corinthians 5:5</note> Hence there is a naming of the "avenging demon" in the works of Orpheus—if perhaps we do not believe our own writers.

But just as every creature hates and curses the crimes of men, so his upright life and instruction are pleasing and acceptable to all. For indeed—if I may put it this way—nothing is unable to be admitted into the participation of both his good and his evil, since they are folded and joined to him by so tight a bond. Hence that Gospel saying: "If a sinner repents, all the angels leap with joy." <note>Luke 15:10</note> Hence the fitting reason for that mystery which was hidden for ages: that our nature, corrupted in the first Adam and disturbed from its state, might be restored through the **cross of Christ**. Clearly, for our sake, the Son of God becomes both man and is fixed to the cross. For it was also fitting that he who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature, in whom all things were founded, should be coupled in an ineffable union with him who was made in the image of God—who is the bond of every creature, in whom all things are concluded. Nor was it right, if all nature was endangered by man's fall, that its loss should be neglected or repaired by any other than the one through whom all nature had been established.

# SIXTH EXPOSITION: ON THE KINSHIP OF THE WORLDS WITH ONE ANOTHER AND OF ALL THINGS

## Preface to the Sixth Book

**G**OD is a unity so distinguished by the triad <note>original: *ternario*, referring to the Trinity</note> that he does not depart from the simplicity of unity. There is a manifold trace of the divine Trinity in the creature. <margin>Trace of the Trinity</margin> Here we shall bring forward this one thing alone—which I believe has been brought forward by no one yet—that the unity we see in creatures, <margin>A triple unity in things</margin> we perceive divided by a triple reason. 

For first, there is that unity in things by which each thing is one with itself, and is consistent and coherent within itself. Secondly, there is that by which one creature is united to another, and by which finally all parts of the world are one world. The third and most principal of all is that by which the whole universe, with its Maker, is one—just as an army is one with its leader. This threefold union is present in every single thing through its own single, simple unity derived from that One who is both the first One and Triune and One all at once: from the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. <margin>Father, Son, Holy Spirit: the Root of all ordered charity <note>original: *caritatis*, meaning divine love</note></margin> For the power of the Father, producing all things, grants its own unity to all; the wisdom of the Son, rightly arranging all things, unites and couples all things to one another; and the love of the Spirit, turning all things toward God, joins the whole work to the Maker with a bond of charity. 

But just as he is more intimate, so is God more one with us than we are with ourselves. Again, each thing is more closely joined to itself than to other parts of the world; thus, having been taught the order of universal charity, if we wish to follow the divine law inscribed on the tablets of nature, we will love first God himself above us and above all things; in the second place, ourselves; and thirdly, our neighbor. Our Prophet, however, said enough about that unity by which each thing is one with itself when he examined the nature of all things individually. Regarding that unity by which we are united to God, it will be dealt with in the next discourse, where we shall discuss the height of happiness. What remains is that unity by which diverse parts are coupled to one another in a mutual covenant, which is what we must deal with at present.

# **Chapter One.**

After we have observed the distinct natures of things and seen them arranged in separate stations (so to speak), we should not believe the universe is made into a single whole simply because individual parts are contained by their own natural conditions, as we showed above. The prophet <note>Likely referring to Moses, the traditional author of Genesis.</note> also wished to indicate this in his own narrative: how many and what kind of ways the natures of things were coupled together. He does this not only to invite us to this scholarly understanding, but to instruct and demonstrate the path and reason by which we might be joined to those things which are better than ourselves. As I considered how many modes of connection exist or could be imagined—through which things might obtain either an affinity or a bond—and as I ran through all the doctrines of the philosophers which I have studied since childhood, no more than fifteen types occurred to me. Approaching the writings of Moses, I saw these indicated by him so clearly and so appropriately that I believe no one could be better instructed in these matters anywhere else.

## **Chapter Two.**

<margin>The essence of the thing to which it belongs</margin>
<margin>The property of the essence</margin>
<margin>Form: to the Subject</margin>
<margin>The transmuter: to the transmuted</margin>
<margin>Art: to the matter</margin>
<margin>Heaven: Earth</margin>
<margin>Earth: emptiness</margin>
<margin>Abyss: Darkness</margin>
<margin>Spirit of God: waters</margin>
<margin>Light: bodies</margin>

Immediately, then, on the first day, he encompasses five modes—I know not whether more briefly or more clearly—by which one thing can be joined to another. For that which is joined to another is either its **essence**, or it is a **property** of that essence; or it exists within it as a **form** <term>Form: in classical philosophy, the 'form' is the essence or defining characteristic that makes a thing what it is.</term> exists in a subject; or it touches it either as a **transmuter** acting upon that which is being changed, or as **art** acting upon its underlying matter. Similarly, we read in Moses five pairs, as if compared and connected: heaven and earth; earth and emptiness; the abyss and darkness; the spirit of God and the waters; light and bodies.

The first mode of connection is designated for us by the earth being "empty and void" <note>original: "terra inanis et vacua"</note>; for the earth—that is, matter—is by its own nature empty unless it is filled from elsewhere by forms. The second mode is indicated by the "darkness upon the face of the abyss." For the abyss is by its own nature neither bright nor dark; yet darkness follows its nature unless the approaching light puts it to flight. In the same way, darkness and the emptiness of privation follow the lack of form in matter until the arrival of specific forms expels them. The third mode is shown by the light arising upon bodies. For light exists in them like a form in a subject. The fourth is heaven and earth; for heaven does not inherent in the earth like a form or an <term>accident</term> <note>Accident: a quality that does not belong to the essence of a thing, like the color of a shirt.</note> exists in the thing it completes, but it is joined to it as an **efficient cause** <term>Efficient Cause: the agent or force that brings something into being or initiates change.</term> to a passive subject, and as a transforming cause to the body being transformed. The example of the last mode is the "spirit of the Lord" <note>original: "spiritus domini"</note> which "moved over the waters." For the craftsmanship of the Lord's wisdom and his spiritual nature—totally separated from the commerce of the body—is understood to be joined to bodies in no other way than art, which exists in the mind of the architect, is joined to the cement, wood, and stones.

Furthermore, consider this logic of sequence: the earth is empty of itself and possesses its own inherent darkness; then it is joined most closely to the light through light, to heaven through heaven, and to spiritual substance through the spirit. But let us see how these things behave within us. The "earth" is the earthly body, empty of life and void of sensation; over it is "darkness," which is death, torpor, powerlessness, and lack of feeling; "light" is the life which nourishes, excites, drives, moves, and fills it with sensation...

->### Chapter Three<-

Let us examine what Moses intends in the following passages: and we shall see ten other modes suggested by him, through which we may understand a mutual alliance between things. For besides those we have already mentioned, there are also these which we shall enumerate: since something is either a part of another or an effect. Likewise, if it is a part, it is either an inseparable part of its whole—in the same way that the sun, moon, and stars are in the firmament—or it is separable, just as portions of water are from the integrity of their own element, toward which they have flowed together. If it is an effect, it either buds forth from an intrinsic <term>seminal reason</term> <note>original: "seminaria ratione." This refers to the Stoic and Neoplatonic idea that God or Nature implanted "seeds" or blueprints in the physical world that allow life to develop according to a plan.</note> just as plants sprout from the earth—yet remain attached to their parent and connected by natural bonds and ligaments—or it consists of and is fashioned from its own principles, like a mixture of elements. In this way, the bodies of animals are made from water and earth; or it has an external cause, which can be divided three ways into the efficient, the exemplary, and the final <note>These are three of Aristotle's traditional "Four Causes." The efficient cause is the agent that makes something; the exemplary (or formal) is the model or pattern; the final is the purpose for which it exists.</note>. We have examples of these three from Moses: while God creates and effects man; and creates him in His own image as if according to a pattern; and the beasts are subject to man and exist for the sake of man as their end.

->### Chapter Four<-

We have spoken of the part and the effect, and by the same logic, of the whole and the cause. For these concepts correspond to one another. But we have not yet completed all the types of kinship. For regarding the cause, there remains that species of affinity in which a secondary cause obeys and is joined to the primary one. Just as when God produces, the waters produce; <margin>Primary cause</margin> and these indeed produce first because they are the immediate cause, but not otherwise than by God's command, because the primary cause has a greater influence <margin>has more influence</margin> than the secondary <margin>than the secondary.</margin>. Similarly, there is a secondary end attached and annexed to the principal one, which Moses wisely signifies by saying that the stars were placed to shine in the heavens and to illuminate the earth. For the well-being of lower things is not the primary purpose of the celestial bodies. Rather, they first intend this: that they might shine for themselves; and then finally, that they might also illuminate us. Therefore, in <margin>Homer</margin> Homer, we read that both the dawn and the sun rise and bring light first for the immortals, and then for mortals as well. Besides all these, there is also a kinship between man and man, and lion and lion; yet a lion is neither a part nor an effect of another lion if it was not sired by it. The prophet <note>Refers to Moses as the traditional author of the Pentateuch.</note> signifies this when he gathers and unites together the fish, the birds, and the beasts of the earth. There is a final type of affinity: that which stands in the middle of nature between the extremes. For man agrees with man and animal with animal because they participate in the same essence, whether specific or general. But the "medium" [the middle state] is not of the same essence as the extremes; rather, it is tempered in some way from them, so that it differs from both while communicating with both. This was indicated to us by Moses when he placed the firmament as a medium in the waters, dividing the super-celestial waters from the waters that are beneath the heavens. There he sufficiently reveals the nature of the medium, just as we have abundantly declared in the preface of the first book and the second chapter of the fifth.

If this practice most helps and suits any kind of person, it is especially useful and fitting for those who have given themselves to the study of literature and the leisure of contemplation. For such people, nothing is more necessary than to purify with integrity of life those eyes of the mind which they repeatedly turn toward divine things; they must illuminate them more abundantly with light sought from above through the support <note>literally "the rod," implying a tool or guide</note> of prayer. Thus, being always reminded of their own constant powerlessness, they may say with the Apostle: *Our sufficiency is from God.* <note>original: "sufficientia nostra ex deo est." Referring to 2 Corinthians 3:5.</note>

# Chapter six.

<margin>A deeper mystery</margin>

Let us examine again what the arrangement of the water and the earth teaches us. ### Chapter Seven.

But that greatest thing of all which the doctrine of the **firmament** <term>firmament: In biblical cosmology, the expanse or "sky" created on the second day to separate the waters above from the waters below.</term> signifies to us: where we see that the lower waters cannot be enriched by any benefit of the higher waters except by the intervention of the heaven, which is placed in the middle between them. ->**THE SEVENTH EXPOSITION ON HAPPINESS, WHICH IS ETERNAL LIFE.**<-

#### Preface to the Seventh Book.

If we have completed the levels, order, and nature of the whole world in the sixth exposition, as if in six days: it remains that in this seventh treatise, as if in the **Sabbath** of our commentary, we treat the Sabbath of the world and the rest of creatures, whose nature we established in the previous parts—that is, we shall treat their **happiness**; or (to say it more correctly) let us listen to Moses treating it as a true prophet of all future things. <margin>A double happiness</margin> 

Happiness, however (as the theologians preach), is of one kind which we can attain through nature, and another through grace. They call the former "natural" and the latter "supernatural." Enough was said about the first—that is, the natural—by Moses [in the preceding books], because once the nature of things is known, we also know their natural happiness. It remains, therefore, for the prophet to teach about the second, showing himself as a prophet rather than a teacher; for when Moses wrote, **grace** did not yet exist, but it was to come.

But since I seem to see certain dabblers—should I call them scoundrels or rather worthless fellows?—who call themselves philosophers when they are nothing of the sort: they immediately mock both grace and supernatural happiness as if these were empty names and old wives' tales. For this reason, I wanted to create a very brief disputation on this matter as a preface to the seventh book. This subject is both useful to everyone on its own and extremely necessary for the work <margin>How true and stable the theologians' opinion is regarding supernatural happiness</margin> we have undertaken; here we shall clearly prove that the opinion of the theologians stands supported and established by the deepest roots of philosophy. I define **Happiness** as follows: the return of each thing to its own principle <note>In this context, "principle" (Latin: *principium*) means the originating source or beginning from which a thing arises.</note>. For happiness is the "highest good," and the highest good is that which all things seek. However, that which all things seek is the very thing <margin>Alexander</margin> which is the principle of all things, as <term>Alexander of Aphrodisias</term> <note>A famous commentator on Aristotle who lived around 200 AD.</note> attests in his commentaries <margin>Greek interpreters</margin> on First Philosophy <note>The term used for Metaphysics.</note>, and as the Greek interpreters attest regarding Aristotle’s *Ethics*. Therefore, the same end <note>The "end" or *finis* refers to the final purpose or goal of a thing.</note> of all things is that which is the principle of all things: the one God, almighty and blessed, the best of all things that can either exist or be imagined. From this come those two primary names <margin>Pythagoreans</margin> among the Pythagoreans: **the One** and **the Good**. He is called "the One" <margin>Two names of God</margin> because He is the principle of all things, just as "unity" is the principle of all numbers; but He is called "the Good" because He is the end of all, the rest of all, and absolute happiness. We can now see, <margin>The root of twofold happiness</margin> if we are a little more observant, the reason for a twofold happiness. For happiness is the possession and attainment of this First Good. Created things can attain this Good in two ways: either in themselves, or in Him. For this Good is both exalted above all things, dwelling in the abysses of His own divinity, and found diffused through all things. In some places He is found more perfectly, in others more imperfectly, according to the condition of the things <margin>Poets</margin> by which He is shared. Whence (as the poets write): "Jupiter is whatever you see" and "all things are full of Jupiter" <note>original: "Iuppiter eſt quodcũq; uides: & Iouis omnia plena ſunt." This is a reference to Virgil and Lucan, used here to show that God's presence is everywhere in the natural world.</note>. Therefore, since every nature has God within itself in some way—because <margin>What natural happiness is</margin> it has as much of God as it has of goodness (and all things which God made are good)—it follows that when a thing has its own nature perfected in every part, having attained itself, it also attains God within itself. And if the attainment of God is (as we have proven) happiness, then in some way it is happy in itself. This is **natural happiness**, which different things have been allotted, greater or lesser, according to the diversity of their natures. Fire is a thing lacking a soul, yet <margin>How fire participates in God</margin> it participates in God in many ways. For first, it *is*, and each thing that *is* participates in God, who is Being itself. Likewise, because fire has a certain "form" and "act" <note>In scholastic philosophy, "form" gives a thing its identity, and "act" is its state of being or operation.</note>, it is similar to God, who is the first form and the first act. And while fire produces fire, it imitates the divine fecundity; while it keeps itself within the boundaries of its own sphere, it imitates justice; while it serves us, it imitates beneficence according to the small measure of its nature. When fire acts having attained its own perfection, it is happy as far as it is capable of happiness. Plants are happier, for they possess life in addition; animals are happier still, having been allotted cognition as well. As they find more perfection, so they find more of the divinity within themselves. **Man is in the best condition of all mortals**, <margin>Man is in the best condition of all mortals</margin> who, just as in nature, so in natural happiness excels the others; he is endowed with intelligence and freedom of will, which are the primary gifts and most conducive to happiness. Supreme among creatures is the **angelic mind**, both in the nobility of its substance and in the attainment of its end, of which it participates most greatly because it is both joined and closest to Him. Truly, as we said above, through this happiness neither plants, nor beasts, nor man, nor angel reach God—who is the highest good—in God himself, but only in themselves. <margin>The imperfection of natural happiness; the opinion of the philosophers on happiness</margin> Therefore, according to the capacity of their various natures, the logic of happiness varies by degrees. For this reason, the philosophers, speaking only of this natural kind, placed the happiness of each thing in the "best operation" of its own nature. 

Regarding the angels, whom they call minds and intellects: even if these philosophers admitted that the angels' highest perfection was to understand God, they nevertheless established no other knowledge of God for them than that by which they know themselves. Thus, they understand only as much of God as the nature of God is represented within their own substance. 

Concerning man, although various thinkers have held various views, they all kept themselves within the narrow limits of human faculty. They defined human happiness either in the search for truth itself—as did the <term>Academics</term> <note>The "Academics" refers to the followers of the later Platonic Academy, often associated with skepticism and the belief that absolute truth is difficult to grasp.</note>—or rather in its attainment through the study of philosophy, as <term>Al-Farabi</term> <note>A renowned 9th-10th century Islamic philosopher who integrated Aristotelian and Platonic thought.</note> said. <margin>Academics, Al-Farabi, Averroes, Avicenna, Ibn Bajja, Alexander, Platonists</margin> Averroes, Avicenna, <term>Abubacher</term> <note>Likely referring to Ibn Bajja, an Andalusian philosopher known in Latin as Avempace or Abubacher.</note>, <term>Alexander</term> <note>Likely Alexander of Aphrodisias, a major commentator on Aristotle.</note>, and the Platonists seemed to grant something more, anchoring our reason in the <term>Active Intellect</term> <note>original: "intellectu qui actu est." In medieval philosophy, this was the "higher" mind that allows humans to think abstractly.</note>—or some superior power related to us—as if that were our ultimate goal. Yet not even these thinkers lead man back to his own origin nor to the highest good.

I neither reject nor despise these arguments and opinions of theirs, provided they profess to speak only of *natural* happiness. For it is certain that through such means, neither man nor angels can be raised higher than what these philosophers describe. <margin>Man cannot be joined to God by his own powers</margin> This is best proven by this reasoning: since nothing relying on its own strength can rise above itself (otherwise it would be stronger than itself), certainly nothing striving by itself toward happiness will be able to attain anything greater or more perfect than its own nature. 

But let the philosophers tell me: if this is the only happiness found in things, why do even they admit that among all animals, only man is born for happiness? <margin>He establishes supernatural happiness</margin> Since creatures other than man also reach their own natural ends, we could say that the happiness of others is lesser than that of man; but how shall we defend the idea that they have *no* happiness at all? Nay, since other creatures below man never deviate from the end established for them by nature, while man almost always goes astray, the human condition would seem the most unhappy of all, unless man can boast of some other privilege. 

Let us therefore listen to the holy <margin>Theologians</margin> theologians reminding us of our dignity, and the divine gifts freely offered to us by a most generous Father. Let us not, I pray, be cruel to our own souls and ungrateful toward God the Creator by rejecting them. 

We said above that the height of happiness lies in the attainment of God, who is the highest good and the source of all things. <margin>What the difference is between supernatural and natural happiness</margin> This can happen in two ways: either we reach God in His creatures (in which God shares Himself), or we reach God in God Himself. We have shown—and will show—that created things cannot by their own powers reach this latter state, but only the former. 

If we pay attention, that natural happiness is a shadow of happiness rather than true happiness, <margin>Natural happiness does not have the character of true happiness</margin> just as the creature in which you reach God is not the highest goodness, but only a thin shadow of divine goodness. Furthermore, through natural happiness, things are restored to themselves rather than to God; they have not achieved a return to their origin, but only succeeded in not departing from their own nature. 

But true and perfected happiness carries us back and leads us to gaze upon the face of God—which is all good, as He Himself said—and to a perfect union with that Source from which we flowed. To this, the angels...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of happiness, distinguishing between the natural drive of physical elements and the supernatural grace required for humans and angels to return to God.</meta>

<margin>Who are capable of supernatural happiness and how</margin>
...they can indeed be lifted up, but they cannot ascend <note>meaning, they cannot climb by their own natural power</note>. This is why Lucifer sinned, saying: *I will ascend into heaven.* <note>original: "Ascendam in caelum"</note>. Man cannot reach this happiness on his own; he can only be drawn to it. This is why Christ said of himself—being happiness itself—*No one comes to me unless my Father has drawn him.* <note>John 6:44; original: "Nemo uenit ad me niſi pater meus traxerit illum"</note>. However, brute animals and those things lower than man can neither go to it nor be drawn to it. Therefore, only man and the angel were created for that happiness, which is the true happiness.

<margin>An example of both kinds of happiness in physical bodies</margin>
A vapor can rise high, but only if it is pulled by the sun’s ray; a stone or any heavy, solid substance can neither receive the ray fully nor be lifted into the heights by it. We call this ray, this divine power, this internal flow, **grace** <note>original: "gratiam"</note>, because it makes both man and angel pleasing to God. Philosophers have a clear example of this teaching in physical bodies. Some bodies move in a straight line, while others move in a circle. Straight motion—by which the <term>elements|The four basic substances of the ancient world: earth, water, air, and fire</term> are carried to their proper places—symbolizes the happiness by which things are stabilized in the perfection of their own nature. Circular motion—by which a body revolves back to the same point from which it started—is the most perfect image of true happiness, through which a creature returns to the same Beginning from which it first came. 

But see how everything fits together on both sides. Only immortal and incorruptible bodies move in a circle. Only an immortal and eternal substance returns to God. To complete their movements, the elements require no force other than the natural drive—whether the weight of heaviness or the lightness of levity—implanted in them from their birth. In the same way, individual things are carried toward their **natural happiness** by their own drive and their own power. But even though the heavenly bodies are suited for circular motion, they are not sufficient in themselves to complete this movement; rather, they need a **divine Mover** <note>In the science of the time, God was the "Prime Mover" who kept the stars and planets in their circular orbits</note> to turn them and guide their revolution. Finally, those bodies are perpetually fit for circling in such a way that they do not *create* the motion, but rather *receive* it. 

It is no different for us and the angels. By nature, we are of such a kind that we cannot turn ourselves or reflect ourselves back <note>toward our divine origin</note>; instead, we can be turned by the moving power of grace and reflected back into God. From this comes the saying: *Those who are led by the spirit of God, these are the sons of God.* <note>Romans 8:14; original: "qui aguntur ſpiritu dei hii filii dei ſunt"</note>. Note that he said *those who are led*, not *those who lead*. We differ from the heavens in this: they move by the necessity of nature, but we move by our own freedom. For the Spirit-Mover constantly knocks at your soul. If you ignore it, you are left to yourself—to your own sluggishness and weakness, miserable and unhappy. But if you admit it, you are immediately filled with God and carried back through the circle of <term>religion|Derived from the Latin 'religare', to bind back or reconnect to the source</term> to the Father and the Lord. There, you will possess life forever—the same life you already were, even before you were created. 

<margin>The height of true happiness</margin>
<margin>Christ</margin>
<margin>Paul</margin>
This is true happiness: that we may be one spirit with God; that we may possess God in God's presence, not in ourselves, knowing just as we are known. For He knew us not through us, but through Himself; likewise, we shall know Him through Himself and not through ourselves. This is the whole reward; this is eternal life; this is the wisdom that the "wise of this world" did not know: that we may be brought back from all the imperfection of the many into unity, through an unbreakable bond with Him who is **Oneness** itself. For this happiness, Christ prayed to the Father in this way: *Father, grant that just as I and You are one, so also they may be one with us.* <note>Refers to the prayer in John 17</note>. Paul hoped for this, saying: *I shall know, not in part, but even as He is.* <note>1 Corinthians 13:12</note>. And since he hoped for it, did he not rightly say: *Who shall separate me from the love of Christ?* <note>Romans 8:35</note>. He desired to be dissolved so that he might become one with Christ.

## Chapter Six

From this, the solution to the question that has long tormented interpreters of this book is manifest: **Why on the second day was it not said: "And God saw that it was good"**? <margin>Why on the second day it was not said that it was good</margin> 

If we say what is usually said—that it happened because the work of the waters was not finished on that day, but only on the third day when the waters under the heaven flowed together into one place—the answer will seem hardly sufficient. For the proper work of the second day is not the arrangement of the waters, but the arrangement of the **firmament**, which was fixed in the middle place between the waters. On that day there was both the making of the firmament—when God said "Let there be a firmament"—and the distinction of the waters—when He said "And let it divide the waters from the waters"—which were both quite complete. 

The collection of the waters called the "sea," the revealing of the dry land, and the production of plants belong to an entirely different work; just as they were completed on another day (the third) to which they belonged. Therefore, a reason must be sought from a deeper mystery. The **firmament** (as we showed above) figures the Law <note>The Mosaic Law or the Old Testament.</note>. And the firmament was, like something unformed, not simply perfect until it was furnished with the sun, moon, and stars. It is the firm opinion of all the ancients—which they confirm with one voice as beyond doubt—that the complete knowledge of all arts and of all wisdom, both divine and human, is included in the five books of the Mosaic Law. They believe this knowledge is disguised and concealed within the very letters with which the words of the Law are woven, in a manner we shall now declare. 

<margin>A paradoxical doctrine of the ancient Hebrews</margin>

Let us take, for example, the first small part of the book of Genesis: specifically from the beginning up to the place where it is written, *And God saw the light, that it was good.* That entire passage is joined together from one hundred and three elements <note>The author uses "elements" to refer to individual letters of the alphabet</note>. When these are arranged in the way they appear there, they constitute the words we read, which offer nothing but common and trivial matters. This order of letters constitutes the **rind** <note>original: "cortex"; a common metaphor in mysticism for the literal or outer meaning of a text</note> of the text, while the **marrow** of hidden mysteries lies hidden within.

<margin><unclear>unclear</unclear></margin>

If this were done throughout the entire Law, then finally, from this rightly established position and connection of the elements, all learning and the secrets of all liberal disciplines could be brought to light. 

I said, however, "if we are capable of receiving this enclosed wisdom." For we cannot *learn* doctrines and teachings there for the first time; we can only *recognize* them. 

As for me, I do not assert or attest to these things as if I "prove" them, for I have neither put them to the test, nor do I trust that I am able to do so. ...we arrange: it becomes **Sabbath** <note>original: "שבת" (Shabbat), transcribed as "sciabat"</note>. If we set the first three letters in the order they lie: it becomes **He created** <note>original: "ברא" (Bara)</note>. If the first is omitted and the next three taken: it becomes **Head** <note>original: "ראש" (Rosh), transcribed as "rosc"</note>. If, omitting the first three, we join the fourth to the last: it becomes **Foundation** <note>original: "שת" (Sheth), transcribed as "seth"</note>. Again, if we join the second to the first: it becomes **Great** <note>original: "רב" (Rab)</note>. If the last is joined to the first: it becomes the last and twelfth word, which is **Good** <note>original: "טוב" (Tov), transcribed as "thob"</note>, by changing the letter *thau* <note>the Hebrew letter ת</note> into *thet* <note>the Hebrew letter ט</note>, a substitution which is most frequent among the Hebrews. 

Let us see now what these words mean first in Latin <note>the scholar's language of the time</note>, and then what mysteries concerning all of nature may be revealed through them to those not ignorant of philosophy. **Ab** signifies *Father*. **Bar** signifies *in the Son* and *through the Son* (for the preposition *Beth* signifies both). **Reshit** signifies *Beginning*. **Shabbat** signifies *rest* and *the end*. **Bara** signifies *He created*. **Rosh** signifies *head*. **Esh** signifies *fire*. **Sheth** signifies *foundation*. **Rab** signifies *of the great*. **Ish** signifies *of the man*. **Berith** signifies *by a covenant*. **Tov** signifies *by the good*. 

And if we weave the whole speech together in the following order, it will be of this kind: **"The Father, in the Son and through the Son, created the beginning and the end (or rest), the head, the fire, and the foundation of the Great Man, by a good covenant."** This entire sentence results from the breaking down and re-composing of that first word <note>"Bereshit"</note>. How deep and full of all doctrine this meaning is cannot be obvious to everyone. But let some things be immediately open, though not all things are for everyone, which are signified to us through these words. It is known to all Christians what it means for the Father to have created *in the Son and through the Son*. Likewise, it is known that the Son is the *beginning and the end* of all things: for He is the **Alpha and Omega** 

<margin>John</margin>

(as **John** writes) and He called Himself the **Beginning**; and we have demonstrated that He is the **End** of all things, so that all may be restored to their source. 

Other things are a little more obscure: namely, what those terms *head*, *fire*, and *foundation of the Great Man* mean; what that *covenant* is, and for what reason it is called *good*. For it is not immediately easy for everyone to see explained here the whole nature of the **four worlds** <term>the four levels of existence in Kabbalistic thought: Atziluth (Emanation), Beriah (Creation), Yetzirah (Formation), and Assiah (Action)</term> of which we are treating, as well as their kinship and happiness, about which we have recently disputed. 

First, therefore, it should be noted that the **World** is called a **Great Man** by Moses. For if man is a *small world* <term>the microcosm</term>, then certainly the world is a *great man* <term>the macrocosm</term>. Taking this opportunity, he most aptly represents the three worlds—the intellectual, the celestial, and the corruptible—through the three parts of a man. In this figure, he indicates not only that all worlds are contained within man, but also briefly declares which part of man corresponds to which world.

<margin>Which part in man corresponds to which world</margin>

Let us therefore consider three parts in man: first the supreme part, the **head**; then that which extends from the neck to the navel; and thirdly, that which extends from the navel to the feet. For these are also distinguished and separated in the figure of man by a certain variety. But it is wonderful how beautifully and precisely, by the most exact reasoning, these correspond in proportion to the three parts of the world. 

<margin>Knowledge, Motion, Generation</margin>

->GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA SENDS GREETINGS TO LORENZO DE' MEDICI<- <note>The original Latin abbreviation "S." stands for *Salutem*, a formal greeting wishing health/salvation.</note>

I have dedicated my **Apology** <note>The *Apologia* was Pico's defense of thirteen of his nine hundred theses which had been challenged by a papal commission.</note> to you, Lorenzo de' Medici, not because (I call God to witness) it seems to me a work worthy of such a great man, but because it is owed to you by that right by which I realize I have long owed all that is mine to you. I say less than I would wish, and these words are altogether colder than to sufficiently express what I feel—that is: with what love, what loyalty, and what respect I follow you, and for many years now have followed you. I am moved both by the many favors conferred upon me which clearly testify to your most loving spirit, and by your own [virtues], which belong not so much to fortune as to the soul; those same rare, or rather unique qualities, which your own modesty does not allow me to recount at present. 

I return to the *Apology*: I pray that you may receive it with a cheerful countenance. It is a small gift indeed, but truly a significant testimony of my loyalty and respect toward you for all time. I did not dedicate it to you so that you might recognize in me an excellence of talent or learning that I do not possess, but so that I might know—for I will say it again—that whatever I am, I am most devoted to your greatness.

### THE APOLOGY OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA, COUNT OF CONCORDIA. <note>Concordia was the small principality ruled by Pico's family.</note>

**W**hen I had recently come to Rome, I kissed the feet of the Supreme Pontiff Innocent VIII <margin>Innocent VIII, Supreme Pontiff</margin> <note>Pope Innocent VIII (reigned 1484–1492) initially supported Pico but later suspended the debate after a commission found several theses heretical.</note>—to whom the name "Innocent" is most deservedly given from the innocence of his life—according to the custom, as if kissing the feet of God. So that I might not depart from my usual practice of always studying and handling something concerning literary matters, and to do something worthy of the city of Rome according to my strength—something pleasing to a Christian prince and useful to myself and to students—I proposed nine hundred questions on divine and natural things. These I was prepared to answer in a public assembly of most learned men. 

Hardly had they come into public view when, among some who might approve of my talent or learning, or at least my devotion to the liberal arts <term>bonarum artium: literally "the good arts," referring to the humanities and philosophy</term>, a manifold crowd of detractors arose. And although the distastes, the upturned noses, the censures, and the overall judgments of each person were varied to see (as always happens when we attempt something new and non-trivial), there were about five principal points that these whisperers, one after another, condemned in me. 

For some altogether disparage philosophy and letters, doing so even so that they might seem like "know-it-alls" <term>scioli: people who have a superficial smattering of knowledge</term>. Sometimes they add that Adam was cast out of paradise because, through the knowledge of good and evil, he wished to make himself equal to the gods. They argue that, by a similar example, those who wish to know more than is fitting should be exterminated from the court of Christ. Others do not so much disapprove of philosophy as this very type of disputation and this institution of publicly debating on letters, [viewing it] rather as a display...

...barking that these things were offered more for a display of talent and learning than for the purpose of acquiring knowledge. Some called me bold and reckless because at this age—not yet having reached my twenty-fourth year—I did not hesitate to propose a debate in that most famous city <note>Rome</note>, before a most grand assembly of the most learned men, concerning the highest reaches of philosophy, the sublime mysteries of Christian theology, and unknown branches of study. Many accused me of acting superfluously, ambitiously, and beyond my strength—calumniating me not only for doing this in Rome, and as a youth, but for intending to dispute such a great number, namely nine hundred, questions <note>original: "nōgentis... q̃ōnibus"; these are Pico's famous 900 Theses</note>. Among those who professed the study of wisdom—that is, the study of theology—there were some who, not content with perhaps lighter insults, proclaimed me to be not merely bold, nor reckless, nor boastful, but a magician, an impious man, and a new leader of heresy <term>heresiarch</term> <note>A "heresiarch" is the founder or leader of a heretical movement or sect.</note> within the Church of Christ. 

I call God to witness that I deliberated for a long time whether I should wash away these accusations or whether they should instead be passed over in silence. Two things in particular moved me to remain silent. First, because I always abhor contention and strife, I have always loved the peace of the mind and the tranquility of a most placid life, which my studies have provided for me; nor have I hated any task of writing more than that which is established in dispute and bitter altercation of any kind—for I have never judged it to be the mark of a good man or a philosopher to return an injury or an insult, any more than to inflict one. The second reason was this: I felt I could easily ignore the hatred and the insults of wicked men, being content with the judgment of the Supreme Pontiff <note>Pope Innocent VIII</note>—whose memory I must always rightfully celebrate—and of many in the most holy Apostolic Senate <note>The College of Cardinals</note>, whose kindness and most benevolent spirit toward me I can and should never forget. Indeed, regarding all other matters, I was of the opinion that those critics were unworthy of a response. 

But regarding the one charge of the crime of heresy leveled against me, I feared that if I did so <note>remained silent</note>, I would seem to acknowledge a crime that I did not wash away. For Rufinus <note>A 4th-century monk and theologian</note> writes most wisely that it is indeed glorious to endure injuries patiently after the example of Christ, but he who bears or ignores a mark of heresy is not a Christian. And our Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Bible into Latin</note> exclaims with the greatest possible effort of mind and in a most clear voice: "I do not want anyone to be patient under suspicion of heresy." Jerome, therefore, does not want me to be silent; by all the authority he possesses, he draws and impels even an unwilling and idle man to write. Therefore, if there are any who perhaps wish me to be silent, let them know that their controversy is not with me, but with Jerome, who wishes me not to be silent. Who can fail to listen to Jerome without disgrace? 

Therefore, with him persuading—indeed, even compelling me—I have set out to write a brief <term>Apologia</term> <note>In this context, a formal written defense of one's opinions or conduct.</note>. I do this not to tear into or accuse anyone, but so that I may rightly clear myself of the great crime of impiety that is unjustly charged against me. I beg my detractors to endure this with the same spirit with which I have always endured their unfair offense. Let them endure, I say, that I—who am a Christian born of Christian parents, who bears the standard of Jesus Christ on my forehead, and who would even gladly die for the faith of Christ—should exclaim as if with Paul, while they listen with an even mind: "I am no magician, no Jew, no Ishmaelite <note>A term used in the Renaissance to refer to Muslims.</note>, no heretic; but I worship Jesus, and I carry the cross of Jesus in my body, through whom the world is crucified to me, and I to the world" <note>original: "per quem mihi mundus crucifixus est & ego mundo"; a reference to Galatians 6:14.</note>. Finally, since I have never claimed for myself the distinguished titles of holiness or wisdom, or anything of that kind...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's defense of his upcoming public debate. In the previous section, he likely introduced the idea of a philosophical tournament. ...for this kind of combat—that is, literary combat—is unique in that there is profit in being defeated. Thus it happens that even the weakest person not only can, but rightfully should, desire these contests rather than avoid them. For he who yields receives a benefit from the victor, not an injury; indeed, through the victor, he returns home wealthier—meaning more learned—and better prepared for future battles. 

Inspired by this hope, I, a weak soldier, have not feared to undertake such a serious battle against the strongest and most vigorous of men. Whether this was done rashly or not should be judged by the outcome of the battle rather than by my youth <note>Pico was only 23 years old when he proposed these debates.</note>. It remains for me to respond to those who are offended by the vast number of propositions I have put forward, as if this burden rested on their shoulders and not rather on me alone, who must endure whatever labor is involved. 

It is certainly unseemly and overly <margin>Cicero</margin> irritable to wish to set limits on someone else's industry, and, as **Cicero** says, to desire moderation in a matter that is better the larger it becomes. In such a grand undertaking, it was inevitable that I would either fail or succeed. If I succeeded, I do not see why performing well in ten questions should be praiseworthy, while performing well in nine hundred <note>Pico’s famous "900 Theses," which he intended to defend in Rome in 1487.</note> should be considered blameworthy. If I failed, those who hate me would have cause to accuse me, and those who love me would have cause to excuse me. Since in a matter so serious and grand, it is more fitting to grant pardon than accusation to a young man who failed due to limited talent and little learning. Indeed, as the poet says: if strength fails, there will certainly be praise for the daring, and **in great things, to have willed is enough.** 

If in our own age many have imitated <margin>Gorgias of Leontini</margin> **Gorgias of Leontini** <note>A Greek Sophist known for claiming he could speak on any subject.</note> and have been accustomed—not without praise—to propose debates not just on nine hundred questions, but on every question regarding all the arts, why should I not be allowed, at least without blame, to dispute many questions, but ones that are certain and defined? 

But they say this is "superfluous" and "ambitious." I, however, contend that this was done not only out of necessity but that they themselves, if they consider my method of philosophizing, must clearly admit it, even if unwillingly. For those who have devoted themselves to one of the <margin>Thomas, Scotus</margin> schools of philosophers—for example, to **Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas, the heavyweight of Dominican theology.</note> or **Scotus** <note>John Duns Scotus, the influential Franciscan philosopher.</note> who are now most widely read—can certainly test their learning in the discussion of only a few questions.

Therefore, since I had to speak on all of them, lest by being a defender of a single private doctrine I appeared bound to it and neglected the rest, the total number of points brought forward could not help but be very many, even if only a few things were proposed about each school. Nor should anyone condemn me for "being carried as a guest wherever the storm takes me." <meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s defense of his nine hundred theses, specifically addressing his methodology of "syncretism"—the reconciliation of seemingly opposing philosophical schools—and his introduction of "mathematical philosophy."</meta>

Just as a husband hates barrenness in a wife, surely so much more will the divine mind—joined and associated with the soul for so long—hate an unfruitful soul, insofar as a far more noble offspring is desired from that union. Therefore, not content with common doctrines alone, I have proposed for dispute much from the **Ancient Theology** <term>Prisca Theologia: The idea that a single, true theology exists which threads through all ancient religions, given by God to humanity in antiquity</term> of **Hermes Trismegistus**, much from the teachings of the **Chaldeans** and **Pythagoras**, and many things added from the more secret mysteries of the **Hebrews**. I have also proposed many things discovered and meditated upon by us concerning natural and divine matters. 

<margin>The harmony of Plato and Aristotle</margin>
We have proposed, first, the harmony of **Plato** and **Aristotle**, which has been believed by many before now but proved sufficiently by no one. Among the Latins, **Boethius** <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher who intended to reconcile the two Greeks but died before finishing the work</note> promised he would do this, but he is never found to have actually done what he always wished to do. 

<margin>Simplicius</margin>
Among the Greeks, **Simplicius** <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist commentator</note> professed the same; would that he had proved as capable as he was promising! 

<margin>Augustine</margin>
**Augustine** also writes in his *Against the Academics* that there were several who attempted to prove the same with their most subtle disputations: namely, that the philosophy of Plato and Aristotle is one and the same. 

<margin>John the Grammarian</margin>
Likewise, **John the Grammarian** <note>John Philoponus, a Christian philosopher and scientist in Alexandria</note>, although he says that only those who do not understand Plato’s words think Plato differs from Aristotle, nevertheless left the proof of this to posterity. 

<margin>Note</margin>
Furthermore, we have added several passages in which we assert that the opinions of **Duns Scotus** and **Thomas Aquinas**, as well as those of **Averroes** and **Avicenna** <note>Key figures of Scholasticism and Islamic philosophy respectively</note>, which are considered discordant, are in fact in agreement. 

<margin>New dogmas devised</margin>
In the second place, we have arranged seventy-two new physical and metaphysical dogmas which we ourselves devised within both Aristotelian and Platonic philosophy. If anyone holds to these, they will be able—unless I am mistaken—to resolve any question proposed concerning natural or divine things by a logic far different than that taught to us in the schools and cultivated by the doctors of this age. 

<margin>Note</margin>
Nor should anyone wonder that I, in my early years and tender age—during which it was hardly permitted, as some boast, to read the commentaries of others—should wish to bring forth a new philosophy, rather than simply praising it if it is defended or condemning it if it is rejected. Finally, since these discoveries are ours and belong to our own study, it is for the judges to weigh not the years of the author, but rather the merits or demerits of the works themselves.

<margin>A new institution of philosophizing through numbers</margin>
However, besides that, there is another new method of philosophizing through numbers which we have introduced. 

<margin>Plato</margin>
This is indeed ancient, observed by the earliest theologians—especially by **Pythagoras**, **Aglaophemus**, **Philolaus**, **Plato**, and the earlier **Platonists**. But in this age, like many other noble things, it has grown so obsolete through the neglect of those who followed that hardly any traces of it can be found. 

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
**Plato** writes in the *Epinomis* <note>A dialogue attributed to Plato or his pupil Philip of Opus</note> that among all the liberal arts and contemplative sciences, the most chief and divine is the science of numbering. Likewise, seeking the reason why man is the wisest animal, he answers: "because he knows how to count."

<margin>Note</margin>

...to make public the hidden secrets of the most profound divinity. He decreed that the wise men who then survived should be called together, and each should bring forward what he remembered about the mysteries of the Law. Scribes were employed to compile seventy volumes (for there were approximately that many wise men in the Sanhedrin). Those who do not believe me on this matter should hear Ezra himself speaking: <margin>Ezra</margin> "After forty days had passed, the Most High spoke, saying: 'The first things you wrote, place in public; let the worthy and unworthy alike read them. But the last seventy books you shall keep, to hand them over to the wise among your people. For in these is the vein of understanding, the fountain of wisdom, and the river of knowledge.' And so I did." 

These are Ezra's words, verbatim. These are the books of the science of the Kabbalah, in which Ezra rightly proclaimed with a clear voice that there was a "vein of understanding" (that is, an ineffable theology regarding the substantive deity), a "fountain of wisdom" (that is, an exact metaphysics regarding intelligible and angelic forms), and a "river of knowledge" (that is, a most firm philosophy regarding natural things). These books Pope Sixtus IV <margin>Sixtus IV</margin>—the Supreme Pontiff who immediately preceded Innocent VIII, under whom we now happily live— <margin>Innocent VIII</margin> ordered to be translated into Latin for the public benefit of our faith.

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's defense of his "900 Theses," specifically addressing the formal structure of his debate and beginning his point-by-point refutation of the charges of heresy. It follows his introductory remarks about his intentions and the nature of his intellectual project.</meta>

I could have condensed the chapters of this debate. If I had wanted to divide it into its individual members and tear it apart, as others are accustomed to doing, the number would have surely grown to an infinite count. And to say nothing of the rest, who is there who does not know that a single dogma out of the **nine hundred questions** <note>original: "nōgētis q̃. s̄." referring to Pico’s famous 900 Theses</note>—specifically the one concerning the reconciliation of the philosophies of **Plato and Aristotle**—could have been drawn out by me into six hundred chapters (not to say more) without any suspicion of trying to inflate the numbers? I could have done this by enumerating one by one every point in which others think they disagree, but I believe they agree. 

But why do I linger longer on these things? Why do I not rather come to the point for which this entire work was undertaken: to prove as clearly as light, and beyond all controversy, that not only am I not impious, but that those men are impious and heretical who do not blush to say that I am or have been a heretic? I shall do this not with insults and abuse, but by bringing into the open the facts and reasons themselves: what I have said, what I have written, and what I have felt. Likewise, let us see what those men have said and felt. 

These matters will then be examined by other learned and distinguished men in both our own and foreign Universities. The **Holy See** <margin>The Holy See. Innocent.</margin> will judge, as will **Innocent VIII** <note>Giovanni Battista Cibo, Pope from 1484–1492, who initially suspended Pico's debate and formed the commission that condemned the theses.</note> who sits upon it. To neglect or violate his judgment is an abomination and a crime. He is the supreme judge on earth, representing Him who is the judge of the living and the dead. He is the storehouse and the secret cabinet of truth, acting in the place of Him who is Truth itself, who was made flesh and dwelt among us to announce the truth to us.

But now let us descend to examining the questions themselves which those masters condemned as if they were heretical. In doing this, my way of speaking must change. For I must hold discourse with <term>barbarians</term> <note>Pico uses "barbarians" to refer to the Scholastic theologians who used technical, often "clunky" Medieval Latin, as opposed to the elegant Classical Latin of the Humanists.</note>, and as the witty proverb says: <margin>A witty proverb.</margin> "stutterers understand only stutterers."

->### FIRST QUESTION CONCERNING THE DESCENT OF CHRIST INTO HELL.<-

The **FIRST** conclusion from those proposed by me in my debate, which those men condemned, was this: **"Christ did not truly and in terms of real presence descend into hell as [Saint] Thomas and the common path posit, but only in terms of effect."** <note>original: "quo ad effectum." Pico argues that Christ’s soul didn’t physically travel to the underworld, but his power/divinity achieved the salvation of the souls there.</note>

Regarding this conclusion, I first wish to <margin>How he proceeds to clarify the conclusion.</margin> declare my meaning and what my mind and opinion are concerning the manner of Christ’s descent. It was my intention to explain this in the proposed conclusion and to show it to be not only Catholic and believed and approved by many Catholic doctors, but also far more probable than its opposite. 

**Secondly**, I will declare how even the proposition itself, by the virtue of its speech and according to the force of its words, is in no way to be judged heretical or even simply "tasting of heresy" by learned men. 

**Thirdly**, I will declare that they themselves err in the faith if they persist in the opinion that I cannot defend my conclusion from heresy, even in the sense permitted by the force of the words. 

**Fourthly** and lastly, I will show in abundance that they can in no way excuse themselves for the fact that their condemnation was made without due consideration. 

But before I explain the manner in which I hold that Christ descended into hell, I wish to premise this: although we are bound to believe explicitly and in particular that Christ descended into hell as an **article of faith** handed down and promulgated to us by **Philip** <note>The Apostles' Creed was traditionally believed to have been composed by the twelve apostles, with each contributing one article. The descent into hell was attributed to St. Philip.</note>, such that even a protestation like mine would not save a person who...

<meta>This page continues the theological investigation into how Christ's soul descended into hell and the nature of how spiritual beings occupy space.</meta>

...granted that it does not belong to it to be placed or moved locally except by reason of its action. Therefore, I say that to have descended into hell, or to have been in hell locally, does not seem to have belonged to Christ except by reason of his action <note>The author is arguing that Christ's presence in the underworld was defined by what he did there, rather than a physical body taking up space.</note>, so that although the soul of Christ was truly and essentially in hell, his substance itself was not the reason for his presence, but only his action. 

To understand these words more fully, it must be noted that there are two opinions <margin>Two opinions of those who posit that separated substances are in a place through a passing action.</margin> among those who claim that separated substances <note>Spiritual beings like angels or souls that are not currently joined to a physical body.</note> are in a place only through a "passing action" <note>An action directed toward something else.</note>. 

Some say that to incorporeal <note>Non-physical or spiritual.</note> substances, by reason of their substance, a place is in no way owed—just as such a substance is truly never "white" or "black." Thus, according to them, it can reasonably be said that such a substance is not in a place and is nowhere, just as it is truly said to be neither hot nor cold. 

As for the authorities of Scripture <margin>Gregory of Nyssa</margin> <margin>First opinion</margin> that seem to give a place to angels when they say they are in heaven, or sent to this or that place, they are to be understood in this way: not that the angels are actually "here" or "there"—since they are not properly in a place—but that they act here or there, or begin to act where they did not act before. These thinkers rely heavily on the words of Gregory of Nyssa <note>A 4th-century Christian theologian and philosopher.</note> who says that when we ought to say a spirit *acts* here, we use language loosely and say it *is* here. Thus, this opinion holds that the substance of an angel or a separated soul can never be called "present" to this or that place, except in a negative sense (meaning it is "not distant"). 

But if it is ever said to be or to have been somewhere, that is the same as saying it acted or had acted somewhere. They add that this way of speaking is borrowed from physical things; because we see that physical things cannot act unless they are present (at least according to common opinion), we conclude the same for incorporeal things—believing that wherever they act and wherever their action is found, there also is their substance locally present. 

They conclude finally that it is a lack of mental sophistication and a failure of imagination to be unable to understand that something can be a real being and yet not be in a physical place. They argue it is a frivolous argument to say that "being" must come before "acting," for while that statement is true in the sense that a non-existent thing cannot act (for an agent must be in a state of actuality), it is not true in the sense that acting in a place requires being in a place. It is possible for an actor to be of such a nature that local presence or distance is no more applicable to it than whiteness or blackness. 

Therefore, those of this opinion would say that the soul of Christ, while separated from his body, was neither in hell nor outside of hell according to its substance, but was truly nowhere. It is said to have been in hell because it acted in hell; and it is said to have been most principally in that part of hell where it most principally acted. 

Although many learned doctors hold this opinion regarding the mode of being present in a place, I do not hold it, nor have I followed it in my conclusion. Instead, I held the one I will immediately subjoin. 

There is, therefore, another opinion <margin>The second opinion, which the author held</margin> which says that a separated substance, such as an angel or a soul not united to a body, is indeed truly in a place. It is "definitively" <note>Term: <term>definitively present</term>; in Scholastic philosophy, this means a spirit is in a place because its power is focused there, even if it has no physical size.</note> present locally just as a physical thing is "commensuratively" <note>Term: <term>commensuratively present</term>; this describes how a physical body occupies a space that exactly matches its own dimensions.</note> present locally. In this regard, this path agrees with the common view of Scotus and all the Scotists <note>Followers of John Duns Scotus, a major medieval philosopher.</note>. 

But they differ in this: <margin>The difference between this opinion and the opinion of the Scotists</margin> the Scotists say that the limitation of the essence and the final internal determination of the substance is the reason for the separated substance being in a place. However, this opinion which I have followed in my conclusion says that although a physical substance is commensuratively in a place, the reason for its being so is not its "substantiality," but its quantity, which is an external factor...
