<meta>This page continues the author's defense of his theological propositions, specifically addressing how an incorporeal soul can be said to exist in a physical location like Hell.</meta>

...external to the reasoning of its substance. Thus, even though an incorporeal substance <note>such as a soul or an angel</note> truly exists in a place "definitively" <term>definitively: a technical term meaning the entity is present within certain limits of a place, but without occupying physical volume like a body does</term> and is locally present, nevertheless the reason for its being in that place is not its own substance, but rather its operation <note>original: "operatio"; here meaning the soul's action or influence</note> passing from it to the outside.

<margin>Declaration of the opinion</margin>
I judge that this opinion should be understood in this way, and so understood, I judge it not only to be non-heretical, but even more probable than its opposite. This is because, even if the finiteness or limitation of a separate nature <note>a "separate nature" refers to a soul separated from the body</note> is the reason why it is not everywhere at once, or the reason why if it is in one place it is not simultaneously in another as a whole, it is still not the reason for its existence simply within the place of the substance itself. Rather, it is there by its effect or operation—taking "operation" to mean every relationship toward a body or a place that functions by way of active or passive action, distinct from the relationship of being physically present in a location. I understand this as a matter of fact, without denying other possible modes of descent or location for the separate soul (as I say in the following conclusion), though such modes remain unknown to us.

Having followed this opinion in my conclusion, I say that **Christ was in Hell only through His effect**, because he was not there except according to his soul. Following this opinion, it must be said that just as it is not appropriate for a physical substance to be anywhere "commensuratively" <term>commensuratively: occupying a space that exactly matches the physical dimensions of the object</term> except through its physical bulk, so it was not appropriate for that soul to be in Hell (where it is believed to have been) except through effect and operation.

But just as the reason for the presence of the souls of the Holy Fathers <note>the "Holy Fathers" refers to the righteous people who died before Christ, believed to be waiting in the "Limbo of the Fathers"</note> was their relationship to that place—functioning as a kind of **detention and binding** to that location until they were brought out by the Redeemer after the gate was opened—likewise, the reason for the presence of Christ's soul was the operation which he performed there. I will demonstrate below that this was my intention and that the words of my conclusion imply this, where I will declare that the conclusion itself, even by the force of the speech and the power of the words, is not to be judged heretical.

<margin>Note.</margin>
However, as to which opinion is truer regarding the way separate substances exist in a place—whether that of the Scotists <note>followers of the philosopher Duns Scotus</note> or those whom I have followed—I do not determine. I only say this: my opinion has been believed and held as most true by so many great Catholic masters, doctors, and those most celebrated for their learning and holiness, that those who dare to judge the opinion of such proven doctors as "heretical" or "savoring of heresy" should be judged far more reckless than I, who prefer the authority of those ancient theologians over the rulings of the more recent ones.

<margin>Bernard of Gannat</margin>
For this opinion which I follow is held affirmatively not only by **Durandus**, but also by **Bernard of Gannat** <note>original: "Bernardus de gannaco"</note> in his attacks on Henry’s second *Quodlibet*.

<margin>Thomas the Englishman</margin>
**Thomas the Englishman** <note>Thomas of Sutton or Thomas Jorz</note> holds it in his *Quodlibets*.

<margin>Herveus the Breton</margin>
**Herveus the Breton** <note>Herveus Natalis</note> holds it in his second book on the *Sentences*.

<margin>Saint Thomas / Archbishop of Amalfi</margin>
**Saint Thomas Aquinas** also held it in his first book on the *Sentences*, although elsewhere he may seem to follow another opinion. The **Archbishop of Amalfi** holds it in his second book. **John of Paris** holds it in the *Correction of the Corruptor*.

<margin>John of Paris</margin>
Why should I list more? I believe more than a hundred highly proven Catholic doctors have held this opinion, whose books have not only not been rejected by the Church, but are publicly read and celebrated in all Christian universities. If anyone wishes to consult them, they will be able to see the foundations of the opinion and recognize its probability. I do not intend to do that here; I only act to explain the conclusions I have proposed so that the simple-minded may not have cause for scandal, nor detractors (if there are any) have cause for slander.

<margin>Third</margin> <margin>Giles</margin> <margin>Note</margin> ...[anima]ted, or is in a place unless it acts upon something or is acted upon by the place or by a thing existing in that place. <note>The text begins mid-sentence, likely discussing how spiritual beings relate to physical locations.</note> However, Giles of Rome <note>original: "Egidius"; a prominent 13th-century theologian and pupil of Thomas Aquinas</note> and many others say that one should not worry about those articles <note>Refers to the 219 articles condemned by the Bishop of Paris in 1277, which sparked intense debate over the limits of divine and natural power.</note> because they were made without summoning all the doctoral masters of Paris, but only at the request of certain heads of the chapters.

Wherefore, even if my conclusion were against an article, those who condemned me should remember that they were entirely in error in condemning me, because they said my conclusion was against the Apostles' Creed, when they ought to have said it was against the "Parisian Creed"—and even that is false, as we have shown before. It seems to me that the true understanding of those articles is this: in Article 204, if it speaks of "operation" <note>The act of a spiritual being exerting power or influence on a physical location.</note> in the commonly accepted way mentioned before, the intent is that even if all operation were set aside, the finiteness or limitation of a separate nature would still be the reason it is not "everywhere," or the reason that if it is in one place, it is not simultaneously in another whole place, and in both by its very nature. Regarding Article 218, I believe the intent is that the substance, or the finiteness of the substance, is not the reason for an angel being simply in a place. By explaining the articles in this way, there is no contradiction; and articles understood thus are not only not against my position, but they totally confirm it on both sides, as is clear from the explanation of the position set forth above.

<margin>Solution to the second argument according to many</margin> <margin>Solution of the three problems touched on earlier in the argument</margin> To the second point, many respond by granting that it is possible for an incorporeal substance to exist without an "operation" passing outside of itself. However, this being granted, the argument seems to suggest that one of three absurdities <note>original: "inconvenientibus"; in medieval logic, an "inconvenience" is an unacceptable or contradictory consequence.</note> would follow. 

<margin>Of the first</margin> <margin>"Part" is understood in two ways</margin> The first of these problems is that, since the being is a part of the universe, it would be absurd for it not to be "in" the universe. To this, they would say that the one arguing is using the word "part" in two different senses. For if by "part of the universe" he understands that which has a determined position <term>position: "situm," one of Aristotle's categories describing the arrangement of parts</term> in the universe, then they would say that an angel cannot be called a part of the universe whether it is operating or not. But if he understands "part" as being one of the things that exist—that is, one of the entities and natures of the universe—then they grant that it is then a part of the universe, and indeed one of the more noble ones. But from this, it does not seem to follow that it must have a specific position or a definition related to a place.

<margin>Of the second</margin> <margin>"Being everywhere" is understood in two ways</margin> The second problem is that it cannot be said to be "everywhere," because that is a property of God alone. To this, it is said that "being everywhere" in the way theologians say God is everywhere—namely by essence, power, and presence—is indeed proper to God and cannot belong to any created nature. However, "being everywhere" in the sense of being "here or there" indifferently, or being everywhere by "indistance" <note>Lack of distance or separation from any point in space.</note>—that is, truly existing according to a substance that is not distant from any place—whether this is repugnant to a creature, you may hear Henry <note>Henry of Ghent, a major 13th-century philosopher.</note> in *Quodlibet* 7, question 9, saying thus: 

<margin>Henry</margin> <margin>A double limitation</margin> "In a creature, a double limitation can be understood. One is in nature and essence, by which it is finite and contained within certain bounds; in this way, God alone is unlimited and infinite in nature. Another limitation of nature can be understood which is a limitation of position <term>position: "situm," referring to the category of "Ubi" or "Where"</term>, by which it is so finite and contained within certain limits that it must be somewhere—not nowhere, and not everywhere—but so 'here' that it is not 'there'; or, even if it is not determinately 'here' or 'there,' it is still under the determination of 'either here or there' or 'somewhere.' This limitation pertains to the category of 'Where' <note>original: "ubi"; one of Aristotle's ten categories.</note>, such that every creature differs from God by this first limitation of its own."

To the third, I say that that argumentation proceeds from an incomplete understanding of our position. <margin>Operation</margin> For the position does not understand "operation" <note>The activity or causal influence exerted by a spiritual being</note> (by which an incorporeal thing is said to be located) to mean only that operation which is an external local motion or a real alteration—as we also touched upon somewhat in the response to the first point in the exposition of the <term>Articles of Paris</term> <note>The Condemnations of 1277, a list of forbidden theological propositions</note>. <margin>To be taken in two ways</margin> Rather, it takes "operation" broadly for every motion or influence or relation signified by the mode of a "transient operation" <note>an action that passes from the agent into an external object</note> into a body and proceeding from the angel, or vice versa. These are Thomas's words verbatim. 

From these words, the response to the argument is clear: because although angels have no operation toward the <term>Empyrean heaven</term> <note>The highest, purely spiritual part of the heavens</note> that would constitute local motion or real alteration, they nevertheless have something that functions by way of a transient operation, such as presiding or something similar.

For when the essence of an angel is said to be "finite," the limit is taken as the limit of essence and power—just as a definition is called a "term"—and not as a limit of physical dimension. <margin>End [limit] to be taken in two ways</margin> A place, however, is called "finite" according to the three dimensions of quantity. A "limit" according to each of these two meanings has no shared measurement or proportion. Therefore, it is not necessary that what is finite in essence be limited by the boundaries of a place. These are the literal words of Thomas. From which it follows that, if Thomas is not lying, this Master is "crude" who called his own crude proof a "demonstration."

It is certainly clear that it would not, for it is by this very fact that a unity is distinguished from a point: a point has position, but a unity does not. 

Yet it is manifest that an angel, and any incorporeal substance, is even more abstract than any quantity, whether "continuous" <note>such as a line or a shape</note> or "discrete" <note>such as a number</note>. Metaphysics, as is clear to everyone, deals with higher abstractions than arithmetic (which is one of the mathematical sciences). Therefore, it is even less possible to say that an angel has a physical position. 

If this master cannot imagine the abstraction of an angel, let him at least consider the abstraction of a unity. Let him hear what should be said about himself according to Henry <margin>Henry</margin> <note>Henry of Ghent, a famous 13th-century theologian</note>. "Those who cannot understand an angel according to the nature of its own substance—as a unity without the concept of a point—are those of whom the Commentator <note>Averroes, the great Andalusian philosopher</note> says, in his notes on the second book of the *Metaphysics*, that their 'imaginative power' dominates their 'cognitive power.' Therefore, as he says, we see that such people do not believe in logical demonstrations unless a mental image accompanies them. For this reason, such people are melancholic <note>In the medieval theory of the four humors, "melancholy" was associated with a literal-minded focus on physical, heavy things</note> and they become excellent mathematicians, but they are naturally inept at the study of nature." 

Thus far Henry, word for word. From this it follows that, according to Henry, this master is poorly suited for the study of natural philosophy, worse for the study of metaphysics, and worst of all for the study of theology, which also deals with abstractions. There remains for him only an aptitude for mathematics, and since he has not practiced even those, let the judgment of his character be left to his own conscience.

<margin>Albert the Great</margin>
Now that I have resolved the arguments commonly brought against the foundations of the position I followed in my conclusion regarding the manner of Christ’s descent, I also wish to bring forward the words of our Albert—truly no less "Great" <note>a pun on Albertus Magnus (Albert the Great)</note> in his teaching than in his surname. I remember reading his thoughts on this matter in his book on *Physics*. In the first treatise of the fourth book, in the first chapter, he explains Aristotle's point that the ancients were deceived. They believed that just as "that which does not exist is not in a place," so too "nothing exists unless it is in a place." Albert then digresses on this passage and says:

"There are, however, many modern thinkers who concede the conclusion of this argument, even though they know the argument itself is invalid. From logic, we know that an argument is not valid when it proceeds from the destruction of the 'antecedent' to the destruction of the 'consequent' <note>A logical fallacy: just because "Non-existence = No Place" is true, it does not mean "Existence = Place" must also be true</note>. Therefore, although it is true that 'that which does not exist is nowhere,' it does not follow from this that 'that which exists is somewhere.' And although this does not follow logically, there are many who claim that everything that exists is in a place, using the following reasoning: everything that exists is a particular thing; a particular thing is 'here and now'; and whatever is 'here and now' is in a place. Therefore, everything that exists is in a place. Furthermore, they say everything that exists has a definite essence, because it is confined within its own limits; and what has a definite essence is 'defined' in a place; and what is 'defined' in a place is in some specific place."

These thinkers make a distinction based on John of Damascus <note>An 8th-century Church Father</note>, who says that being "in a place" can be meant in two ways.

2. Something is in a place **definitively** <term>definitively: when an essence is limited to a certain area such that it is not found outside of it, yet it does not occupy physical space</term>. In this way, they say indivisible things, like intelligences <note>angels</note> and souls, are in a place.

And in his *Questions on Boethius' On the Trinity*, he <note>Referring to Thomas Aquinas, the "Angelic Doctor" of the 13th century.</note> holds the view of the Commentator <note>The "Commentator" refers to Averroes (Ibn Rushd), the influential Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were central to medieval university life.</note> regarding **indeterminate dimensions**. Likewise, in the first book of the *Sentences* <note>Peter Lombard's *Sentences* was the standard theological textbook of the Middle Ages; every master had to write a commentary on it.</note>, he says that the intelligible thing itself and the act of understanding it are understood by the same action. But in the first part of the *Summa* and in the third book of the *Sentences*, he holds that the reflexive action <note>The mind turning back to look at its own process.</note> differs from the direct action.

Likewise, in his writing, he holds that the soul of Christ, insofar as it was capable of being joined to the body, was like the soul of a **wayfarer** <note>original: "viator"; a technical term for a person still living on earth, traveling toward God.</note>; but insofar as it was joined to the Word <note>The "Word" or Logos refers to the Second Person of the Trinity (the Son).</note>, it was like the soul of a **comprehensor** <note>original: "comprehensor"; one who has already attained the "Beatific Vision" of God in heaven.</note>. In the *Summa*, however, he holds that the soul of Christ was totally and in all respects like the soul of a comprehensor, and that the fact it did not transmit the gift of clarity and impassibility <note>The state of being unable to suffer or feel pain, a quality of glorified bodies in heaven.</note> into his body was due to a divine dispensation. Likewise, he thinks one way concerning the knowledge of Christ in his [early] writing and another way in the *Summa*, and so it is with many other things.

Thus it can be seen in which matters he followed different opinions in different places. If these men <note>Pico's critics and accusers.</note> contend completely that the opinion concerning the "manner of being in a place by way of operation" <note>The idea that a spirit is "present" in a place only because it is acting or working there, not because it occupies space.</note> is also Thomas’s view, they will have nothing more against me—except that my opinion on the manner of Christ’s descent is so much more probable and should be judged less heretical, insofar as it is true even according to the opinion of Saint Thomas.

Because of this, I marvel all the more that these masters <margin>Note.</margin> condemned my conclusion before they had even judged it heretical. I had not only explained my intention regarding it to them in these words, but I had even dictated it to be written down and noted, saying thus: "Let no one understand me to say, based on this conclusion, that the soul of Christ did not descend to the underworld, or that the soul of Christ was not in hell during the three-day interval <note>The time between the Crucifixion and the Resurrection.</note>; on the contrary, I confess both. But I say that neither physical motion nor being located in a place befits any **separate spirit** <note>A soul or spirit not currently united to a physical body.</note>—such as the soul of Christ then was—except by reason of its operation."

I announced these precise words and no others, word for word, for them to note as a brief declaration of this conclusion. How they could still judge it heretical afterward, when they could now hold it as orthodox, I do not see.

<margin>He argues against his opponents</margin> And to show briefly, by way of a summary argument, that those who believe my proposition cannot be defended from heresy are erring in the faith, I argue thus: One who posits a conclusion that is in itself heretical can be accused of heresy, insofar as heresy exists in the intellect. But one who posits my aforementioned conclusion cannot be accused of heresy from the way it is positioned; therefore, the aforementioned conclusion is not heretical in itself. They themselves grant the major premise of this argument.

[If] proposition *a* is such that one cannot be accused of heresy for it, then even the person who posits proposition *a* cannot be accused. But the person who posits everything from which my conclusion follows—in the way I have posited it—cannot be accused of heresy; therefore, the person who posits the proposition itself as I have posited it cannot be accused.

I prove the minor premise <note>The second part of the logical syllogism.</note> thus: The contradictory of this statement—"The reason for being in a place (that is, 'here' or 'there') for separate substances is operation, not the limitation of nature"—is not a matter of faith <note>original: "non est de fide"; meaning it is a matter of philosophical debate, not an established dogma that must be believed for salvation.</note>. And the contradictory of this statement—"It is not permitted to argue from a whole conjunction to one of its parts"—is not a matter of faith. And the contradictory of this statement: "If someone, having made a negative or affirmative assertion, adds the authority of some Doctor with a qualifying word like 'as' [*ut*], it can be taken just as well in a specific sense as in a relative sense." Because it can just as well be equivalent to the phrase "in the manner in which" as to the word "that," [this] likewise is not a matter of faith. And the contradictory of this statement: "Through the common way in theological matters, we can appropriately understand the way that is commonly held in that university..."

# On the Descent of Christ into Hell

The argument proceeds as follows, and it seems that Christ did not descend into hell according to his soul because a finite thing cannot be in different places at the same time. However, the soul of Christ was a finite creature, and immediately after death it was in paradise with the soul of the thief to whom it was said in Luke 23: "Today you will be with me in paradise." <note>original: "Hodie mecum eris in paradiso"</note> Therefore, at that time at least, he could not have been in hell. Furthermore, those things which Christ did and suffered in his assumed nature were ordained for human salvation. But it would not have been beneficial for this salvation for Christ to descend to the underworld, because through the passion which he endured in this world, he liberated us from all guilt and punishment; therefore, it seems that Christ did not descend to the underworld.

On the contrary is what is stated in the **Creed**: "He descended into hell." <note>This refers to the Apostles' Creed, a foundational statement of Christian belief.</note> And the Apostle says in Ephesians 4: "Now that he ascended, what is it but because he also descended into the lower parts of the earth?" <note>original: "descendit ad inferiores partes terre"</note> The <term>Gloss</term> <note>A standard medieval marginal commentary on the Bible.</note> interprets this as "to the underworld."

I respond that since it is an article of faith that Christ descended into the underworld, and this cannot be understood by reason of his divinity—according to which he is everywhere—nor by reason of his body—according to which he was in the tomb—it remains that it must be understood by reason of the soul of his human nature. Presupposing this, two things must be seen: first, the manner in which the soul of Christ descended into hell; second, to which "hell" he descended.

Regarding the first point, it should be known that since a <term>separated soul</term> <note>A soul that has been parted from the body after death but before the final resurrection.</note> is neither a body nor a power within a body, it cannot be said that the soul of Christ descended to the underworld by that kind of movement or descent by which bodies are moved. 

<margin>How angels move to a place</margin>
Whether it is by the kind of movement by which angels are moved is not clearly evident. For angels are said to move from place to place insofar as they work successively in different places. A separated soul is not said to have any operation regarding a place, or regarding a body existing in a place, because since by its nature it is determined to a specific body, it cannot move or act upon another except through the mediation of its own body. But it lacks that body while it is separated. Therefore, the soul cannot be moved from place to place by reason of an operation it has concerning a place or a body existing in a place. 

<margin>The soul descends to hell in two ways</margin>
Nevertheless, notwithstanding this, a separated soul can be said to have descended into hell in two ways. One way is by **assignment**. In this way, the souls of the damned are said simply to descend into hell because they are simply assigned there so that, once they have resumed their bodies, they may be in hell; because of this, they are said to be where they are simply assigned. However, the souls of the holy Fathers are said to be in <term>Limbo</term> <note>A region of the afterlife where the souls of the righteous who died before Christ were thought to wait.</note> or to have descended to Limbo because of an assignment that was not simple but conditional: that is, they would stay there upon resuming their bodies unless they were liberated by the Redeemer. However, the soul of Christ is not said to have descended to hell in this way—namely, by assignment—because every such assignment is due to contracted or committed sin, which was not in Christ.

In another way, the soul of Christ can be said to descend into hell according to its **effect**. In this way, the soul of Christ is said to descend into hell because of the double effect it had on those who were in hell. One effect was the display of the divine vision which they lacked, toward which the passion of Christ acted as a form of merit; and because all merit depends principally on the act of the soul, this effect is attributed to the soul as the principal beginning of meriting. Likewise, by <term>appropriation</term>, <note>A theological method of attributing certain works or attributes to one person of the Trinity or one part of Christ's nature for the sake of clarity.</note> just as Christ was blessed according to his soul, so according to it, he is attributed as being the cause of beatitude in others. For it is fitting that a being in potentiality be brought to actuality by that which is already in actuality. Another effect was according to certain ones to whom...

<summary>This page explores the theological arguments for how Christ's soul descended into hell after his death, clarifying that he did so not by physical movement or as a punishment for sin, but through the "effect" of his presence and merit.</summary>

<meta>This page continues a theological discussion regarding the nature of Christ's descent into hell (the "Harrowing of Hell") during the three days between his death and resurrection, specifically focusing on whether this was a physical movement or a spiritual effect.</meta>

...the soul of Christ acted directly as an active cause, namely, to illuminate the souls of the fathers who were in <term>Limbo</term><note>A state or place where the souls of the righteous who died before Christ's resurrection were said to wait.</note> and [to teach] concerning the mysteries that are revealed through divine grace. For according to Dionysius <margin>Dionysius</margin> in the seventh chapter of *The Celestial Hierarchy* <note>original: "celeſtis gerarchie." Dionysius here refers to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a highly influential early Christian theologian.</note>, Christ, according to his soul, has the task of teaching the angels; and by reason of this twofold effect, the soul of Christ can be said to have descended into hell. 

This is confirmed, however, by a threefold reasoning. The first is because <margin>First reason</margin> movement or "descent" belongs to a <term>separated soul</term><note>A soul that has been parted from the body after death.</note> not in the manner of bodily movement, but in the manner that movement belongs to a spiritual spirit. But for other spiritual substances—namely God and angels—movement from place to place does not belong to them by a movement that exists within themselves as subjects, but through the effect they have on other things; therefore, in a similar way, it belongs to a separated soul, and belonged to the soul of Christ. 

The second reason is this: <margin>Second</margin> Christ is said to have descended into hell so that he might illuminate the souls of the holy fathers to see God. In that same instant in which Christ died, the holy fathers saw God. However, in that same instant, Christ's soul could not have been in hell by means of physical travel. Therefore, he did not descend there by a movement within himself, but by the effect he had on others. 

Likewise, just as during those <term>three days</term><note>original: "triduo." The period between Good Friday and Easter Sunday.</note> Christ's soul is said to have been in hell <margin>Third</margin> with the souls of the holy fathers, so in those three days or part of them he is said to have been in paradise with the soul of the thief <note>Referring to the "Good Thief" crucified alongside Jesus.</note>. To whom it was said in Luke 23: "Today you will be with me in paradise." But this cannot be understood as a physical location reached through movement; since according to those who hold that a spirit is in a place <term>definitively</term><note>A technical term meaning a spirit is "where its power acts," rather than filling up space like a physical object.</note>, when it moves from place to place, the same spirit cannot be in several places at once, nor move simultaneously with several movements tending toward several places. Therefore, it must be understood according to the effect. 

For if anyone says that "Paradise" is spoken of in two ways: <margin>Paradise spoken of in two ways</margin> In one way as a physical place, namely the Empyrean heaven, and thus Christ's soul was not in paradise except after the <term>Assumption</term><note>Here referring to the physical entry into heaven.</note>. In the other way, paradise is called the vision of the divine essence; and thus Christ's soul was in paradise from the moment of conception, and the soul of the thief on the very day of the Passion. In this way, it is not contradictory for Christ's soul to have been simultaneously in paradise—meaning he saw God—and to have been locally in hell. 

If this were said, it would not be valid, because just as paradise is spoken of in two ways, so is hell. For in one way, hell is called a place corresponding to the interior of the earth. <margin>Hell spoken of in two ways</margin> In the other way, it is the lack of the divine vision. Therefore, just as the soul of the thief is not said to have been with the soul of Christ in paradise except because, by the merit of Christ’s Passion, the thief’s soul saw God; so Christ’s soul is not said to have been with the souls of the chosen fathers in hell except because their souls—which lacked the divine vision and thus were said to be in hell—were purged of this lack by the merit of this Passion. 

Therefore, both should be understood equally in terms of effect, not in terms of location or physical movement within the soul itself. However, while this may be a probable explanation and seems sufficient to preserve the Article of Faith and the words of Scripture, because divine power is not fully grasped by human reason, it should not be stubbornly asserted that Christ's soul could not have descended to hell by some other way unknown to us. 

To the first argument, it must be said that the same finite thing cannot be in several places at once <term>definitively</term> or <term>circumscriptively</term><note>Scholastic terms: "circumscriptive" presence is how bodies occupy space (filling it), whereas "definitive" presence is how spirits occupy space (by being limited to a certain area).</note>, nor is it claimed in this way that Christ's soul was in paradise and hell at the same time. But according to the effect, nothing prevents the same finite thing from being said to be in several places when the effects are compatible and simultaneously subject to the power of the same agent. And thus the soul of Christ is said to have been in paradise and in hell at once, because by his merit the soul of the thief saw [God]...

### Main Text

...confirms. Likewise, Jerome, in his commentary on the Gospel of Matthew, says that the words of the Psalm, "their sound went out into all the earth" <note>Psalm 19:4, original: "in omnem terram exiuit sonus eorum"</note>, and the statement of Christ that the Gospel would be preached in the whole world, were already fulfilled by the apostles. Augustine, however, in his letter to Hesychius <note>The OCR reads "Exitium," likely a transcription error for Hesychium</note>, with whom Origen agrees in his commentary on Matthew, holds that this has not yet been fulfilled.

Likewise, Jerome, in his commentary on the Letter to Titus, holds that angels existed for many ages before the visible world and served God; Ambrose also holds this in his *Hexameron* <note>A treatise on the six days of creation</note>. Augustine, however, in his commentary on Genesis, holds that they were created at the same time as the <term>empyrean heaven</term> <note>In medieval cosmology, the highest part of heaven, believed to be made of pure light and fire.</note>.

Likewise, Jerome, in his prologue to the Book of Wisdom, maintains that this book belongs to Philo and is not to be counted among the sacred scriptures. Augustine, however, in the third book of his *Retractions*, shows that he once held it was published by Jesus son of Sirach, though he retracts that there; and although he does not explicitly state who published it, in his book *On Christian Doctrine*, he nevertheless counts it among the sacred books.

Likewise, Jerome, in his book *Hebrew Questions*, says that before God made the heaven and the earth, He had previously established Paradise, because of the verse stating, "God had planted a paradise from the beginning." Augustine, however, in his literal commentary on Genesis, explains "from the beginning" to mean on the third day.

Likewise, Augustine, in his book *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, asserts that the entirety of Peter’s denial took place in the courtyard of Annas, and that the things said later, after Jesus was sent to Caiaphas, were stated as a recapitulation. Jerome, however, in his commentary on Matthew, seems to believe that Peter denied Christ in the courtyard of Caiaphas. Bede, in his commentary on Luke, seems to agree with him.

Likewise, Jerome, commenting on that passage of Habakkuk, "your eyes are pure," denies that individual angels are placed in charge of individual physical creatures; but Augustine, in his *Eighty-Three Questions*, holds that they are. Origen and John of Damascus agree with Augustine.

Likewise, Jerome, commenting on that passage of Jonah, "Take me and cast me into the sea" <note>Jonah 1:12, original: "Tollite me & mittite ī mare"</note>, says that it is permissible to perish by one's own hand when chastity is at risk. Augustine, however, in his book *The City of God*, affirms the opposite.

Indeed, many such things are found in which the <term>holy doctors</term> <note>The "Doctors of the Church," highly influential early Christian theologians.</note> wrote contrary views among themselves <term>preserving the faith</term> <note>original: "salua fide"; meaning they disagreed on secondary details without abandoning Christian doctrine.</note>. But not all examples come to mind in this great haste; nor was I able to work on this task with more exact diligence because I wished to immediately counter the disease of unjust infamy that was coming upon me. I intend to write elsewhere on this matter so that, with more leisure and care, I may add more and perhaps better points.

I will, however, add what now occurs to me from Jerome’s letter to Augustine, where he says: "Do not wonder if, in your books, and especially in the exposition of the Scriptures—which are most obscure—some things seem to deviate from the straight line. And I say this not because I judge anything in your works to be worthy of blame—for I have never devoted effort to reading them, nor is there a supply of these copies among us, except for the books of your *Soliloquies* and certain commentaries on the Psalms. If I wished to discuss these, I would not say they differ from me (who am nothing), but I would show they differ from the interpretations of the ancient Greeks." This is what he said.

Therefore, just as they could differ among themselves, so too can we differ from them in many things, while <term>preserving the faith</term> and the truth of Scripture and the determinations of the Holy Church.

The **third proof** is taken from the special prerogative of Sacred Scripture and the decrees of the Universal Church, to which alone we grant the excellence of <term>infallible truth</term>. Hence Augustine, writing against Jerome in a letter to him, says: "For I confess to your charity that I have learned to yield this fear and honor only to those books of Scripture which are now called canonical, so that I believe no author of these..."

It is presumptuous to call the opinion of Durandus <note>Durandus of Saint-Pourçain (c. 1275–1334), a Dominican theologian known for his independent and often controversial "Modernist" views.</note> simply heretical. But if it were found to be so, it is necessary that Durandus should patiently bear this mark. But someone will say: granted that your meaning, which you declared <margin>Objection</margin> you intended by that proposition, is Catholic. Granted also that the force of the words allows it, could not your proposition also give rise to that meaning of Durandus which you yourself detest? And therefore, you have erred in setting forth a conclusion that could cause scandal in the minds of the faithful.

To this, I say first that the nature of things proposed for debate is one thing. <margin>First Response</margin> Another is the nature of those things handed down in writing to be read as doctrine. For when something is proposed for debate, a brief, concise, and unexplained proposition is put forward which, in itself, enfolds multiple difficulties of words and meanings to be resolved in the meeting of the debate itself. Otherwise, if everything were explained there, no room would be left for debate; therefore, one who proposes an ambiguous, obscure, or equivocal proposition for debate is excused, because he will distinguish and clarify it during the debate. But those who commit something to writing as doctrine do by writing what occurs here by debating. Therefore, in that case, everything ought to be clear, transparent, and ready. 

Second, let these most severe censors consider that it is not only difficult but almost impossible to <margin>Second [Response]</margin> so weigh and examine the words of all propositions which one puts forward that no ambiguity of meaning can exist, and no erroneous opinion can be drawn from them. Nor indeed do I wish to claim this for my own propositions, which many Evangelical and Apostolic <note>Referring to the Gospels and the Epistles of the Apostles in the New Testament.</note> propositions do not possess. For many are found among them that have multiple interpretations and can be twisted to an erroneous meaning. Indeed, some even seem to sound like heresy at first glance. 

From this, all heresies have sprouted: <margin>Where heresies sprouted from</margin> namely, while some did not look so much into the depth of the meaning as they attended to what the "bark" <note>original: *cortex*; a common medieval metaphor for the literal surface of a text as opposed to its spiritual "pith" or "marrow."</note> of the Gospel words sounded like. From this, Arius, hearing "the Father is greater than I," <margin>Heresy of Arius</margin> <note>John 14:28</note> believed the Father was greater than the Son and said the Son was a creature. From this, Helvidius, hearing that Joseph "did not know Mary until she brought forth her firstborn son," <margin>Heresy of Helvidius</margin> <note>Matthew 1:25. Helvidius was a 4th-century writer who argued against the perpetual virginity of Mary.</note> attending more to the grammatical force of that word "until" <note>original: *donec*</note> than to the truth of the Gospel sense, doubted the perpetual virginity of Mary. 

From this, Marcion, reading that saying of Paul, "But the law entered in that sin might abound," <margin>Heresy of Marcion and the Manicheans</margin> <note>Romans 5:20</note> believed the Law of Moses to be evil and from an evil principle, according to the Manichean view. And Basilides, reading "I once lived without the law," <margin>Heresy of Basilides</margin> <note>Romans 7:9</note> believed that the soul of Paul had once lived in another body <note>Referring to the doctrine of metempsychosis or reincarnation.</note>. 

From this, Eunomius, hearing Christ responding to the Jews accusing him of calling himself the Son of God, where it was written, "I have said, you are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High," <margin>Heresy of Eunomius</margin> <note>John 10:34 quoting Psalm 82:6. Eunomius was a leader of the extreme Arians.</note> attended more to the thing said and the response itself than to the intention and purpose of the speaker, and believed that Christ is called the "Son of God" in the same way any holy person is called a son of God. Similarly, this proposition, "nor does the Son know that day," <margin>Error of many</margin> <note>Mark 13:32, regarding the end of the world.</note> was an occasion for many to believe that the Father understands more than the Son knows. For if we interpret it according to the sense the words commonly make, it seems to suggest that, yet the truth of the hidden meaning is otherwise. 

I could bring forward infinite similar propositions from the canon of the Scriptures. <margin>Gregory</margin> Gregory says that we should not always understand words as they seem to sound at first glance, especially where they are ambiguous; rather, we must return to the intention of the speaker. <note>original: "intentionem loquentis"</note> And Gregory says that often, while the literal property of words is focused upon, the sense of truth is lost. And in the twenty-sixth book of his *Moralia in Job*, <note>A massive and influential commentary on the Book of Job written by Pope Gregory the Great in the 6th century.</note> Gregory says: No one should consider the words, but rather the will and the intention. For the intention should not serve the words, but the words should serve the intention.

<margin>Jerome</margin> And Jerome, in his commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, testifies that the Gospel consists not in the words of the scriptures, but in their meaning; not on the surface, but in the marrow; <note>Jerome uses "marrow" (medulla) to mean the deep, nourishing inner essence of a text, as opposed to the "skin" or surface-level reading.</note> not in the leaves of talk, but in the root of reason.

<margin>Ockham</margin> For this reason, Ockham, in his *Dialogue*, <note>William of Ockham (c. 1287–1347) was a famous English Franciscan friar and philosopher, famous for the principle of "Ockham's Razor."</note> proves false this common proposition: "words are to be understood not from the opinions of individuals but from common usage." He says this especially regarding the second part of the statement. For he says that in ambiguous and complex words, one must not return to the common understanding, but rather to the intention of the speakers. And so, when there is ambiguity in the teaching of someone speaking or writing, one must similarly return to the intention of the speaker so that they may explain themselves and express the true sense which the force of the words allows. They should not be rejected unless it can be proven that such a true sense is contrary to their other sayings or is irrelevant to their purpose. Even in simple speech, the same doctor <note>In a medieval academic context, "doctor" refers to a recognized authority or teacher of the Church.</note> says we must return to the intention of the speaker, and we must stand by their interpretation unless it is established—or probably or strongly presumed—that they used such an ambiguous way of speaking to deceive or for some other evil end.

<margin>Epilogue</margin> From all these things, I conclude that I was not the one who erred. I am the one who, while under a "protestation," <note>A formal declaration often made by medieval scholars at the start of a debate, stating that they did not intend to say anything contrary to the Christian faith.</note> probably put forward a complex proposition to be clarified during the dispute. This proposition can yield no sense that some approved doctor—or one not yet declared as such by the Church—has not held. Rather, those have erred who judged a proposition to be simply heretical, even though it has a Catholic <note>Meaning "orthodox" or "correct" in the context of the universal Church.</note> sense allowed by the force of the words, and even after that Catholic sense had already been declared to them by the person proposing it. Even if they had done this before I declared my meaning, they might have erred more excusably; however, if they are truly learned, they could have recognized for themselves that the proposition had a double meaning. Taking note of this, they should not have simply condemned it, but rather should have interpreted it in its good sense.

<margin>Augustine</margin> For Augustine, in his book *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, explaining that passage from Matthew, "Do not judge, and you will not be judged," <note>Matthew 7:1.</note> says: "In this place, I believe nothing else is commanded except that we interpret those deeds, where it is doubtful with what intent they were done, in the better light." For concerning neutral deeds which can be done with either a good or bad intention, it is rash to judge, and especially to condemn. Therefore, what Augustine says about things that are *done*, let us likewise understand to be said about things that are *spoken*. Applying Augustine's sentiment to speculative matters, let us conclude that in these sayings which can have both a good and a bad sense, it is rash to judge, and especially to condemn.

-># SECOND QUESTION CONCERNING THE PUNISHMENT OF MORTAL SIN<-

Now, the second conclusion which those men <note>The author's critics or the faculty of theology</note> condemned is this: **for a mortal sin of finite duration, an infinite punishment in terms of time is not owed, but only a finite one.**

And because, when I set down this conclusion in my booklet, these words were prefaced: "Unless there were the sayings of the saints <note>original: "dicta sanctorum"; referring to the Church Fathers and established authorities like Augustine or Jerome</note> which, in the clear meaning of their speech, seem to say the opposite, I would firmly assert the following conclusions. I do, however, assert that they are probable and can be reasonably defended." The first of these is this: **Mortal sin is in itself a finite evil.** The second is this: **for a mortal sin of finite duration, etc.** A certain master <note>A university professor or "Magister"</note>, holding a dispute with me regarding this conclusion, said: "What other testimony do we seek that your conclusion is heretical, since you yourself clearly say it is against the sayings of the saints? For the following logic holds: it is against the sayings of the saints, therefore it is heretical." I showed him then, as I will also show below, how my conclusion was in no way repugnant to the opinions of the saints, and how their words were to be understood. But even if it had been the case that the conclusion was against the sayings of the saints, how much his "logical consequence" was worth—and how unworthy it was of a doctor who boasts of being a theologian—can be clear to anyone from what was said above regarding the first conclusion. I know what I could say here about that master. For he is the one who so often sent letters back to our homeland about me, promising something like a trophy or a triumph over me.

<margin>What he is about to do regarding the declaration and in what order</margin>
<margin>A manifold proposition</margin>
But I wish first to declare that the conclusion itself is Catholic <note>meaning "orthodox" or "correct doctrine"</note> and in harmony with the sayings of almost all the <term>doctors</term> <note>the "Doctors of the Church," authoritative theologians like Thomas Aquinas or Duns Scotus</note>, even though the masters judged both the conclusion itself and the responses I gave them when they questioned me on it to be false, erroneous, and heretical. I say "my conclusion," because if you take it in a sense other than the one I intend for it, then it is no longer my conclusion which I proposed. For a proposition can be <term>multiplex</term> <note>having multiple layers of meaning or interpretations</note>, and can thus be many propositions. Therefore, I wish to declare that my responses themselves are also sound, both regarding the conclusion and the responses themselves, always declaring my own meanings—that is, those which I intend through them—as the force of the words allows.

<margin>The first thing to be noted regarding sin</margin>
<margin>Turning toward</margin>
<margin>Turning away</margin>
For the declaration of the conclusion, five things must be noted. **First**, it must be noted that in sin, two things can be considered: the <term>turning toward</term> <note>original: "conversio"; seeking satisfaction in worldly things</note> a created good, and the <term>turning away</term> <note>original: "aversio"; rejecting God</note> from the unchangeable and uncreated good <note>God</note>. In the first way, sin is a finite evil, even according to all the doctors. In the second way, sin is a finite evil according to the "common way" <note>the standard theological consensus</note>. And because the turning toward a created good—which the sinner uses wrongly in the act of sinning—belongs to the <term>intrinsic nature</term> of the sin itself, it is therefore said that sin is an **intrinsically finite evil**. However, the turning away from the uncreated good makes it **extrinsically infinite**, only because it is called an infinite evil insofar as it is a turning away from an infinite good. Therefore, it only remains that it is an <term>extrinsically and objectively</term> infinite evil.

<margin>The second thing to be noted</margin>
<margin>Time of the way and the end</margin>
**Second**, note that by "time," we can understand only the <term>time of the way</term> <note>original: "tempus vie"; the span of a human life on earth</note>. In this sense, it is certain that neither sin nor anything else pertaining to man can be infinite in terms of time, since the "time of the way" for any traveler <note>a living person journeying toward eternity</note> is not only finite in duration but also brief. In another way, we can understand by "time" both the "time of the way" and of the <term>end</term> <note>original: "termini"; the state after death or eternity</note> and...

<summary>The author begins defending his second thesis: that mortal sin committed in a finite lifetime does not strictly deserve an infinite duration of punishment. He argues that while sin is "objectively" infinite because it offends an infinite God, it is "intrinsically" finite as a human act.</summary>

<meta>This page continues a theological defense regarding the nature of sin and its punishment. The author is distinguishing between the temporary act of sinning and the lasting state of guilt that follows it.</meta>

<margin>Third. 
Mortal sin is understood in two ways: 
As an act 
As guilt</margin> 
...is understood in this way in the conclusion, and thus something in a human can last for an infinite time, as is evident. Third, note that **mortal sin** can be understood in two ways. In one way, it refers to a forbidden act or the omission of an act commanded by God. In another way, it refers to the **guilt** <term>guilt: The Latin *reatus* refers to the legal or spiritual liability to punishment that remains after the sinful deed is done</term> left behind by that forbidden act or omission. Indeed, in many places in Holy Scripture, this guilt is called "sin," and a person is named a "sinner" because of such guilt even when the act of sinning (in the first sense) has ceased or passed away. 

From this third point, it is clear that it is reasonable to say that although the sin for which a person is damned may sometimes end in terms of its "intrinsic entity"—meaning the actual performance of the act—the sin does not end in terms of its guilt. In fact, if the guilt ended in that way, eternal punishment would not be owed to the person. Thus, a sin to which infinite punishment is owed is "infinite" in terms of time regarding its guilt. 

<margin>Fourth. 
"To be owed" is understood in two ways</margin>
Fourth, it must be noted that "to be owed" <note>original: "deberi"</note> is understood in two ways, or it can be understood in two ways that some punishment is "owed" for a sin. In one way, something is said to be owed to someone because it will actually be rendered or given to them at some point. In this sense, it is said reasonably and according to Catholic teaching that a sin of finite time (in terms of both its intrinsic entity and its guilt) is not owed a punishment that is infinite in time. This is the sense of the present conclusion: that for a sin of finite time, such punishment is not "owed." For every sin to which punishment is "owed" in this way—meaning punishment will actually be rendered—it must be infinite in time in the manner described. 

However, the conclusion also has another Catholic sense: namely, that infinite punishment is never "owed" (in the sense of being rendered) to someone unless they are finally **impenitent** <note>Meaning they refuse to repent until the end of their life</note> and cease to repent without end for the sin they committed or omitted in life. Thus, for a temporal sin, infinite punishment is "owed" in the aforementioned way if the sinner does not return to justice. 

<margin>The vengeance which God seeks from the sinner, and what it is.</margin>
For just as repentance ends a sin in terms of its "disacceptance" <note>The state of being rejected by God</note>—according to the saying: *at whatever hour the sinner shall groan [in repentance], etc.* <note>original: "quacūq; hora igemuerit peccator"; a reference to Ezekiel 18:21-22</note>—so too does impenitence regarding a sin perpetuate that sin in its guilt and its rejection, leading to infinite punishment. Thus, infinite punishment is never owed to anyone in that first sense unless they possess a sin that is infinite in time. Indeed, the **vengeance** which God seeks from the sinner is that the sinner should return of their own accord to their duty of obedience, grieving for their contempt; otherwise, they will be tormented until they are willing to do so.

<margin>Note: A common distinction regarding the word "owed." 
Epilogue.</margin>
In another way, something can be understood as "owed" to someone because they are worthy of it by merit or demerit, and it *would* be rendered to them if they were to depart this life in that state. In this sense, for a mortal sin of finite time, infinite punishment is "owed," because whoever sins mortally in the space of a single hour is worthy of infinite punishment, and it will be rendered to them if they finally depart this life in that state, even assuming they have no other sin that is infinite in time. 

This distinction regarding the word "owed" is in frequent use among theologians. Hence, following this usage, the **Doctors** <note>The "Doctors" refers to established, authoritative university theologians of the Middle Ages</note> say that eternal life is not "owed" to a **foreknown person** <term>foreknown: Latin *prescito*, referring to someone God knows will ultimately be damned</term> even when they perform a meritorious act while in a state of grace, if we take "owed" in the first sense (because it will never actually be rendered to them). Similarly, it is said that eternal punishment is not "owed" to a **predestined person** <term>predestined: Latin *pđestinato*, someone chosen by God for salvation</term> while they are in a state of mortal sin, because it will never be rendered to them, since that sin will be ended and they will not die in it, but in grace.

From the foregoing, it is clear that my conclusion has a Catholic sense, even according to the customary way of speaking used by Catholic Doctors. Nor should it have been condemned as heretical, false, or erroneous, since its opposite is rather the thing that is false.

...and erroneous. It was the height of ignorance to believe that from the aforementioned conclusion I intended to deny the eternal punishment of the damned. On the contrary, from my conclusion one finds an investigation into the cause for which the damned are punished eternally. This cause, I stated, is the perpetuation of guilt in the soul of the sinner through their final impenitence <note>The state of refusing to repent for one's sins before death.</note> and the perpetual failure to lament their sin. This opinion not only seems not to be heretical, but is so Catholic that no one—if they are truly Catholic and trained in the Sacred Scriptures—could rightly or reasonably deny it. <margin>Note</margin> That the proposition, by the force of its own terms, carries this meaning is clear. For the proposition says: **"Eternal punishment in time is not owed to a mortal sin of finite duration."** <margin>He explains the conclusion from the force of the terms</margin> In this proposition, I take "to be owed" to mean that which will at some point be paid off <note>The author is arguing that "owing" a debt implies it can be settled; if it is eternal, the language of "debt" changes.</note>; that this is common usage among the Doctors <note>Highly respected theologians of the Church.</note> has already been shown above. And I take "sin" to mean the offense and the guilt <term>guilt: original Latin "reatus," meaning the legal or moral liability to punishment that remains even after the act of sinning is over</term>. This usage is not only not improper or abusive, but frequent in Sacred Scripture. <margin>Not being heretical</margin> After the Master of the Sentences <note>original: "Magister sententiarum"; referring to Peter Lombard, whose textbook was the standard for medieval theology.</note> <margin>The Master of the Sentences</margin> asks in the second book whether, when the act of sinning passes, the sin remains in the one who sinned until they repent, he responds: "It must not be ignored that sins exist in a person and pass away in two ways: namely, by the act and by the guilt." Durandus <note>Durandus of Saint-Pourçain, a 14th-century philosopher known for his independent thought.</note> <margin>Durandus</margin> also says in the same place that sin is understood to be ended in two ways: <margin>Sin is ended in two ways</margin> one way through the mere cessation of the act, and the other through the remission <note>The forgiveness or cancelling</note> of the sin. That "guilt" is also sometimes called "sin" is expressly stated by Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas.</note> <margin>Thomas</margin> in the same place, saying: "Guilt, mediating between the fault and the punishment, takes on the name of both extremes." But is sin not also taken for guilt in that passage: *It is therefore a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead, that they may be loosed from sins* <note>A reference to 2 Maccabees 12:46.</note>? For those dead for whom we must pray to be loosed from sins are not "in sin" if we take "sin" to mean a mortal fault—nor are they loosed from such sin after death—but they are loosed only from sin taken as the punishment or the guilt of punishment. In this way also "sin" is understood in the passage: *Redeem your sins with alms* <note>A reference to Daniel 4:27.</note> and so in many other passages of Scripture. 

If, therefore, both the sense of the proposition is Catholic and the definition of terms in the proposition is Catholic and most proven, what reason was there to condemn this conclusion of mine as heretical? Now I come to my responses. <margin>Responses which the author had given</margin> And first, I said that if anyone perseveres only for a finite time in mortal sin, he will not be punished except for a finite time. <margin>First</margin> This statement is verified in three ways: First, when we take "mortal sin" to mean guilt and not the act of commission or omission, as was said in the declaration of the conclusion. Second, it should be noted that the term "mortal sin," by the rigor of logic, is taken non-specifically <note>original: "confuse"; in medieval logic, this refers to a term that refers to a general class rather than a specific, individual instance.</note> rather than determinately. <margin>Second</margin> Third, because it is true that if this person who sinned persevered only for a finite time in a specific sin—for instance, in the omission of repenting for their sin—such that they eventually repented of it, they would not be punished for it except for a finite time. <margin>Third</margin> That I intended these Catholic meanings and nothing discordant with the faith is clear from what I added in the response when I said that it remains true that anyone dying in mortal sin will be punished forever. 

When I was further asked <margin>Question</margin> whether someone who sins only for a finite time with one mortal sin and dies impenitent is punished eternally, I responded <margin>Response</margin> that they are. ->### QUESTION THREE: CONCERNING THE ADORATION OF THE CROSS AND OF IMAGES<-

[Large initial T] **HE** third conclusion which they <note>likely referring to a group of university masters or a specific theological faculty</note> condemned was this: **Neither the cross of Christ nor any image is to be worshipped with the worship of *latria* <term>Latria: the highest form of worship, which according to Catholic theology is reserved for God alone, as opposed to *dulia*, which is given to saints.</term>, even in the manner that Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican theologian.</note> proposes.**

I believe this conclusion, which was condemned by those men, is not only Catholic <note>meaning "orthododox" or in line with Church teaching</note> but even truer than its opposite, which is this: **The cross of Christ and images are to be worshipped with *latria* in the manner Thomas proposes.** <margin>Thomas</margin> For Thomas’s opinion in this matter seems less reasonable to me <margin>Durandus</margin> than the opinion of Durandus <note>Durandus of Saint-Pourçain, a philosopher known for his independent mind.</note>, Henry of Ghent, <margin>Henry of Ghent</margin> John of Guarra, Robert Holcot, <margin>John of Guarra</margin> Peter of Aquila, <margin>Robert Holcot</margin> and many others whom I follow in this conclusion. <margin>Peter of Aquila</margin> To make this clear, I will first set forth the opinion of Thomas, which I do not hold, <margin>The opinion of Saint Thomas</margin> and then the opinion of the doctors whom I do follow. From these it will be clear that the determination of those masters regarding my conclusion—besides being neither right nor just—presupposes the complete opposite of what I intend in the conclusion.

Thomas says, therefore, that because (as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in the book *On Memory and Reminiscence*) there is a twofold movement of the soul toward an image: one toward the image itself insofar as it is a certain thing <note>for example, looking at a painting as just paint and wood</note>, and the other way toward the image insofar as it is the image of another. Between these two movements there is a difference, because the first movement, by which something is moved toward the image as a thing in itself, is different from the movement toward the thing of which it is an image. The second movement, however, which is toward the image insofar as it is an image, is one and the same as that which is toward the thing itself. Therefore, he concludes that although worship is not owed to the image of Christ as it is a thing in itself, yet as it is an image, the same reverence is owed to it as is owed to Christ himself, which is the worship of *latria*.

This is Thomas’s method, which rightly seems strange and dangerous to other doctors. For the image itself, even as an image, is distinct from the thing imagined; for it refers to the thing imagined as to something distinct from itself. Therefore, if it were to terminate <note>meaning "to be the end point of"</note> the worship of *latria* in this way, it seems to follow that something other than God would be worshipped with *latria*, which is absurd.

<margin>Against the response of Capreolus</margin> Nor can it be said, as Capreolus <note>Jean Capreolus (c. 1380–1444), a major defender of Thomism.</note> says (wishing to save Thomas’s statement), that the image itself is not worshipped separately, but the image and the thing imagined are one total object of worship. Because either one part of this total object is the image itself (which is a created, relative being) or it is not. If it is not, then it should not be said that one total object is made from those two, because from such a statement it follows that each of them is a partial object, even if one is more primary. If it is so, it follows that some created thing of the genus of "relation" would, at least partially, terminate the worship of *latria*; to say this certainly seems "poorly Catholic" <note>original: "male catholicum"; i.e., bordering on heretical</note>. All the more so because not only can this not be said of a created thing, but even the Persons in the Godhead <note>the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit</note>, by reason of their relative properties, are not the formal terminus of worship <note>the author is arguing that we worship the Divine Essence, not just the relationships between the Persons</note>.

<margin>Against the foundation of the opinion</margin> Moreover, Thomas’s foundation seems hardly effective. For when the Philosopher says that the movement of the soul toward the image and the thing imagined is the same, he does not mean it in the sense that the soul declares the image (as it is an image) to be the same as the prototype <note>original: "exemplari"</note> and thus whatever is owed to one is also owed to the other; rather, the Philosopher only intends this...

->### FOURTH QUESTION: WHETHER AN IRRATIONAL NATURE CAN BE ASSUMED INTO PERSONHOOD BY GOD<-

The fourth conclusion condemned by those critics is this: "I do not assent to the common opinion of theologians who say that God can assume any nature whatsoever into personhood; rather, I concede this only regarding a rational nature." <note>original: *suppositare*. This technical term refers to the "hypostatic union," the theological concept where a nature—like human nature—is taken up into the Person of God the Son.</note>

By this conclusion, I do not intend to deny that God *could* assume any nature into personhood. Instead, I only intend to deny a particular and explicit assent to this assertion. There is a great difference between these two intentions: "God can assume any nature into personhood" and "I do not explicitly agree that He does." For even if this were among the possibilities according to the **absolute power** of God <note>original: *potentia absoluta*. This refers to the theoretical extent of God's power to do anything that does not involve a logical contradiction.</note>, a proposition that—**by the literal force of the words**—merely denies a positive, explicit assent to that specific statement does not detract from God's omnipotence, nor does it smack of any heresy.

The reason for this is that not every faithful person is bound to assent explicitly and specifically to every possibility within God’s absolute omnipotence, nor to profess these things in detail. Rather, it is sufficient to believe some such things in a general and implicit way, provided one does not stubbornly disbelieve them. Therefore, it was not without a deeper meaning <note>original: *non sine misterio*</note> that I did not phrase my conclusion as "God *cannot* assume any nature," but rather: "I do not assent to the opinion saying that God can assume any nature into personhood." From this phrasing, it cannot be inferred that God lacks the power to do so; nor can it be said that I am asserting a denial. This is not found in the first part, which is negative, nor in the second part, from which it only follows that I hold a specific and distinct act of concession regarding **rational nature**.

Therefore, I deny within myself a particular and explicit assent to this assertion: "God can assume any nature into personhood." And I can deny this reasonably. This is partly because, even if the opposite were true, it remains unknown to us in its specifics; thus, it seems I am not obliged to believe it explicitly. Furthermore, it is not easy to prove that the opposite assertion—"God cannot," etc.—is false or that it actually detracts from God's omnipotence. This is strongly confirmed by the authority of the **Solemn Doctor, Henry of Ghent**, who, after previously holding the opposite opinion (namely, that any nature could be assumed), later leaned toward the view that only a rational nature can be assumed.

<margin>Henry of Ghent</margin>
<margin>Henry's words</margin>
Henry writes as follows: "Regarding the possibility of a nature being assumed, there is no doubt whether God could take to Himself any nature that is *capable* of being assumed. Therefore, the entire difficulty of this question turns on the 'assumability' of the nature itself." Regarding this, there are two famous positions.

<margin>The first position which Henry recounts</margin>
He says: "The more common and solemn position—to which I myself was once somewhat accustomed to assent—is that any nature subsisting in creatures can be assumed." Those who hold this believe that a certain nature can be "elevated" even if the corresponding power within it is not itself capable of such elevation. This, however, does not seem to me to be a position that can be reasonably maintained. 

<margin>An argument against this position: That God has being in creatures in two ways.</margin>
To understand this, it must be noted that God has "being" in His creatures in two ways. One way is **naturally** and in a manner suited to nature; the other is **voluntarily** and in a manner that transcends the limits of nature. In the first way, He has being through His "inflow" in every nature and creature. In the second way...

# Notes on Scribe Abbreviations and Paleography

The letter **p** is frequently written with an added stroke. It is represented as **ꝑ** <note>original: "p with a stroke"; this symbol is a common <term>siglum</term> or shorthand for the Latin words *per* (through/by), *par*, or *por*</note>.

In the word **promotes** <note>original transcription: "pmouet", where the "p" features a curl. This is the Latin word *promovet*</note>, the **p** has a curl. This specific character **ꝓ** <note>Unicode U+A753</note> is the standard abbreviation for the prefix **pro-** (for or forward).

In this transcription, I will use the closest Unicode characters available or describe them if they are too obscure, though most can be represented in modern digital formats. For a transcription intended to be "exactly as it appears" in the original manuscript, I will use the specific characters.

### Catalog of Special Characters

*   **p** with a stroke: **ꝑ** <note>Used for *per*, *par*, or *por*</note>
*   **p** with a curl: **ꝓ** <note>Used for *pro*</note>
*   **q** with a stroke: **qđ** <note>The addition of the 'd' is a shorthand for the Latin word *quod*, meaning "that," "which," or "because"</note>.

In the manuscript, this often appears as a **q** with a bar through the tail, known as **ꝗ** <note>Unicode U+A757</note>. However, in this specific text, it is written as **qđ**.

Other common markings include:
*   **q** with a semicolon: **q;** <note>This represents the suffix *-que*, the Latin word for "and"</note>
*   **q** with a bar: **q̄** <note>An alternative shorthand for the suffix *-que*</note>
*   **p** with a bar: **p̄** <note>Typically used for the prefix *pre-* (this mark is not present in the current section, which favors the stroke **ꝑ** instead)</note>
*   **pp** with a bar: **pp̄** <note>A bar over a double "p" usually abbreviates *propter* (on account of) or, in religious texts, *papa* (Pope)</note>.

I will prioritize standard characters combined with marks where possible to ensure the best possible compatibility with modern reading software.
