<meta>This page continues a scholastic theological discussion regarding the "assumption" (the union of a creaturely nature with the Divine) and the concept of "circumincessio" (mutual indwelling). It follows a previous discussion of two specific points or operations of God.</meta>

...those two. But no creaturely nature is receptive, nor can it be capable of the indwelling <note>original: "illapsus," referring to God flowing into or permeating a creature</note> of God to receive into itself, in a way consistent with nature, the first aforementioned operation of God, unless it is also receptive in itself to the second operation. This is because no creature can exist as a substance if it cannot also possess some operation through its power. For according to the Philosopher <margin>The Philosopher <note>A standard medieval reference to Aristotle.</note></margin> at the end of the fourth book of *Meteorology*, all things are defined by their operations and they exist only as long as they can perform their proper operations; when they cease to be able to perform their proper operations, they simultaneously cease to exist. 

For as Damascus <margin>Damascenus <note>St. John of Damascus, an 8th-century theologian.</note></margin> says in the same place, chapter seventeen: "An intellect that is not wise and is deprived of cognition would never truly exist at all." If it is incapable of operation and immobile, it is entirely non-existent. By this, he openly suggests that if a nature could not be elevated through its intellect, the substance of the intellect itself would not be "assumable" <note>Capable of being taken up by God, as in the Incarnation.</note>, nor would the man himself be. This is because he would not truly be "man," according to what is stated just before: "Since man is a rational, intellectual being, how then was God made man if he had assumed flesh without a soul, or a soul without an intellect?" <note>original: "sine intellectu." The author is arguing that for God to become truly human, the human nature must include a functioning intellect.</note> For that would not be a man. 

Therefore, in a similar way, no creaturely nature is receptive, or can be receptive, to the mutual indwelling <term>circumincessio: a theological term (perichoresis in Greek) describing the mutual indwelling or "inter-penetration" of the Divine and human natures</term> of God—to receive the aforementioned first operation of God within itself beyond the limits of nature—unless it is also receptive in itself to the second operation. However, a nature is not receptive to the second operation except through the powers of the intellect and the will; therefore, [only intellectual natures can be so united].

Consequently, although the argument of Augustine <margin>Augustine</margin> mentioned in the first reason does not hold purely by its logical form, it does not fail in any specific subject matter. It follows that if a nature (such as human nature) can be elevated according to its essence, it must necessarily be simultaneously elevatable according to its power; and if it cannot be elevated according to its power, it cannot be elevated according to its essence. This follows the same logic as saying: "if the soul of a brave man is immortal, then every man's soul is immortal; and if not every soul is immortal, then neither is the brave man's." This is because the principle of immortality or mortality is the same in all of them. Therefore, such an argument holds well because of its subject matter, just as if it held by its logical form, for it truly holds by the power of its form when considering the common principle that applies to a specific nature (such as the immortality of the soul). That principle is the same in every soul.

Let us therefore look at the possibility and impossibility of this "assumption" <note>The act of God taking a created nature into union with Himself.</note>. Regarding God’s part, as we said, there is no doubt. But because the capacity on the part of the recipient is unknown to us, it is difficult for us to understand the truth of this question. 

For this reason, there is another position different from the one mentioned above; although it is less common <margin>Another position cited from Henry <note>Likely referring to the theologian Henry of Ghent.</note></margin>, it is more appealing to the mind. Even if it does not seem as true because it is unfamiliar, it is perhaps truer: namely, that no nature is receptive to God in the aforementioned way through mutual indwelling unless it is an intellectual nature. This view pleases me more. 

Holding this opinion for the present, I speak first to the opposing view regarding the incorporeal nature of the rational soul or an angel, and the nature of the body in man insofar as it is ordered toward the soul, like a thing to be perfected is ordered toward its perfection. It is in the body that the soul performs its intellectual operation more effectively (once every accidental hindering disposition is removed) than when it is separated from it. Thus, the whole composite of body and soul, with its intellectual power, is the recipient; the body is the recipient through the mediation of the soul's substance and in relation to that substance, as the soul is an intellectual power. Thus, in no way can something be a recipient of this union if it does not possess an intellectual power—understanding "intellectual power" to include everything in which the "essence of the image" <note>The *Imago Dei* or Image of God, which traditional theology locates in the human intellect and will.</note> principally consists within the substance of the soul.

<summary>The author argues that only intellectual beings (humans and angels) are capable of being united with God in "mutual indwelling." He bases this on the Aristotelian principle that a thing's existence is tied to its ability to perform its highest function, which for humans is the use of the intellect.</summary>

<meta>This page continues a theological discussion regarding the "Assumption" of natures by God—specifically the debate over whether God could unite Himself to an irrational creature (like a stone or an animal) or if he is restricted to intellectual natures like humanity.</meta>

...nor Robert of Colletorto <margin>Robert of Colletorto</margin> <note>original: "Robertus de collotorto"; Robert was a prominent Dominican theologian in the early 14th century.</note> nor Bernard of Gannat <margin>Bernard of Gannat</margin> <note>original: "Bernardus de gannaco"; another influential Dominican scholar of the period.</note>, both of whom I have seen reciting the opinion of Henry <note>Henry of Ghent (d. 1293), one of the most important philosophers of the late Middle Ages.</note>, ever judged it to be heretical or to savor of heresy. Lest they themselves appear to have acted irrationally, I wish to briefly set forth the way in which it seems Henry defends his position.

There are, however, two main reasons against Henry: <margin>Two reasons against Henry</margin>
**The first reason** stands in this: that in God is every principle of <term>substantiating</term> <note>The act of giving a "substance" or individual existence to a nature.</note>, because He is the fullness of all being. Therefore, it seems that He could give individual existence and <term>personality</term> <note>original: "suppositare"; the technical theological term for God acting as the "person" or foundation (supposit) for a nature, as in the Incarnation.</note> to any nature whatsoever. 
**The second reason** is that during the <term>three days</term> <note>original: "triduo"; the period between Christ's death on the Cross and his Resurrection.</note> God sustained the body that was in the tomb, which was not a rational [living] being at that time. And just as He sustained it for those three days, He could have sustained it for as long as He wished.

These are the two main foundations of the opposing opinion; and Henry himself, as was seen in the recitation of his opinion, brings these against himself.

To the first reason, as we have seen, <margin>Solution to the first</margin> he responds that it is true that the fullness of all being is in God, and every principle of substantiating and providing personality is found most fully in Him. However, this is not the *total* cause of why a nature can be assumed [by God]; rather, it is a "co-cause." For if that power were not in the one assuming, He could not assume. But beyond this, something is required in the nature being assumed so that it is "assumable." This is the quality of being in the <note>original: "ratio imaginis"; referring to the "Image of God" found in humans.</note> **image** [of God] and, finally, a supernatural aptitude for being raised to the **beatific operation** <note>The "Beatific Vision," or the direct experience of seeing God in heaven.</note>. Since this is found only in an intellectual nature, it seems appropriate that only such a nature is "assumable." For it seems reasonable that a nature which cannot be raised to the "second act" [spiritual activity] also cannot be raised to the "first" [union with God's person].

By this response, Henry seems to want to maintain that nothing is taken away from **divine omnipotence**. When people place all those powers in God, they conclude only that He *has the power* to sustain a nature in this way. Henry also attributes all of this to God; he does not deny that the reason for what is required on the part of the one assuming [God] is found most fully in Him. Rather, he says that the irrational nature itself is not "assumable"—not because of a defect in divine omnipotence, but rather because of the excellence of the divine nature and the "deformed deficiency" of an irrational nature.

To the second reason, it seems many things can be said: <margin>A manifold solution to the second</margin>
**First** is the response of Henry, <margin>First</margin> who says that He assumed the nature of that body [in the tomb] insofar as it was still ordered toward the intellectual soul. By reason of this ordering, the body itself can be called "intellectual" in a serving and preparatory sense. To answer more completely, it should be said that when it is stated that nothing can be assumed by God except an intellectual nature, it is understood that nothing *besides* that can be assumed as the **primary** thing assumed, or as the whole and adequate subject of the assumption. The body in the three days [of the tomb] was not assumed in that way, but only as a part of the rational nature which was the total and primary thing assumed.

Furthermore, <margin>Second</margin> someone might perhaps say that it was not properly "sustained as a person" in those three days, because a body is not a nature that can be its own person. Consequently, one might argue not improbably that terminating the dependence of that body's nature is not the same as giving it personality. Otherwise, anything that supports the weight or dependence of a part would be "giving it personality," which is not said. And so, although the **Word** [the Son of God] in those three days terminated that dependence of the body which the whole of humanity would have terminated—by virtue of which the body in the three days communicated to Christ its "property" of lying in the tomb—He did not, however, properly provide personality to the body as He would to a human nature. The most evident sign of this is that the nature of that body did not communicate the property of being a "body" to Christ in those three days in the same way that the human nature had communicated it to Him—and still communicates it—concretely as a "man."

->## FIFTH QUESTION ON NATURAL MAGIC AND THE KABBALAH OF THE HEBREWS.<-

$\quad$ The fourth conclusion condemned by those men was this: **No science makes us more certain of the divinity of Christ than magic and Kabbalah.**
$\quad$ In explaining this conclusion, I said that among the sciences—which are "sciences" in such a way that they do not rely on revelation through their method of proceeding, their principles, or their conclusions—there is none that makes us more certain (in the way that sciences discovered by humans can provide certainty) than that **magic** which is a part of natural science, and that part of **Kabbalah** which is a science and not <term>revealed theology</term>. <note>The author is distinguishing between human intellectual systems like "Natural Magic" and knowledge directly given by God via scripture or tradition.</note> These masters said that my explanation did not fit the purpose of the words of the aforementioned conclusion, and that the conclusion **by its literal force** was false, erroneous, and heretical. Let us look at how many things in their condemnation deserve to be condemned, point by point. First <margin>First</margin>, let them tell me how my explanation could more closely fit the purpose of the words of my conclusion. For what is in that explanation other than explicitly declaring the force of each individual term placed in the conclusion? For there, I first explain what I mean by "science" when I say "no science," and what I mean by "to make certain," and by "magic," and by "Kabbalah." I do not see what remains to be further explained. Second <margin>Second</margin>, I want to show that not only is it not false and heretical by its literal force, but rather that its opposite is false and, according to them, totally heretical. For the said conclusion is a negative one, which is explained <term>disjunctively</term> <note>A logical statement using "or" (either/or)</note> through three categorical statements like this: "No non-revealed science etc., other than magic and Kabbalah, makes us certain of the divinity of Christ; OR magic and Kabbalah do not make us certain etc.; OR magic and Kabbalah make us more certain of the deity of Christ than other non-revealed sciences." Now, this disjunction is true and orthodox because it has at least one true part. And so it is now clear that by the literal force of the words, it is not false. But it is also clear that its opposite, according to them, would be heretical. For the opposite of this statement—"no non-revealed science etc. makes us more certain etc."—is this: "Some non-revealed science makes us more..."

<meta>This page continues the author's defense of his "magical conclusions," specifically addressing the linguistic ambiguity of the word "magic" and how his use of "natural magic" differs from forbidden sorcery.</meta>

...nor can any scandal arise from the ambiguity of this name "magic." Having distinguished it in such a way—approving of "natural magic" while rejecting that which is superstitious and diabolical—it is not only not a cause for scandal, but can even be a means of edification for simple people.

Among these people, I have seen many who, hearing that the Magi <note>The Three Wise Men or "Kings" from the biblical Nativity story.</note> came to worship Christ, <margin>Note</margin> and believing that this name "magi" means nothing other than "necromancers" <note>Those who practice communication with the dead or demonic spirits.</note>, take this as an argument that magic is not forbidden, nor against the faith of Christ, since practitioners of magic were the very first to worship Christ himself. It is useful, therefore, to have taught the faithful so that when they hear the word "magus," they do not always assume it means a worshiper of demons. And when they hear that among the Persians, magi were held in the highest honor and reverence for their learning and wisdom, they should know that those men were philosophers, not necromancers. For all nations have always pursued and detested necromancers as destructive, harmful, and indeed pestilential to the people, casting them out and holding them in ill repute.

Similarly, when they read that Albert <margin>Albert <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a highly influential medieval scholar and theologian known for his work in the natural sciences.</note></margin> spent much time on natural magic among his experiments, they should understand this as referring to that which is not forbidden. Otherwise, following the example of such a great man, they might devote themselves to forbidden arts, presuming that what was permitted to him is also permitted to them.

Therefore, our magical conclusions remove scandals from the minds of the faithful rather than creating them. For if they ever read in the works of the Doctors <note>The authoritative theologians of the Church.</note> that all magic is forbidden, they will immediately understand from the reasons for that prohibition that those authors are speaking only of the kind that involves commerce with demons, and that they intend nothing regarding natural magic. For, as Hilary <margin>Hilary <note>St. Hilary of Poitiers, a 4th-century bishop and theologian.</note></margin> says, "the understanding of what is said must be derived from the reasons for saying it." <note>original Latin: "intelligentia dictorum ex causis assumenda dicendi"</note>

But if they wish to resort to the strict force of words, they can know from logic <term>dialectics: the formal art of logical argument and terminology</term> that a negation or distribution of a multi-valued term does not negate or distribute it for every underlying instance of every meaning collectively. Therefore, since this term "magic" is ambiguous—referring to both the superstitious and the natural—a general rule applied to it will not apply to every possible meaning at once. Instead, from the statement "all magic is forbidden," it will only be understood that all types of superstitious magic—which are all grouped under one name and one definition—are forbidden. For many types are indeed forbidden; and all these things are clear and lucid even to those who are only moderately learned.

Therefore, my magical conclusions should in no way have been suspicious to these masters. As I said in my first conclusion, I reject all magic forbidden by the Church, condemning and detesting it, and protesting that I speak only of natural magic. I declared this more explicitly through a specific conclusion, stating that through this magic we perform nothing except by activating or uniting natural virtues.

For so says the eleventh of the magical conclusions: "The wonders of the magical art exist only through the union and activation of those things which exist seed-like and separately in nature." <note>original Latin: "Mirabilia artis magice non sunt nisi per unionem & actuationem eorum quae seminaliter & separate sunt in natura"</note> And it is the same as what I said in the thirteenth conclusion: that to practice magic is nothing other than "to marry the world." <note>original Latin: "magiam operari non est aliud quam maritare mundum"</note>

I intend for the aforementioned specification and restriction of my meaning—limiting it to natural magic—to be applied to every individual conclusion. Thus, when I speak of the activity of characters and figures <note>Symbols, shapes, or inscriptions used in esoteric practices believed to have natural resonances.</note> in a magical work, I am speaking of their true and natural activity. For it is clear that they possess such power according to all philosophers, both in their action and in their manner of acting and being acted upon. And although, according to the Peripatetics <term>Peripatetics: followers of Aristotle's philosophy</term>, they are of far less activity and power than are...

These are Hilary's words verbatim. From this, it is most clearly evident that number provides power and efficiency.

<meta>This page continues the argument regarding the "Rule of Faith" and the importance of apostolic succession in counteracting heretical teachings. It specifically focuses on the Church of Rome as a primary example of preserved tradition.</meta>

# On the Tradition of the Apostles

The **tradition** of the **Apostles**, <note>original: "traditionem Apostolorum"</note> which has been made clear in all the world, is present in every church for all who wish to see the truth. We are able to list those who were **ordained** as bishops by the Apostles and their **successors** even down to our own time. These men neither taught nor knew anything like the frenzied schemes of the heretics. 

Yet, if the Apostles had known any **hidden mysteries**—which they used to teach the "perfect" privately and apart from the rest—they would have surely delivered them especially to those to whom they were committing the churches themselves. For they desired that these men, whom they left behind as their **successors** and to whom they gave over their own office of authority, should be **perfect** and **blameless** <note>original: "perfectos et irreprehensibiles"</note> in all things. If these men acted correctly, it would be a great benefit; but if they failed, it would be the greatest calamity.

Since it would be far too long in a volume such as this to list the successions of **all** the churches, we shall confound all those who—in whatever manner, whether through self-satisfaction, vainglory, blindness, or wicked opinion—assemble in unauthorized meetings. We do this by pointing to the tradition of the greatest, oldest, and most famous church, founded and established at **Rome** by the two most glorious Apostles, **Peter and Paul**. 

By pointing to the **tradition** which this church has from the Apostles, and the faith which she announces to all people, which has come down to us through the **succession** of bishops, we put to shame all those who stray from the truth. For with this church, because of its superior origin, it is necessary that every church should agree—that is, the faithful from everywhere—since in her the tradition from the Apostles has always been preserved by those who are from everywhere.

The blessed Apostles, having founded and built up the church, committed the office of the <term>episcopate</term> <note>The office or tenure of a bishop, from the Greek 'episkopos' meaning 'overseer'.</note> into the hands of **Linus**. Paul makes mention of this Linus in the Epistles to Timothy. To him succeeded **Anacletus**; and after him, in the third place from the Apostles, **Clement** was allotted the bishopric. 

This man, Clement, had seen the blessed Apostles and had moved among them. He might be said to have the preaching of the Apostles still echoing in his ears, and their **tradition** before his eyes. Nor was he alone in this, for there were many still remaining who had been taught by the Apostles. 

In the time of this **Clement**, no small dissension having occurred among the brothers at Corinth, the Church in Rome sent a most powerful letter to the Corinthians, exhorting them to peace and renewing their faith, and declaring the **tradition** which it had lately received from the Apostles. 

This tradition proclaims that there is one God Almighty, Maker of heaven and earth, Creator of man, who brought on the flood, and called Abraham, who led the people out of the land of Egypt, spoke with Moses, set forth the law, sent the prophets, and who has prepared fire for the devil and his angels. From this very document, those who wish to do so can learn that He, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, is announced by the churches, and can also understand the apostolic tradition of the church, since this letter is older than those who now teach falsely and **invent** <note>original: "confictum"</note> another God above the Creator.

To this **Clement** succeeded Evaristus, and to Evaristus, Alexander; then Sixtus was appointed the sixth from the Apostles, and after him Telesphorus, who suffered martyrdom gloriously; then Hyginus; after him, Pius; then Anicetus. Soter having succeeded Anicetus, **Eleutherius** now, in the twelfth place from the Apostles, holds the inheritance of the episcopate. In this order, and by this **succession**, the ecclesiastical tradition from the Apostles and the preaching of the truth have come down to us. 

And this is the most abundant proof that there is one and the same vivifying faith, which has been preserved in the Church from the Apostles until now, and **communicated** <note>original: "cõicarentur"</note> in truth. This is **not a fabrication**, but the **true exposition** of the scriptures according to the succession of the bishops.

Moreover, the spiritual law pertains to him who, according to Paul, is a viewer of things in secret, not to him who looks at what is manifest. As for their claim that they wonder why the doctors of the Church never made mention of this doctrine, we have shown sufficiently above that Hilary, Origen, and Ezra—and alongside them Paul and the Gospel—remembered this science. 

It should also be noted that you will never, or very rarely, find any of our doctors—I speak of the ancients—citing any of the Hebrews by name. Instead, you will see them speaking only in general terms, saying: "so the Hebrews say," or "this is the opinion of the Hebrews." Indeed, I do not remember finding this except once in Origen, who cites the patriarch Huillus, his contemporary. Therefore, it is no wonder if you never hear the authors of the Kabbalah cited by them by name. 

However, we see our doctors placing such trust in the testimony of the Hebrews that, as our Jerome says: when they wish to prove what they say—especially Eusebius, Origen, and Clement, and many others—they always refer back to the Hebrews, saying: *"a Hebrew reported to me," "I heard from a Hebrew,"* or *"this is the opinion of the Hebrews."* <note>original: "referebat mihi hebreus. audiui ab hebreo. hebreorū ista snĩa est."</note> And Jerome himself even calls them "masters," saying: *"this is the opinion of the masters."* <note>original: "hec ē snĩa magistroꝝ"</note> There should be no doubt that they mean the teachers of the Kabbalah, which can be demonstrated by clear reason. 

For the entire school of the Hebrews is divided into three sects: into the Philosophers, into the Kabbalists, and into the Talmudists <note><term>Talmuticos</term>: followers of the Talmud, the body of Jewish civil and ceremonial law.</note>. It is not to be believed that the Talmudists were cited by our ancient doctors, both because Clement and many others who cite the Hebrews lived before the composition of the Talmud itself (which was more than 500 years after Christ's death), and because the Talmudic doctrine was entirely fabricated by the Hebrews themselves against us, as they were already fighting against Christians. Therefore, our ancestors would not have paid such honor to that doctrine as to think something said by them was particularly firm when corroborated by the testimony of the Jews. 

Likewise, it is certain they do not cite the philosophers, because those who began to explain the Bible according to philosophy <note>the rationalist Jewish tradition</note> began only a short time ago. For the first was Rabbi Moses of Egypt <note>Maimonides</note>, in whose lifetime Averroes of Cordoba flourished; and three hundred years have not yet passed since the death of Averroes. <margin>The first and true Kabbalah</margin>

<margin>The Hebrews honored two sciences with the name of Kabbalah. The Art of Raymond</margin>

Catholics grant so much from the testimony of Jerome <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the scholar responsible for the Vulgate Latin Bible</note>, and they so thoroughly approve of it, that it is the very thing which our own teachers confess and believe was revealed by God to Moses, and from Moses through a line of succession to other wise men. It is this which, because of this manner of transmission, is called <term>Kabbalah</term> <note>From the Hebrew root *QBL*, meaning "to receive"; it refers to an oral tradition received from a predecessor</note>, which I often see designated by our authors in this way: "as the ancient tradition says." This is the first and true Kabbalah, of which I believe I was the first among the Latins to have made explicit mention. It is the one I use in my <term>conclusions</term> <note>Refers to the author's "900 Theses," intended for public debate in 1487</note> which, since I set them forth expressly against the Hebrews for the confirmation of our faith, I do not know how these masters could have held as suspect in the faith.

But because this way of transmitting by succession, which is called "kabbalistic," seems to suit every secret and mystical matter, it is for this reason that the Hebrews have usurped the term so that they call every science that is held among them as secret and hidden "Kabbalah." Thus, everything knowable that is obtained from some source through a hidden path is said to be obtained "through the way of Kabbalah."

In general, however, they have honored two sciences with this name also. One is called <note>original: *Harsit*—likely a corruption of *Ars* or a Hebrew term</note> that is, the **art of combining**. This is a certain way of proceeding in the sciences, and it is something similar to what is called among our people the **Art of Raymond** <note>Raymond Lull (c. 1232–1315), a philosopher who created a logical system using rotating disks to combine concepts and discover universal truths</note>, although they perhaps proceed in a different way.

The other is about the powers of superior things that are above the moon, and it is the highest part of **natural magic**. Both of these are also called Kabbalah among the Hebrews for the reason already stated, and we have also sometimes made mention of both of these in our conclusions. For that "art of combining" is what I call in my conclusions the **alphabetic revolution** <note>A technique of rearranging or substituting letters to find hidden meanings in text</note>. And this other one, which concerns the powers of superior things, can be understood in one way as a part of natural magic; in another way, as a thing distinct from it, it is that of which I speak in the present conclusion, saying that it helps us in the knowledge of the divinity of Christ in the manner already declared.

And although the name "Kabbalah" does not suit these two sciences by its primary and proper definition, it could nevertheless be applied to them metaphorically. Truly, just as long ago the <term>Magi</term> <note>original: *magi*—originally meaning Persian priest-scientists, but later evolving into the word "magician"</note> meant only wise men, but later necromancers and diabolical men—falsely claiming for themselves the name of a wise man—called themselves "Magi," so also certain people among the Hebrews, promising divine things through false and vain superstitions (indeed, in truth differing almost not at all from necromancers), said that they possessed the secret names of God and the powers by which they might bind demons and perform miracles, and that Christ performed miracles in no other way. These people falsely claimed the name "Kabbalists" for themselves, saying that their art was that true Kabbalah which God revealed to Moses. Just as necromancers also say that they received their incantations and brutalities from Solomon, Adam, Enoch, and similar figures.

This "falsely named Kabbalah," however, I have not only not approved in my conclusions or followed, but have expressly rejected, setting forth a specific conclusion directly against that which says the miracles of Christ could not be done through the way of Kabbalah. Let these things suffice for the present conclusion, which would require a special book if we wished to declare exactly what natural magic and what Kabbalah are. Here it is enough to have shown that nothing is contained in them which is repugnant to the Catholic and orthodox faith.

<meta>This page continues a scholastic disputation regarding the theology of the Eucharist. ->### SIXTH QUESTION CONCERNING THE SACRAMENT OF THE EUCHARIST.<-

**IF THE COMMON PATH** regarding the possibility of <term>assumption into a person</term> <note>original: "suppositationis"; the theological concept of a nature (like humanity) being "taken up" and supported by a divine Person (like the Word)</note> with respect to any creature is held, I say that without the conversion of the substance of bread into the body of Christ, or the annihilation of the "bread-ness," it is possible for the body of Christ to be on the altar according to the truth of the sacrament. This is said when speaking of what is *possible*, not of what is *actually the case*. By this conclusion, I do not intend to say that bread is *not* converted into the body of Christ, or that the body of Christ is in fact in the sacrament—as it was actually instituted by Christ—by having the body of Christ present alongside bread that has been assumed or supported by the Word <note>The "Word" refers to the Second Person of the Trinity (the Son)</note>. I expressly reject those claims regarding the "actual state" at the end of the conclusion where it says "this is said of what is possible, not of what is actually the case." Here, I want the term "possible" to refer not only to the preceding statement about Christ assuming the bread, but also to the truth of the sacrament of the Eucharist and to the sacrament itself; indeed, even to the presence of Christ's body along with the assumed bread. Thus, perhaps it would not be necessary that, by virtue of this "assumption" of the bread by the incarnate Word, the bread would become the body of Christ which he already took from the Virgin. Nevertheless, it is possible that he would be on the altar together with the bread if it were assumed by Christ. 

I speak, therefore, in the present conclusion about a *possible* sacrament, and its *possible* truth, and the *possible* presence of Christ's body together with this "assumable" bread. Therefore, I wonder why the present conclusion was condemned as erroneous on the grounds that the aforementioned things are false regarding the sacrament of the Eucharist as already instituted (which they claim I am speaking about), when I explicitly profess in the conclusion to be speaking about a *possible* sacrament and its *possible* truth. Therefore, let them consider the words of the conclusion more attentively before they condemn a conclusion that so expressly rejects the meaning they are condemning. Indeed, let them consider that their own determination can hardly be defended from error. For if it were the case that the conclusion intended to uphold the truth of the sacrament according to Christ’s institution as the Church holds it (as they say), then it would be not only "erroneous" but simply heretical. However, if the meaning of the conclusion is the one explained by me, it is not only not erroneous in faith, but rather it is erroneous to say the opposite! For there are many things which are heretical if said to be "actually the case," yet the opposite of which would be heretical if said to be "possible." For example, to say that the Father is incarnate <note>The Father being "incarnate" would mean the First Person of the Trinity became man, which contradicts the dogma that only the Son became man</note> as a matter of fact is heretical; but to say the Father *could* be incarnate is not only not heretical, but it is heretical to say the opposite <note>meaning, it is heretical to limit God's power by saying He *could not* have done so if He chose</note>. 

<margin>Question</margin> And let these things suffice for the clarification of the conclusion and its defense. But for the sake of scholastic exercise, leaving aside my conclusion, let us see whether this might be true: that the body of Christ could be saved as being on the altar through another mode than through the conversion of the bread into itself. Namely, through the <term>sustenance of the bread-ness</term> <note>original: "substentationem paneitatis"; the idea that the "essence" of the bread remains while being supported by a divine person</note> in the divine Person together with the assumed humanity, so that there would be one Person in three natures: namely, divinity, humanity, and bread-ness. By reason of this one Person, each nature could be predicated of the others in relation to that Person; there would be a <term>communication of properties</term> <note>original: "comunicatio idiomatum"; a theological rule where properties of one nature, like "being bread," could be attributed to the person, "God"</note> such that "God is bread" and "man is bread" and vice versa. And thus, "Christ as man" is on the altar just as "Christ as bread" is on the altar, and so on. And this would be "sacramentally" or by virtue of the sacrament, if the power for this were given to it.

<summary>The author defends a theoretical proposition that God could have chosen to remain present in the Eucharist by "assuming" the nature of bread (similar to how he assumed human nature) rather than by changing the bread into his body. He emphasizes that while this is not what the Church teaches is happening, it is a logical possibility that cannot be condemned without limiting God's absolute power.</summary>

Secondly, it is argued <margin>Second argument.</margin> because, according to **Augustine** in his letter to Volusianus, in miraculous things, the entire reason for the deed is the power of the Doer. To restrict this wonderful sacrament to a specific mode of defense that is not expressly found in the canon of Scripture or the determination of the Church is to restrict divine power to the capacity of our intellect—which is dangerous. It is also against **Augustine**, who says in the same place: "If a reason is sought, it will not be a miracle; if an example is provided, it will not be unique." <note>original Latin: "Si ratio queritur non erit mirabile si exemplū ponitur non erit singulare."</note> Let us grant that God can do something that we must confess we cannot investigate.

Thirdly, it is argued <margin>Third argument</margin> because that whose opposite is not clearly found in the sayings of the Saints can much more easily be held as a possibility. Likewise, **Ambrose** <margin>Ambrose</margin> says that the power of God, which creates creatures from nothing, here "changes the creatures." And other authorities who say that the bread and wine do not remain after consecration but are converted, are explained thus: that the "bread" which was bread does not remain, even though the same "bread-ness" exists, because it now exists through a different person <term>suppositum</term>. This term "bread" signifies a person in the nature of bread-ness, and this does not remain. 

However, there is a great difference between saying that the bread-ness remains "hypostatized" <note>existing as a reality within a Person (Hypostasis).</note> in the divine person, and that it remains in its own person; because in this second way, there would be no "communication of properties" <term>communicatio idiomatum | the theological doctrine that the attributes of both the divine and human natures are predicated of the one person of Christ</term>, which occurs in the first way. However, I believe these authorities are entirely against those who posit this as a matter of fact and as being the case, rather than only as a possibility.

This is because the assumption of breadness into the subject of the Word is a greater difficulty than creation itself, given that the divine Being is further removed from the nature of breadness (to which it is said to be communicated in the "assumption") than "being" is from "non-being." And yet, the power of creation cannot be shared with a creature through its own operating or co-operating; therefore, neither can the power for such an assumption.

<margin>Eighth.</margin> Furthermore, if that were granted, after the reception of the sacrament, the priest would no longer be fasting, and it would not be a spiritual food only, but also a physical one. This is contrary to the dignity of the sacrament. <note>In medieval theology, the Eucharistic fast required that the priest's stomach be empty of ordinary food; if the bread remained physically "bread" after the union, it would technically break the ritual fast.</note>

<margin>Ninth.</margin> Likewise, Christ would be discarding something after he had assumed it into the unity of his subject, because he would assume "breadness," which he would then discard when the bread is converted into the members of the body <note>i.e., when the bread is digested and becomes part of the physical body.</note>.

Because God is man and man is God, they share their "properties" <term>idiomata: the communication of properties, where attributes of the human nature are attributed to the divine person and vice versa</term>: where God is, there is the man. <meta>This page continues a complex scholastic argument regarding the metaphysics of the Eucharist, specifically exploring how the Body of Christ can "support" the qualities of bread through the power of the Divine Word (the second person of the Trinity).</meta>

[The Word] does not give substance to the assumed nature <note>The "assumed nature" refers to the human nature taken on by God in the person of Jesus.</note> except by reason of its own infinite being. To whatever nature it draws to itself in union and association, and to whichever nature it communicates its infinite being, it also communicates the power to support another nature united to it. In this same way, a substance, insofar as it draws an accident <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a quality (like color or shape) that cannot exist on its own but must exist in a substance.</note> to its own being—because an accident is not a "being" except insofar as it belongs to a being—gives to that accident the power to support another accident coming upon it (just as an "act" comes to "potentiality") within itself and within its own being. 

Therefore, the Body, taken as a part that is united to and supported by the Word in its own being—which is the being of the Word communicated to it—is able to give substance within itself to the nature of bread (which is capable of being assumed and has the quality of an accident). For it is supposed that just as God gives the mode of substance to accidents, so He can give the mode of an accident to "breadness" <note>original: "paneitati"; the essential quality of being bread</note> by supporting it in something else that relates to it as a subject. Nor does it matter for this purpose whether the subject is a complete species or not, because sometimes the subject of an accident is incomplete as a species, such as a head or a hand. 

Just as God produces some creatures directly and others through intermediaries, and just as He terminates some creatures in Himself as their final end through others, so also the Word can terminate in Himself—as the supporting <term>suppositum|the individual, self-subsisting subject or "person" that carries a nature</term>—some creature through the mediation of another. And just as the creatures through which God produces things are called "producers," and those through which He terminates things in Himself as their end are called "ends" or "sub-ends," so the creature through which the Word gives substance to another will be said to "substantiate." 

Therefore, by reason of such substantiation in the body of Christ as a "quasi-subject" and immediate support, it will be said in concrete terms that "the bread is the body" and vice versa, just as "the Son of God is man" and vice versa. And they will share their <term>properties|specifically the "communication of idioms," where attributes of one nature are predicated of the other</term> in the manner described, like a surface and a colored object. For "bread" stands for that which supports "breadness," just as "white" stands for that which supports "whiteness." 

For as the <margin>Aristotle</margin> Philosopher says in the first book of the *Topics*, "white" is a body having such a color. <margin>Damascene</margin> Damascene <note>John of Damascus, an 8th-century theologian who wrote on the nature of Christ.</note> says in Book 3, Chapter 11: "God is He who has a divine nature, and man is he who has a human nature," and so on for the rest. And just as it makes no difference for something to be "white" whether the thing in which the whiteness is supported is a complete species or not, so it makes no difference for something to be called "bread" whether that which is the "breadness" is supported—that is, immediately substantiated—is a complete species or incomplete, or a nature or a part of a nature. 

<margin>Against.</margin> **On the contrary:** because an assumed nature or part of an assumed nature does not have the character of a <term>suppositum</term>, nor does it have the "being of subsistence" in itself; for although the being of the Word is communicated to it, yet insofar as it belongs to the nature, it is not the "being of subsistence," but rather of "existence in another." Therefore, the assumed nature, as it is united, cannot support another nature in itself, nor draw it to the <term>suppositum</term>, since it does not itself have the character of a <term>suppositum</term>. 

<margin>Response.</margin> **Response:** But if this concludes the matter, would it not also conclude that a surface cannot substantiate color in itself? For the "being" that belongs to subsistence regarding substance—when communicated to an accident—is one of "existence," and thus a surface could not be the subject of color because the surface itself is an accident. Should we say that the being of the Word, as it belongs to the assumed humanity in relation to the Word, is one of "existence," but as it belongs to that same humanity in relation to "breadness," it is one of "subsistence"? However, as it belongs to the nature assumed last, it is "existence" simply, just as might be said of a surface. 

<margin>Against again.</margin> **But against the aforementioned things, it is argued again:** a nature is immediately united to the <term>suppositum</term>...

<margin>How an accident depends on substance.</margin> For an accident depends on a substance only regarding its existence—at least according to the common way—not according to its essence. Therefore, although the essence of the bread remains, since the <term>subsistence</term> of the bread (through which the accidents subsisted) ceases to be there, it remains that the accidents subsist by themselves, unless we posit that they migrate from one subject to another.

<margin>Second.</margin> Second, it is argued that this position is more fitting because more difficulties are resolved by it. For here, the only difficulty is regarding the union. <meta>This page continues a dense scholastic debate regarding the metaphysics of the Eucharist, specifically focusing on the difference between the "annihilation" of the bread versus its "conversion" into the Body of Christ. The text engages with the arguments of Durandus of Saint-Pourçain, a prominent medieval theologian.</meta>

...having been made capable of being <term>assumed</term><note>In theology, "assumption" refers to a higher nature (like the Divine Word) taking a lower nature (like humanity) into its own personal existence.</note> into a new personal existence [suppositum], that which simply ceases to be is annihilated. Thus, its reproduction would be a creation, and annihilation is entirely irrelevant to this, whether one posits that something succeeds it or nothing succeeds it, because this is entirely external to the thing which ceases to exist.

<margin>Conversion.</margin>
However, that which remains according to its essence, but loses its own personal existence [suppositum] and passes into the existence of another person, is truly **converted**, and truly becomes that person. This is the true nature of conversion, in which two things are understood in the converted object:

<margin>The nature of conversion.</margin>
first, that it remains in its essence (which distinguishes it from something annihilated), and second, that it becomes something else by reason of its personhood (which distinguishes it from something that remains unconverted). And as it becomes something else, it lets go of the nature of its own personhood, and by this, it is distinguished from something merely "assumed." Holding the common view of conversion, however, the bread is not converted but annihilated. Those who wish to maintain that it is a conversion and not an annihilation seem to satisfy the problem with words rather than with reality.

Hence, many from that school of thought have conceded that it is an annihilation, etc.

<margin>Arguments for the opposing/true side.</margin>
On the contrary, for the true side, it is argued that the opinion claiming the sacrament of the Eucharist is actually brought about by the "assumption" of <term>bread-ness</term><note>original: "paneitatis"; the essential quality or substance of being bread.</note> is inappropriate and irrational.

<margin>The first argument of Durandus.</margin>
First, **Durandus**<note>Durandus of Saint-Pourçain (c. 1275–1334) was a Dominican theologian known as the "Resolute Doctor" for his independent thinking.</note> argues that it is ridiculous for one nature—or rather many—to be assumed by the divine person every day and then set aside every day. This would be the case if the substance of the bread in this sacrament were newly assumed, because there would be as many "assumptions" as there are consecrations, and as many "depositions" [settings aside] as there are receptions of the sacrament.

<margin>Response.</margin>
But perhaps this "ridiculousness" does not prove the falsity of the premise.

<margin>Second [argument].</margin>
Second, it is argued that it seems impossible for such an assumption to occur through some created medium, as the aforementioned opinion suggests. For that medium would have to act either as the <term>efficient cause</term><note>The agent that brings something into being.</note> of the assumption or as its end-point. But nothing created can stand in relation to the "assumption" in either of these ways, therefore, etc.

The minor premise is proven because it is clear that nothing created can be the efficient cause of such an assumption. This is because such an assumption happens when a thing loses its own natural way of being and takes on another; it seems only the **Author of Nature** [God], who alone established the natures of things, can do this. Thus, He alone seems able to change them.

<margin>Response.</margin>
This argument of Durandus perhaps shows that a created thing cannot be the *principal* efficient cause. By the same logic, it seems that nothing created can be the end-point of such an assumption, because something cannot be attributed to a nature if it is above nature and the entire course of nature. This [act] is to provide the underlying support [subsistence] for another nature which is born to subsist in itself.

And perhaps this erroneous opinion mentioned above would believe it could escape [these arguments] through the points made earlier. For falsehood is not always easily convicted of its own falsity by evident reasoning; so weak is the light of our intellect, being as it is the lowest within the hierarchy of intellectual natures.

<margin>Third [argument]. Body. As a part. As a whole.</margin>
Furthermore, Durandus argues as follows: whatever may be said about the position of such an assumption, it is nonetheless entirely inappropriate for it to occur by means of a "body-part." For a body—when understood as a part of human nature, assuming there is only one <term>form</term><note>In Aristotelian thought, the "form" is the organizing principle that makes matter into a specific thing (like a human).</note> in a human—cannot name only the matter. Instead, it must necessarily name the composite of matter and the form that gives it bodily existence. It is necessary that "human body" refers to the whole in reality and not just a part, even if, conceptually, it can name a part because the soul provides all...

For by the same reasoning that the body of Christ would be in the sacrament of the altar through the assumption of the substance of the bread, by that same reasoning the blood would be in this sacrament through the assumption of the substance of the wine. But this is not true, as will be proven, therefore etc. 

The premise is proven because if the blood of Christ were in this sacrament through the assumption of the substance of the wine, just as is posited for the body of Christ through the assumption of the substance of the bread, then it would follow that just as the bread is assumed by means of the body (which belongs to the unity of the <term>person</term> <note>original: "suppositum"; the individual substance or "subject" that acts</note> who assumes it), so the wine would be assumed by means of the blood belonging to the unity of the person who assumes it. Now, it is clear that the blood of Christ does not belong to the identity of the person of Christ, since blood is not yet under the human form, but is a fluid <note>original: "humor"; following medieval biology, blood was seen as a transitional substance being processed into flesh</note> on the way to being converted so that it may come under the human form. Therefore, it cannot be assumed by the person of Christ by means of the blood, unless perhaps it were said that in every performance of this sacrament there was an immediate assumption of Christ's blood, and an assumption of the wine by means of that blood. In this way, every day there would be an assumption of a new nature—namely, blood—without any relationship to the assumed nature of the bread (which others deny), and the wine would be assumed through that. 

But in this matter, many would perhaps not only reject the reasoning of Durandus [margin] Response [/margin] but would rebuke him no less than the aforementioned opinion—specifically regarding his claim of the non-assumption and lack of <term>hypostatic union</term> <note>The union of divine and human natures in the one person of Christ</note> of the blood of Christ shed on the cross and presented in the sacrament to the person of the Son. For it seems that according to this view, that blood would not have been a sufficient price for the redemption of the human race, since it would not have been united personally to the divinity. 

Wherefore [margin] Saint Thomas [/margin] Saint Thomas Aquinas, in his sixth book of *Quodlibetal Questions*, question 6, says: "The blood of Christ shed in the Passion sanctified the human race, according to the end of the letter to the Hebrews: 'Jesus, that he might sanctify the people through his own blood, suffered outside the gate.' [Hebrews 13:12] Furthermore, the humanity of Christ possessed life-giving power from the power of the Word <note>The "Word" or Logos: the Second Person of the Trinity</note> united to it," as [margin] Damascene [/margin] John of Damascus says in his third book. Whence it is manifest that the blood shed in the Passion, which was the supreme source of salvation, was united to the divinity, and therefore it was necessary that in the Resurrection it be joined to the other parts of his humanity, etc. Thus says Thomas.

This is clear because the word "this" always refers to the same numerical thing that preceded it. But Christ, in instituting this sacrament, said "This..."

It is not there actually because the assumption of two natures by one Person is not enough for one nature to be wherever the other is. For if the Person of the Son had, from the beginning, assumed the humanity of Peter in Rome and of Paul in Judea, it would not follow that wherever Peter was, Paul would be there too, and vice-versa—except in regard to the Person, which is predicated of both and of whom both are predicated <term>concretely|referring to the whole person rather than an abstract quality</term>. 

Similarly, granted that the Person of the Son assumed both humanity and bread-nature, it does not follow that where the nature of bread is, there the nature of humanity must be. Nor, by reason of the Person, could it be said that where the bread is, there is the body of Christ because of the communication of idioms; for according to that opinion, the name of the Person does not receive the predication of the "assumed bread" nor of the "parts of the body." For it is not true to say, according to those thinkers, that the Son of God is "bread" or a "body" which is a part. Therefore, by reason of a common Person, one cannot be predicated of the other so that one is said to be the other, or one is said to be where the other is. 

Nor is it like the "tooth of an Ethiopian" and its whiteness, where the tooth is called white and the white thing is called a tooth, and where one is, the other is—because this is because they are one in their underlying subject, and consequently indistinguishable in subject and place. the assumed bread-nature. And whatever the case may be regarding this argument, this much is true: that just as it does not follow by necessity, it nevertheless follows by possibility, etc.

From these words, it seems that it is not the intention of Damascene that the substance of the bread and wine remain and are "assumed" by the divine person, but that they pass into the body and blood of Christ and are thus united to the divinity. 

However, those <note>the opponents of this view</note> insist, <margin>Objection.</margin> asking how that which is annihilated—that is, it truly ceases to be in itself—is united? And they insist on that comparison of the coal, in which it is said that just as a coal is not simple wood but wood united to fire, so the bread of communion is not simple bread but bread united to the divinity. And it is said <margin>Solution.</margin> that the coal and fire are not the same person; however, one passes into the other through its corruption. Thus the bread of communion is not one person with the divinity, but by its ceasing to be, it passes into the body of Christ which is united [to the divinity].

Those things which are inconsistent, I judge should be cast out and rejected.

->### SEVENTH QUESTION: ON THE SALVATION OF ORIGEN.<-

It is more reasonable to believe that Origen is saved than to believe that he is damned. <note>Origen of Alexandria (d. 254 AD) was one of the most influential early Christian theologians, but his views on the pre-existence of souls and the eventual salvation of all beings led to fierce debates and posthumous condemnations.</note>

These masters have said that this conclusion is rash, reprehensible, "smelling of heresy," and against the determination of the universal Church. But I, to speak of them more modestly, wish to show that their judgment is not correct, and that this conclusion is not against the determination of the Church; and what is more, even if everything they bring against me were true, it still cannot be said that this conclusion is heretical or "smells of heresy." For a fuller declaration of this matter, there will be seven articles. In the first, it will be seen whether Origen ever wrote or believed any heretical opinion concerning matters of faith. <margin>Seven articles: how to proceed in the declaration of the conclusion.</margin> In the second, granted that he did write such things, whether he wrote them dogmatically, or with firm adherence, or merely in an investigative manner. In the third, granted he wrote with adherence, whether he sinned mortally in writing them so that he could be called a heretic. In the fourth, granted that he wrote and wrote in such a way that he erred, <margin>For the first article.</margin> whether he ever repented for such things. In the fifth, granted that neither his repentance nor his lack of repentance is certain, whether it is more reasonable to believe him damned or saved. <margin>Rufinus, Jerome, Augustine.</margin> In the sixth, what is to be judged from the text of the decrees regarding what the Church has determined about Origen. Rufinus is of the opinion that the heretical dogmas found in the books of Origen were falsely inserted by heretics who corrupted his books, and that they do not represent Origen’s true mind. Jerome feels the opposite. But let us see what probability each opinion holds, and it will perhaps appear that—while preserving the faith <note>original: "salua fide"</note> and fully satisfying all those things which we are bound to believe for the necessity of salvation—one can still freely and probably believe that those principal heresies for which Origen’s sin and subsequent condemnation are proven were not from Origen’s mind. Instead, they were falsely imposed upon him by treacherous heretics who corrupted his books. 

Supporting this side is, first, the authority of Pamphilus the martyr, whose book is circulated in defense of Origen. In this work, the most glorious martyr shows—using Origen’s own words quoted from his books—that Origen held orthodox <note>original: "catholice"; here meaning in accordance with the universal church</note> views on the very points where he is accused of heresy. Jerome, however, denying that this book belongs to Pamphilus, says the following in his responsive apology to Oceanus and Pammachius: "If you say that Origen's books were violated by his enemies to defame him, why should I not be allowed to say that a volume was composed by his friends and followers under the name of Pamphilus, which would vindicate him from infamy through the testimony of a martyr?" From these words, it seems notable that Jerome presents both possibilities as probable, implying that just as Rufinus cannot be proven wrong in saying those books were corrupted, neither can Jerome himself be proven wrong in saying that the book is not by Pamphilus. 

And Jerome adds further down: "The very name 'apology' indicates an excuse. For nothing is defended unless it is accused of a crime." <note>Jerome is arguing that by writing a "defense," one admits there is something wrong that needs defending.</note> But someone might say: "If that is so, then since Jerome labels this very treatise in which he writes these things with the title of 'apology'—in which he defends himself, saying he followed Origen’s teaching but not his dogma—he likewise shows himself to be guilty of a crime, since nothing is defended unless it is accused of a crime." And thus no one could be justly excused if an excuse always presupposes a just accusation. 

But let us now see by what conjectures Jerome is moved to believe the book is not by Pamphilus. The first thing that moves Jerome is that the same things are read in the first book by Eusebius, among those six books he wrote in defense of Origen. The second is that Eusebius himself, when writing the *Life of Pamphilus*, said that Pamphilus wrote no original work of his own. For Jerome says this in his first book against Rufinus, addressed to Pammachius and Marcellus: "Eusebius, Bishop of Caesarea—once the standard-bearer of the Arian <term>Arianism: a heresy holding that Jesus was a created being, not equal to God the Father</term> faction—wrote six books for Origen, a very extensive and elaborate work. And with many testimonies he proved Origen to be orthodox according to him—which is to say, an Arian according to us. Of these, you translate the first book under the name of the martyr [Pamphilus]." And further down: "If this book belongs to Pamphilus, then which of the six books is the first one by Eusebius?" 

Likewise, Eusebius—the friend, herald, and companion of Pamphilus—wrote three most elegant books containing the *Life of Pamphilus*, in the third of which he says this about Pamphilus: "And he himself indeed wrote nothing at all of his own work, except perhaps letters which he sent to friends." To such an extent had this defender of Origen and praiser of Pamphilus humbled himself in his humanity that he says Pamphilus composed nothing at all, not even of his own speech; and he said this after Pamphilus was already crowned with martyrdom, so that you might have no refuge [to claim he wrote it] after the books published by Eusebius...

->### Concerning the book of Pamphilus the Martyr<-

Therefore, it cannot be well understood how the same things read in the book of Pamphilus could also be read in the first book of Eusebius, unless perhaps they shared some common points regarding Origen that did not pertain to the specific point of the conclusion being discussed here. Nor does it seem as marvelous as **Jerome** marvels that **Pamphilus** and **Eusebius** wrote similar things, since, as Jerome himself says, they were close companions <note>The Latin term "contubernales" refers to tent-mates or close associates, emphasizing their shared intellectual life in Caesarea.</note>. Thus, Eusebius could have reported in his own books things he had read in Pamphilus’s work, or, as happens daily, he could have discovered and thought them out for himself through a similar movement of the mind. And these are the points concerning the first book of Eusebius.

However, regarding what Jerome says—that Eusebius writes in the *Life of Pamphilus* that out of humility, Pamphilus wrote nothing of his own work except for letters—and his further point that Eusebius (a defender of Origen and a praiser of Pamphilus) says this: **Rufinus** would perhaps respond that this does not do much to damage his own case. 

<margin>First.</margin> First, because that little treatise by Pamphilus leans more toward the brevity of a letter than toward the scale of a proper book. 

<margin>Second.</margin> Second, because that brief *Apology for Origen* perhaps cannot correctly be called a "personal work," since Pamphilus does not establish any dogma there <note>The author distinguishes between original "dogmatizing" (creating new doctrine) and merely defending an existing person.</note>. Indeed, no universal question is treated there; rather, it deals briefly only with a particular man—namely, Origen—and whether his books were corrupted or not. To write such a thing is not to "compose a personal work," nor is it a matter of his humility lifting itself up by avoiding the name of an author. 

<margin>Third.</margin> Third, it is possible that this book simply did not come to the notice of Eusebius, both because of the book's small size and because of the very humility Eusebius attributes to him; for a man who writes nothing "great" might prefer to hide rather than show off even those thin and tiny things he did write. 

<margin>Fourth.</margin> Fourth, Rufinus will say it is also possible that Eusebius—as a defender of the **Arian** treachery <note>Arianism: A major heresy that claimed Jesus was a created being, not co-eternal with God the Father. The author suggests Eusebius had a motive to lie about the book's authorship.</note>—wished not only to hide the book of the martyr (which deprived his sect of Origen's testimony) but also to act through this indirect testimony of his so that posterity would believe the work was not by Pamphilus. 

Therefore, when Jerome says—as if to strengthen his reasoning—that the "defender of Origen" says Pamphilus wrote nothing, etc., it is actually more against Jerome than for him. This is because, since Eusebius defended Origen not as a Catholic but as an Arian, he could justly be suspected in this matter, as I have said. 

But why is it necessary to labor over these points? Or how can Jerome prove at all from Eusebius's testimony that the *Apology for Origen* is not by Pamphilus, when Eusebius himself, in the sixth book of his *Ecclesiastical History*, says that the defense for Origen was written by the holy martyr Pamphilus? 

Furthermore, when Jerome adds: "What will the letters of Bishop **Theophilus** do? What of **Pope Anastasius**?" and so on, Rufinus would perhaps say that the book of Pamphilus does not fight against their primary intention. For their purpose was to root out from the world those worst heresies and poisonous dogmas, whoever they belonged to, because this pertained to the faith and the strengthening and stability of the Church. Whether those views were actually Origen's (as many believed) or were not, those most religious pontiffs would have cared little. On the contrary, it would perhaps have been desirable and most acceptable to them if it could have been proven by certain and valid arguments that those heretical opinions were *not* believed by Origen; for this would be done for the faith, not against the faith—against heretics, and not for heretics.

The author argues that even if Pamphilus claimed to write nothing but letters, this brief defense might not have been considered a "formal work," and notes that Eusebius's own history contradicts Jerome's claim.</summary>

They relied quite heavily on the testimony of such a great man, who was so highly praised by Catholics, and they defended their own error with his authority. Therefore, Pamphilus’s book would fight against those letters <note>original: "epistolas," referring to Jerome’s polemical letters against Origen's supporters</note> if the heresies of which they were accused were excused within it. However, if the entire effort of that book is to deprive the supporters of those views of such a good patron, then what if those letters follow him? It is certain that they only pursue him as the leader of their school of thought <term>heresiarcham: the founder or leader of a heretical sect</term>. To the points Jerome brings forward in his second book, one might perhaps respond in this way: First, regarding his statement that he himself once believed and even wrote that this was Pamphilus’s book, before he had read in Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), the famous church historian and companion of Pamphilus</note> that Pamphilus had written nothing, and so on. From this statement of Jerome’s, Rufinus might argue against him like this: 

"If, O Jerome, you once believed and wrote that the book you read was indeed by Pamphilus: tell me, I pray, what lies did you read in it? Did you recognize heresies or a favoring of heresies there? Or was it rather truths, or things resembling the truth, that in no way harmed the Catholic faith? If it was false and heretical, how could you be led to believe the author was a Catholic martyr <note>referring to Pamphilus of Caesarea, who died for the faith in 309 AD</note>—someone whose testimony and words no one could suspect of wrongdoing without being scandalous themselves? If, however, it was both Catholic and worthy of a Christian martyr, why do you now condemn those same things and call them fabrications? Why do you say they were spread to introduce heresies? In short, why do you now judge as unworthy of a martyr the very things you once judged worthy? For the text remains the same as what you read then and what you read now. Even if we set aside the author’s name, let us consider the arguments made there in defense of Origen <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–253 AD), a brilliant but controversial early theologian whose works were the center of this dispute</note> on their own merits. If they are evil, why did you then judge them to belong to a holy martyr? If they are good, why are they not accepted as good now, regardless of who wrote them? 

Furthermore, how can you say, O Jerome, that I spread this book to introduce heresies? In that book—as has been said above—nothing else is attempted except to ensure that heretics cannot bolster themselves with Origen’s testimony. This acts to uproot heresy, not to spread it. Moreover, this book is found not only in Latin but in Greek. I, Rufinus, made the Latin version by translating from the Greek. Who published the Greek if not Pamphilus? Certainly not I, Rufinus—especially according to you, who accuse me of ignorance of Greek literature. I could not have written a book so Greek and so eloquent that it matched the style of Eusebius. If another author is suggested, Jerome responds that it belongs to Didymus <note>Didymus the Blind (c. 313–398 AD), a famous Alexandrian theologian who was one of Jerome’s teachers</note> or someone else. Rufinus will insist: 'Whoever that other person may be, I, Rufinus, am no longer the one held guilty of this crime, but another. And if Didymus is a liar and a deceiver according to you, then your own teacher Didymus is a liar—the man you named in your own books as a "seeing prophet," as the "eye of the bride" from the Song of Songs, and as an apostolic man. If he is a liar, it is because he published the Greek text and falsely attributed it to Pamphilus; it is not I, who simply found the Greek under Pamphilus’s name and shared it with Latin speakers under that same author’s name. Nor should you be surprised that I believed Didymus in this matter, since you yourself believed him in his explanations of the Scriptures.' 

As for Jerome’s claim that the Latin version differs from the Greek, Rufinus would say: 'Why do you not produce the passages that were badly translated, O Jerome? Is it so that I cannot defend myself against the charge? You act just as you did when Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), the famous bishop who corresponded with Jerome</note> wrote to you saying that certain parts of your translation from Hebrew were being condemned, yet he did not specify the exact passages.'"

If there are some faults in books, even if you do not know the causes of those faults, you do not immediately judge their authors to be heretics. <meta>This page continues a theological defense of the early Christian scholar Origen, specifically addressing accusations that his teachings on the Trinity and the eventual salvation of all beings (including the devil) were heretical. Jesus Christ, through whom all things [exist]. They deny that the Son of God ought to be professed as God, lest they seem to profess and speak of two gods; and what will they do with this passage of the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul, often called "the Apostle" in this period.</note> in which Christ, through whom all things [exist], is clearly described as being **God over all**? But they do not notice that those who feel this way [err], because just as he did not speak of the one Lord Jesus Christ in such a way that God the Father should not be called Lord, so also he did not speak of God the Father as being the one God in such a way that the Son should not be believed to be God. For the Scripture is true which says: *Know that the Lord himself is God.* <note>Psalm 100:3</note> However, both are one God, because there is no other beginning of divinity for the Son than the Father; rather, as Wisdom says, the Son is the **purest emanation** <note>original: "purissima manatio" — a term used to describe how the Son "flows" from the Father without being a separate being.</note> of that one paternal fountain. Therefore, Christ is God over all things—all those things, without doubt, which we mentioned a little while ago: over principalities, and powers, and virtues, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the one to come. <note>Referencing Ephesians 1:21.</note> Moreover, he who is over all things has no one above himself. For he is not "after" the Father, but "from" the Father.

This same thing concerning the wisdom of God must also be understood regarding the Holy Spirit, where it is said: *The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world*, and *that which contains all things has knowledge <margin>Note.</margin> of the voice.* <note>Wisdom of Solomon 1:7</note> If, therefore, the Son of God is said to be "over all things," and the Holy Spirit is remembered to "contain all things," and God the Father is "from whom all things [come]," then the nature of the Trinity and the **one substance** <term>substance: in Greek "ousia," the essential "stuff" or being of God that the Father, Son, and Spirit share.</term> which is over all things is clearly shown. These are the words of Origen, quoted word-for-word.

And elsewhere, upon that [saying] of Paul, *How then shall they preach unless they are sent?*, <note>Romans 10:15</note> he says: "For there are some who indeed announce and preach concerning the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, but not sincerely or with integrity, as are all the heretics who indeed announce the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, but do not announce them well or faithfully. For they either wrongly separate the Son from the Father, saying the Father is of one nature and the Son of another, or they wrongly confuse them, so that they make God a composite of three, or merely a threefold naming. But those who announce good things well will give to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit their own respective properties; yet they will confess that there is no diversity in substance or nature." These are the words of Origen.

Regarding these words, what could be more **Orthodox** <note>original: "catholicum" — meaning universal or in line with the established church.</note> or more clearly expressed? It is necessary, therefore, that if anything is found written differently in the books of Origen, it is not Origen’s own work, but that of heretics who, through the corruption of his books, wished to have Origen as a patron <margin>For the second [heresy]</margin> of their error.

Regarding the <margin>heresy which to the same [is attributed]</margin> second heresy, there exists such clear testimony that, in my judgment, <margin>objection defense</margin> it can hardly be denied. For in his own letter, Origen himself—even according to the <margin>Origen himself denies</margin> translation of Jerome, who makes mention of that letter—expressly denies that the **devil can <margin>& asserts the contrary.</margin> ever be saved**. He says that not even a madman could say this. Furthermore, <margin>Dialogue of Origen.</note> there exists a dialogue between Origen and Candidus, a follower of the Valentinian doctrine <note>Valentinianism was a major Gnostic movement that Origen fought against.</note>, in which Candidus threw this same error in Origen’s face, and Origen refutes it and denies that he holds this view. And upon that passage of Paul, *Have they stumbled so as to fall?*, Origen says this: looking at this "fall" of which Christ said *I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven*, he denies that Israel has fallen [in that way]. For their conversion will occur at the end of the age, then when the fullness [of the Gentiles] has entered, all Israel shall be saved. But for him who is said to have fallen from heaven, there will be no conversion, even at the end of the age. These are the words of Origen. This also [refutes] that heresy which is imposed upon him, [claiming] that the Spirit does not understand the Son, and the Son does not understand [the Father...]
