For he says thus: he calls this depth of God "inscrutable" to every creature, but he could not say these things regarding the Son and the Holy Spirit. For the Son says to the Father in the Gospel: *Father, all mine are yours and yours are mine* [John 17:10]. And concerning the Holy Spirit, Paul himself declares, saying: <note>original: "Nemo ſcit hominum quæ fūt hominis niſi ſpiritus hominis qui in ipſo eſt. ita & quæ in deo ſunt nemo cognouit niſi ſpiritus dei"</note> *For what man knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man which is in him? Even so, no one has known the things of God except the Spirit of God* [1 Corinthians 2:11]. Therefore, when Paul says, "Who has known the mind of the Lord?" he speaks of <term>creatures</term><note>In this theological context, 'creatures' refers to all created beings, including humans and angels, as distinct from the Creator.</note>; but Origen excepted the nature of the Trinity from this statement. 

It seems that one heresy remains attributed to Origen: <margin>Regarding the heresy of the creation of souls</margin> namely, the opinions concerning the soul—that they were created from eternity and <margin>The objection made</margin> descend from heaven into bodies. Regarding the soul, Origen himself writes in his <margin>defensio (defense)</margin> commentaries on the Epistle of Paul to Titus that he can accept nothing as a <term>determined</term><note>Latin: "determinati." To "determine" a doctrine meant to set it down as an official, binding Church teaching.</note> ruling from Church dogma except that all souls are of the same species, that they possess free will, that they are rational, that they are immortal, that they were created by God, and that they will face punishments for evil deeds and rewards for good ones. 

He says he affirms only these things regarding the soul because there is evident testimony for them in the Scriptures. In other questions about the soul, however, he says he states only what seems more probable to him, proceeding by way of <term>inquiry</term><note>Latin: "inquiſitiue." Origen often framed his more radical ideas as philosophical explorations rather than rigid doctrines.</note> rather than by a final ruling, because nothing regarding those matters is firmly established in Church dogma. 

However, all agree that it seemed more likely to Origen that souls were created before bodies and lived in the heavens. <margin>Rufinus</margin> And Rufinus, in his apology to Anastasius, the Bishop of the City of Rome <note>Pope Anastasius I, reigned 399–401 AD.</note>, after he recounted three different opinions on the soul, says this at the end: "But I, having read each of these, say with God as my witness that until the present I hold nothing certain or defined regarding this question, but I leave it to God to know what is the truth, and to whom He himself deigns to reveal it. However, I do not deny that I have read these individual points, and I confess I am still ignorant—except for this which the Church clearly teaches: that God is the creator of both souls and bodies." ...afterward it was then determined: Indeed, not only in the time of Origen but even in the time of Augustine—who lived 200 years after Origen—nothing had yet been determined by the Catholics (that is, by the universal Church) regarding the soul. For Augustine himself was doubtful in his opinion about the soul, as is clear from his letter to Jerome: namely, whether individual souls are created for individual bodies <note>original Latin: "singule singulis"</note>, as the orthodox tradition now holds. From one opinion, it seemed to Augustine to follow that God would be unjust; or whether, from that one soul made in Adam by God, others were then propagated as a body is from a body. Do not believe that Augustine doubted this matter only in his youth; for in the first book of his *Retractions* <note>A work written late in life where Augustine reviewed and corrected his earlier writings</note>, which was among his last works, he doubts this question. For he writes thus in the first book: "Without controversy, therefore, God is a certain original region of the soul's happiness, who did not indeed beget the soul from himself, but created it from no other thing, just as he created the body from the earth. These are Augustine's words, verbatim.

From this it clearly appears that because of the aforementioned erroneous opinion about the soul, Origen can in no way be called a heretic. The second proposition which I state is this: that if it is true what Thomas [Aquinas] says in his *Quodlibets* <term>scholarly theological exercises where questions on any topic were debated</term>—as will appear more extensively in the seventh article of the defense of Origen—and if it is good theology that we are not bound by the necessity of salvation to believe not only the doctors of the Church (such as Jerome, Augustine, and the like) but not even the Church itself, except in those things which pertain to the substance of the faith; and if we add that it pertains not at all to the substance of the faith whether Origen was the author of those heresies, or someone else (provided we confess that those heresies are indeed heresies—that is, impious dogmas). 

It seems to follow that a faithful man and true Christian is not bound by the necessity of salvation in this question to believe Jerome—even if the Church leans more toward him—rather than Athanasius, Didymus, Methodius, or Rufinus. The faith of [Rufinus] is said to have been proven by prisons and exile in the holy Church of Alexandria during the time of the persecution of heretics; indeed, it is better to believe the words of Origen himself. So perhaps also in this case—where Jerome prefers to think that the writings demonstrating Origen to be Catholic are faked and corrupted, rather than those which prove him a heretic—it is neither impious nor seemingly ruinous to the faith not to adhere to him [Jerome] entirely. Rather, it seems to confirm the faith to take away the defense and testimony of Origen from the heretics, rather than to weaken it. ...even Jerome and later members of the church were of this opinion: that those heresies were not from the mind of Origen, but were falsely ascribed to him by heretics. In this matter, as in all others, I always place the judgment of the Church before the judgment and reasoning of all others.

Regarding the second article, it seems more reasonable that Origen should be excused because, if he wrote anything not accepted by Catholics, in those writings he proceeded neither **dogmatically** <note>original: *dogmatice*; presenting an idea as an absolute, unchangeable truth of the faith</note> nor **assertively**, but always **doubtingly** and **inquisitively** <note>original: *inquisitive*; as a search for truth rather than a final statement</note>. <margin>For the second article.</margin> Wherefore, just as in the books of Augustine <margin>Augustine.</margin> *On Genesis* there are many things not accepted, yet they are excused by us because, as he himself says in his book *Retractions*, more things in that book were "questioned than found" <note>original: *plura in eo libro sunt quesita quam inuenta*</note>. So too there may be many things in the books of Origen to be rejected and condemned which, because he spoke them not by determining them but by inquiring, he should not be called a heretic; for <term>heresy</term> <note>a persistent, stubborn denial of a truth of the faith</note> properly means a dogma asserted against the expressed truth of either Scripture or the determination of the Church. <margin>Heresy properly defined.</margin>

That Origen always spoke in this way is clear from many places. <margin>Note.</margin> For even after a disputation on the soul, he says: "Let these things, according to our opinion, not be dogmas, but only questions sought out and put forward so they would not seem entirely unaddressed." And on the *Epistle to the Romans*, in the second book: "Let these things be said by us with the rule that if anyone says something better and more reasonable, those things should be held rather than these of ours." And in the fourth book: "These things were brought forth as we were able in such arduous and difficult places. And in the fifth book: "In the meantime, these things were able to occur to us in the present place. If anyone perceives something better, let him not be reluctant to look at those things while setting these aside."

And more is read in the book *Peri Archon* <note>original: *periarchon*; Origen's major work *On First Principles*</note>. <margin>The book *Peri Archon*.</margin> We see that he proceeds in this order: he first puts down those things which seemed to him to be expressly determined in the Scriptures, and in those, he deviated in nothing from the Church. Other things he says are doubtful to him, and he wishes to inquire about them, asserting that for all of them, only that truth is to be received which in no way opposes apostolic and ecclesiastical dogmas. <margin>For the third article.</margin>

...that he dictated to Ambrose <note>Ambrose of Alexandria (died c. 251), Origen’s wealthy patron who provided shorthand writers and copyists.</note> in earlier years, before he had yet discovered anything of the truth, intended to be communicated only to Ambrose himself in private and not to be published. This was because Origen did not yet know these things to be safely certain or in harmony with apostolic truth. Ambrose, however, brought those secretly produced works into the public. Later, once the Catholic <note>In this context, "Catholic" refers to "orthodox" or universally accepted Church teaching.</note> truth was discovered by Origen—who was by then a sixty-year-old—he began to write boldly for the public in an orthodox manner. He grieved deeply that those works he had written for Ambrose’s private use had already been published by him. In his own defense—as gathered from the words of Jerome and Eusebius concerning the sequence of the whole affair—he provided testimony about his Catholic faith in a letter to Pope Fabian of Rome, recounting the facts: namely, that the writings found earlier were not written by him for the purpose of being published, as he himself was doubtful whether they <margin>Jerome</margin> were Catholic or not. But Ambrose published them. This is indeed what Jerome says: Origen himself, in the letter he wrote to Fabian, Bishop of the city of Rome, expresses repentance for why he wrote such things, and he blames the rashness on Ambrose, who brought into public what had been produced in secret. Eusebius, moreover, recounting what Origen wrote after his sixtieth year—after he enumerated the book *Against Celsus*, twenty-five books of *Commentaries on Matthew*, and twenty on the *Prophets*—adds: "He wrote also to Fabian, Bishop of the city of Rome, and to many other leaders of the churches concerning his Catholic faith." These are his words. Therefore, let it be true that before his sixtieth year, Origen was doubtful about many mysteries of the faith. And let it be true that he privately communicated many things in writing to Ambrose—things he then held not by firm adherence but by doubtful inquiry—which are now not to be received by Catholics. And thus Jerome speaks the truth: that the things found in many of Origen's books, even those that are not Catholic, are indeed by Origen, because they were truly dictated by him, though not as things believed, but as things questioned rather than discovered. Consequently, they should not be culpably attributed to Origen (who later discovered the Catholic truth), and in which many things were also devised by heretics, according to Rufinus. We can also accept this as true, especially since Origen himself complained of this very thing while he was alive. Let it therefore be true, according to Eusebius in the *Ecclesiastical History* (which was approved as true by Jerome), that Origen does not hold as his own works—that is, those in which he says something definitively and with adherence—except those he wrote after his sixtieth year. And let it be true also according to Jerome that he repented of the things rashly published by Ambrose earlier, and consequently died a Catholic. Thus, not only according to Rufinus, Pamphilus, and Eusebius, but also according to Jerome, it is more reasonable to believe that he is saved than to believe that he is <margin>For the fifth article.</margin> condemned. For the fifth article, I say this proposition: however much anyone sins mortally and gravely in life, and it is established that he has sinned mortally, unless <margin>First proposition.</margin> his final impenitence is established, it is rash to assert truly that he is condemned. The truth of this proposition is evident from the common opinion of all the doctors <note>The 'Doctors' refers to the authoritative theologians and scholars of the Church.</note> consenting to the said proposition. From this proposition, I infer two <margin>First corollary proposition</margin> corollary <note>A 'corollary' is a logical consequence that follows naturally from an already proven statement.</note> propositions. The first is this: Not because someone has sinned mortally in life—and it is not certain to us that he did not repent—must we firmly judge that he is in hell. This is evident because, once a mortal sin is posited, that entire state from which eternal damnation follows is not yet fully established. Rather, it is necessary to go beyond the sin and be certain...

...concerning final impenitence <note>original: "de finali impenitentia"; the state of refusing to repent for one's sins up until the moment of death</note>. Nor do I firmly deny that it is to be believed that he is in hell. I have to show you his repentance. But you, who assert that he is damned, have the burden of proving his impenitence. And toward this, the saying of Henry of Hesse <margin>Henry of Hesse <note>A prominent 14th-century German theologian and philosopher</note></margin> contributes much, who in his exposition of the third chapter of the book of Genesis says these formal words: "If, therefore, the argument of some were effective by which they persuade that someone is damned—as they do concerning Solomon, because Scripture commemorates his sin and makes no mention of his righteousness or repentance—then the first man [Adam] would be convicted of being damned for his sin in the same way as the first angel [Lucifer]." This is Henry's point. For nowhere is mention made of the repentance of Adam, but only of his sin. Similarly, in Judges chapter 8, we read of the sin of Gideon and not of his repentance; and yet it is well believed by the Doctors of the Church to speak of his salvation. And you can see that by this same argument, certain people were deceived and erroneously said that Moses was damned, because his sin at the waters of contradiction <note>original: "aquis contradictionis"; a reference to the Waters of Meribah, where Moses struck the rock in anger</note> was recorded, and nothing was explicitly recorded regarding his repentance. And yet God said to Joshua: "Moses my servant is dead" <note>Implying Moses remained a "servant" of God even in death</note>.

The second corollary proposition is this: <margin>Second corollary proposition</margin> no one can be certain that anyone is damned to hell unless they have this from a special revelation from God or from those to whom it is believed God has revealed it. The truth of this is clear from the preceding propositions, because no one can be certain of final repentance or impenitence except the one who knows the secrets of the heart and the person to whom He wished to reveal it. For since no one is as certain about the state of another as they are about themselves—because no one knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man which is in him, as it is said in 2 Corinthians—and since a man cannot be certain about himself whether he is worthy of hate or love, as it says in Ecclesiastes 9, how much more can he not be certain about another unless he has a special revelation concerning it?

Now, from this principal proposition and its corollaries, I infer for the purpose of my conclusion that even granting that Origen <note>A prolific and influential early Christian scholar (c. 184–253 AD) whose works later became the subject of intense theological controversy</note> may have sinned mortally by erring in those ways, nevertheless, since we are uncertain about his final impenitence or repentance, to assert that he is damned is an altogether rash judgment and is to be rejected. Since, therefore, we can be certain neither of his salvation nor of his damnation, it is nonetheless pious and very reasonable to believe, as I have said, that God saved him—a man of such and so great knowledge.

Concerning him, Jerome says in his preface to the Song of Songs: <margin>The words of Jerome</margin> "While in other matters he surpassed all others, in this he surpassed himself," and of him that saying is verified: "The King has brought me into his chamber." O ingenious reader, pay diligent attention and understand through these things for yourself what I do not express. In the preface to his *Hebrew Questions*, Jerome, speaking of the same Origen, says this: <note>original: "In prefatione autem hebraicarum questionum de eodem loquẽs Origene sic inquit"</note> "I say this one thing: that I wish I possessed his knowledge of the Scriptures, even if I had to bear the envy attached to his name." He treated as worthless the images and shadows of ghosts—whose nature is said to terrify children—and their chattering in dark corners. I pass over what Jerome further proclaims of him: that he trampled upon greed and that he castrated himself out of zeal for God <note>A famous, though debated, account that Origen took a biblical verse literally to ensure his chastity while teaching both men and women.</note> (though not according to knowledge); that he sweated through days and nights in the explanation of Scripture, which will grant eternal life to those who clarify it, as the Wise Man says. And as is written to Vigilantius, he explained the obscurities of the prophets and revealed the greatest mysteries of both the New and the Old Testaments.

I pass over the fact that he was not only the son of a martyr, but he himself was very close to the merit of martyrdom. For Eusebius <note>The "Father of Church History" (c. 260–339 AD).</note> says that even as a small boy, he burned with such ardor for attaining martyrdom that he would willfully throw himself into dangers. Later, during the time of the **Decian persecution**, he endured new crosses, new kinds of punishments, and torments unheard of in all previous ages, so much so that Eusebius says he was tormented by "a thousand deaths" <note>original: "mille mortibus"</note> so that the one death he truly desired would not be granted to him. The persecutor acted with the greatest effort to ensure that neither a quick end was provided nor the punishment ceased. 

See how close he was to the glory of martyrdom, which so many of his disciples achieved under his leadership and encouragement. I say again, he was certainly very close to the glory of martyrdom; indeed, he earned a merit that was almost equal. For Augustine also says in his book *On the Good of Marriage* that the merit of martyrdom is not unequal between **John**, who did not suffer death, and **Peter**, who did. Note these words of Augustine well: just as John, although he did not pass by the sword, was nevertheless ready to endure martyrdom when he was cast into a vat of boiling oil, so too was Origen. Although he did not undergo death by martyrdom, he was nevertheless ready—indeed, most eager—to undergo it. He suffered so many torments, as Eusebius says, that he underwent a thousand deaths in place of one. 

This is what Bernard says in his sermon on the holy martyrs: that there is a **triple martyrdom**. There is martyrdom of the will alone; martyrdom of the deed alone; and martyrdom of both deed and will. John the Evangelist suffered the martyrdom of the will alone, of whom it was said to him and his brother, "You shall drink my cup" (Matthew 20). Regarding this, Cyprian <note>Bishop of Carthage and an early Christian martyr.</note> says: "Among the servants of God, where martyrdom is contemplated and the mind is conceived as devoted to good, it is crowned by God as judge. For it is one thing for the spirit to be lacking for martyrdom, and another for martyrdom to be lacking for the spirit." <note>Meaning it is one thing to be a coward, and another to be willing to die but never given the chance.</note>

Therefore, if the spirit was never lacking for Origen’s martyrdom, and he underwent a thousand deaths for one, how could we not believe he is crowned by God the judge—unless the martyr Cyprian is lying? And if he was "damned," who, I ask, damned him to the death of Gehenna <note>term: Gehenna (Hell)</note>? Was it Jesus Christ, for whom he wished to die so many times? Rather, just as Augustine says of Cyprian that the blood of martyrdom washed away every stain of heresy in him, so too we piously believe of Origen: that the blood of martyrdom—poured out by him not so much outwardly upon the earth, but inwardly upon his celestial soul burning with zeal for God and charity—washed away every stain of heresy. We say with David <note>The author is adapting the language of Psalm 1 and Psalm 32 to Origen.</note>: 

**Blessed is Origen**, who, although he once walked in the counsel of the erring, did not stand in the way of sinners through his repentance, and never sat in the seat of pestilence through obstinacy, but his will was in the law of the Lord, and in His law he meditated day and night. 

**Blessed is Origen**, whose iniquities are forgiven through baptism, and whose sins are covered through repentance, and to whom the Lord has not imputed sin because of his martyrdom. Finally, for such a man and so great a man...

Even if this man sometimes erred in the mysteries of the faith due to a defect of his intellect and not from any malice of his will, let us believe that he was not abandoned by the Lord in his final moments. Rather, we should believe that through the visitation of God's most kind mercy, he was illuminated regarding those secrets of faith in which he might have erred, and was called back from the path of error to the path of salvation. 

I understood this in my brief response when I said elsewhere: since he was not found to have been <term>pertinacious</term><note>In canon law, 'pertinacity' is the stubborn, conscious refusal to correct an error in faith; without it, one is not technically a heretic.</note>, it is plausible to believe that God saved him—visiting him with the illumination I mentioned, most mercifully placing him in a state worthy of salvation, and calling him to a saving repentance for those secrets of faith in which he erred. 

Whether this actually happened or not, no one can know with certainty unless it has been revealed to them from above. But to believe that it happened, rather than that it did not, seems more consistent and reasonable to anyone considering the acts and life of Origen. For in matters of doubt, one must always adhere to the more favorable side. These things are said so they may carry weight even if Origen’s repentance were not established; however, we have already shown very clearly in the preceding pages, through the testimony of the most blessed Jerome, that his repentance is indeed established.

### The Sixth Article <margin>Regarding the sixth article.</margin>

Regarding the sixth article, I say that it does not seem believable that the Church ever decreed Origen’s soul is damned to hell. I prove the truth of this proposition with two reasons.

**The first reason** is this: <margin>The first reason.</margin> concerning a matter where one side or the other cannot be determined with certainty except by a reckless judgment, one should not believe a determination has been made by the Church. But regarding this question of whether Origen is saved or damned, no side can be determined except recklessly, or at least without a special revelation from God. Therefore, since no such revelation is established, it should not be believed that the Church has made a determination on this matter. The <term>major premise</term><note>The first part of a logical argument (syllogism).</note> is well known, and to believe the opposite would be an insult to the Church—namely, that she could judge anything unadvisedly or recklessly. The <term>minor premise</term><note>The second part of a logical argument.</note> is evident from the articles discussed above.

**Confirmation:** <margin>Confirmation</margin> The Church could not be certain of Origen's damnation except through a special revelation made concerning him. But there is no mention anywhere that such a revelation was ever made; therefore, etc.

**The second reason** is this: <margin>The second reason.</margin> if there is anything that might persuade someone that the Church determined Origen's damnation, it is certain texts in the <term>Decretals</term><note>Collections of papal letters that form the basis of Church law.</note> which seem to suggest this to those who interpret them in a crude manner. However, when they are rightly examined, they work for us rather than against us.

1. 4. From the section on heretics, the chapter "Brotherhood," it is written: "Since Celestinus and Pelagius were condemned in the <margin>Synod of Ephesus.</margin> Synod of Ephesus, how can their chapters be accepted when their authors are condemned?"

### QUESTION EIGHT: CONCERNING THE FREEDOM OF BELIEF

<margin>Proof of the conclusion for its first part. Aristotle.</margin>
**Just as no one holds an opinion precisely because they want to hold that opinion, so no one believes something to be true precisely because they want to believe it.**

<margin>Proof for the second part. Augustine.</margin>
From this conclusion, I infer the following as a corollary: **It is not within the free power of a human being to believe an article of faith is true whenever it pleases them, or to believe it is not true whenever it pleases them.** Those Masters <note>The "Masters" likely refers to the university faculty or ecclesiastical judges who had previously condemned the author's propositions.</note> judged that this proposition, along with its corollary, was erroneous and "savored of heresy." <term>Savoring of heresy</term> <note>A technical legal term in the Inquisition meaning a statement that sounds heretical or leads toward heresy, even if not explicitly condemned.</note> I, however, consider the main conclusion to be not only Catholic but most true, and far truer than its opposite. I say the same of the corollary when it is understood correctly; its meaning, if taken according to my intent, should not be understood otherwise than as it follows from the main conclusion of which it is the corollary.

<margin>Pierre d’Ailly. Henry of Oyta. Henry of Hesse. The University of Paris.</margin>
That the conclusion is not only Catholic but also most true is clear. For the first part—which is that no one holds an opinion on something precisely because they want to—Aristotle supports this in the second book of *On the Soul*, text of the commentary 253, where Aristotle establishes the difference between imagination and opinion. <note>Aristotle argued that while we can imagine whatever we like, forming a belief or opinion requires being convinced by some evidence.</note> This sentiment of Aristotle has not only never been rejected, but has indeed been unanimously approved by all our theologians. 

The second part of the conclusion—which is that no one believes something is precisely true just because they *want* to believe it is true—is found in several places in the works of Augustine. He says quite often that one cannot believe by free will alone—that is, by the mere command of the will—without the persuasion or motive of reason. My entire conclusion (which summarily holds that when a doubtful proposition is presented, the mere grasp of terms and the mere command of the will are not enough for someone to believe or disbelieve it) is held by **Pierre d’Ailly**, **Henry of Oyta**, and **Henry of Hesse**. <note>These were prominent 14th-century "Nominalist" theologians associated with the University of Paris.</note> And when I was in Paris, almost the entire **University of Paris** held this view. Indeed, many Catholic doctors consider it so true that they regard its opposite as impossible. In fact, I have not yet read a single teacher who contradicts this opinion. 

<margin>Explanation of the corollary proposition.</margin>
The corollary proposition is not to be understood or accepted in any other way than with the restriction or definition placed in the preceding statement: namely, that it is not in the free power of the will to believe an article of faith is true whenever it pleases, and to believe it is false when it pleases. It does not follow that the intellect believes *precisely* because it pleases the will to believe; such an understanding of one proposition linked to another is not unusual. Indeed, in Holy Scripture, the meaning of the letter is often taken from what precedes or follows it, which is especially the case...

<meta>This page continues a scholastic defense regarding the relationship between the human will and the act of faith, specifically addressing whether a person can choose to believe something simply by willing it.</meta>

...it ought to happen through our [will] because I have said this. It is not in our power, etc. I do not propose this as a statement in itself and a separate conclusion, but I propose it as a corollary <note>A "corollary" is a proposition that follows naturally from one already proved.</note> from the preceding point. If it does not please them to accept the meaning of the present corollary from its principal proposition to which it is annexed and linked, let them attend to the fact that something is said to be in "freedom" or in the "free power of the will" in two ways. <margin>In two ways something is said to be in the freedom or in the free power of the will.</margin>

**In the first way**, because once an apprehension <note>In medieval logic, "apprehension" is the simple act of the mind grasping a concept or "article" of faith without yet judging if it is true or false.</note> is placed in the intellect, with no other act of the intellect required, it is within the commanding power of the will to produce that act [of belief]. And thus it is denied in this conclusion that the act of believing is in the free power of man; <margin>First.</margin> nor is it necessary for every commanded act—whether meritorious or demeritorious—to be in the power of man in such a way. For the mere apprehension of the terms of an article of faith is not sufficient for believing; rather, beyond this, persuasion or some "probable reason" is required, as is cited from Augustine. <margin>Augustine.</margin>

**In the second way**, something is said to be in the free power of the will because, when all other things required for that act are in place, the will can choose to bring it into being or not; <margin>Second.</margin> nor is the will forced into this act even when all other conditions are met. In this way, the act of believing an article of faith is indeed in the free power of the will. This is the intended meaning of the corollary proposition. From what has been said, anyone with an understanding can see that those masters were not correct to say absolutely that my position is "erroneous" or "savors of heresy."

Furthermore, the fact that the opinion of those doctors whom I follow—who say that the mere apprehension of terms combined with a simple command of the will is not enough to cause the assent of faith—is probable and reasonable can be clearly shown. This is evident not only by the authority of Augustine (who, as I said, affirms this in many places) but also by most effective reasons. 

**First, it is argued thus:** <margin>It is argued first.</margin> It is not in the free power of a man to form an opinion that something is "this way" or "that way" whenever he wants; therefore, it is not in the free power of a man to believe something is "this way" or "that way" whenever he wants. The logical consequence is clear: if a more likely case does not hold, then the less likely one does not either. <note>This is an "a fortiori" argument: if we can't even control our weak opinions, we certainly can't control our firm beliefs.</note> It is less difficult to hold an opinion while fearing the opposite might be true than to believe something without any such fear. This premise is expressly stated by Aristotle in the second book of *On the Soul* (commentary 153). <margin>Aristotle.</margin> 

This is also clear through experience. Everyone experiences within themselves that when a doubtful proposition is presented, if it is purely a matter of doubt, they are not inclined to give their assent to either side until some new "appearance" of truth arrives—whether through a logical argument (a syllogism), through intuitive knowledge, through the testimony of many people, through the authority of a speaker, or something similar.

**Secondly, it is argued thus:** <margin>Second.</margin> It is not in the free power of a man to make something "appear true" to his intellect or to make it "appear false." Therefore, it is not in the power of a man to believe "this" or "that" is true or false. The consequence holds because it is a contradiction for someone to believe something and give assent to it if it does not appear true to him. The premise is proved because for something to appear a certain way to the intellect is for that thing to be "represented" to the intellect; this cannot depend on a command of the will because the representation must happen *before* the will can act upon it.

**This is confirmed** <margin>It is confirmed.</margin> because the reason something appears a certain way to the intellect is that the object being represented is a certain way, or because the evidence (or whatever makes it credible) is a certain way, or because the intellect itself is disposed in a certain way. But making the object be a certain way, or making the intellect be a certain way, is not within the choice of the will...

->II ii<- <note>Signature mark for the gathering of pages.</note>

<summary>The author argues that belief (faith) is not a simple choice of the will triggered by hearing a concept; rather, the intellect must first perceive the concept as "credible" or "true" through evidence or reason before the will can act. He defends this position against accusations of heresy by citing Aristotle's psychology and Augustine's theology.</summary>

<meta>This page continues a scholastic debate regarding whether the act of faith is a product of the will (desire/choice) or the intellect (reason). It specifically addresses the "Third," "Fourth," and "Fifth" arguments in a sequence.</meta>

...of [truth]. Therefore, for a thing to appear in this or that way to the intellect is not within the power of the will.

<margin>Thirdly.</margin>

Thirdly, it is argued as follows: Whenever there is a power that is purely neutral and indifferent toward two opposite **secondary acts**, it cannot move into one of them unless it is first determined by something that serves as a **primary act**—or something that stands in place of a primary act—regarding one of those secondary acts.
<note>In scholastic philosophy, a "primary act" (actus primus) refers to a capacity or a state of being, while a "secondary act" (actus secundus) is the actual exercise of that capacity. For example, knowing a language is a primary act; speaking it is a secondary act.</note>

But it is the case that the intellect is a power that is purely neutral and indifferent toward the **specification** of any of its secondary acts. 
<note>original: "specificationem." In this context, "specification" refers to the specific content of a thought—what makes a thought about "a tree" different from a thought about "a house."</note>

Therefore, it cannot be determined toward any such specification unless something else arrives that is either a primary act or stands in place of a primary act regarding such a determination.

From this reasoning, I take the following consequence: a mere act of the will cannot serve as a primary act regarding the specification of the acts of the intellect. Therefore, by the command of the will alone, the intellect cannot be determined toward such a specification. This consequence is well-known from the previously assumed reasoning. Furthermore, the premise is clear from the common opinion of all the Doctors <note>The "Doctors" refers to established Church authorities and university professors.</note> agreeing on this point: that although the act of the intellect depends on the will regarding its **exercise**, it does not depend on it regarding its **specification**.
<note>The distinction here is that the will can "turn on" the intellect (exercise), like choosing to open a book, but the will cannot force the intellect to see a false statement as true (specification).</note>

With these things established, I argue for the point as follows: The act of assenting and the act of dissenting are acts that have opposite specific natures. Therefore, the intellect cannot be determined toward assent or non-assent by the command of the will. Consequently, the fact that someone believes through the intellect that an article of faith is true—or does not believe it—is not precisely because they "want" or "do not want" to believe. Rather, it is because of something else determining the intellect (which is neutral in itself) toward the specification of such an act.

<margin>Fourthly.</margin>

Fourthly, it is argued thus: A person is not determined toward believing something precisely through an act of the will if, when asked why they believed it, they do not point to a precise act of the will as the reason. But it is the case that if someone is asked why they believe the Christian faith rather than the faith of the **Muslims**, they will not point precisely to an act of the will. Therefore, they are not inclined toward believing by a precise act of the will.
<note>original: "maumethensium," referring to the followers of Muhammad.</note>

<margin>Eight reasons assigned by our theologians for why we should believe the Gospel.</margin>

That a mere act of the will is not the cause is evident from experience and from the writings of our theologians, by whom these eight reasons are commonly cited for why we ought to believe the Gospel:
1. Prophetic pronouncement.
2. The harmony of the Scriptures.
3. The authority of the writers.
4. The rationality of the contents.
5. The irrationality of individual errors.
6. The stability of the Church.
7. The clarity of miracles.
<note>The text mentions "eight" reasons in the margin, but only seven are listed in this specific passage; the eighth, often the "efficacy of the doctrine," may have been omitted by the scribe or appears on the next page.</note>

Fifthly, it is argued as follows: Whenever two people are determined to believe opposite things, and each of them is determined precisely because they *want* to be so determined—being completely indifferent to judgment or the persuasion of reason—it cannot be said that one is moved to believe more reasonably than the other. But given two people, where one wants to believe that "A" is true and the other does not want to believe it, we are able to say that this one wills more reasonably and the other more irrationally. Therefore, they are not determined to will this way or that way simply because they precisely want to.

<margin>Albertus.</margin>

The major premise of this reasoning is well-known because, as **Albert** says in the third book *On the Soul*: when the will acts precisely because it wants to act that way, it is like a **tyrant**. In a tyrant's action, the reason for the act is not sought, because their acting is not according to reason, but according to their own pleasure. 
<note>Referring to Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280), a dominant figure in medieval philosophy.</note>

The minor premise is manifest, because daily we say that the Muslims or the Jews act irrationally in the fact that they do not believe, and we act reasonably...

### QUESTION NINE ON THE ACCIDENTS IN THE SACRAMENT <note>The "accidents" are the physical properties of the bread and wine—such as taste, color, and smell—which Catholic theology teaches remain after the "substance" has changed into the Body and Blood of Christ.</note>

Whoever says that an **accident** cannot exist unless it exists within the Eucharist <note>The author is discussing whether physical properties need a physical "anchor" or subject to exist.</note> could still hold to the sacrament while also holding that the substance of the bread does not remain. Indeed, these masters have not said that this conclusion is heretical or "tastes of heresy," but only that it is erroneous. If they had brought forward any reasons for their opinion, I could either believe them or respond to them. 
<margin>Note / For the declaration of the conclusion.</margin> 
But they have not brought forward any reasons that I have seen, neither in the condemnation of this conclusion nor in others. I say this for the sake of clarifying the conclusion: by this statement, I do not intend to say categorically and absolutely that an accident cannot exist without a subject, or that in the sacrament it is *in fact* <note>original: "de facto"</note> in a subject. On the contrary, I hold firmly with the Church that the sacramental accidents are *in fact* without a subject. 

<margin>Thomas</margin> 

But I say that someone who would say that accidents cannot exist without a subject—and who held, with **Thomas** <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas, whose theology of the Eucharist became the standard Catholic model.</note>, to the real distinction between the bread’s "existence" and its "essence"—could say that it does not contradict divine omnipotence to preserve the *existence* of the bread without its *essence*. Just as God preserves an act, whether substantial or accidental, without its own power, so too in that "being" of the bread, the accidents could be hosted even though the substance of the bread does not remain. In these accidents, the body of Christ could have a real presence, just as it now has in accidents that are hosted in no subject at all. 

And whatever the case may be regarding the Sacrament of the Eucharist as it was actually instituted by Christ and believed by the Church—in which it is harmoniously held that nothing of the bread remains, such that its reproduction would be a new creation—nevertheless, if one holds the aforementioned opinion of **Thomas** regarding the real distinction of essence from existence, and taking the "Sacrament of the Eucharist" in an extended sense to include what is or what can be (as it is taken in my conclusion, which is a "divided modal statement" <note>A logical term referring to a proposition that discusses what is *possible* rather than just what *is*.</note>), not only is the present conclusion probable and not erroneous, but rather it is erroneous to say that there could not be some Sacrament of the Eucharist in which the accidents were in a subject. 

<margin>Note</margin> 

I do not know by what logic these masters saw fit to condemn a "divided statement of possibility" simply because of the falsehood of a "statement of fact" constructed from the same terms. I wonder that they do not know it is a fallacy of the consequent <term>fallacy of the consequent: a logical error where one assumes that because a specific result is true, only one specific cause must be responsible</term>, arguing from the less broad to the more broad when...

And indeed, they say it is clear that this is possible; for although essence is prior to being—from which it would seem that since it is prior, being could be separated from the latter—it is more possible for essence to be separated and exist without being than vice versa. However, considering from the other side that essence relates to being as potential relates to act, and as matter relates to form (because the "act" depends less on the "potential" than vice versa), it seems more feasible for being to exist without essence than the reverse. But God, in the incarnation of the Word, made the essence of humanity exist without its own being (as is said by many doctors); therefore, He can much more easily make the being of the bread exist here without its essence. Thus, just as in the Incarnation the essence was assumed and remains but the being does not remain, so here, through conversion, the essence can be changed and not remain, while the being is not converted and will remain.

Secondly, they show that this is not only possible but necessary, because nothing created can be converted into the uncreated; but one created thing can be converted into another when they share in matter and in genus <note>In logic, 'genus' is a broad category. Now, the essence of the bread and the essence of the body of Christ agree in matter and genus; hence, one can be converted into the other, even by nature, if the body were mortal. But the "being" (*esse*) of the bread does not share in matter or genus with the substantial "being" of the body of Christ, since that [Christ's being] is uncreated and divine, belonging to the divine person, since in Christ there is only one being of actual substantial existence. Therefore, it is impossible for the "being" of the bread to be converted, and it is necessary for it to remain.

I am of the opinion that it is not necessary for it to remain. <margin>Opinion of the author.</margin> Both because if it cannot be converted, it can nevertheless be annihilated, or it can be corrupted by yielding into the potency of matter. Just as humanity could be assumed without its "being" being assumed (instead remaining in the potency of matter), so too the essence can be converted without the "being" being converted (instead being reduced into the potency of the essence)—though, to tell the truth, these "reductions" are more easily said than understood. Furthermore, although the being of the bread cannot be converted into uncreated being, it can nevertheless be converted into a created essence, because those things which share in matter are [convertible]...

->### QUESTION TEN: CONCERNING THE WORDS OF CONSECRATION<-

**THOSE WORDS** "This is [my] body" <note>original Latin: "hoc est corpus"</note> which are spoken in the consecration are held **materially** and not **significatively**. <note>This is a technical distinction in medieval logic. That this is so will be clearly evident once the meaning of the conclusion is understood.

[Margin: Note well.] <margin>Note well.</margin> First, it must be noted that I do not intend for these words to have been taken "materially" when they were first uttered by Christ, but only when they are uttered by a priest of the Gospel when he is consecrating. For in all these places, I remember that angels were called by the name of "souls" by Augustine—though I have not seen everything, nor can I remember every single place where I might have read the holy doctors calling angels by this name. Indeed, it is a point that, when read, does not usually require much attention. 

When I said that it is more "improper" to say God is "Intellect," I intended nothing other than this: that angelic knowledge—which claims the name of "intellectual knowledge" for itself—is further removed from the infinite knowledge of God (who knows all things through His own essence) than it is from the reasoning knowledge proper to the rational soul or to humans. If, indeed, it is inferred from the present conclusion that God is "improperly" said to understand (just as a comparative implies a positive), let that consequence be accepted only in this sense: God is not called "Intellect" according to the narrow or specific definition of the word "understand," etc., but according to the common, less specific path, as was clear from Dionysius's way of speaking.

### QUESTION XIII. CONCERNING THE HIDDEN INTELLIGENCE OF THE SOUL.

The soul understands nothing actually and distinctly except itself. 
In explaining this, I said that I was speaking of the "hidden understanding" <note>original: "intelligere abdito"</note> mentioned by Augustine in his book *On the Trinity* and by Henry <margin>Augustine. Henry.</margin> <note>Henry of Ghent, a major 13th-century philosopher</note> in his *Quodlibeta* <note>A collection of various theological and philosophical questions</note>. These masters said that my conclusion did not match the meaning of the doctors I cited in my response. I do not know how they can say such a thing if they have actually seen those doctors' works. And because this matter of "hidden understanding" is...

<summary>The author defends his use of Dionysian terminology regarding God's knowledge, arguing that while God knows all, human terms like "intellect" or "reason" are technically inadequate. He also begins a new section on the soul's self-knowledge, citing Augustine and Henry of Ghent.</summary>
<keywords>Pseudo-Dionysius, Augustine, Henry of Ghent, divine knowledge, angelic intellect, rational soul, hidden understanding, scholastic debate</keywords>

...subtle and profound, I do not wish to explain it more broadly here. Since those critics did not otherwise condemn the conclusion, I wish to say only two things. First, that I do not intend to universally deny to the soul—in whatever state it may be—any distinct knowledge of things other than itself. I grant that the soul of Christ understands other things actually and distinctly; and similarly, I grant that the souls of the blessed <note>those in heaven</note> do so through revelations or "infused species" <note>concepts or forms of knowledge placed directly into the mind by God rather than learned through the senses</note>. 

Second, I say that I am speaking of that **hidden understanding** <term>intelligere abditum: a term for the soul's deep, internal activity independent of the physical body</term> which exists without a "phantasm" <note>a mental image derived from sensory experience</note> or the support of the senses or imagination. Furthermore, I am not speaking of just any such understanding, but of that hidden understanding which is direct and permanent. Concerning this, I placed a conclusion next to this one, stating: **"The soul always understands itself, and in understanding itself, it in some way understands all beings."** 

And so, in all my conclusions, there is always a certain hidden "concatenation" <note>a logical chain where one idea links to the next</note> which perhaps my critics do not notice. But returning to the point, I say that the soul, through such direct and permanent hidden understanding, actually and distinctly understands nothing except itself. From this, it is clear that the present conclusion, when understood this way, should not have been condemned outright as "erroneous," even if in some other sense it were not true. For if we judged things so strictly, many propositions of both philosophers and theologians—and even Sacred Scripture itself—would be condemned.

<margin>Habakkuk. Matthew.</margin> For example, there is that passage from Habakkuk, chapter 1: "Your eyes are [too] pure to see evil, and you cannot look at iniquities" <note>original: "mundi sunt oculi tui ne uideas malum & ne despicias iniquitates"</note>. And similarly, that passage in Matthew 25 concerning the foolish virgins: "I do not know you" <note>original: "nescio uos"</note>. For although the vision of God or His knowledge is unique and most simple, and although these stated propositions seem to deny such vision or knowledge universally—even regarding God—because of the negation placed before the verb "to see" or "to know," they are nevertheless explained by the Doctors <note>learned Church authorities</note> specifically as referring to God’s *approving* vision or knowledge. The negation in those verses is not taken to mean that God lacks all possible modes of vision or knowledge. 

<margin>Psalms.</margin> This must be the case because the Psalmist also says: "My sins are not hidden from you" <note>original: "Delicta mea a te nō sunt abscōdita"</note>. Therefore, if many such passages are "distinguished" <note>clarified by making logical distinctions</note> by commentators and Doctors and guided toward a true meaning rather than being condemned, I do not know why my own conclusion deserved to be so simply condemned—especially after it had been explained and clarified to the judges in the manner I just described.

Let these words be dictated by me now with a "hurrying pen" <note>written in haste</note>; I intend to write at another time with more leisure and care, providing more and perhaps better arguments. This very work, such as it is, was labored over for twenty nights <note>the author is emphasizing that this defense was written in only three weeks</note>, and in publishing it, speed was more necessary for me than diligence. For it was necessary to provide my friends with something they could throw to my barking enemies—like a morsel of meat thrown to Cerberus <note>the three-headed hound of the underworld in Greek mythology</note>—so that I might immediately confront the disease of unjust infamy that was spreading against me. 

<margin>Note.</margin> However, whatever I have written and shall write in the future, let it always be prefaced by this: that only that should be held as valid and holy which the Supreme Pontiff <note>the Pope</note> and all those whose judgment he approves shall decree as valid and holy. And I wish that he had already decreed something concerning these opinions of ours which have been called into doubt, according to his wisdom and authority. If he had, it would not have been a "rash" undertaking for me to defend what he condemned, nor "superfluous" to defend what he approved. 

Therefore, while we cannot yet make use of the sentence of such a great judge, let us write these things so that detractors may not have anything sinister to say about the questions I proposed for dispute, and so that the "unlearned and simple" <note>the general public or non-theologians</note> do not have cause for suspicion. For it can happen that when someone less learned touches upon these matters, reading a proposition like "Christ did not truly and [as much as]..."

...to the real presence, as the common way posits it, he descended into hell <note>original: "descendit ad inferos." This refers to the "Harrowing of Hell," a doctrine stating that Christ descended into the underworld after his death.</note>. If someone is cunningly—not truthfully—offended by that wording, he might believe the sense of the proposition is that the article of faith concerning the descent of Christ is not true. Likewise, when he reads that infinite punishment is not due to a mortal sin of finite duration <note>Pico argued that because a human act is finite in time, its punishment should logically be finite, a view that challenged the standard doctrine of eternal damnation and was condemned by the Church.</note>, he might suspect me of holding the heresy that the punishment of Gehenna <note>Gehenna: a historical term for Hell.</note> is not eternal. And when he understands that I think well of Origen's salvation, he might suspect that I love not so much the life, character, teaching, and repentance of Origen <note>Origen (c. 184–253 AD) was a highly influential but controversial early Christian theologian whose views on the pre-existence of souls and universal salvation were later declared heretical.</note> as I do the dogmas believed by Origen. It is similar with many other propositions which might perhaps have, on the surface, what I call "holy simplicity"—that is, they might offend ears that are as unlearned as they are pious.

For that reason, just as we have written these things so they may be read so that no one thinks ill of us or of the orthodox dogma of our holy religion, so too I would not want those "raw" and unexplained propositions—if I may call them that—to be read by our people unless they have first reached these [explanations]. This is especially true for the more dull-witted and those who are unrefined and unaccustomed to more remote doctrines.

I therefore pray, beseech, and <margin>Note.</margin> entreat friends and enemies, the pious and the impious, the learned and the unlearned, by the heart <note>original: "viscera," literally 'entrails' or 'inmost parts,' signifying deep compassion.</note> of Jesus Christ our Lord, by the wondrous mystery of his descent into hell, by the eternal fire of the damned which is not extinguished—owed especially to heretics and the enemies of the most holy Roman Church—by the sacrament of the true and mystical body and blood, by the omnipotence of God, by the reverence to be shown to the images of his Son and his co-heirs: let them read what we now write without malice and without envy. Let them not read the former things—that is, the propositions themselves, unnarrated and unexplained—since we proposed them to be disputed among the learned and did not publish them to be read everywhere by everyone. 

For there, too, are many impious dogmas of the ancient philosophers <margin>Averroes Alexander.</margin> Averroes <note>Averroes (1126–1198): An Islamic philosopher from Spain whose commentaries on Aristotle were central to university debates but often clashed with Church doctrine.</note> and Alexander <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias (fl. 200 AD): A commentator on Aristotle who argued that the human soul was not immortal, a view Pico presented for debate but did not personally adopt.</note> and many others, which we—even if we have always professed, asserted, and preached them publicly and privately—consider to be no less alien to true and right philosophy than they are to the faith. Nevertheless, practicing scholastic exercise according to the custom of the academies, we undertook to dispute them in a private gathering among a few learned men. 

Whoever reads the booklet of propositions for dispute, as they might be warned by its title, will see that I distinguish between what is said from my own opinion and what is said from the opinion of others. I do not propose those [other views] as my own or as true opinions, but as views believed by them. Thus one might suspect that even if the dogmas and discoveries of others are stated, both these and those seemed to me true and probable. Therefore, let those who hate me not read them because they are ours; let those who love me not read them, because from those things which are mine, they might imagine many things which are not ours.

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's "900 Theses," specifically concluding a section on theology and beginning a famous defense of "natural magic" as a tool for understanding the divine.</meta>

### xvi. conclusion.
The way of worshiping images and the cross proposed by Peter of Aquila, Henry of Ghent, Johannes Guarra, Durandus, Robert Holcot, and commonly by all the Scotists <note>Followers of the philosopher John Duns Scotus, known for their subtle logical distinctions.</note>, is more probable than the way proposed by Thomas <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas, the 13th-century Dominican theologian.</note>.

### xvii. conclusion.
Simply because someone denies that images should be worshiped in the specific way Thomas describes, it does not follow that they deny images should be worshiped in the way the Church itself prescribes.

### xviii. conclusion.
Since the fullness of all being resides in God, God—by His own power—is able to give every nature a hypostasis <term>hypostasis: From the Greek for "substance" or "standing under"; in theology, it refers to a distinct personhood or individual reality, such as the three "Persons" of the Trinity.</term>.

### xix. conclusion.
Regarding the question of whether an irrational nature <note>Such as a plant, animal, or inanimate object.</note> is—due to the lack in its own nature—incapable of being "assumed" into the divine nature in a union of personhood <note>original: "unitate suppositi"</note> (as Henry of Ghent believed), or whether it is not incapable (as the common view holds): a Catholic may remain so undecided as to not take a positive action of contradicting Henry’s opinion.

### xx. conclusion.
A proposition that denies agreement with a certain statement does not, by the literal power of the words, imply a positive agreement with the opposite statement.

### xxi. conclusion.
All magic that is commonly called necromancy <note>Literally "corpse-divination," but used here to mean any magic involving demons.</note>, and every art or science—if such things can even be called arts or sciences—that involves a pact or communication with demons in any way, whether explicit or implicit, central or secondary, occurring before, during, or after, or in any way whatsoever, is a forbidden and superstitious thing, and is rightly condemned by the Church.

### xxii. conclusion.
That science which is rightly called the practical branch of natural philosophy, and which William of Auvergne <note>Pico refers to him as "Guilelmo Parisiensi."</note>, Roger Bacon, and all Greek authors call natural magic <term>natural magic: Unlike demonic magic, this was the study of the hidden (occult) properties of herbs, stones, and stars to produce marvelous effects through nature alone.</term>, contains nothing in itself that is contrary to the Catholic and orthodox faith.

### xxiii. conclusion.
There is no science—extending the name "science" to include both revealed and unrevealed knowledge—that can grant us certainty about the divinity of Christ other than the teaching of the Gospel and the science of Christian theology.

### xxiv. conclusion.
Among the sciences that are not revealed, but are humanly discovered and acquired in all their parts, there is none that helps us more in knowing the divinity of Christ than that through which we understand what can be done by the power of natural agents, both earthly <note>original: "sublunarium," or things below the moon.</note> and celestial. From this, we may then comprehend from the works of Christ that he was truly the Lord and Author of nature, because he performed by his own power things that exceed the limits of all natural power, both heavenly and earthly.

### xxv. conclusion.
A believer is not obligated to always use the term "science" <note>original: "scientia"</note> in every speech as if it were a common term for both revealed and unrevealed knowledge.

->KK ii<-

28th conclusion.

The act of believing is a free act.

30th conclusion.

These words, "This is my body," etc., when they were uttered by Christ, were held **significatively**, not **materially**. <note>In medieval logic, "significative" means the words were used to perform the action or convey their meaning directly, whereas "materially" refers to using the words as a quote or an object of speech.</note>

**41st Conclusion.**

<meta>This page begins the official papal brief from Pope Alexander VI to the philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. It follows the historical timeline after Pico's 900 theses were condemned by the previous Pope, Innocent VIII. This document serves as a formal clearance of Pico's reputation.</meta>

### Brief of Alexander VI, Supreme Pontiff, to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, Count of Concordia.

#### To our beloved son, the noble man Giovanni Pico, Count of Mirandola.
->**POPE ALEXANDER VI**<-

**BELOVED** son, greetings and apostolic blessing. As far as we are able with God's guidance, we look to the peace and reputation of all Catholics, especially those who are recommended by nobility of birth, the discipline of letters <note>In this context, "letters" refers to humanistic education and classical scholarship.</note>, and integrity of life and orthodox faith. Some time ago, when you first presented yourself to our predecessor of most serene memory, Pope Innocent VIII, and the Roman Curia, you posted nine hundred conclusions in theology and other faculties to be publicly disputed, as is the custom, with the permission of our aforementioned predecessor. You offered to maintain these conclusions under the correction of the Apostolic See. 

However, the said predecessor understood from certain people that some among those conclusions were contrary to our faith and religion—erroneous, scandalous, ill-sounding, and suspected of unhealthy doctrine. Wishing then to look after the integrity of the faith, lest the minds of the faithful (and especially the simple folk who are accustomed to flock to such public disputes) be corrupted, he commissioned and commanded—through his letters in the form of a brief—certain venerable brothers (then his, now our bishops) and other professors of Sacred Theology and of both branches of law <note>Civil and Canon (Church) law.</note> named by him. He ordered them to examine the contents of the said conclusions to see whether any of them, by the force of their words, were discordant with the Catholic faith, or savored of heresy, or were doubtful and ambiguous such that they could be drawn toward an erroneous sense. They were to report back to the predecessor himself, as is more fully contained in the said brief, so that after receiving a faithful report from them, he might provide a timely remedy. 

These bishops and professors indeed reported back to the same predecessor that certain conclusions seemed to them to be suspicious and, as they asserted, savored of heresy. Nevertheless, you had published those conclusions only for the sake of scholastic dispute and intended for them to be disputed under the correction of the Apostolic See; you finally professed that you would hold them to be whatever they were judged to be by our same predecessor, promising by an oath that you would assent to whatever declaration the predecessor himself might happen to make regarding this matter. 

Afterward, however, it was accepted by the said predecessor that you had published another book, an *Apology* <note>Pico's *Apologia*, written in 1487 to defend his 900 theses.</note>, in which you interpreted those same conclusions by declaring them in a better and Catholic sense, and you explained the understanding of the sincere faith regarding them. Lest the aforementioned propositions should in any way corrupt the hearts of the faithful, the same predecessor forbade the reading of the little book of the nine hundred conclusions; however, he declared that you had incurred no mark of diminished reputation on account of the premises, as is more broadly contained in those same letters, the tenor of which we wish to be considered expressed here. 

But later, since some were suggesting to the same predecessor that you had contravened your aforementioned oath under the pretext of the said *Apology*, he commanded that you—then staying in France—be summoned to the Curia. Having received his commands with reverence, you set out on the journey to return to the Roman Curia. When you had arrived in Italy, you remained in the regions of Florence by the good pleasure of the predecessor himself. In the meantime, the premises having been brought to our notice and the truth of the entire business having been investigated by us, it was found—and especially reported by our venerable brother George, Bishop of Albano and Lisbon, and our beloved sons Giovanni Battista Orsini (priest of the title of Saints John and Paul) and Francesco of Saint Eustachius (deacon), Cardinals of the Holy Roman Church. We had specifically commissioned them to accurately inform themselves and report to us, having called upon our beloved son Paolo Genovese, professor of theology and of the Order of Saint Dominic and Master of the Sacred Apostolic Palace. They reported that nothing further had subsequently been acted upon, proceeded, or attempted against you, and that in the same *Apology*, you had written your mind in a way that should be relieved of any mark of suspicion regarding the orthodox faith among all people...

# **GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA: ON BEING AND THE ONE, TO ANGELO POLIZIANO.**

## PREFACE.

**Y**ou were telling me <note>Latin: *Narrabas*</note> just the other day about the discussion **Lorenzo de' Medici** had with you concerning "being" and "the one." This took place while he was arguing against **Aristotle**—whose *Ethics* you are publicly lecturing on this year—by relying on the reasoning of the **Platonists** <note>Followers of Plato's philosophy</note>. Lorenzo is a man of such effective and multifaceted genius that he seems suited for all things. In him, I especially admire this: although he is always extremely busy with the affairs of the Republic <note>Referring to the state of Florence</note>, he is always either discussing or meditating upon some literary or scholarly topic.

Because those who believe that **Aristotle** disagrees with **Plato** also disagree with me—as I maintain that the philosophy of both is in harmony <note>Pico was famous for his "syncretism," the attempt to reconcile different schools of thought</note>—you asked how **Aristotle** might be defended in this matter and shown to agree with his master, **Plato**. I told you then whatever came to my mind, confirming the responses you yourself had given **Lorenzo** during the debate rather than offering anything new.

But this was not enough for you. You insistently demand that, even though I plan to write more extensively on these subjects in the *Concordance of Plato and Aristotle* which I am currently "bringing to birth" <note>original: *parturio*; Pico uses the metaphor of labor to describe his work-in-progress on reconciling the two philosophers</note>, I should nevertheless summarize the main points for you in this brief commentary...

# Second Chapter 
### In which it is asked where Plato spoke about being and the one, and it shows that his words favor the opinion that says the one and being are equal, rather than those who want the one to be superior to being.

<margin>What should be thought of Plato's *Parmenides*.</margin>

<margin>The utility of logic.</margin>

They rely on these arguments; before we dismantle them, it would not be out of place to bring into the open what can be found expressed by Plato regarding this question. I find Plato discussing being and the one <note>original: "de ente & uno"</note> in two places: namely, in the *Parmenides* and the *Sophist*. The Academics <note>Pico is referring to the Neoplatonists, later followers of Plato who argued that "The One" was a mystical principle higher than "Being" or existence itself.</note> contend that in both places, the "one" is placed above "being" by Plato. 

But I will first say this regarding the *Parmenides*: nothing is asserted in that whole dialogue; nor, even if it were asserted most strongly, could anything be found clearly enough to allow us to ascribe a dogma of this kind to Plato. Certainly, the book should not be counted among the dogmatic <note>In this context, "dogmatic" refers to works intended to teach a specific, settled doctrine rather than those meant for training the mind.</note> works, since it is entirely nothing else than a certain <term>dialectical exercise|A method of logical investigation through question and answer, often used to test the consistency of definitions rather than to state a final truth.</term> which is so far from my own opinion that the dialogue itself...

Zeno had judged this to be the duty of old age. Even if we do not believe these testimonies, let us run through the dialogue itself <note>The dialogue referred to here is Plato’s *Parmenides*, a famously difficult work about the nature of the "One."</note>. We shall see that nothing is affirmed anywhere. Instead, it is only asked everywhere: "If this thing exists, what will follow?" and likewise, "What if it does not exist?" The Academics <note>The "Academics" were later followers of Plato who embraced skepticism, arguing that nothing can be known for certain.</note> seized the opportunity for their own opinion regarding being and the one from this source. Indeed, in the first proposition, he exercises himself with this problem to see what would follow if all things were one. He responds that it would follow that the "one" we suppose to exist would be impartible <note>original: "imptibile" (impartibile); meaning it cannot be divided into parts.</note>, would be infinite, would be nowhere, and after enumerating many things of that kind, he also brings this up among others: it would follow, namely, that the "one" is not being <note>original: "ens"</note>. 

Pay attention, however, even if this is not merely a dialectical exercise but a dogma being handed down concerning being and the one: consider how much these two things differ—namely, to assert that the One is *above* being, and to assert that it would follow that *if* all things are one, that "one" would not be being. Enough has been said regarding Parmenides. Indeed, in the *Sophist* <note>Another of Plato's dialogues.</note>, he speaks rather in favor of the view that the One and Being are equal <margin>What he says in the *Sophist* regarding being and the one</margin> rather than the One being superior to Being. I do not find where he explains this otherwise. He signifies this in many ways, as through these words: "For considering it thus, you confess it is necessary that he who says 'something' says 'one' thing," and shortly after: "Truly, he who does not say 'something' must say 'nothing' at all." These are his words. Therefore, for him, "not one" and "nothing" are equal—indeed, they are the same; likewise, "one" and "something" are equal. After this, he likewise proves that it cannot be said that "non-being is one." And thus he concludes: "Being does not happen to non-being; therefore, the 'one' does not happen to non-being." He is speaking, however, about the "one" which he had said above was equal to that which is "something." He seems, therefore, to take it as granted that the "one" is "being." But let us grant that Plato affirmed this—though he certainly affirmed it nowhere. Come, let us examine in what sense it could truly be said, first laying the foundations of Aristotle’s own opinion in this manner.

### Chapter three, in which he declares how "being" is understood by Aristotle when he makes it equal to the "one" and encompassing all things. <margin>Being can be understood in two ways. He proves the word is correctly understood in the way Aristotle understood it. First testimony. Second, Simplicius defending Parmenides. Solution to the first argument of the Platonists.</margin>

This word, "being" <note>original: "ens"</note>, about which there is doubt as to whether it is equal to the "one," can be accepted in two ways. The first is that when we say "being," we understand everything that is "outside of nothing" <note>original: "extra nihil"</note>. Aristotle used it in this way when he made being equal to the one. Nor did he use the word this way without reason: for as it is truly said, we ought to think like the few, but speak like the many. We think and hold opinions for ourselves; we speak to others—that is, to the multitude—and we speak so that we may be understood. The common people, and anyone from their midst, understand "being" in such a way that everything is called "being" which does not lack "to be" <note>original: "esse"</note>, and which cannot truly be called "nothing." 

But even among those who are considered the wisest, even among those who hold the opposite view, we find this word used in this way. For Parmenides the Pythagorean, when he said "the One is that which is," he understood God. If we believe Simplicius <note>A 6th-century commentator on Aristotle who tried to harmonize different Greek philosophies.</note> and many others who wish to defend Parmenides against those who misrepresent him—as if he had said that *all* things are one—they respond with one voice that it was never believed by Parmenides that there is no division, multitude, or plurality in things. He openly confesses this elsewhere in his poems. But when he said "the One is that which is," he judged that the name of "being" truly fits that which is truly only "One"—which "One" is God. Therefore, if we believe Parmenides and his defenders and the Platonists, the "one" cannot be above "being" unless it is above God. So far is Parmenides from denying that God is "being," that he grants the true name of "being" to God alone.

And so, the solution to the first argument of the Platonists <note>Followers of Plato who, in this era, often argued that the "One" (the ultimate source) was superior to and separate from "Being."</note> presents itself to us in passing. But even Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A 5th-6th century theologian whose writings were a cornerstone of medieval Christian philosophy; he was often used to support the idea that God is "beyond" Being.</note>—whom those disputing against us claim as a supporter of their own opinion—will not deny that it was truly said by God to Moses: "I am who I am." This we read in Greek as "I am the one who is" <note>original: *εγω ειμι ο ων* (ego eimi ho on)</note>, that is: "I am <term>Being</term> <note>The author uses the Latin word *ens*, referring to the fundamental state of existence or "that which is."</note>." 

Indeed, since they themselves say that "nothing" (or non-being) is the opposite of Being, just as "multitude" is the opposite of the One, they must necessarily concede that whatever is not Being is nothing (or non-being). Just as that which is not "one" is "many" (or a multitude). Therefore, if they follow the same rule of logic, they must admit that God is either "nothing"—a thought the ears themselves dread to hear—or that God is Being. In this way, when we accept the concept of Being, we establish that first axiom <note>A self-evident truth that requires no proof.</note> and universal principle: that of any thing, it must necessarily be said that it either is, or is not.
