God is the one who is the fullness of all existence: who alone is of Himself, and from whom alone—with no intermediary standing between—all things have proceeded into being. For this reason, we truly say that God is not "being," but rather "above-being" <note>original Latin: *super ens*</note>, and that God himself is something higher than being. Since the name of "the One" is given to Him, it follows that we must confess the One to be above being. However, we call God "the One" not so much to declare *what* He is, but rather *how* He is all things that He is, and how other things come from Him. For "the One," as Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian theologian and philosopher whose works were highly influential in the Middle Ages and Renaissance</note> says, is a name given to God because He is all things in a unique way. Again, He is called "the One" because He is the principle of all things that exist, just as the number "one" <note>original: *unitas* (unity)</note> is the principle of all numbers.

<margin>Why God is called "the One."</margin>

Therefore, if—as the Academics <note>Followers of the later Platonic school</note> claim—Plato affirms in the first part of the *Parmenides* that the One is superior to being, that "One" will be none other than God. This they themselves admit, asserting by common consensus that the first principle of all things is what Plato is treating there. But someone might say that in this respect, at least, Aristotle disagrees with Plato: for Aristotle never treats "being" <term>ens; the concept of existence</term> in such a way that it falls under the "One," nor does he fail to include God within it, as Plato does. Those who say this have not read Aristotle. He, in fact, does this too, and far more clearly than Plato. For in the sixth book of *First Philosophy* <note>Aristotle’s *Metaphysics*</note>, he says that "being" is divided into "being in itself" <term>ens per se; something that exists fundamentally</term> and "being by accident" <term>ens per accidens; a property or quality of something else</term>. Since "being in itself" is divided into ten categories <note>The ten Aristotelian categories (substance, quantity, quality, etc.)</note>, there is no doubt among good interpreters that God is not contained under this "being," for He is neither "being by accident" nor is He contained under any of the ten categories into which "being in itself" is divided.

<margin>How it could be said by Plato that the One is above being, if indeed he said this.</margin>

<margin>So also by Aristotle, who sometimes takes the view that God should be called not "being" but "above-being."</margin>

Likewise, that division is common among the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school</note> where being is said to be divided into "substance" and "accident." When this occurs, we understand "being" in such a way that God is above being, and not contained under it, just as Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas</note> teaches in the first book of his commentary on the *Sentences*. I will add this as well: some Platonists boast unfairly, as if they possessed a mystery unknown to Aristotle when they say there are two proper names for God—namely, "the One" and "the Good"—and that "the Good" and "the One" exist before "being." Just as we have shown that it was not hidden from the Peripatetics how God can be understood as "above being," we can also show that Aristotle gave these two names, "the Good" and "the One," to God above all others. For in the twelfth book of *First Philosophy*, after he disputed concerning the whole of being and the separate intellects <note>the "unmoved movers" or celestial spirits</note>, he asks at the end (as if turning after everything else to investigate the properties of God alone) whether, besides the "good" that exists within the university of beings (like the order in an army), there is some "Separate Good" acting as the leader of this army. He determines that this Good is God. Consequently, in the same chapter, he proves God's unity, citing that famous line from Homer as testimony after his strong arguments: "Let there be one leader, one king." <note>original Greek: εις κοιρανος εστω. εις βασιλευς (eis koiranos estō. eis basileus)</note> Where, then, is Aristotle false? Where is he discordant with Plato? Where is he profane? Where does he think of God less honorably than is fitting?

<margin>That Aristotle gives these two greatest names—the One and the Good—to God.</margin>

...nor anything of those things that are not; nor is He among those things that are. Neither do the things that exist know Him as He is, nor does He know the things that are as they are. Let us recall what we have said, and we will see that in the **first step** we learn that God is not a body, as the <term>Epicureans</term> <note>Followers of Epicurus who believed the world was material and made of atoms; here accused of thinking God is a physical being.</note> believe, nor is He the "form" of a body, as those wish to claim who assert that God is the soul of the heavens or the universe. <margin>Against the Egyptian Epicureans, Varro, and others.</margin> This was the opinion of the Egyptians, as Plutarch writes, and of Varro, the Roman theologian. But there are even some among the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle, who traditionally taught in the "peripatos" or covered walkway of the Lyceum.</note> who are so dull-witted that they confirm this to be the true opinion of Aristotle. They are like men resting in a prison as if stuck in the mortar, <note>original: "ī calce" — likely referring to being trapped in the "lime" or building materials of the physical world.</note> believing they have reached the heights of God while they are still lying on the ground, having not yet moved a foot toward Him. For if they were right, God would be neither a perfect life, nor a perfect being, <margin>The fifth decade of the Concord of Plato and Aristotle.</margin> nor even a perfect intellect. We learn in the **second step**—which fewer people attain correctly, and in which we are more likely to fail if we stray even a little from true understanding—that God <margin>The second step.</margin> is neither life, nor intellect, nor something that can be understood; rather, He is something better and more excellent than all of these. <margin>Dionysius and the Platonists.</margin> For all these names express a *particular* perfection, yet no such particularity exists in God. Recognizing this, both Dionysius and later the Platonists deny that life, intellect, wisdom, and similar things exist in God. But since God, by His unique perfection—which is His infinity and His deity—unites and collects in Himself the total perfection of all these things (which in us are many and divided), He is not like "one" thing among those many, <margin>The Peripatetics.</margin> but the "One" who exists *before* the many. <margin>The Parisian theologians.</margin> Therefore, others, and especially the Peripatetics (whom the <term>Parisian theologians</term> <note>The Scholastic scholars at the University of Paris, then the center of Catholic theological study.</note> imitate in almost everything as far as they can), concede that all these things *are* in God. By saying and believing this, we not only speak and believe correctly, but we also speak in harmony with those who deny these attributes. <margin>Augustine.</margin> This is true if we always keep before our eyes the words of Aurelius Augustine: that the wisdom of God is no more "wisdom" than it is "justice," and the justice of God is no more "justice" than it is "wisdom."

In the same way, life in Him is no more "life" than it is "knowledge," nor is His knowledge more "knowledge" than it is "life." For all these things are one in God—not through confusion or mixing, or as if distinct things were penetrating one another—but through a simple, supreme, ineffable, and foundational unity. In this unity, every act, every form, and every perfection—just as in a primary and most eminent leader—is so excellently enclosed within the deepest treasures of divine infinity, above and beyond all things, that God is not only intimate to all things, but is more "one" with all things than they are with themselves. Truly, words fail, <margin>To love God. Note.</margin> and everything we say is less than what we can conceive.

But see, my dear Angelo, <note>Addressing his friend, the famous humanist scholar Angelo Poliziano.</note> what madness holds us? While we are in the body, we can love God more than we can either speak of Him or know Him. By loving Him, we benefit ourselves more, labor less, and obey Him more. Yet we always prefer to go on seeking through knowledge, never finding what we seek, rather than possessing it through love—for without love, even if He were found, He would be found in vain. But let us return to our subject: it is now clearly evident to you how God may sometimes be called Mind, Intellect, Life, and Wisdom, and yet at other times be placed above all these things. <margin>Plato.</margin> Both views are proved to be true and harmonious. Nor does Plato disagree with Aristotle on this point; for in the sixth book of the *Republic*, when Plato speaks of the God whom he calls the "Idea..."

<meta>This page continues the philosophical argument regarding the relationship between "the One" (unity) and "Being" (existence), specifically refuting the Neoplatonic view that the One is superior to Being. It transitions into a discussion of the four "transcendentals" (Being, One, True, Good) and how they derive from God.</meta>

...the root of multitudes: Prime matter, therefore, according to that man who is so great among the Platonists that he is called "divine" <note>likely referring to the philosopher Plotinus</note>, is not only not "one," but is a multitude—or rather, the root of all multitude found in things. We have said these things to throw their own arguments back at them. However, prime matter is not entirely devoid of unity, just as it is not entirely devoid of being. It receives its exact unity from the same source from which it receives its being: from *form*. I pass over the disputes regarding its unity—whether affirmative or negative—as all these matters are well known to those who have even slightly walked with the Aristotelians <note>original: "de ambulatiūculam fecerint," a punning reference to the Peripatetics, or "those who walk about."</note>.

### Chapter Seven, in which he resolves the third argument of the Platonists regarding multitude, and shows that for those who say the "One" is more common than "Being," they must concede something that Plato himself denies.

<margin>Solution to the third argument.</margin>
<margin>Argument against the Platonists proving that, according to Plato, the One cannot be superior to Being.</margin>

They are greatly mistaken in their third argument. For multitude is not opposed to the "One" in the same way that "non-being" is opposed to "being." The latter possess a **contradictory** opposition <note>A logic term where one must be true and the other false, like "alive" and "not-alive."</note>; the former possess either a **privative** or **contrary** opposition, which the Aristotelians discuss at length in the tenth book of the *First Philosophy* <note>Aristotle’s *Metaphysics*.</note>. But let them see what ruins they fall into, those who are called Platonists and claim the "One" is higher than "Being." It is certain that whenever two categories are related such that one is under the other (as a specific type is under a more general one), it is possible for something to escape the scope of the lower category while still remaining within the higher one. This is exactly why the higher category is said to be "more common." 

A ready example: because "animal" is more common than "man," it can happen that something is "not-man" while still being an "animal." By that same logic, if the "One" were more common than "Being," it would be possible for something to be "non-being" (nothing) while still being "one." Thus, unity would be claimed for "nothingness," a concept that Plato expressly refutes in his dialogue, the *Sophist*.

### Chapter Eight, in which he declares how these four—namely Being, One, True, and Good—exist in all things that come after God.

<margin>Followers of Avicenna. Averroes. Plato.</margin>
<margin>The order among these four.</margin>

The truest opinion, therefore, is that there are four properties that encompass all things: **Being**, **One**, **True**, and **Good**. This holds if we understand their opposites to be nothingness, division, falsehood, and evil. To these four, two others were added—namely, **Something** and **Thing**—by later thinkers following Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina, a Persian philosopher whose works heavily influenced Western thought.</note>. Avicenna interpolated the philosophy of Aristotle in many places, which led to great intellectual battles with Averroes <note>Ibn Rushd, an Andalusian philosopher known as "The Commentator" on Aristotle.</note>; but as far as this specific matter is concerned, there is little actual discord. For these thinkers divide what is understood as the "One" into "One" and "Something" (an idea not foreign to Plato, who in the *Sophist* lists "Something" among these related terms), and they divide what is contained under "Being" into "Being" and "Thing." 

But regarding those two, we shall speak elsewhere. To follow what we have begun, these four exist in God in one way, and in those things created after God in another; for God possesses these from himself, while all other things have them from Him. Let us first see how they exist in created things. All things that come after God have an <term>efficient, exemplary, and final cause</term> <note>"Efficient" is the maker, "exemplary" is the blueprint or Idea, and "final" is the purpose.</note> because all things are *from* Him, *through* Him, and *for* Him. 

Therefore, if we consider things as they are established by God as the **efficient cause**, they are called **beings** because they participate in existence through His making. If we consider them according to their **exemplary pattern**—which we call the "Idea" according to which God created them—they match and correspond to that pattern; thus they are called **true**. (For example, a "true" image of Hercules is one that actually conforms to the real Hercules). If they tend toward Him as their **ultimate end**, they are called **good**. If, however, each thing is taken absolutely in itself, it is called **one**. The order among them is as follows...

<meta>This page continues the metaphysical investigation into the nature of existence, specifically focusing on the "transcendental" properties of Being—Unity, Truth, and Goodness—and how they relate to the Creator and the created world.</meta>

First, everything should be conceived under the <term>concept of being</term><note>original: "sub entis ratione"; the philosophical framework used to understand existence</note>, since the agent first causes everything so that it is something in itself; otherwise, it would not proceed from the agent according to the whole of what it is. From this, it follows that nothing exists after God <note>in the hierarchy of being</note> such that, in conceiving it, we do not understand it as a being from another, a finite being, or a <term>participated being</term><note>a being that does not have existence by its own nature but receives it from a higher source</note>. Unity follows after Being. The third property is Truth, because after something exists in itself, it must be seen whether it is such as the exemplar according to which it was formed; if it is found to be similar to that exemplar, it remains for it to turn toward that source—as if toward a kinsman or relative—through Goodness. <margin>Plato.</margin> Who does not see that these properties are equal in scope? Grant that something exists, and it is certainly "one." For he who does not say "one" says nothing, as Plato says in the *Sophist*. For whatever exists is undivided in itself and divided from all others which are not itself. This is what we understand when we say "one," <margin>Truth is convertible with being.</margin> or to speak in Plato's words, it is "identical to itself and other than others," which he himself confirms in that same dialogue as applying to every single thing. It is also necessarily "true." For if he is a man, he is certainly a true man; it is the same as saying that "this is not true gold" and "it is not gold." For when you say it is not true <margin>Augustine.</margin> gold, you mean this: it looks like gold and is something similar to gold, but it is not gold. Therefore, Aurelius Augustine, defining what is "true" in his *Soliloquies*, says: "The true is that which is" <note>original: "verum est id quod est"</note>. This should not be taken to mean that "being" and "true" are the exact same thing. For although they are the same in reality, they are different in concept and definition. Therefore, one should not be defined by the other, but Augustine wanted to express this: a thing is then called "true" when it is that which it is called and is said to be—as gold is then "true" when it is gold and <margin>Good is convertible with being.</margin> nothing other than gold. This, therefore, is what he meant by "the true is that which is," though some people, not paying attention, find fault with the definition. In the same way, a thing is also "good," because whatever exists is good insofar as it exists. <margin>Arguments against Olympiodorus.</margin> Olympiodorus is far from the truth, in my opinion, believing he can prove that "good" and "being" are different because we desire "good" simply, but we do not desire "being" simply, but "well-being" <note>to live well or happily</note>; and therefore, it could happen that if things go badly for us, we might desire not to be. For—to set aside the question of whether those who are in a bad and miserable state can seek not to exist by a right and natural desire—he does not notice that just as "being" is manifold, so goodness is manifold. For there is first the natural being of things, as for a man to be a man, for a lion to be a lion, or for a stone to be a stone; a natural goodness follows this being inseparably. There are other ways of being which can be called "accidental" <note>original: "adventitia"; qualities that are added to a thing but are not part of its essential definition</note>, such as for a man to be wise, to be beautiful, or to be healthy. Just as wisdom and beauty are different kinds of "being" from humanity, so they are different kinds of "good." For the "good" of humanity (by which a man is a man) is one thing, and the "good" of wisdom (by which he is not just a man, but a wise man) is another; just as the former is one kind of being and the latter is another. Therefore, just as all things seek the "good," so all things seek "being." And first, they seek that goodness which follows natural being, because this is the foundation of the goodnesses that follow; all those others come to the thing in such a way that they cannot stand without that foundation. For how will he be happy who does not exist at all? Truly, that goodness which they first acquire when they exist is not enough for them, but they desire to reach the remaining ones which complete and adorn that first one. Just as we say truly that other "goodnesses" are sought by them besides the first, so we can truly say that other "beings" are desired by them besides the first—because "being happy" is one kind of being, and "being a man" is another. And if anyone grants that it is possible for someone to be unwilling to exist if he is not happy, it does not follow (as Olympiodorus thinks) that "good" is one thing and "being" is another; rather, it follows that being a "man" is one thing and being "happiness" is another, and likewise, the goodness of a man is one thing and the goodness of happiness is another.

### Chapter nine, in which he declares how those four properties are in God.

Let us examine again how these properties exist in God, in whom they do not exist in relation <margin>e</margin> to a cause, since he has no cause. For he is himself the cause of all things and is from no one. However, these can be considered in God for two reasons: either insofar as he is the cause of others (a distinction that does not apply to created things as far as the present business is concerned, since God can exist without being a cause); or because other things cannot exist without being from him. 

Therefore, we first conceive of God as being the "universality of all act," the fullness of being itself. This understanding is followed by the fact that he is "One," so that even the opposite cannot be conceived. See how far they wander who invent several first principles or many gods! Immediately, it is also "most true"; for what can he have that appears to be and yet is not, <margin>The three conditions of the Good according to Plato.</note> since he is "Being" itself? It follows certainly that he is Truth itself. But he will also be "Goodness" itself. For there are three conditions of the "Good," as Plato writes in the *Philebus*: that it be "Perfect," "Sufficient," and "Desirable." Moreover, that which we conceive of in this way will be Perfect, because nothing will be lacking to Him who is everything. He will be Sufficient, because for those possessing Him, nothing will be lacking, as they will find all things in Him.

### THE FIRST OBJECTIONS OF ANTONY OF FAENZA AGAINST THE LITTLE BOOK ON BEING AND THE ONE.

<margin>The first objection.</margin> If any little book deserves to be inscribed "On Being and the One," it is necessary that it explain the nature and properties of being and the one. However, in this little work which recently came into my hands, and which is titled *On Being and the One*, many things are treated that are almost foreign to the title and inscription. Indeed, the author's primary purpose is to dispute whether, according to Plato, Being and the One follow each other mutually <note original: "sese inuicem mutuo cōsequātur">This refers to the concept of "convertibility," where Being and the One are considered different words for the same reality.</note>, or whether, as the Academics <note>The "Academics" refers to the followers of Plato's Academy.</note> think, the One is more common than Being. But this is not to treat "of being and the one" but of the mutual conversion of being and the one—and not even absolutely, but only according to Plato. For if any philosopher were to debate only the question of whether the soul is immortal, he would not thereby be "disputing about the soul," but a treatise would be held specifically "on the immortality of the soul."

<margin>The second objection.</margin> The author of the work says, moreover, that the Academics think God (according to Plato) is not truly and properly Being, which indeed I wonder at greatly. If he means all the Academics or Platonists, as his phrasing seems to signify (otherwise he would not pronounce absolutely that the Academics feel this way), it perhaps does not lack a falsehood. 

<margin>Themistius.</margin> For Themistius, an author of no small nobility among the Platonists, testifies that the Idea which is the principle of things is, in Plato’s opinion, truly and properly "Being" and "the One." Indeed, the Platonists—either all or most of them—do not think the Idea is one thing and God, the craftsman of things, another.

<margin>The third objection.</margin> Proceeding further, he says: "If it can be defended in any way that according to Plato the One is more common than Being, it must be judged thus." He says that words which in the Latin name are called "concrete," such as *white*, *shining*, or *being*, signify something foreign [to the essence] by whose presence the things receive the name. For whiteness is one thing, a white object another; humanity is one thing, a human another. Therefore, that will be called "Being" in which "to be" is one thing, and that which subsists is another. Therefore, God, who is "Being" itself, cannot be judged "a being," but "the One," because he contains and closes off all things. But does not this sort of defense lack coherence with itself?

For by the same reasoning that "white," "man," and "being" signify something distinct, it must also be that "one," "blessed," "God," and many similar terms signify something distinct. Therefore, God—who is Unity, Blessedness, and Divinity all at once—could not be called "one," nor "blessed," nor even "God" at all <note>The author is exploring the "apophatic" or negative theology tradition, which suggests that human language and categories are insufficient to describe the Divine essence.</note>. How then is He not "Being," but "The One"?

Furthermore, "being" is said of that which exists. <margin>Confirmation</margin> Just as it is impossible for one who sits not to be "sitting," it is also impossible for Him who truly and <margin>Fourth [argument].</margin> properly is "Being" not to exist; for God says, "I am who I am" <note>original: "ego sum qui sum"; a reference to the divine name revealed to Moses in Exodus 3:14</note>.

But it may seem even more remarkable that he <note>The author of the text being discussed.</note> tries to defend the idea that God is not "Being," not only according to Plato, but he even tries to pull Aristotle himself into the same opinion. For in the book of the *Metaphysics* <note>Aristotle's primary work on the nature of reality and existence.</note>, he says: "Being" is divided into <term>being through itself</term> <note>original: "ens per se"; things that exist by their own nature rather than as a property of another thing</note> and <term>accidental being</term> <note>original: "ens per accidens"; properties that happen to belong to a thing, like its color or size</note>. "Being through itself" is then divided into the ten <term>categories</term> <note>original: "praedicamenta"; Aristotle's classification system for all aspects of reality, such as substance, quality, and quantity</note>. ->**Response to the first objections.**<-

**GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA SENDS GREETINGS TO ANTONIO OF FAENZA.**

I have read your questions regarding that little book which I recently published, *On Being and the One*, with as much pleasure as the affection and freedom of mind with which you wrote them. I owe you much for this service. If we were to spend ourselves more freely upon our friends—or more willingly demand the same from them—we would certainly be far better and more learned than we currently are. But this deadly delusion has seized the minds of men: that we think we do not please those whom our errors do not please. We interpret the free judgment of friends as either hatred or grumpiness, while we interpret flattery as love and natural goodness. Thus it happens that while we prefer to be praised when undeserving rather than be corrected when we deserve it, we are always mocked and never truly earn praise. See how much we err! For almost all praise is always useless, and often harmful. For if it is true, what utility does it bring? If it is false, it surely makes us, who are praised, insane—and makes those who praise us ridiculous. 

Criticism, certainly, is always useful: if it is just, it leads us to knowledge; if it is less than just, it rouses us to the defense of the truth. Finally, what else is it to be corrected than to become better through another's labor? Or what else is it for a friend's book to shine under the "file" <note>original: "lima"; a metaphor for the polishing or editing of a text</note> than for you to benefit from his long nights while you are sleeping? Therefore, I cannot help but owe you much, as I was saying. Regarding the things in my book that pleased you less, you signaled your feelings to me freely. I recognized in your writings, besides your benevolence, that dexterity of mind already known to me. I immediately began to examine quite severely whatever you had noted—not as a father <note>i.e., not as the protective "parent" of the text</note> but as a judge—since your testimony had already brought those things into suspicion of being false. But as I thought about it, several points occurred to me by which those ideas seemed capable of being defended and vindicated from fault. I wanted to write these back to you freely, lest I myself fail to embrace the very virtue I praise in you; so that if I do not imitate your judgment in criticizing those points, I might at least imitate your freedom in defending them. 

<margin>Solution to the first objection. The Title. The Prologue.</margin> You say it is not right for the book to be titled *On Being and the One*, since you do not deal in it with the nature and all the properties of "being" and "the one," but only with the interchangeability <note>original: "conversione"; the metaphysical concept that "Being" and "One" are different names for the same reality</note> of the one and being. What is the Prologue but an expanded and explained Title? The title promises a treatise on "being" and "the one"...

But I say that the chimera we conceive in the mind does not exist for the very reason that the parts of which we understand it to consist are divided in the nature of things, rather than united. And just as a thing does not exist if its constituent parts are divided, so too a thing not only does not exist, but *cannot* exist, if its parts are neither united nor able to be united by the force of nature. Therefore, we say a chimera does not exist—and we believe it is impossible for it to exist—for no other reason than this: it is not credible that the beasts from which we imagine it will ever come together into a single animal composition. 

Again, you insist that because a diameter is incommensurable <note>original: "diametrum non esse commensurabilem." Something is detected as false to the extent that it fights with itself and includes a contradiction. And what else is it to include a contradiction than to be "divided" within itself? Therefore, every truth is "one" because it is consistent and harmonious with itself; every falsehood is "divided" because it fights with itself and is not coherent. 

Many have believed that the false is the negation of the true—a fact that is not hidden from you. <margin>Solution to the sixth objection</margin> Nor do the arguments you bring forward stand in the way. Although false gold is not only *not* gold, but is also something *other* than gold, it nonetheless happens to be something else besides gold only insofar as it is "false"; it is false because it is not the gold it appears to be. 

Therefore, it is false gold because it does not fit the "idea" <term>idea: In this context, the perfect, essential pattern of a thing as it exists in the mind of God or the nature of reality.</term> of gold; but because it fits the idea of bronze or silver, it is not entirely false. It is only false gold, just as it is not entirely "non-being"; for although it is not this specific thing (gold), it is nonetheless something else—say, bronze, lead, or silver. <margin>What absolute falsehood is</margin> But that which corresponds to no idea is entirely and absolutely false, just as it is entirely non-being—such as what we call a chimera. 

See, therefore, how they proceed in a parallel course: non-being, the divided, and the false. Thus, a chimera can rightly be called "false," and every false thing can be called "divided." <margin>Solution to the seventh objection. Albert. Thomas.</margin> Indeed, evil is not opposed to good by a "contrary" opposition <note>In logic, a "contrary" is a polar opposite (like black and white), whereas a "negation" is a lack of something (like the absence of light).</note> as you think; Albert <note>Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280), a foundational scholar of the Middle Ages.</note> teaches this in his exposition of Aristotle’s *Categories*, and your Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the most influential Scholastic theologian.</note> discusses it at great length in the first question of his work *On Evil*. <meta>This page continues a philosophical debate regarding the nature of truth, falsehood, and the classification of Good and Evil, likely responding to a previous letter or objection concerning Aristotelian logic.</meta>

...a falsehood, in so far as it is false, is false—not "not false"—but it is true <note>The author is using a logical paradox: it is "truly" a fact that the falsehood is false.</note>; and for that reason, it is not divided, but one.

<margin>Another solution</margin> 

You add that I say falsely that what is false encloses a contradiction. You argue this because there are many false things which, by the power of either nature or man, are capable of being true. But you should consider this: everything that is false, for as long as it remains false, encloses a contradiction. However, just as some things are false in such a way that they *could* become true, others are false in such a way that they can *never* be true. So too are there some things so contradictory to themselves and so at war with themselves that they can never return to a state of friendship and concord. Others hate one another in such a way that they can nonetheless eventually return to favor. 

<margin>Example</margin>

This will be made manifest by an example: to say "a man is a lion" is always false, because it always encloses a contradiction, and just as it can never be reduced to a unity, so can it never be reduced to a truth. But for me to say "I am sitting" is neither true nor false <note>This refers to a "contingent" statement—it depends on the physical act.</note>. If, however, you add that I am sitting *while I am standing*, you immediately introduce a falsehood. In the same way, you also bring in a contradiction. For "me sitting while I stand" includes a contradiction; and as soon as it ceases to be false—as when I actually begin to sit—it immediately returns from division back to unity. 

<margin>Another solution</margin>

Furthermore, the objections you raise concerning the opposition of the false and the true were already resolved in my earlier letter. For you say: "if it is true, it is that which is seen to be what it is; if it is false, it is that which is seen to be what it is not." Since there is no contradiction between "seeming to be what is" and "seeming to be what is not," you argue that the false is not the negation of the true. 

<margin>Another solution</margin>

But I do not accept the definition of the "false" in that way: namely, that it consists in something appearing to be what it is not. Rather, I want its definition to be this: that it is *not* that which it is said to be. 

<margin>Note</margin>

For example, "false gold" is false precisely because it is *not* gold; and as far as the definition of the false is concerned, it happens to either seem to be, or actually be, something other than gold. 

As for your claim that I have not resolved your argument by which you prove that Good and Evil are contraries, I will speak frankly. I did not think a solution was needed where there was no real knot to untie. Your argument is of this sort: "The Good is to be sought. The Evil is to be fled. Seeking and fleeing are contrary motions. Therefore, Good and Evil are contraries." To me, this reasoning of yours seems so effective and of such great power that it proves not only that Good and Evil are contraries (about which someone might perhaps doubt), but also that **Being** and **Non-Being** are contraries—even though everyone knows those are actually <term>contradictories</term> <note>In formal logic, "contraries" (like black and white) allow for a middle ground, while "contradictories" (like being and non-being) do not.</note>. For we would conclude thus: "Being is to be sought; Non-being is to be fled; seeking and fleeing are contrary motions; therefore, Being and Non-being are contraries." Either you must grant me that Being and Non-being are contraries, or I will not grant you that Good and Evil are contraries.

<margin>Another solution</margin>

But, you will say, another argument must be resolved. "Non-being" is not a <term>genus</term> <note>A general category in logic.</note>; how then is "Evil" nothing, when Aristotle says in the *Categories* <note>original: "predicamentis"</note> that Good and Evil are the genera of contraries? 

<margin>Aristotle</margin>

All the interpreters of Aristotle are full of solutions to this question, to whom I referred you in my previous letter, lest I entangle us both in unnecessary labor.

Aristotle often uses examples in his logical commentaries based on the opinions of others rather than his own. If you pay attention, you will see why he wishes this to be so: because evil itself is entirely ignorant of the property of a contrary. For he concedes that these things can be allotted the name of a "contrary" in some way only to the extent that they do not possess the full nature of evil, but retain something of the goodness which they have not yet lost. Therefore, they are in some way contraries only insofar <margin>He argues against the opponent.</margin> as they are, in some way, not entirely evil. 

But if I were to set death or blindness before you, I would ask <margin>the opponent.</margin> whether these are "true evils" according to the opinion of Thomas, and again, whether they oppose each other through that species of contrariety you describe. I do not see at all what you would answer. For if these are evils—and in that very passage from which you bring forth testimony from Thomas—he would contend with great assertiveness that these cannot possibly be contraries through that very species of contrariety you put forward. With what mind do you affirm this as being the opinion of Thomas? You ought to have known that what is conceded regarding certain "imperfect" evils (due to the mixture of goodness they still retain) must not be transferred to the pure and absolute nature of evil itself.

[Marginal notes]

<margin>m. These "restricted" and "unrestricted" categories are your own inventions, not those of Thomas Aquinas.</margin>

<margin>n. To give a ridiculous answer to a question that was not asked ridiculously is absurd, even if many things are asked foolishly and answered foolishly—that is, they are answered so they don't appear unsolved simply because they *cannot* be solved. Therefore, to someone asking "is the moon a being?" it is rightly answered that it is a being. But to someone asking further "what kind of being is it?" it is certainly a ridiculous answer to simply say "it is a being."</margin>

<margin>o. You are saying nothing. For who does not know that a thing is "not something" because it is neither a substance nor an accident?</margin>

<margin>p. These points are the same as those in the first question concerning evil, and they support my position just as those did.</margin>

[Main text]

...that God is not "being" in the first sense: for although He belongs to no <term>category</term><note>Latin: *genus*. In Aristotelian logic, these are the ten classifications of reality, such as substance, quality, or quantity.</note>, nothing prevents Him from truly and properly existing in the nature of things; and the question "Does He exist?" can be answered truthfully. How then could it be unknown that there is another way of "being"?

Furthermore, your reasoning has no strength. For the sense of Thomas’s words is this: <term>being</term><note>Latin: *ens*. The most fundamental concept in medieval philosophy, referring to anything that exists in any way.</note> is spoken of in one way as signifying the nature of the ten categories: that is, signifying substance and accident, and all things that are entirely "positive" which are contained in the ten categories. These are included either through themselves (such as species and genera) or as certain principles, whether <insert>m</insert> "restricted" or not (such as <term>prime matter</term><note>The purely potential "stuff" of the universe before it takes a specific shape or form.</note> and form in the category of substance; and God; and all substantial differences). In this first sense, certainly, negations and <term>privations</term><note>The absence of a quality that should normally be present, like blindness being the absence of sight.</note> cannot belong to a category.

In the other way, "being" is said of that which can answer the question "Is it?"—whether the thing is a true and positive being or not. Hence, adding an example, Thomas says: "and in this way, evil is; just as blindness is." This means: "and in this way evil is a being, just as blindness is a being." For in Thomas's usage, there is no difference whether one says "it is" or "it is a being." 

However, when he adds that "to be something" does not only signify [a category], he does not mean (as you <insert>n</insert> seem to have thought) that it is a reasonable answer to someone asking "What is the moon?" or "What is thunder?" to simply say "it is a being" or "it is something." Such a solution would be ridiculous. 

Rather, it is this: "to be <insert>o</insert> something" signifies (especially according to the first sense) that which can be reasonably answered to the question "What is it?" For instance, it signifies that it is a substance, or an accident, or an animal, or a color, or something of this sort which <insert>p</insert> can rightly be answered to a questioner. But blindness and evil are none of these things. 

Thomas himself explains in the *First Part, Question 48, Article 2* <note>Referring to the *Summa Theologiae*, where Aquinas discusses whether evil is a real thing in the world.</note> that he does not wish the first part of this division to be interpreted with your mindset. Answering the second argument there, he says:

> As is said in the sixth book of the *Metaphysics*, "being" is used in two ways. In one way, it signifies the entity of a thing as it is divided into the ten categories; in this sense, "being" is interchangeable with "thing," and in this way no privation is a being, and thus neither is evil. In another way, "being" is used to signify the truth of a proposition, which consists in composition, the indicator of which is this word "is"; this is the "being" that answers the question "Is it?" In this sense, we say that blindness is in the eye, or any other privation. In this way, even evil is called a being. (Thus says Thomas.)

Death indeed takes away life completely, but neither the body nor primary matter <note>The most basic, formless substratum of all physical reality in Aristotelian philosophy.</note>. That which deceived you, therefore, is: that blindness is the precise privation of sight, and death of life; but it ought not therefore to have been believed that it is the precise privation of good. Does Thomas not openly confess to you and say that evil is contrary to good just as sick is to healthy, not as blindness is to sight? Blindness, therefore, insofar as it is evil, leaves something of the good upon which it rests; but insofar as it is blindness, it permits nothing of sight to exist. But what Thomas says—that good and evil are opposed as habit and privation—is most true: for in that place Thomas [discusses] those things properly [called] habit...

<meta>This page continues a metaphysical debate regarding the distinction between a thing's "essence" (what it is) and its "act of being" (that it exists). It specifically addresses the Fourth Objection in a series of logical challenges regarding the nature of God and created objects.</meta>

## Fourth Objections

It was not stated that God is not a **being** <term>ens; a thing that exists</term> because, in God, "to be" <term>esse; the act of existing</term> stands for His essence. Rather, it is because being is not something distinct from essence—which is a very different matter. Otherwise, the very being of a stone—which stands for its essence—would be considered neither a "being" nor "good." For the being of a stone is not essence in an abstract sense, but is the stone itself: its own "to be" and its own essence.

If we cannot ask "what is it?" regarding negations <note>the absence of something, such as "nothingness"</note> and privations <note>the lack of a quality that should naturally be there, such as "blindness"</note>: Since these do exist in a certain way, it is not enough to form the question "what is it?" simply by knowing that the thing in question exists. Rather, one must know more: both that it exists, and that it is *something* specific. Therefore, when someone asks "what is it?", it is ridiculous and irrational to respond with "a being" or "something," regardless of whether "being" is understood in the first sense <note>referring to a real entity in the world</note> or the second <note>referring to the logical truth of a statement</note>. Thus, if one asks what "sin" is, the question is about the name rather than a physical reality.

If a thing is a "being," then according to your position, it is a being because its "to be" is a different thing in reality from its essence. You argue that "humanity" is one thing, while "a human" is another; that "whiteness" <note>the abstract quality</note> is one thing, and "a white object" <note>the thing that possesses the quality</note> is another. Therefore, if an **Idea** <note>referring to the eternal archetypes or patterns of things held in the divine mind</note> is a being, it would be a being because the "to be" of the Idea is different from the Idea itself. However, the Idea is God; therefore, [the conclusion of your logic would be that] the being of the Idea is something different from God. <note>This is presented as a logical trap, as orthodox theology of this period held that God is simple and has no internal divisions.</note>

For if every human is simply and absolutely <term>capable of laughter</term><note>Latin: "risibilis." In medieval logic, being "capable of laughter" was the standard example of a "proprium"—a characteristic that belongs only to humans and to all humans, but is not part of their core definition.</note>, there is no need to add a condition to restrict it, such as saying: "every human is capable of laughter as long as they are human." Nor should such a restriction be added just because not all false things are divided equally, or because not all beings are equally good—nevertheless, all things are absolutely good in their being.

How we conclude that good and evil are opposites will be easily established if you understand that "pursuing" and "fleeing" are opposites, and if the logic of opposing motions has been sufficiently understood by you.

Why do you wonder if I say that the Latin scholars do not deny Aristotle—whom Simplicius <note>Simplicius of Cilicia (c. 490–560 AD) was one of the last great pagan Neoplatonist philosophers who wrote influential commentaries on Aristotle.</note> denies, but Boethius <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 477–524 AD), a Roman senator and philosopher who translated Aristotle into Latin and served as a bridge between Antiquity and the Middle Ages.</note> does not? Does it follow that I am either failing to imitate Boethius or exalting the "barbarians"? You call me a strange man; but I would call you "wonderful" instead—you who think that because I imitate Boethius and set aside Simplicius for a moment, I am scorning Boethius and following the barbarians.

If good and evil are opposites, you wish to prove that a <term>Chimera</term><note>A mythological beast, used in logic to represent an impossible object or a "non-being" that can be thought of but does not exist in reality.</note> is something that exists in the nature of things. But if you understood the logic by which I called good and evil opposites—which you either do not yet wish to or cannot understand—you would have proven nothing regarding the Chimera.

You are greatly surprised that I call certain <term>privations</term><note>A "privation" is not just the absence of something, but the absence of a good that *ought* to be there, like blindness in an eye.</note> "Half-full," and you try to prove they do not exist this way: "Evil is nothing; therefore, it is not a half-full privation." But following your own argument, I would say: sickness is evil; therefore, it is nothing; therefore, it is not a half-full privation. Yet, sickness is a certain kind of privation. Therefore, it is not a "half-full" privation of health or of some good, but rather a "full" and "perfect" one? That is impossible. Therefore, privations are "half-full" (incomplete) in the way that sickness, rarity, or ugliness are. Blindness is a "perfect" (complete) privation of sight, but an "imperfect" privation of the good—for it does not take away the entire good that exists in the one who cannot see.

If it is true, as you write, that every evil leaves something of the good behind, then the Chimera—which is entirely "non-being"—would also retain something of the good. If it preserves something of the good, it is not entirely evil, nor entirely non-existent. Granted, the "power" by which it could be created and exist is in God, and the "notion" by which it can be understood is in the mind; nonetheless, it remains that the Chimera is "good" and "being" only in terms of potential. For it is the power of God, and it is a "Chimera" for different reasons. We do not deny that the Antichrist is "good" in potential, whose power to exist is partly in matter and partly in the heavens and in man. Furthermore, how is the Chimera—if all thought and the power of God are excluded for a moment—entirely non-being and evil? For if it were non-being, it certainly could not be evil. For evil is a privation, which exists in a <term>subject</term><note>In this context, the "subject" is the physical thing or person that possesses a quality.</note>; and that subject must necessarily participate in goodness. Otherwise, it could not be a "subject" at all. For that which is entirely nothing cannot be the subject of anything.

You have not yet disproven what I said; and you try to confirm your view with the authority of Simplicius, except that Simplicius does not say what you claim. But there was no reason for you to boast; for I did not say that Aristotle felt that everything which exists does so either through itself or by accident, nor did I falsely attribute anything to the Blessed Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent Scholastic theologian.</note> because of it.

Although every privation is a kind of negation, it is not yet established that there isn't one kind of opposition for affirmation/negation and another for privation/habit. Nor does it follow that if evil is the privation of good, "evil" and "not-good" must be interchangeable terms.

As for your defense, by which you want to protect the idea that "God is not God," I attribute this neither to the truth nor to the Blessed—

I think this is consistent with Dionysius; nor did the blessed Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century theologian famous for "negative theology," which argues God is best described by what He is NOT.</note> ever deny that God is God. 
But as Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Scholastic philosopher and theologian.</note> interprets it, no name can fully explain the nature of God; nor for any other reason does he think affirmations are applied to God. Truly, you say that if the name of God has a description, it has a meaning <note>original: "rationem"</note>, not just a predicate. But even if this is granted, the argument stands: For let *.a.* be the meaning of the name. Let it be said in this way: "God is *.a.*" For the meaning of anything is predicated of that which it defines. Therefore, by a simple conversion, "*.a.* is God." Therefore "God is God." Likewise, you say that when one asks whether God is something other than God or not, it must be established what is conceived by the name of God. You say that whatever else is given, I will say it is God; for He is above everything that can be conceived. But does not this sort of solution contradict itself? For if you admit a proposition of this kind—that God is above that which can be conceived—do you not clearly affirm something about God? Let there be, then, a definition of the name that is "everything which is above that which can be conceived," and the argument will still hold. Furthermore, it follows that "God is above everything that can be conceived," therefore "God cannot be conceived"; otherwise, the same thing would be above itself. Therefore, He could neither be loved nor worshiped.

Finally, you might think the power of gold is so great that, whether we wish it or not, in reality or in the mind, it necessarily drags God along with it in this way: "Gold exists. Therefore, Being itself exists. Therefore, God exists." <note>This is a critique of a logical argument where the existence of a finite thing is used to prove the existence of the Absolute.</note> Likewise, you argue: "God is. Therefore, the Infinite is. The Infinite is, therefore it is nothing." If you say the Infinite Being is, then the finite is not—as if you were arguing: "The finite is not; therefore, it is nothing." Then you say: "The Infinite is, therefore the Infinite is not; for the Infinite," you say, "destroys itself." Truly, I think that if anyone had written such arguments to Nicoletto <note>Likely Nicoletto Vernia (d. 1499), a famous and controversial professor of philosophy at the University of Padua.</note>, he would have answered nothing. Nor will I oppose anything against them, lest I seem to doubt a matter that appears clearer to me than light. Indeed, if you try to prove your "refinement" <note>original: "politiōem"</note> with these arguments, I truly fear you may lose your gold.

If you wish, reply something to these objections, my best friend, so that we may now bring this disputation to an end; for we have played enough. Moreover, I would not want you to think I turned to these things out of hatred or ill-will. I know you remember that before I wrote anything to you, I asked if you were willing. Indeed, I call God to witness that I love and venerate my companion from Mirandola <note>Referring to his uncle, the famous Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.</note>. If you ever care to put it to the test, you will recognize that I have told no lie.

<meta>This page appears to be the beginning of a preface or dedicatory letter by Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola, the nephew of the famous philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. He is describing his efforts to collect and publish his late uncle's papers.</meta>

Consulting the needs of men, I hurried to Florence by the fastest possible journeys. I applied myself with whatever means I could to ensure that whatever had been noted by him <note>Referring to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), the famous Renaissance philosopher.</note>, even if unpolished and unexamined, might be committed to our authority. Our efforts were not entirely in vain; for even if the wills <note>original: "tabule"; referring to the legal tablets or documents of inheritance.</note> had not yet been opened, nor the heir known, the chests were nonetheless opened in such a way that we might inspect and turn over all the commentaries. We saw in those scattered paper codices the man's incredible zeal: universal reading, and concepts admirable beyond the grasp of the human mind. But in organizing the writings, there was a lack of care that is not to be praised; everything was cut up and scattered here and there. But about these things, I shall speak elsewhere.

While we were unrolling these with diligent care, his little work *On the One and Being* <note>original: "de uno & ente"; a famous treatise by Pico attempting to reconcile the philosophies of Plato and Aristotle.</note>, published about four years before his death, fell into my hands together with three letters written by you to him regarding it, and their replies. Because of the novelty of the matter, I did not just read through these, but drank them in—indeed, almost devoured them, as they say (for I knew by rumor that this had been done, but I had not sufficiently explored what importance they brought). I began to think and debate with myself whether I should give that work to the printers publicly with the other works I had gathered and judged for publication, making no mention of your objections; or whether it would be more prudent if it went out to the public both attacked here by objections and fortified there by defenses. 

After a long discussion of the matter, a final opinion at last settled in my mind. Certainly, it would seem to bear marks of infamy if encountered by learned men, if it did not just fear accusers, but also did not dare to summon them to judgment, as if it lacked faith in its own conscience. Likewise, it seemed opportune for it to go accompanied by the replies, as if with witnesses to defend the cause of its innocence. I did not doubt that this plan of ours would be praised by upright men, since I should either have allowed my late uncle—a man who had truly earned my greatest gratitude—to be defrauded in some part of his famous teaching by not publishing such a little book, or, if it went out alone, to leave a handle for the most wicked vituperations and accusations forever, by not calling into the forum <note>A metaphor for the public sphere of scholarly debate.</note> those things which had been composed on both sides in several letters of objection and rebuttal. 

But when some letters were presented from our Christopher Saxolus <note>A local scholar and physician who was part of Pico's circle.</note>, both a citizen and a physician, by which it was signified to us that you had composed a fourth letter on that business which lacked a reply (as you said), the matter was called back into doubt. And again becoming of a wavering opinion, I thought the judgment, already balanced, must be weighed more exactly, since the last accuser was pressing the case and there was no one to act as defender. Then a certain urge to undertake a defense entered my mind, though it was not readily apparent how I should turn myself toward maintaining silence. 

From one side, the man's modesty and kindness toward everyone moved my mind, as did the cleverness and sharpness of his talent in untying and washing away difficult knots on the spot and in inexplicable riddles <note>original: "scyrpis"; literally "bulrushes," used idiomatically for riddles or thorny problems.</note>—so that I judged that your last letter had not been safely delivered. I thought it would have been easy for him to have replied. If, however, your letters were delivered by a faithful messenger, they might have perished through the negligence of the couriers (for that happens often) or by some other accident on the journey. Finally, it occurred to me in the explanations of your earlier questions that there was a complaint that the same things were often repeated by you and the same things often doubted; because of this, I immediately ran through the main points of your entire controversy to see if anything could be found in the first replies that could show the fourth letter had been sufficiently answered in part...

Otherwise, my dear Antonio, I would have very willingly left aside the work undertaken even from the beginning. This was both so that I might not seem to be initiated into controversies, from which I shrink even if I were pleading a most just cause, and so that I might not deviate from the true path of philosophy. This is the path which—after horses and arms <note>Gianfrancesco refers to his noble upbringing and military training, which he set aside for a life of study.</note> (though I have smelled some small flowers of letters since childhood)—and after the dealings of great leaders, I began to measure out with my uncle Giovanni Pico and our Giovanni Mainardi <note>Giovanni Mainardi (1462–1536) was a celebrated physician and a close friend and editor to both Picos.</note> as my guides. At that time, the knowledge of nature ought to invite us—not to exhaust ourselves in literary contests, but to recognize the Creator of nature himself. Philosophical meditations should always, of their own accord, invite us to investigate the innermost meanings of the divine words. This is the end of all studies; by these, the path to heaven is revealed to us, provided we do not cultivate them for the sake of capturing our own glory, but so that we might be able both to know our God more easily and love him more fervently. Thus, we may more promptly follow what he commanded to be done and flee what he taught must be avoided. 

Behold, the reason for this burden I have undertaken and the business with you is explained. It is most just, as you see, and therefore to be borne by you with an even mind. Indeed, I might perhaps have thought that I could use these writings of ours as messengers to confirm the kindness already begun and contracted with you in Ferrara. Otherwise, the very "being" of a stone, which stands for its essence, would be neither being nor good; for the "being" of a stone is not essence, but is itself both its "to be" and its essence.

...to have understood that a question can be formed to which an affirmative and correct answer can be given. First, if you think that a question cannot be correctly formed unless the thing being asked about is of such a nature that a response can be provided through it, I do not agree with you. 

For it is Aristotle’s opinion <margin>Aristotle</margin> <note>Aristotle (384–322 BCE) was the foundational figure for medieval and Renaissance logic; the author here is likely referencing his *Posterior Analytics*.</note> that one can inquire whether a centaur exists or not, even though a centaur is not the kind of thing where the question "does it exist?" can be answered <note>original: "an est," a standard logical inquiry into existence.</note> affirmatively, since it is a mere fable, a mere fiction. 

Similarly, I also oppose the view if you believe that the questioner must already know this same thing. For, as we have shown, a person who correctly asks *what* a thing is does not need to know more than the fact *that* it exists. Therefore, if someone knows a thing is "something," it is not a ridiculous response to say it is "something" to an ignorant person who is asking about it. 

However, for those who ask the question "what is the thing?", I have not been in the habit of teaching them that it is either a <term>being</term> <note>original: "ens." <meta>This page continues a philosophical defense of the Platonic "One," reconciling it with Scholastic and Stoic definitions of substance, essence, and existence.</meta>

For even if in created things the essence differs from being in reality, it does not follow from this that whatever can in any way be called "being" must necessarily be composed of essence and being—or existence—as if from parts <margin>The Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school of philosophy.</note></margin>. Therefore, the "Idea," which is the pattern or exemplar of created things, does not consist of essence and existence as distinct realities <margin>Antipater <note>A Stoic philosopher and student of Diogenes of Babylon.</note></margin>. However, we may speak of such a composition existing within the "Idea" <margin>Posidonius <note>A versatile Greek Stoic philosopher and scientist.</note></margin> when we consider it as the exemplary cause of the essence and being (or the being and existence) found in created things <margin>Seneca <note>The Roman Stoic philosopher and statesman.</note></margin>. We apply this composition and distinction equally even to the simplest things; we call it a "conceptual" distinction <note>original: "secundum rationem," meaning a distinction made by the mind to help us understand, rather than a physical split in the object itself.</note> when our intellect has constructed it. 

The Peripatetics use this common distinction very frequently—a distinction which, as that author says, was repeated by Antipater and mentioned by Posidonius in his letters to Seneca. Therefore, in this manner, we can say that the "Idea" is composed of essence and existence conceptually, and we can call it a "being." That is, we consider it the exemplar of creatures which are composed of essence and being (which differ in reality). However, we do not place this composition in God when we contemplate Him not as the exemplar of others, but as He is in the innermost sanctuary of His own divinity, enjoying Himself.

Fourth, you ask—according to the definition of "denominatives" <note>Words derived from another, like "brave" from "bravery." The objection suggests "One" is just a derivative label for God, not His actual nature.</note>—if a thing is called "one" because of its "unity" <margin>Solution to the fourth objection</margin>. But according to your position, God is called "one" because of His *likeness* to unity. Therefore, the predication by which the Platonists say "God is one" does not actually pertain to the substance of God. Furthermore, when we say "God is one," you think it signifies not *what* He is, but *how* He is; however, "how" belongs to the category of accidents <note>In philosophy, "accidents" are non-essential qualities, like the color of a shirt.</note>. Therefore, the word "one" as applied to God is not a substantive noun. 

Either I have not learned the Platonic sect well enough, or I am ignorant of the Greek language, for that is not enough to defend the discipline of the Academics. But the response is easy: for when it is said by the Platonists that the "One" predicated of God is substantive and not merely denominative, it is rightly asserted. And again, when it is asserted that He is called "One" because He is like Unity, this is not inconsistent. It cannot be said to be non-substantive for that reason. For even if a name is adapted to something because of a certain property or likeness, it does not necessarily follow that the name is not substantive, provided it is accepted as a substantive name that signifies not as an "adjacent quality" <note>original: "per modum adiacentis," like an adjective.</note> but as something "standing by itself" <note>original: "per se stantis," like a noun.</note>. It is clear enough that the "One" predicated of God is understood not as something inherent but as something standing by itself, so that it needs no proof. 

Thus, you have a property from which the name is applied without taking away its status as a substantive. For your Thomas <margin>Thomas <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas, the 13th-century Dominican theologian.</note></margin>—indeed *our* Thomas—both in other places and in the first part [of the *Summa Theologiae*], reports that the thing a name is meant to signify differs from the reason why the name was first given. For example, he explains that this name "stone" <note>Latin: *lapis*.</note> is given to signify that substance so named, but it is called so because of a related property: namely, that it "hurts the foot" <note>original: "pedem ledit." A popular medieval etymology: *lapis* was thought to come from *laedens pedem* (foot-hurter).</note>. Hence, in another place, he teaches that it is used by grammarians to write that a name denotes "substance with quality." John Scotus <margin>John Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus, a major late-medieval Franciscan philosopher.</note></margin> also affirms this in the first book of his commentary on the *Sentences* <note>The standard theology textbook of the Middle Ages by Peter Lombard.</note>. Therefore, my dear Antonio, when we speak of the "One" in relation to God, we speak of it truly and as a substantive name, because we both conceive and predicate it as "standing by itself." Again, when we say it is imposed because of a likeness to unity and its properties, we speak of the truth...

The author also defends the use of the term "One" for God as a substantive noun rather than a mere descriptive quality, citing Thomas Aquinas and Duns Scotus.</summary>

<meta>This page continues a philosophical and theological defense, likely written by Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola, responding to objections raised against the teachings of his famous uncle, Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. The discussion centers on the nature of God’s "Oneness" and the logical relationship between God and the existence of created things.</meta>

We approach as closely as is permitted to us because, clearly, we use a suitable term to indicate that deity which is—above all created things—ineffable <note>original: "ineffabilem"; meaning that which cannot be expressed in words</note>. Just as unity is the principle of all numbers, so too is God the principle of all things that exist. From these words, you will also gather the solution to your other argument regarding the *manner* of being; you claim that "oneness" is merely a category of "accidents" <note>In Aristotelian logic, an "accident" is a quality that a thing has (like being tall) but which is not essential to its being what it is.</note>. In this proclamation—"God is one"—you ask how He can be one while the word "one" remains a substantive name for God. <margin>A brief solution from the words of the uncle.</margin> If you consider the source from which the name originates and what it is attributed to denote, you can recognize the solution to your doubt quite briefly from the words of my uncle. 

He says: "Why do you say I follow the reasoning of the Platonists rather than Dionysius <note>Referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a highly influential Christian mystic and philosopher.</note>, when—as you boast with such a loud voice—you have never actually read Dionysius or the Platonists?" But you should know that for the Platonists, the "Type" of God is **Unity**, while for Dionysius, God is "all things in a unified way." No one could rightly desire a more direct solution. For when it is said that the "Type" of God is **Unity**, it refers to His likeness and manner; but when it is said that God is "all things in a unified way," it refers to His substance, which is asserted to be entirely the same. Furthermore, in the Greek language (which my uncle knew well), an abstract term can sometimes be signified by a concrete word.

To provide the solution to your fifth doubt, many words are not needed. He says: "If God did not exist, and gold were gold, then gold would not be gold." <margin>Solution to the fifth objection.</margin> You add these words: "Therefore, would it be gold? What if the definition of truth stands? It will be a truth that corresponds to no 'Idea'." <note>The author is discussing "Ideas" in the Platonic sense—perfect eternal forms of things.</note> Add, I pray, these few things which he said follow from his words, and you will recognize how there will be a "truth corresponding to no Idea." What do I mean by this? Something impossible. Namely, an impossibility gives birth to an impossibility. Therefore, it is no wonder if you make whatever you wish follow from your impossible proposition. For if God did not exist and gold did exist, it would be a truth corresponding to no Idea, since from the impossible, the impossible is produced. Not only the logicians <note>original: "dialectici"</note> but also the theologians agree with this. 

For if you ask John Baconthorpe <margin>John of Baconthorpe</margin> <note>A 14th-century English Carmelite monk known as the "Resolute Doctor."</note>, the Carmelite, whether it could happen that gold exists and God does not, he will answer you in the first book of his *Sentences* that no thing whatsoever can be understood unless God is understood first. Since God is involved in the understanding of all things, you may conclude whether it can be pronounced—beyond all controversy, even among novice logicians—that it is impossible for gold to exist and God not to exist. But we shall speak of this again at the end of the work, if you later consult the Cardinal of Cambrai <margin>Cardinal of Cambrai</margin> <note>Pierre d'Ailly (1351–1420), a famous French theologian and astrologer.</note>. You will hear that man, who was well-practiced in all philosophy, saying in his first commentary on the *Sentences* that a contradiction follows from any impossibility.

In the sixth place, you said that if "Socrates is sitting" were neither true nor false (which my uncle had asserted because it was not a *necessary* truth), you could defend the idea that a negation or affirmation is not true in every case, since in some cases neither one nor the other possesses a necessary truth. <margin>Solution to the sixth objection.</margin> Solving this objection, we respond that this speech—namely, "Socrates is sitting"—does not, insofar as it depends on itself, necessarily determine its own truth or falsehood. However, it does not follow from this that an affirmation is not true or a negation is not true regarding any given thing—provided you understand it in the way that he himself teaches.

<summary>This page defends Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's views on the Oneness of God by reconciling Platonic and Dionysian philosophy, while also arguing that without God as a primary principle, all logical existence and understanding (such as the existence of "gold") would collapse into impossibility.</summary>

<meta>This page continues a philosophical or theological dispute, likely between the author and a respondent named Antonio, regarding the nature of truth, existence, and the categorization of "good" and "evil" versus "truth" and "falsehood" in the tradition of Aristotelian metaphysics.</meta>

<margin>The seventh objection and solution.</margin>

You could also deny that in every case an affirmation or negation is true in such a way that one side of the contradiction is necessarily true. For he says that "I am sitting" is always either true or false because I am always either sitting or not sitting. However, what is said—"that I am sitting"—is in itself neither true nor false; that is to say, this proposition does not determine truth or falsehood for itself from its own nature, as necessary propositions <note>A "necessary" proposition is one that must be true by definition, such as "a circle is round."</note> do. But since it is possible for it to be true when I actually sit, and false when I do not sit, it is, by its own nature, indeterminate toward either possibility.

Furthermore, you press against some of his words concerning good and evil, and truth and falsehood, which he had proposed were located in things and in the soul <note>In medieval philosophy, "things" (res) refer to the external world, while the "soul" (anima) refers to the mind or intellect.</note>, in this way: "If good and evil are in things, while truth and falsehood are in the soul, where is your opposition between affirmation and negation? For a negation posits nothing. How, then, can a chimera <note>A mythological beast; in philosophy, it is used as a classic example of an impossible object that does not exist in reality.</note> be both in things and in the soul if it is entirely a non-entity and is "false," especially since you think that "non-being" and "evil" are interchangeable terms?"

But I pray you, pay attention and notice: evil and good are said to be "in things" for this reason—because they concern the state of the objects themselves. 

<margin>Aristotle</margin>

In the same way, truth and falsehood concern the soul. For truth and falsehood are not in things themselves, as **Aristotle** writes in the sixth book of *First Philosophy* <note>original: "prime philosophie"; this refers to Aristotle's *Metaphysics*.</note>, but in the mind. It does not necessarily follow from this that a thing which is entirely evil is a "true thing." It is also argued that if good and evil are in things, they cannot be opposed contradictorily. This is because the "evil" which is said to be in things is not said to be there as if it were a "thing" itself, but because it is observed and considered regarding the things themselves—that is, insofar as a thing is deprived of its perfections. This lack is what makes them "not good." A chimera, however, is not "in things" because it is entirely a non-being and entirely evil; yet, if it were possible for nature to produce it as a thing, it would exist and be good <note>The author is following the Scholastic view that "Being" and "Goodness" are the same; if something truly exists, it has a degree of goodness.</note>. It is "false" only insofar as it does not exist at all and fits no universal idea. We do not even affirm that the chimera itself is in the soul, but rather that there is a *notion* of the chimera, which is both a "nothing" and "evil" when considered as a real thing.

<margin>The eighth objection with a solution.</margin>

After this, you believed you could prove that "blindness is true," which the other man had denied. You argued in this manner: "If it is true that 'blindness is blindness,' who cannot see that blindness is true? For they are the same thing. By the very fact that blindness is posited, the fact that 'blindness is blindness' is also posited; if it is taken away, the other is taken away. They are generated together." You also argued that, in Himself, God is the same as "God being God," as both are eternal and the First Truth. 

But I, my dear **Antonio**, contend the opposite. I deny that the things you mention are the same. For when one of those things you bring up is posited, the other is not necessarily posited. If blindness alone were posited, with no intellect considering it, blindness would indeed exist, but the "fact that blindness is blindness" <note>The author distinguishes between a simple quality (blindness) and a complex logical statement about that quality (the proposition "blindness is blindness").</note> would not exist. This also solves the argument about God and the generation of Socrates. For Socrates, by his own nature, generates himself; he does not generate the proposition "that Socrates is Socrates," since complex propositions are not "generated" in that way. Even if I were to grant you that they are the same, we still say that your conclusion does not follow because of the different ways they signify—namely, "complexly" and "incomplexly"—since such an argument would be of no valid weight.

<summary>The author debates the nature of truth and existence, arguing that while good and evil relate to the state of objects, truth and falsehood exist only within the mind. He further distinguishes between simple existence (like blindness or a person) and logical propositions about that existence.</summary>
