<meta>This page continues a philosophical defense of the author's uncle (Antonius) against a series of logical objections, specifically focusing on the nature of truth, existence, and the linguistic structure of propositions.</meta>

This argument—that "blindness" and "the fact that blindness is blindness" are the same—is true; therefore, the other follows by the same token. This is a <term>complexum</term><note>A technical term for a "complex" statement or a full proposition, as opposed to a "simple" term like a single noun.</note>, and yet the other is absurd because "blindness" is a simple name, not a complex statement or any kind of enunciation. Thus, it is one thing for "blindness" to be true, and another for the statement "blindness is blindness" to be true.

And although these points might suffice for my uncle’s defense, do not believe that we lack further ways to protect and fight for his position. So that a more complete response may reach you, I want you to know that according to the opinion of **Gregory of Rimini** <margin>Gregory of Rimini</margin><note>A famous 14th-century theologian and philosopher known for his "nominalist" views on how language refers to reality.</note>, I could have said that even if "blindness" being established led to the statement "blindness is blindness," it does not necessarily follow that they are the same thing. For he denies this consequence—and many others of this kind—where, setting aside everything else except God, one says: "God exists, therefore God is 'God exists'." The **Cardinal of Cambrai** <margin>The Cardinal of Cambrai</margin><note>referring to Pierre d'Ailly (1351–1420), a prominent scholar and cardinal.</note> also denies all propositions in which something is stated about an <term>infinitival phrase</term><note>An "infinitiva," such as "to be human" or "to be blindness," used as a subject in a sentence.</note> used significatively; he asserts they are both false and grammatically incongruous, as appears in the first book of his *Sentences*.

You complain next that a "falsehood" should not have been pronounced as "divided" with this specific condition—namely, "as long as it is false." <margin>Ninth objection and the solution to the objection.</margin> You explain this in these words: "If every falsehood is simply 'divided' (which you do not deny has been proven), let no one hesitate to say that a certain falsehood is divided only with this condition: 'as long as it is false'." For if every man is simply and absolutely <term>risible</term><note>A classic logic example: "risibility" is the unique human capacity to laugh. Scholastics used this to discuss essential versus accidental properties.</note>, there is no need to add a condition to restrict it by saying "every man is capable of laughing as long as he is a man." Nor should the restriction have been added just because not all false things are equally divided or false; for not all beings are equally good, yet all are absolutely good. 

But weigh his words carefully, for through them you can cast aside every scrap of doubt. He says: "Every 'false-divided' thing is not equally false because they are not equally divided, since things that are not necessarily and always false are not 'equally false' as those which are always and necessarily false." Therefore, Anthony, that word "as long as" was rightly added because of things that are not always and necessarily false; for even if they are false, they can become true or be "united" <note>The author is likely referring to the *sensus compositus* (composite sense) and *sensus divisus* (divided sense), a logical distinction about how modal terms like "possible" or "necessary" apply to a sentence.</note> either by nature or by the work of a craftsman. You even said this yourself in your second set of objections: however, as long as they are "divided," they remain false. Truly "always false" things are those that can never return to "friendship" [with truth], as is seen abundantly in the response to the second objections. 

Nor does your analogy regarding beings and "risibility" support you in the least. For beings are always and absolutely good. Although they are not all *equally* good—some participating more in the nature of "good" than others—they are nevertheless always and necessarily good; for insofar as they are beings, they are good, and they cannot become non-beings or non-good unless they are reduced to nothingness. But a "falsehood" or a "divided thing" (which consists in a complex statement) can easily become "non-divided" and "true." Therefore, the analogy does not fit. For although not all false things are equally divided, they are nonetheless false insofar as they are not united and not true. Furthermore, this objection should hardly have troubled us; for who would doubt that one could say a man (who is absolutely and always capable of laughter) will be capable of laughter "as long as he is a man"? Would learned men disprove this phrasing: "a man is capable of laughter as long as he exists"?

The tenth head of your objections brings nothing else against him, except to say that what you said could have been easily established if the theory of "contrary motions" had been sufficiently understood by him. <margin>Solution to the tenth objection</margin>

<meta>This page continues a philosophical or rhetorical dispute regarding the logical relationship between human actions (seeking and fleeing) and moral qualities (good and evil), specifically critiquing the validity of an argument based on Aristotelian physics.</meta>

But he—unless his memory fails him—complained that you have not proven what you claimed so often follows. ...as your Thomas <note>Likely referring to Saint Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican friar and theologian.</note> says, who is not only a Latin author but the most eminent among the Latins; <margin>Thomas</margin> he not only reports this but proves it. To him we also add others who hold the same view, such as Giles <note>Giles of Rome (c. 1243–1316), a philosopher and theologian.</note> in his second book on the *Sentences* <note>The *Sentences* by Peter Lombard was the standard theology textbook of the Middle Ages; most scholars wrote commentaries on it.</note>, as well as many others like Burley <note>Walter Burley (c. 1275–1344), an English logician.</note> and Esculanus <note>Likely Cecco d'Ascoli (1257–1327), an Italian encyclopedist and physician.</note>. <margin>Giles</margin> Furthermore, John [Duns] Scotus, <margin>Burley</margin> in explaining Aristotle's *Categories*, supports our opinion, saying: if "the good" is understood as being interchangeable with "being" <note>In scholastic philosophy, "goodness" and "existence" were considered different ways of describing the same reality.</note>, then evil is nothing, and thus it is not a contrary to the good. <margin>Esculanus</margin> For since it is beyond controversy that both sides of a pair of contraries must be something positive, it follows that something which is "nothing" in the nature of things—which is what evil is—cannot be declared a contrary. <margin>John Scotus</margin> And although you have denied that evil is nothing, appealing to Thomas, Thomas himself not only fails to support your opinion but abundantly refutes it. My uncle <note>The author frequently refers to his uncle’s previous writings or "letters" as the basis for this argument.</note> showed this sufficiently in the margin of the third letter. Nevertheless, we do not think it out of place to touch upon a few points in passing to support my uncle's opinion and to show that not only was Thomas of the view that evil is nothing, but whole crowds of illustrious philosophers and theologians have committed themselves "with hands and feet" <note>original: "pedibus manibusque"; a Latin idiom meaning to support something with all one's might or completely.</note> to this sentiment.

We find that Augustine, <margin>Augustine</margin> in discussing the *Morals of the Manichæans*, said that no nature is evil. Shortly after, lest there be any ambiguity about what he understood "nature" to be, he added: "nature itself is nothing other than that which is understood to be something within its own kind." We have seen that Giles of Rome, in his first book of commentaries on the *Sentences* of the Fathers, left it written that evil, insofar as it is evil, is a pure privation <term>privation: the absence of a quality that should normally be present (like blindness being the absence of sight, rather than a "thing" in itself)</term> and not "something." Gregory of Rimini <margin>Gregory of Rimini</margin> testifies to this same thing in his commentaries on the second book of the *Sentences*: that evil itself is not (to use his term) an "entity," but a pure privation. Many others have judged the same, but to bring them all forward now might perhaps cause boredom for me in writing and for you in reading later. For example, if we speak of "darkness" in God, we do not mean literal darkness, but rather that He is not light—or rather, we say He is "light above light" when the kind of darkness we understand is absent. 

<margin>John Gerson, Chancellor of Paris</margin> The most learned and devout Chancellor of Paris, treating this same opinion, says: "Therefore, whatever we say affirmatively about God includes a certain negation." And a little later, he says for this reason that Dionysius denies God is "being," but affirms He is "above being." <margin>Egidius</margin> Egidius <note>Giles of Rome, a medieval theologian.</note> says in the first book of the *Sentences* that God is wise, but not in the way we understand "wise." Hence he says this is the reason why Averroes <note>An influential Islamic philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> in the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics* pronounces these predications we attribute to God to be similar to mathematical propositions. In the manner of mathematicians, the things we understand are indeed in the objects, but not in the same way we understand them; just as we understand a "line" which exists in matter, but we do not understand it specifically because it is in matter. 

But why should I delay you with many words when I can make you more certain of this truth which we assert with only a few? Namely, so that you may know that whatever we predicate of God signifies something far different from what we conceive and declare.

<summary>This page discusses the theological concept of "apophatic" or negative theology, arguing that God's nature transcends all human language and names, including the name "God" itself. The author cites authorities like Pseudo-Dionysius, John of Damascus, and his own uncle (Pico della Mirandola) to explain that human descriptions of God are only approximations of a divine reality that is "above being."</summary>

<meta>This page continues a theological discussion regarding the nature of God and the limitations of human language in describing the divine. The author is addressing a correspondent named Antony, defending the authority of Dionysius the Areopagite against Antony’s apparent skepticism.</meta>

<margin>Christ
Dionysius</margin>

Jesus Christ himself—who is the power of God, the wisdom of God, and the Truth—asserts, according to the testimony of the Gospel of John, that "God is spirit." <note>original: "deus spiritus est"</note> Dionysius, in his book *On Mystical Theology*, while speaking of God and contemplating the ineffable <term>Deity|The essence of God that is beyond human description</term>, removes many of the predicates that we usually attribute to Him; he argues that God is not "spirit" in any way that we are capable of knowing. See, therefore, that Dionysius does not wish for "spirit" to be predicated of God in the same sense that we understand spirit. By these final words, he intends to teach the reader that while it is true that God is spirit—so as to agree with the Gospel of Christ—He is nevertheless not "spirit" in the way we conceptualize it. This is to ensure we do not believe the nature of God can truly be expressed by us through any name at all.

I suspect you are well aware of how great the authority of Dionysius is, and how his most sacred doctrines have been extolled with praise and celebrated by all the theologians who have graced the schools of Paris. <note>The "Gymnasia" of Paris refers to the University of Paris, the center of medieval and Renaissance scholastic theology.</note> However, since your uncle, in his responses to your objections, hinted that you did not very willingly admit the sayings of Dionysius during your disputation, I would have you know that he was a most faithful disciple of the Apostle Paul in the faith of Christ. By Paul's help, God willed that Dionysius leave behind the errors of the pagans to recognize and follow the truth, eventually being granted the crown of martyrdom for the faith of Christ. Gregory <note>Likely Pope Gregory the Great.</note> spoke great things of his teaching, and Pope Martin, in the synod celebrated at Rome against the heretics, did the same. John of Damascus and many others have extolled him with the highest praise. For a long time, his books were hidden away by heretics and remained unknown to the minds of the faithful—

<margin>Constantine the philosopher</margin>

—until they were brought to light by the word of Constantine the philosopher, who had committed all his books to memory. <note>Constantine the Philosopher is better known as Saint Cyril, the 9th-century missionary to the Slavs.</note> Indeed, if Dionysius had been held in such regard by the many Fathers who fought great battles against the heretics and the enemies of the holy Catholic Church, how much more quickly and easily they would have achieved a triumph over their enemies (which was only accomplished later, slowly and with the exhaustion of great labors).

Now, when you intend to prove that God can be called "God" because of the rational definition of the name which is predicated of that name, I say that you labor in vain, my dear Antony. For you are not stating something about God himself, but about this *name* "God." To make this understood more clearly, I will explain at greater length: I ask you, what do you conceive by the letter "A," which you designated for the sake of the name's definition? If you conceive of nothing, you do not err (to use your uncle's words). If you do conceive of something, I ask again whether you conceive of it as something about which something else can be stated. If you do it this way, you still do not err, because that "A" will again hold the place of the subject, not the predicate. But if you were to conceive of—

<margin>Apuleius
Plato</margin>

—that which is stated about Him, you would wander far from the truth, since God himself is infinitely greater than everything you can conceive. Even the Platonist Apuleius, in his book *On the Doctrines of Plato*, calls Him "unspoken" and "unnamable." <note>Apuleius was a 2nd-century Roman philosopher; he is quoting a tradition from Plato's *Timaeus*.</note> Plato’s own words on this matter were rendered into Latin by Apuleius: "To find God is indeed not easy; to understand Him is impossible." <note>original: "Deum quidem inuenisse haud facile est intellexisse impossibile"</note> Therefore, let us say that all affirmations concerning God are improper; whenever we wish not only to speak but even to conceive of anything, He exceeds it to infinity. Furthermore, we are not only limited while held in this earthly prison of ignorance and misery, but even when we are established in heaven, perfectly blessed in the enjoyment of God, we will not have the capacity to "comprehend" God, but only to "apprehend" Him—to use the terminology of our theologians. <note>In scholastic theology, "apprehend" means to know something truly, while "comprehend" means to know it fully and exhaustively, which only God can do of Himself.</note>

<meta>This page continues a theological debate concerning the "incomprehensibility" of God—the idea that the human mind cannot fully grasp the divine nature—and whether this prevents us from loving or worshipping Him.</meta>

...will be forgiven. Furthermore, you believe that these two propositions contradict each other: namely, that "God is above everything that can be conceived" and that "nothing can be affirmed about God." You argue that if the definition of the name "God" is "that which is above what can be conceived," then your argument holds weight. However, the issue is resolved when we say that "proper affirmations" <note>original: "affirmationes... proprias"; in scholastic theology, a "proper" affirmation is a statement that describes a thing's essence exactly as it is, rather than just using metaphors or describing what it is not.</note> cannot be understood. This simply means that no description can be found that represents the nature of God in its entirety. This phrase—"above that which can be conceived"—means nothing other than that God cannot be fully grasped by the mind, and that what God is in His essence cannot be known. These words, therefore, do not state what God *is*, but rather that what He is cannot be known. Thus, they possess the power of negation <note>Defining something by what it is not (apophatic theology).</note> rather than affirmation. 

Even if I were to grant you that they do affirm something, your argument still would not hold. Otherwise, if someone wanted to know about an unknown thing and asked us about its essence, and we replied to the seeker, "It is that which we do not know, that which we have not yet grasped with the mind, and which we cannot grasp," that person’s request would not seem to be satisfied. They would not be able to make an affirmative statement about that thing based on this teaching, but only a negative one—unless, perhaps, someone could be found who could explain to others what that thing was, even though it was so utterly unknown to men and so far beyond the reach of all thought that it could not be known or conceived even by the speaker himself. 

<margin>Simonides</margin>
Thus, both Simonides <note>Simonides of Ceos (c. 556–468 BC), a Greek poet. When the Tyrant Hiero asked him "What is God?", Simonides continually asked for more time to deliberate, eventually concluding that the more he thought about it, the more obscure the answer became.</note> and the Tyrant who consulted him knew that the name of God represents something of the greatest magnitude; yet one of them desired to know what God was, while the other admitted he did not know. 

Furthermore, you use the following logic: "God is above everything that can be conceived; therefore, God cannot be conceived (otherwise He would be 'above Himself'); therefore, He cannot be loved or worshipped." I respond that God can be fully and perfectly conceived only by Himself, exactly as He is, and by no other intellect. It does not follow from this, however, that He cannot be loved or worshipped. For we conceive of a Deity so great, endowed with such omnipotence, and infinitely surpassing all creatures with every kind of power, that we can only conceive of Him through His effects <note>The "effects" are the created world and its workings, which act as clues to the nature of the Creator.</note>. 

Stirred by this wonder and warmed into a love for Him, we begin to conceive of these effects; we realize He is the Highest Good, and so we admire, worship, and love Him. For once the things God has made are perfectly known—to use the words of Themistius <note>Themistius (c. 317–388 AD), a philosopher and rhetorician who wrote famous paraphrases of Aristotle.</note>—He turns the minds and mouths of all people toward admiration and praise of Himself. 

<margin>Themistius</margin>
Likewise, we read those things which have been divinely revealed, and being endowed with His grace, we conceive through faith that which we cannot fully conceive by our natural power. At the very least, it is necessary for us to love Him above all things, so that when the riddle of this flesh is finally broken <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 13:12: "For now we see through a glass, darkly [in an enigma/riddle]... but then shall I know even as also I am known."</note>, we may be able to contemplate Him as He is, with the greatest joy of both the "inner and outer man," which is our ultimate happiness. 

Furthermore, in order for us to love something, it is not necessary for us to see, know, or conceive of it perfectly. It is enough if we know that it exists, or what it is like, even if that knowledge is confused and obscure, whether it comes from faith or from observing His effects. Thus, even a small amount of prior knowledge, of whatever sort it may be, is enough for us to love such a Being. For we can love anything as long as we do not entirely lack knowledge of it; from the things the soul already knows, it learns to love the unknown, as Gregory <note>Likely Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604 AD).</note> says. Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274). The author is referencing the *Summa Theologiae*, specifically the "Prima Secundae" (First part of the second part), Question 27, Article 2, where Aquinas argues that love does not require perfect knowledge.</note> also proves in his *Prima Secundae* that something can be loved perfectly even if it is not known perfectly, and he proposes God as an example among other things.

<summary>This page argues that although God's essence is "incomprehensible" and beyond human definition, humans can still love and worship Him through faith, revelation, and the observation of His works in the world. The author cites classical figures like Simonides and Themistius alongside theologians like Gregory the Great and Thomas Aquinas to prove that limited knowledge is sufficient to spark perfect love.</summary>

<margin>Solution to the final objection</margin>

Finally, you say my uncle believed the power of gold was so great that, whether we wish it or not, it would by necessity draw God along with it, either in reality or in the mind. But, my dear Antony, he did not think this was about the power of gold, but rather its powerlessness; he was not only of the opinion but was made certain that God is so believed in that gold could neither exist nor even be understood if God were removed. 

And although <margin>John of Bacon</margin> <note>original: "Io. de bachone." My intention is to show (perhaps even in your judgment) that it would have been worthwhile for you to undertake the refutation of those points if you were able; but if not, you should at least have put your hand to the work or frankly admitted that his assertions were true. 

My uncle’s arguments are these, which I will soon explain: it is impossible for anything to exist if <term>Being itself</term> <note>original: "ipsum esse." Therefore, it is impossible for gold to exist if...

...they may satisfy [your requirements], and they will also close my response. I have first brought forward certain points which both strengthen my uncle's opinion and confirm as well as elucidate my own interpretation of his words which we set forth before. For if the first principle <note>The "First Cause" or God.</note> fails, it is necessary that all those things which proceed from it perish, as is gathered from the eighth book of Aristotle’s *Physics* <note>original: "Aristotelis octavo physice auscultationis"</note>. <margin>Arguments to demonstrate the proposition</margin> God, moreover—as the same philosopher witnesses—is the true principle from whom all other true things come; therefore, if God is taken away, it is necessary that all true things perish. But if true things tend toward nothingness, then existing beings are likewise not saved from destruction, since they coincide with an equal scope. <margin>Aristotle</margin>

Likewise, if He who communicates both being and life to things is removed, who would not see that those very things would utterly perish? That God grants this to the things themselves is the opinion of Aristotle in the first book of *On the Heavens* <note>original: "de celo"</note>, who adds that this is communicated more clearly to some and more obscurely to others. <margin>Aristotle</margin> Furthermore, whatever is ruled by the art of the First Cause <term>First Cause: The primary origin of all things, identified by these philosophers as God.</term> falls down if that cause perishes. Averroes <note>A 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were central to Renaissance thought.</note> testifies in the second book of the *First Philosophy* <note>The Metaphysics.</note> that this entire machine <note>The "machine of the world" (machina mundi), a common metaphor for the universe.</note> is governed and ruled by the First Cause, under which no one can doubt that gold is also contained and included. <margin>Averroes</margin>

I could bring many other things into the discussion from the sacred books, such as much from the Gospel itself, much from the most sacred dogmas of the apostle Paul, and very many things from others, such as from Gregory, who said that all things fall into nothingness unless they are preserved by the almighty God. <margin>Gregory</margin> [I could cite] Augustine in *On Genesis* <note>original: "super Genesim"</note>, and Saint Thomas, and John [Duns] Scotus in his treatise *On the First Principle*. <margin>Augustine</margin> <margin>Thomas</margin> <margin>John Scotus</margin> I deliberately pass over these, since it should be enough to have proved it by the natural reasons which you seemed to demand, and by the teachings of the gentile <note>Non-Christian philosophers, specifically the Greeks and Arabs.</note> philosophers—something you did not believe could be proven by him at all.

Therefore, following all these things we have said, I should think that among good minds it will be beyond controversy that all my uncle's opinions have been sufficiently defended, perhaps even in your judgment. However, we have written these things not to clash with you. We also wrote reluctantly, as our friend Giovanni Manardi <note>A famous Italian physician and scholar (1462–1536).</note> and Cristoforo Sasolo of Mirandola <note>A physician and citizen of Mirandola, formerly a student of the recipient.</note>—our fellow citizen, physician, and formerly your student—can testify. <margin>Giovanni Manardi</margin> <margin>Cristoforo Sasolo</margin> We wrote, moreover, without hatred. The greatest proof of this for you is that if you judge anything committed to these papers to be detracting from your honor in any part, I am ready to strike it out and remove it at your discretion before the response reaches the hands of others. I would do this most gladly, since I love you as a man, respect you as a philosopher, and revere you as a Christian. If it should please you to make a trial of my spirit toward you, you will perceive that I have weighed my actions as much as my words.

->FINIS.<-

<meta>This page continues a philosophical and personal correspondence, likely involving Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola, discussing the limitations of human intellect and the value of spiritual friendship over academic rivalry.</meta>

...and if we examine our thoughts with the utmost diligence, we find that for Christians, ambition is a poison that creeps into the heart, later giving birth to a deadly pride. From this, it often happens that those who love this earthly wisdom—in which we involve ourselves daily—completely neglect that wisdom which is begotten and eternal, from which all this flowing and temporary knowledge is derived. They do this because they are puffed up and elated by fleeting glory. 

But I pray, let us see from where we are carried away in spirit, and why we value ourselves too highly. For how small is our knowledge? We grasp only the smallest portion of the science of natural things. Even those many and great things which we do not know cry out silently that we profess or believe ourselves to be learned in vain—and falsely. 

Undoubtedly, even a simple man, a farmer unskilled or entirely ignorant of letters, could ask many questions about things placed right before our eyes, for which a philosopher—otherwise very great—would be unable to give a certain explanation. Indeed, in perceiving <term>substances</term><note>In this context, "substances" refers to the essential nature of things that exist independently, often used in a metaphysical sense to describe beings like angels or the soul.</note> that are entirely separated from sensible matter, how far do we actually proceed in our knowledge? We see them only with the bleary and owl-like eyes of the mind.

But what shall we say of divine matters? We pant and feel anxious not only to know them, but even to track them down; yet we direct our gaze while blinking and stumbling in the dark, covered by clouds that are almost entirely thick. Furthermore, have we not received this knowledge of things of ours either from books or from a teacher? What need is there, then, to boast? We have merely learned the meditations of others and swallowed them, as if listening to someone telling a history. 

But this is a "history" of nature, placed within bitter arguments through various studies and tossed about by different opinions; for that reason, it is uncertain. This is revealed most clearly by the very name "opinion." If we do obtain some small bit of knowledge by ourselves, I ask you, what else is it but a certain uncertainty, rolled up in a thousand wrappings and entangled in a thousand deceits? 

I would pursue this matter further—as if incensed against those who value these studies more highly than is appropriate—had I not already treated this subject specifically in a long inquiry and dedicated a special book to it. For these reasons, I have decided to turn myself to those books whose propositions are stated as <term>dignities</term><note>From the Latin *dignitates*, referring to self-evident axioms or principles that serve as the foundation for a logical argument.</note> and whose conclusions are gathered in an ineffable <term>syllogism</term><note>A form of reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two given or assumed premises.</note> and which render the mind purified (if, however, we take care for that).

But let this be the end of our literary conflict and the end of this letter. Yet see how different the result has been for our controversy compared to others. Once a dispute—whether conducted by voice or in writing—is finished, hatreds and grudges are often exercised between those minds that were in discord. Fraudulent wars are plotted; detractions of honor and reputation gush forth from both sides. 

You, however, and our Pico <note>original: "Picus noster"; likely referring to the famous philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola or a close relative.</note> were "co-parents" even before the dispute—that is, bound by a spiritual knot. Nevertheless, because of this, the former concord of your minds has not been dissolved. As for me, I was known to you only by name while your uncle was alive, and you to me; but this defense has caused a certain treaty of friendship to be struck between us. Take care that this remains stable as long as we shall live; and so that it may persevere eternally after this death which we expect, strive by whatever means you can to live rightly and piously. I shall also strive to do the same. 

In the meantime, do not be reluctant to experience with what love I follow you. Perhaps I shall provide what you have requested more abundantly than I promised at the conclusion of my defense. For there is nothing so difficult that I would not do it for the sake of more readily earning your favor (as you are surely a most serious philosopher). 

->From the citadel of Mirandola, January 4, 1496.<-

<meta>This page serves as the preface or introduction ("Argumentum") written by Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola (1469–1533) for the collected works of his famous uncle, the philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494). It establishes the transition from Pico's early "playful" intellectual exercises to his later, more devout religious writings.</meta>

->### The Argument of Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola, etc., regarding the Oration and Letters of his uncle, Giovanni Pico, etc.<-

a  Receive, reader, these studies <note>original: *lucubrationes*; literally "works produced by candlelight," implying late-night, diligent scholarship</note> of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola as well—works of a lighter nature which perhaps he himself would not have published while living, nor would we have, except for being prompted by the frequent encouragements of celebrated men. You will first read a most elegant oration <note>This refers to the famous *Oration on the Dignity of Man*, intended as the opening speech for a public debate in Rome that was eventually cancelled.</note>, composed with a certain youthful eagerness, yet frequently admired by the more learned for its peak of doctrine and eloquence. Nor should it bother you if many things are seen at its conclusion that are also inserted in the preface of his *Apology* <note>Pico's *Apologia* was a legal and theological defense of his "900 Theses," some of which were condemned by the Church.</note>; since he published the latter but kept the former always at home, sharing it only with friends. 

You will see many of the hidden dogmas of the ancients—previously wrapped in enigmas and the coverings of myths—most ingeniously unlocked. You will also see his attempt, using both intellectual strength and oratorical charms, to show how the "poetic theology" <note>The Renaissance idea that ancient myths (like those of Orpheus or Hermes Trismegistus) contained hidden Christian truths.</note> of the ancient sages served as a handmaid to the mysteries of our own theology. By untying certain knots of both, he invites men to literary wrestling grounds <note>original: *literarias palestras*; a classical metaphor for places of intellectual debate and academic competition</note>. For during that time, he was very active in these debates, which he later left behind as mere "preludes" or "playful battles" to more serious studies. He then turned his mind to working on those things which we have already released and those we are set to release in the future. 

You will also read several letters (for it would be a most laborious task to collect them all). Some are personal letters written both during his tender youth and his more mature years; others were composed after he dedicated his whole heart to God, filled with the holiest advice. You will find that the former smell most abundantly of learning and eloquence; the latter you will perceive to savor of both sufficiently and, beyond this, to breathe most fruitfully the love of Christ.

<meta>This page begins the "Oration on the Dignity of Man," one of the most famous texts of the Renaissance. It was intended as an introductory speech for a public debate in Rome in 1487, though the debate was eventually banned by the Pope.</meta>

# THE ORATION OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA, COUNT OF CONCORDIA.

I have read, Most Reverend Fathers, in the records of the Arabs, that when Abdala the Saracen <note>original: "Abdalam sarracenum"; likely referring to Abd-Allah ibn Qutayba, a 9th-century scholar</note> was asked what he thought was most worthy of admiration on this world's stage, he replied that nothing is seen more wonderful than man. With this opinion agrees that famous saying of Hermes: "A great miracle, O Asclepius, is man." <margin>Hermes Trismegistus</margin> <note>original: "Mercurius"; referring to the legendary figure Hermes Trismegistus, supposed author of the Hermetic Corpus</note> As I pondered the reason for these sayings, I was not satisfied by the many things brought forward by many people concerning the excellence of human nature: <margin>The dignity of man</margin> that man is the intermediary between creatures, intimate with the gods above, the king of lower things, the interpreter of nature by the sharpness of his senses, the investigation of his reason, and the light of his intelligence; the interval between stable eternity and flowing time, and (as the Persians <note>original: "Persae"</note> say) the bond of the world, or rather its wedding song; and according to David, a little lower than the angels. <margin>David</margin> <note>referring to Psalm 8</note> These are great things, certainly, but not the primary ones—that is, those which rightfully claim the privilege of highest admiration. For why should we not admire the angels themselves and the most blessed choirs of heaven more?

At last, I seemed to understand why man is the most fortunate animal and consequently worthy of all admiration, and what that condition is which he has been allotted in the sequence of the universe—a lot to be envied not only by the beasts, but by the stars and the minds beyond this world. A thing beyond belief and marvelous. And why not? For it is for this reason that man is rightly called and considered a great miracle and a truly wonderful animal. But what that condition is, hear, O Fathers, and grant me your kind attention with your usual courtesy.

Already God the Father, the Architect, had built this world-house we see, the most august temple of divinity, according to the laws of secret <note>original: "archanae," i.e., arcanae</note> wisdom. He had adorned the super-celestial region with minds; He had animated the ethereal globes with eternal souls; He had filled the excrement-laden and drossy parts of the lower world with a crowd of animals of every kind. But when the work was finished, the Craftsman desired that there be someone who might weigh the reason of such a great work, love its beauty, and admire its magnitude. Therefore, when all things were now completed (as Moses and Timaeus testify), He thought finally of bringing forth man. <margin>Moses, Timaeus</margin> <note>referring to the Book of Genesis and Plato's dialogue "Timaeus"</note>

But there was nothing in His archetypes from which He might fashion a new offspring, nor in His treasures what He might bestow as an inheritance upon His new son, nor in the seats of the whole world where this contemplator of the universe might sit. All things were already full; all had been distributed into the highest, middle, and lowest orders. But it was not in the Father's power to fail, as if exhausted, in His final birth; it was not the part of His wisdom to waver through lack of counsel in a necessary matter. It was not the part of His benevolent love that he who was to praise the divine liberality in others should be forced to condemn it in himself.

Finally, the Best of Craftsmen ordained that he to whom nothing could be given as his own should share in common whatever had been private to each individual. Therefore, He took man as a creature of indeterminate image and, having placed him in the middle of the world, addressed him thus: "We have given you, O Adam, no fixed seat, no form of your very own, nor any function peculiar to yourself alone, so that whatever seat, whatever form, and whatever functions you yourself may desire, you may have and possess according to your wish and your judgment. The nature of all other creatures is defined and restricted within laws prescribed by us. You, constrained by no limits, may determine it for yourself, according to your own free will, <margin>Free will in man</margin> in whose hand I have placed you. I have placed you at the world's center so that you may more easily look around from there at whatever is in the world. We have made you neither celestial nor terrestrial, neither mortal nor immortal, so that with freedom of choice and with honor, as though the maker and molder of yourself, you may [fashion yourself] in whatever..."

<summary>This page introduces Pico's famous defense of human dignity, arguing that man's greatness lies not just in his place in the hierarchy of being, but in his God-given free will to choose his own nature.</summary>

...[if] you prefer, you may fashion your own form for yourself. You will be able to degenerate into the lower things, which are the brutes; you will be able to be reborn into the higher things, which are divine, by the judgment of your own soul. Oh, the supreme generosity of God the Father! Oh, the supreme and wonderful happiness of man! To whom it is granted to have whatever he chooses, to be whatever he wills. As soon as brutes are born, they bring with them from their mother's womb <note>original: "ebulga matris"</note> (as Lucilius says) all that they will ever possess. The highest spirits <note>referring to angels</note> were from the beginning, or soon after, that which they will remain for all eternity. Upon man at his birth, the Father bestowed seeds of every kind and the germs of every way of life. Whatever seeds each person cultivates will grow and bear their fruit in him. If they are vegetative, he will become a plant. If they are sensual, he will become brutish. If they are rational, he will turn into a heavenly being. If they are intellectual, he will be an angel and a son of God. And if, not content with the lot of any creature, he withdraws into the center of his own unity, he becomes one spirit with God; standing in the solitary darkness of the Father, which is above all things, he will surpass them all.

Who would not admire this chameleon of ours? Or who would admire anything else more? It is for this reason that Asclepius of Athens <note>a figure in Neoplatonic or Hermetic thought</note> said that man was symbolized by Proteus <note>a Greek sea-god who could change his shape at will</note> in the mysteries—on account of this shape-shifting nature that transforms itself. Hence those metamorphoses celebrated among the Hebrews and Pythagoreans. For the secret theology of the Hebrews <note>the Kabbalah</note> transforms the holy Enoch into an angel of divinity—whom they call <unclear>Metatron</unclear>—and transforms others into other spirits. And the Pythagoreans degrade wicked men into brutes, and, if Empedocles is to be believed, even into plants. Following them, Muhammad often had this on his lips: that he who falls away from divine law becomes a brute. And rightly so. For it is not the bark that makes a plant, but its mindless and insensitive nature; not the hide that makes a beast of burden, but its brutish and sensual soul; not the circular body that makes the heavens, but right reason; nor is it the separation from the body, but spiritual intelligence that makes an angel. 

If you see someone surrendered to his belly, crawling on the ground, it is a shrub you see, not a man. If you see someone blinded by the empty illusions of his imagination—as if by Calypso’s <note>the nymph from the Odyssey who detained Odysseus</note> charms—and enslaved to his senses by soothing allurements, it is a brute you see, not a man. If you see a philosopher discerning all things with right reason, revere him; he is a heavenly, not an earthly, being. If you see a pure contemplator, oblivious to the body, withdrawn into the inner reaches of the mind, this is neither an earthly nor a heavenly being; he is a more majestic divinity clothed in human flesh. 

Who would not admire man? He is not without reason designated in the sacred Mosaic and Christian writings sometimes by the name of "all flesh" and sometimes "every creature," since he fashions, builds, and transforms himself into the appearance of all flesh and the character of every creature. Therefore, Evanthes the Persian writes, where he explains Chaldean theology, that man has no native image of his own, but many foreign and external ones; hence that saying of the Chaldeans: <unclear>Enosh</unclear> <note>Hebrew for "man" or "mankind," often implying frailty or mortality</note>, which is to say, "man is an animal of a varied, multiform, and fickle nature." 

But to what end is all this? So that we understand that once we are born in this condition—to be what we wish to be—we ought to take the greatest care that it not be said of us that, though we were in a place of honor, we did not know we had become like the brutes and senseless beasts of burden <note>referring to Psalm 49:12</note>. But let us rather remember the saying of the prophet Asaph: "You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High" <note>Psalm 82:6</note>. Let us not abuse the most indulgent generosity of the Father, who gave us this free choice, lest we turn the gift that should save us into something harmful. Let a certain holy ambition invade our soul, so that, not content with the mediocre, we pant after the highest things and strive with all our strength to attain them (since we can, if we will). Let us disdain earthly...

Who would not wish to be so inspired by those **Socratic frenzies** <note>original: "socraticis illis furoribus." For if, through moral virtue, the forces of our passions have been so stretched to the proper proportions and harmonies that they sound together in an unshakable consonance, and if through **dialectic** <note>The art of logical discussion and investigation of truth.</note> our reason has moved in rhythmic progression, then, inspired by the frenzy of the Muses, we shall drink in the heavenly harmony with our innermost ears.

<margin>Three Delphic precepts</margin>
Then Bacchus, the leader of the Muses, showing the "invisible things of God" to us as we philosophize through his mysteries—that is, the visible signs of nature—will intoxicate us from the abundance of the house of God. In that house, if we are faithful like **Moses**, most holy Theology will approach and animate us with a double frenzy. For, having been raised to its most eminent height, measuring from there the things that are, will be, and have been in an indivisible eternity, and gazing upon the ancient beauty, we shall be the winged lovers of those prophets of Apollo; and finally, stirred by an ineffable charity as if by a divine sting, like burning **Seraphim** <note>The highest order of angels, characterized by their burning love for God.</note> placed outside ourselves, full of divine power, we shall no longer be ourselves, but He himself who made us.

You will see that they warn us of nothing else than that we should embrace with all our strength this three-part philosophy which is the subject of our present dispute.

For that famous saying, **"Nothing in excess,"** <note>original: "μηδεν αγαν" (mēden agan)</note> rightly prescribes the norm and rule for all virtues through the concept of the "mean," which is the subject of **Moral Philosophy**. Let us also consult **Pythagoras**, the wisest of men, who was especially wise because he never deemed himself worthy of the name of "wise man." <note>Pythagoras is credited with coining the term "philosopher" (lover of wisdom) rather than calling himself "sophos" (wise).</note> He first commands that we **"should not sit upon a bushel"**; that is, we should not lose the rational part by which the soul measures, judges, and examines all things through idle laziness, but rather direct and stir it up constantly through dialectical exercise and rules. Then he points out two things we must especially avoid: **"not to urinate against the sun"** and **"not to cut one's nails during a sacrifice."** But after we have, through morality, "urinated away" the flowing appetites of overflowing pleasures, and "cut away" the trimmings of our nails—as if they were the sharp protrusions of anger and the stings of our spirits—only then may we take part in the sacred mysteries of Bacchus, which we have mentioned, and of which the Sun is rightly called the father and leader of our contemplation...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's defense of his upcoming public disputation, transitioning from general justifications to citing the authority of ancient philosophers and scripture regarding the value of intellectual struggle.</meta>

...you are; but with Plato, with Aristotle, and with the most approved philosophers of all ages, it is common to me. To whom it was most certain that nothing was more effective for achieving the knowledge of truth which they sought than for them to be most frequent in the exercise of disputation. For just as by gymnastics the strengths of the body become firmer, so without a doubt in this, as it were, literary wrestling-place <term>palaestra: an ancient Greek wrestling school or gymnasium used for training and competition</term>, the strengths of the mind emerge far stronger and more vigorous. Nor would I believe that either the **Poets** <margin>Poets</margin>—by the much-celebrated arms of Pallas <note>Pallas Athena, the Greek goddess of wisdom and strategic war</note>—or the **Hebrews** <margin>Hebrews</margin>—when they say the serpent is the symbol of the wise—meant to signify anything to us other than that these most honorable kinds of contests are exceedingly necessary for the acquisition of wisdom. Thus it happens perhaps that even the **Chaldeans** <margin>Chaldeans</margin> <note>Ancient Mesopotamian astronomers and sages renowned for their knowledge of the stars</note> in the horoscope of one who is to become a philosopher require that Mars should behold Mercury in a trine aspect <note>original: "Triquetro aspectu"; an astrological configuration where two planets are 120 degrees apart, considered highly favorable for combining energy (Mars) with intellect (Mercury)</note>, as if to say that if you take away these encounters, these wars, all philosophy would become drowsy and dormant. 

But truly, with those who say I am unequal to this task <note>original: "provinciae"; literally a province or administrative duty, here referring to his public defense of 900 theses</note>, my method of defense is more difficult. For if I say I am equal, I may perhaps seem immodest and over-appreciative of myself; if I confess I am unequal, I seem likely to undergo the mark of being rash and ill-advised. See into what straits I have fallen, in what a position I am placed, since I cannot promise about myself without fault what I cannot soon perform without fault. Perhaps I could also bring forward that from **Job** <margin>Job</margin>: "the spirit is in all"; and with **Timothy** <margin>Timothy</margin> hear: "let no one despise your youth" <note>Pico quotes Job 32:8 and 1 Timothy 4:12 to justify his right to engage in high-level intellectual debate despite being only 23 years old</note>; but from my conscience I will say more truly this: there is nothing in us great or singular. I do not deny that I am perhaps studious and eager for the good arts; however, I neither assume nor claim for myself the name of a learned man. Wherefore, the reason I have imposed such a great burden on my shoulders was not because I was unaware of my own weakness, but because I knew that this kind of battle—that is, literary ones—is peculiar in that in them, there is profit in being conquered.

<summary>Pico della Mirandola argues that intellectual debate is essential for sharpening the mind, citing Greek, Hebrew, and Chaldean traditions. He acknowledges his own youth and potential inadequacy but asserts that in philosophical "wars," the defeated party still gains the "profit" of knowledge.</summary>

...they must clearly admit, even if unwillingly, that it is plainly necessary to consider the method of philosophizing. For those who have not pledged themselves to any one of the families of philosophers—namely to **Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the "Angelic Doctor" of the Catholic Church.</note> or **Scotus** <note>John Duns Scotus (1266–1308), a major Franciscan theologian known for his complex logic.</note>, who are now most frequently in everyone's hands—may indeed, by favoring their own side, put their doctrine to the test in the discussion of a few questions. But I have so trained myself that, **sworn to the words of no single master**, I have poured myself through all the masters of philosophy, examined every page, and recognized every school. Therefore, since I had to speak about all of them—lest, if I had defended only a private dogma and neglected the rest, I might seem restricted by it—there could not fail to be many things brought forward from all of them at once, even if only a few were proposed from each. Nor should anyone condemn me for being carried as a guest wherever the storm takes me. For it was once observed by all the ancients that, in unrolling every kind of writing, they passed over no commentary they could read; and especially by **Aristotle**, who for that reason was called by **Plato** <note>original: "αναγνωστησ"</note> **the Reader**. Indeed, it is the mark of a narrow mind to have confined oneself within a single "Porch" or "Academy." <note>References to the Stoic school (the Porch) and Plato’s school (the Academy).</note> Nor can one rightly select a personal favorite from among all the schools if one has not first become familiarly acquainted with them all.

Add to this that in every single "family" there is something remarkable that is not common to the others. And to begin now with our own people, to whom philosophy most recently arrived: there is in **John Scotus** something vigorous and analytical. In **Thomas**, something solid and balanced. In **Aegidius** <note>Giles of Rome (c. 1243–1316), a student of Aquinas.</note>, something polished and exact. In **Francis** <note>Francis of Meyronnes (c. 1288–1328), a student of Scotus known for his sharp distinctions.</note>, something keen and sharp. In **Albert** <note>Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280), teacher of Aquinas and a vast encyclopedist of nature.</note>, something ancient, ample, and grand. In **Henry** <note>Henry of Ghent (c. 1217–1293), a secular theologian known for his independent "sublime" style.</note>, as it has always seemed to me, something sublime and venerable. Among the Arabs, there is in **Averroes** something firm and unshakable. In **Avempace** and **Alfarabi**, something grave and meditated. In **Avicenna**, something divine and Platonic.

Among the Greeks, philosophy is, in general, especially bright and pure. In **Simplicius**, it is rich and abundant. In **Themistius**, elegant and concise. In **Alexander**, consistent and learned. In **Theophrastus**, weightily elaborated. In **Ammonius**, clear and graceful. And if you turn to the **Platonists**, to review but a few: in **Porphyry**, you will be delighted by a wealth of matter and a multifaceted religion. In **Iamblichus**, you will venerate a more secret philosophy and the mysteries of the barbarians. In **Plotinus**, there is nothing specific for you to admire, because he shows himself admirable in every way; the "sweating" Platonists can hardly understand him as he speaks with a learned obliqueness—divinely about divine things, and about human things in a way far above man. I pass over the more recent ones: **Proclus**, luxuriating with Asiatic fertility, and those who flowed from him, **Hermias**, **Damascius**, **Olympiodorus**, and many others, in all of whom <note>original: "το θειον"</note> **"the divine"**—that peculiar symbol of the Platonists—always shines forth.

Added to this is that if there is any sect that attacks truer dogmas and mocks good causes with the slander of its wit, it strengthens the truth rather than weakens it; and like a flame shaken by movement, it is excited, not extinguished. Moved by this reasoning, I wished to bring into the open the opinions not just of one school (as some preferred), but the tenets of every kind of doctrine. My hope was that, through this comparison of many sects and the multifaceted discussion of philosophy, that **"splendor of truth"** which Plato mentions in his letters might shine more clearly upon our minds, like a sun rising from on high. What would it have been if only the philosophy of the Latins—namely of Albert, Thomas, Scotus, Aegidius, Francis, and Henry—had been treated, while that of the Greeks and Arabs was omitted?

<meta>This page continues the defense of "Natural Magic" begun on the previous page, distinguishing it from the forbidden "Goetic" or demonic magic. It concludes the section on magic and transitions into the author's second major theme: the use of Hebrew Kabbalah to support Christian doctrine.</meta>

And that most wise man affirmed: so abhorring the one that when he was called to the rites of evil demons, he said it would be more right for them to come to him than for him to go to them—and rightly so. <note>The "wise man" refers to the Neoplatonist philosopher Plotinus, who famously claimed his guardian spirit was a god rather than a mere demon.</note> For as that first kind of magic renders man a subject and slave to wicked powers, so this second kind makes him their prince and master. Finally, the former cannot claim the name of either art or science. This latter is full of the highest mysteries: it embraces the deepest contemplation of the most secret things and, ultimately, the knowledge of all nature. 

This magic, calling forth into the light as if from hiding places the virtues scattered by God's kindness and sown throughout the world, does not so much perform wonders as it diligently serves nature as she performs them. This magic, having more deeply scrutinized that universal harmony—which the Greeks more expressively call <term>sympathy</term><note>original: "sympatheian" (συμπάθειαν); the Neoplatonic belief that all parts of the universe are interconnected and "feel" together.</note>—and having gained a clear understanding of the mutual connection of all things, applies to each thing its own native allurements—which are called the <term>jynxes</term><note>original: "iunges" (ιυγγεσ); in ancient magic, these were mystical "attractors" or "charms" used to draw down celestial influences.</note> of the magicians. In the recesses of the world, in the lap of nature, and in the storehouses and secrets of God, she brings hidden miracles into public view as if she were the creator herself; and just as the farmer weds elms to vines, so the magician marries the earth to heaven—that is, he joins the lower things to the gifts and virtues of the higher. 

Thus it happens that as much as the former magic appears monstrous and harmful, the latter appears divine and salutary. Chiefly because the former, enslaving man to the enemies of God, calls him away from God; while this natural magic excites that admiration for the works of God which is most certainly followed by ready charity, faith, and hope. For nothing promotes religion and the worship of God more than the constant contemplation of God's wonders. <margin>Note</margin> Once we have well explored this natural magic of which we speak, being more ardently inspired to the worship and love of the Creator, we shall be compelled to sing: <note>original: "Pleni sunt caeli, plena est terra Maiestate gloriae tuae."</note> "The heavens are full, the earth is full, of the majesty of Your glory." 

And this is enough regarding magic, about which I have said these things because I know there are many who, just as dogs always bark at strangers, so they themselves often condemn and hate what they do not understand. 

I come now to those things which, unearthed from the ancient mysteries of the Hebrews, I have brought forward to confirm the most holy and Catholic faith. Lest these things perhaps be thought by those to whom they are unknown to be made-up trifles or the fables of a charlatan, I want all to understand what and of what sort they are, from where they are sought, and by what famous authors they are supported.

<summary>The author distinguishes natural magic as a divine science that weds earthly things to celestial powers, contrasting it with demonic sorcery. He then introduces his study of Hebrew mysteries (Kabbalah) as a tool for defending Christian faith.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s argument regarding the necessity of secret or "occult" wisdom across all major philosophical and religious traditions, leading into his defense of the Hebrew Kabbalah.</meta>

## Pythagoras
## Plato
## Aristotle
## Jesus Christ
## Origen
## Dionysius
## Kabbalah
## Ezra

<margin>Pope Sixtus IV</margin>
<margin>Pope Innocent VIII</margin>
...they observed. Pythagoras wrote nothing except for a very few things which he entrusted to his daughter Damo as he was dying. The sphinxes carved on the temples of the Egyptians served as a warning that mystical doctrines <note>The word "dogmata" here refers to established philosophical or religious principles.</note> should be kept safe from the common crowd, kept inviolate through the knots of riddles. Plato, writing to Dionysius about the highest substances, said: "I must speak through riddles, lest if the letter should happen to fall into the hands of others, what I write to you might be understood by them." Aristotle used to say that his books on *Metaphysics*, in which he treats divine matters, were both "published and not published." <note>Aristotle meant that while the books were physically available, their contents remained hidden to those without the necessary training to understand them.</note> Why say more? Origen asserts that Jesus Christ, the teacher of life, revealed many things to his disciples which they refused to write down, lest they become common knowledge to the masses. This is most strongly confirmed by Dionysius the Areopagite, <note>A 5th-century Christian theologian and philosopher whose works were highly influential in the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note> who says that the more secret mysteries were passed down by the authors of our religion:

that is, from soul to soul, without writing, through the medium of the spoken word. In this very same way, when that true interpretation of the Law was divinely handed down to Moses by God’s command, it was revealed and called <term>Cabala [Kabbalah]</term>, which means "reception" among the Hebrews. This is because that doctrine was received from one person to another as if by a right of inheritance, not through written records, but through the regular succession of revelations. However, after the Hebrews were restored from the Babylonian captivity through Cyrus, and after the Temple was rebuilt under Zerubbabel, they applied their minds to restoring the Law. Ezra, then the head of the Church, after amending the book of Moses, realized clearly that because of the exiles, the slaughters, the flights, and the captivity of the Israelite people, the custom established by their ancestors of passing down the doctrine by hand <note>Meaning "hand to hand" or oral transmission.</note> could not be preserved. He saw that the secrets of the heavenly doctrine granted to them by God would perish, for their memory could not last long without the aid of commentaries. He therefore decided that the wise men who then survived should be called together, and each should bring forward to the group what he remembered about the mysteries of the Law. Scribes were employed to compile seventy volumes (for there were approximately that many wise men in the Sanhedrin). Regarding this matter, fathers, <note>Pico is addressing his audience of churchmen and scholars as "fathers."</note> do not believe me alone; listen to Ezra himself speaking thus: "After forty days had passed, the Most High spoke, saying: 'Make public the first things you wrote; let the worthy and the unworthy read them. But you shall keep the last seventy books, so that you may hand them over to the wise among your people. For in these is the vein of understanding, the fountain of wisdom, and the river of knowledge.' And so I did." These are the words of Ezra, verbatim. These are the books of the science of the Kabbalah; in these books, Ezra deservedly [found] the vein of understanding.

<summary>Pico argues that all great traditions, from Pythagoras to Jesus, kept their highest truths secret, eventually leading to Ezra recording the oral Hebrew "Kabbalah" into seventy books to prevent its loss.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's "Oration on the Dignity of Man," a famous manifesto of the Italian Renaissance. Pico is finishing his defense of the 900 theses he proposed to debate in Rome, specifically justifying his use of esoteric sources like the Kabbalah, Orpheus, and Zoroaster.</meta>

...we read daily in Jerome and Augustine. But in those matters which look toward <term>philosophy: the study of fundamental nature, knowledge, and reality</term>, you would hear Pythagoras and Plato, whose teachings are so related to the Christian faith that our Augustine <margin>Augustine</margin> gives immense thanks to God that the books of the Platonists came into his hands. 

In short, there is almost no controversy between us and the Hebrews about which they cannot be so refuted and convicted out of the books of the Kabbalists <term>Kabbalah: a traditional system of Jewish mysticism and biblical interpretation</term> that not even a corner remains for them to hide in. Of this matter, I have as a most serious witness Antonius Chronicus <margin>Antonius Chronicus</margin> <note>Likely referring to Antonio Vinciguerra, a Venetian diplomat and man of letters</note>, a most learned man, who with his own ears heard—when I was at a banquet with him—Dactylus the Hebrew <margin>Dactylus the Hebrew</margin> <note>A Jewish scholar, possibly a convert, who assisted Pico with Hebrew texts</note>, a man skilled in this science, descend completely <note>original: "pedibus manibusque descendere" — an idiom meaning to agree with every hands and feet, or wholeheartedly</note> into the Christian opinion regarding the Trinity.

But to return to the heads of my own disputation to be reviewed: We have also brought our opinion on interpreting the songs of Orpheus <margin>Orpheus</margin> and Zoroaster <margin>Zoroaster</margin>. Orpheus is read among the Greeks almost in his entirety; Zoroaster is read among them in fragments, but more completely among the Chaldeans <note>The "Chaldeans" here refers to the Neo-Babylonian/Persian tradition from which the "Chaldean Oracles" were thought to originate</note>. Both are believed to be the fathers and authors of ancient wisdom. For, to say nothing of Zoroaster, of whom frequent mention is made among the Platonists (always with the highest veneration), Iamblichus of Chalcis <margin>Iamblichus of Chalcis</margin> writes that Pythagoras <margin>Pythagoras</margin> held Orphic Theology as the model after which he would shape and form his own philosophy. Indeed, for this reason alone, the sayings of Pythagoras are called "sacred," because they flowed from the institutions of Orpheus. From there, the secret doctrine of numbers and whatever great and sublime thing Greek philosophy possessed flowed as if from a primary source. 

But (as was the custom of the ancient theologians), Orpheus so wove the mysteries of his dogmas into the wrappings of fables and disguised them with a poetic veil, that if anyone reads his hymns, he would believe nothing lay beneath except the sheerest trifles and fables <note>Pico argues that ancient myths are actually "allegories" for deep philosophical truths</note>. I wanted to say this so it may be known what labor was mine, what the difficulty was: to draw out the hidden meanings of secret philosophy from the intentional thickets of enigmas and from the hiding places of fables—especially in a matter so grave, so hidden, and so unexplored, without the help of the work and diligence of other interpreters. 

And yet my "dogs" <note>A common metaphor for critics who "bark" at new ideas</note> have barked that I have accumulated certain tiny and light things for a display of numbers—as if all these questions were not the ones most ambiguously and greatly contested, in which the principal Academies <note>Refers to the different schools of philosophy, such as the Peripatetics (Aristotelians) and the Platonists</note> fight; as if I had not brought many things to these very people who carp at mine (and who believe themselves the princes of philosophers) that are completely unknown and untried. 

Indeed, I am so far from that fault that I have taken care to compress the disputation into as few headings as I could. If I had wanted (as others are accustomed) to divide it into its members and tear it apart, it would surely have grown to an infinite number. And to say nothing of the others: who is there who does not know that one dogma out of the nine hundred—namely, about reconciling the philosophy of Plato and Aristotle—I could have deduced into six hundred headings (not to say more), by listing one by one all the places in which others think they disagree but I think they agree? 

But certainly—for I will speak, though neither [arrogantly nor boastfully]—I wanted to give proof by this meeting of mine, not so much that I know many things, but that I know things that many do not know. So that this may now become openly clear to you in fact, most worshipful Fathers; and so that my speech may no longer delay your desire, most excellent teachers, whom I behold with great pleasure prepared and girded for the battle: may it be lucky and auspicious—as if the trumpet were sounding the signal—let us now join hands in combat.

<meta>This page continues the correspondence of the Renaissance philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, specifically a famous moral letter to his nephew. It maintains the encouraging, pedagogical tone found in his other spiritual writings.</meta>

**Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to his nephew Gianfrancesco. Greetings <note>original: "S." for "Salutem," a standard Latin greeting</note> in Him who is true salvation.**

There is no reason, my son, why you should be amazed, nor why you should grieve or be terrified that, upon leaving me, you were immediately presented with so many occasions for evil that disturb you and oppose your resolution to live well. How much more of a miracle would it be if the way to heaven lay open without sweat for you alone among mortals; if the deceptive world and the evil demon now for the first time ceased to be what they are, or if you were not still in the flesh, which lusts against the spirit. Unless we look out watchfully for our salvation, the world alluringly deforms those drunk on Circean cups <note>A reference to the sorceress Circe from Homer's *Odyssey*, who transformed men into animals with a magical drink; here it symbolizes the degrading effect of earthly pleasures.</note> into the monstrous shapes of beasts.

<margin>James</margin>
But James also affirms that you should rejoice, writing: "Count it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various trials." <note>James 1:2</note> Nor is this without merit: for what hope of glory is there if there is no hope of victory? Or what place for victory can there be where there is no battle? He is called to the crown who is provoked to the fight—and especially to that fight in which no one can be conquered against his will. Nor do we need any other strength to conquer than the mere will to conquer itself.

<margin>The great happiness of a Christian.</margin>
**The great happiness of a Christian:** when victory is placed within his own judgment, and the future rewards shall be greater than every wish and every expectation of the victor. Tell me, I ask you, dearest son: is there anything in this life among those things that drive the earthly minds of the lustful for which many labors must not first be undergone, and many indignities and miseries tolerated? A merchant thinks he has done well if, after a ten-year voyage, after a thousand inconveniences and a thousand dangers to his life, he has acquired a slightly more abundant wealth. Regarding the military service of this world, there is no reason for me to write to you, for experience itself has taught you and continues to teach you enough of its miseries. In earning the favor of princes, in reconciling the friendships of equals, in seeking honors—what a mass of troubles! How much anxiety! How much worry! I can learn these things from you rather than teach them to you; for I, content with my books and my little leisure, have learned since I was a boy to live within my fortune, and as much as I can, dwelling within myself, I sigh for or ambition nothing outside of myself. 

Therefore, shall we—sweating and panting—hardly attain these earthly things which are fleeting, uncertain, vile, and common to us and the beasts? And yet toward heavenly and divine things, which "no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor heart conceived," <note>1 Corinthians 2:9</note> shall we be dragged by the gods <note>Pico uses "diis" (gods) in a pluralistic/classical sense common to humanists, referring here to divine influence.</note> while we are entangled <note>original: "foniculosi," likely referring to being bound by the cords of the world or exhausted.</note> and sleeping, and almost against our will? As if either God could not reign or those blessed heavenly citizens could not be happy without us. 

Certainly, if earthly happiness were provided to us while we were idle, someone who shrinks from labor might prefer to serve the world rather than God. But if we are fatigued no less—indeed far more—in the way of sinners than in the way of God, then that cry of the damned must be heard: "We have grown weary in the way of iniquity." <note>original: "Lassati sumus i uia iniquitatis" from the Wisdom of Solomon 5:7.</note> It cannot but be the height of madness to refuse to labor in the place where one goes from labor to reward, rather than where one goes from labor to punishment. 

I set aside how great is that peace, and how great the happiness of a soul that is conscious of no wrong and grows pale at no guilt; <note>A reference to Horace's *Epistles*: "nil conscire sibi, nulla pallescere culpa."</note> which without doubt far outweighs all pleasures that can be possessed or desired in this life. For what is desirable in the pleasures of the world? While they are sought, they exhaust; when they are acquired, they fail to satisfy; when they are lost, they torture. 

Do you doubt, my son, that the minds of the impious are agitated by perpetual cares? It is the word of God, which can neither be deceived nor deceive: their heart is like a boiling sea that cannot rest. <note>original: "cor ip̃i q̃i mare feruẽs" from Isaiah 57:20.</note> For nothing is safe for them, nothing is peaceful; everything threatens fear, everything brings care, everything points toward death. Shall we then look to these people? Shall we emulate them? And, forgetting our own dignity, forgetting our homeland and our heavenly Father, shall we—though we were born free—voluntarily make ourselves slaves? And living miserably with them, and dying even more miserably, shall we at last be afflicted by eternal fires? O, the blind minds of men! O...

<summary>In this letter, Giovanni Pico della Mirandola encourages his nephew Gianfrancesco to persevere through spiritual trials, arguing that the effort required for virtue is no greater than the exhausting labor men endure for fleeting worldly success.</summary>
<keywords>Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola, spiritual warfare, Circe, merchant metaphor, Christian happiness, peace of conscience, worldly vanity, James 1:2</keywords>

...blind hearts! <note>original: "pectora caeca"</note> Who would not see, even more clearly than the light of day, that all these things are truer than truth itself? And yet, we do not do the things we recognize ought to be done; instead, we still hesitate, wishing in vain to pull our feet <note>original: "plantam," literally the sole of the foot</note> out of the mud. <note>The "mud" or "mire" is a common metaphor in Renaissance spiritual literature for the clinging nature of worldly sin.</note> Do not doubt, my son, that in these very places where you live, there will arise innumerable obstacles at every hour to deter you from your resolve to live holily and well; and unless you are on your guard, they will drive you headlong to ruin.
