<meta>This page concludes a letter of spiritual advice—likely from Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to a friend or relative entering a religious life—and begins a new correspondence with the famed scholar Filippo Beroaldo. The tone shifts from pious exhortation to humanist literary modesty.</meta>

->**Two Most Wholesome Remedies**<-

**Fasting and prayer.** <note>The original shorthand "f. atq; oŕo" stands for *jejunium atque oratio*.</note> For what can we do without the help of God? Or how will He help one who has not called upon Him? But He will certainly not hear you when you call if you have first looked down upon your fellow man when he called to you. It is written: *with the measure you use, it will be measured back to you* <note>original: "in qua mensura mensi fueritis remetietur vobis"; a reference to Matthew 7:2</note>; and elsewhere: *blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.* <note>Matthew 5:7</note> 

<margin>Prayer</margin> When I invite you to prayer, I do not invite you to that which consists of many words, but to that which happens in the secret retreat of the mind, in the inner chambers of the soul. Speak to God with your very heart. In the **most luminous darkness of contemplation**, <note>A reference to "apophatic" or mystical theology, where God’s light is so intense it appears as darkness to the human mind.</note> do not merely present your mind to the Father, but unite it with Him in certain ineffable ways known only to those who have experienced them. I do not care how long your prayer is, but how effective it is, and how burning—interrupted by sighs rather than a continuous series of phrases spread out in a rhythmic count. 

If your health is dear to you, if you wish to be safe from the devil's snares, from the storms of the world, and from the ambushes of enemies; if you desire to be pleasing to God and finally to be happy: let no day pass in which you do not approach your God at least once through prayer. Prostrate before Him with the humble affection of a repentant mind, cry out—not from the tips of your lips, but from your innermost depths—with the Prophet: *Remember not the sins of my youth and my ignorances, but according to your mercy remember me, for your goodness’ sake, O Lord.* <note>Psalm 25:7 (Vulgate 24:7)</note> 

The Holy Spirit <note>original: "ipse qui interpellat pro nobis," referring to the Spirit interceding for us as in Romans 8:26</note> will suggest to you what to ask of your God every hour, as will your own necessity. **Sacred reading** will also suggest it to you; I ask you again and again that, casting aside the fables and trifles of the poets, you always keep the scriptures in your hands. You can do nothing more pleasing to God or more useful to yourself than if you never cease to *turn the sacred pages by night and by day.* <note>An adaptation of Horace’s advice to poets to study Greek models "nocturna versate manu, versate diurna."</note> For there lies hidden in them a certain celestial power, living and effective, which—if one treats them purely and humbly—transforms the soul of the reader into divine love by a certain wonderful power.

But I have already exceeded the limits of a letter, drawn along by the subject matter itself and by a certain wonderful charity with which I have followed you in spirit, especially from that hour when I was informed of your most holy purpose. <note>Likely referring to the recipient's decision to join a religious order.</note> Finally, I would wish you to be reminded of this, of which I often spoke with you when you were here with me: never forget these two things: both that the Son of God died for you, and that you too, even if you live long, will soon die. With these twin spurs—one of fear, the other of love—urge your horse through the short course of this momentary life toward the rewards of eternal happiness. We neither should nor can set any other goal for ourselves than to enjoy the infinite Good without end, with perpetual peace for both parts of man. <note>Refers to the peace of both soul and body.</note>

Farewell. And fear God. Friday, May 15, 1492.

***

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Filippo Beroaldo, Greetings.
<note>Filippo Beroaldo (1453–1505) was a famous Italian humanist and commentator on classical texts.</note>

I received from you, most learned Beroaldo, a letter that was as lovely as it was erudite, along with many verses that surely challenge antiquity itself. That gift was most pleasing to me. Therefore, for your sake, I have spent my leisure hours well in a good pursuit; I could not have enjoyed myself in any matter more pleasantly or more honorably. 

<margin>Note</margin> Truly, I would act as a most ungrateful man if I wished to repay your excellent works with my own, which are the worst—exchanging "Suffenus’s poison" for Catullian wit. <note>Pico is using "humanist modesty." Suffenus was a notoriously bad poet mentioned by the Roman poet Catullus; Pico is jokingly comparing his own poetry to Suffenus's trash.</note> For I am no better in poems than he was, except in this: I recognize that I am a Suffenus, and I see "what is in the bag on my back." <note>An allusion to Aesop’s fable that we carry our own faults in a bag behind us where we cannot see them, while others' faults are in front.</note> Yet you demand this of me: namely, that I give you something of my own writings. And you demand it in such a way that you seem to be making a formal request, as if you would not take a rejection lightly. Wherefore, even if it brings me...

...therefore, if you hold any opinion of me, it must be satisfied. You have, therefore, two letters: one to Lorenzo de' Medici, the other to Ermolao <note>Ermolao Barbaro (1454–1493), a Venetian scholar and diplomat who famously debated Pico on the merits of "barbarian" scholastic philosophy versus elegant humanism.</note> concerning the style of the philosophers <note>original: "de genere dicendi phōrū [philosophorum]"</note>. To these I have also added certain short verses which escaped me during these days while I was occupied with other matters. You will read these in such a way that you remember I have engaged in these "less-than-humane" studies <note>A self-deprecating reference to his technical philosophical work as opposed to "humane" or elegant literary studies.</note> with hurried care and in my spare moments, as one who has devoted his primary labor and—as they say—his serious lamps <note>original: "seriosas... lucernas." A classical idiom for late-night study and deep intellectual labor.</note> to the philosophers. Among them, I hope I have made as much progress as you have among the rhetoricians and poets; among whom (I speak from the soul) I do not see why you should not by right claim the first prize. Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), the preeminent poet and scholar of the Medici circle.</note> is entirely yours; he loves you as much as any man can. Regarding me, you may promise yourself anything that is within my power. Farewell.

## Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Lorenzo de' Medici, heartiest greetings.

1. I have read <note>The text reads "Egi," likely a transcription of "Legi" (I have read).</note>, Lorenzo de' Medici, your verses <note>original: "Rythmos." This refers specifically to Lorenzo's Italian-language poetry.</note> which the vernacular muses <note>The "vernacular" muses represent poetry written in the common Italian tongue rather than the formal Latin of scholars.</note> suggested to you in your tender youth. I recognized in them the legitimate offspring of the Muses and the Graces; I did not, however, recognize in them a work of a "tender age" <note>Pico is complimenting Lorenzo by saying his early poems are far more mature than his age would suggest.</note>. For who would not see in your rhythms and the melodic joining of your verses the Graces dancing to the beat...

...so that whoever takes away from you mutilates the work, while whoever shears or prunes from him <note>The author is likely comparing the recipient (Lorenzo de' Medici) to a predecessor like Petrarch or Dante</note> actually cleans it up. Even if we were to grant—which I never will—that what he wrote is more charming and more elegant than yours, it was easy for a man to excel when he did not have to struggle and fight with the very meanings of the words. But those sharp, subtle, and (to put it in a single word) **Laurentian** <note>Refers to the specific intellectual and poetic style of Lorenzo "the Magnificent" de' Medici</note> thoughts of yours can hardly be said to reject "curling irons" <note>A metaphor for artificial stylistic embellishment or excessive "dolled up" prose</note> and unwillingly admit those "dyes" <note>fucos: literally seaweed used for rouge; a metaphor for deceptive or superficial beauty in writing</note>. If that other author, whom we read as soft, polished, and pleasant, had been required to handle your subject matter, we would surely read him as thorny, squalid, and ungrateful. Indeed, one can see him, whenever he attempts anything sharp, intricate, or knotty, failing as much in his style as he rises in his thought.

When, however, he shows off that "furniture" of his words—his ointments, curls, and flowers—Castritius <note>Titus Castricius, a teacher of rhetoric mentioned by the ancient author Aulus Gellius</note>, if he were present, would often warn him as he warned Gracchus: that we should not be deceived by the rounded sound and the flow of the verses. Instead, we should examine what lies beneath: what seat, what foundation, what depth the words have. If you were to do this there, you would sometimes see an "Epicurean void" <note>A philosophical joke suggesting there is no substance or "atoms" beneath the surface</note>: so that there is either no meaning beneath, or what is there is cold and trivial. In this regard, which is the most important part, even if you did not surpass him, I do not see at all why he should be considered superior to you for the sake of speaking gracefully. For words could not be more illustrious than they are in your work, and their arrangement is so fitting that they could not possibly cohere better, flow more roundly, or fall more rhythmically in any way.

<margin>Note</margin> But now let us weigh Dante against you, about whom perhaps more people will stir up controversy. For there are many who, in comparing writers, do not weigh merits so much as they count years; they command others to read the ancients with reverence, while they themselves cannot read their contemporaries without envy. Certainly, as far as style is concerned, I think no one will deny you the first place. Dante is sometimes so rough, harsh, and thin—even crude and unpolished—that even his own "goldsmiths" <note>aurarii: likely a reference to Dante’s ardent commentators or those who try to "gild" his reputation</note> admit it. But they throw the blame for this onto the age and the century in which he lived. You are entirely more refined in your speech, and he is not "grander" than you. 

But they will say he is "grander and more sublime" in his meanings. I ask you, what is so wonderful about him speaking of philosophical matters when nature itself compels this and freely supplies the thoughts? <margin>Augustine. Thomas</margin> If the subject is God, the soul, or the blessed, he merely brings forward what Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas</note> or Augustine have written on these things. And he was as frequent and assiduous in meditating on and treating these things as you are in carrying out the greatest public and private business. It was not so remarkable for Dante to have done this as it would have been shameful for him to have failed at it.

But it was, without a doubt, a work of the highest genius that you yourself excel in making philosophical those things which are amorous; and those things which are somewhat harsh in their own severity, you make lovely by introducing "Venus" <note>The quality of charm, grace, and beauty</note>. Thus, in your verses, the serious matters of philosophers are so mixed with the playfulness of lovers that the former gain dignity from the latter, and the latter gain cheerfulness and grace from the former. By this union, both together and each individually are better than they were before. 

But this is not as admirable as that which moved me most: that these ideas were introduced by you not as if imported, but as if dug out from the very lap of the subject matter you are treating. From that very subject—as if you were watering the soil—they seem to bloom, so that they appear native, not foreign; necessary, not brought in; entirely genuine, not counterfeit. This is what I cannot admire enough, and it is why you seem to me to have surpassed Dante. For even if he flies high, he is lifted by the wings of his subject matter; you, even though the subject resists and pulls you downward, are raised on high by the wings of your genius; and so raised...

<meta>This page continues a detailed literary and philosophical critique, likely addressed to Lorenzo de’ Medici, comparing his poetic compositions and "paraphrase" to the works of the Italian masters Petrarch and Dante.</meta>

...so that you do not depart from the subject matter: but rather that you raise it up along with yourself, as much as you have deserved from it as much as it deserved from Dante himself. Now it is possible to see what difference there is between you, Francesco <note>original: "Franciscum"; referring to Francesco Petrarch (1304–1374), the famous Italian poet and humanist.</note>, and Dante: to which I would add that Francesco sometimes does not live up to his promises—having something that charms at first glance, but does not satisfy further. Dante has something that sometimes strikes one as harsh upon the first encounter, but delights more as one penetrates into his inner depths. Your works have no less in their conclusion to hold the reader than they have in their first appearance to capture them. Add to this that those men sang their poems in retreats, in the shade, and in the highest tranquility of their studies; you sang yours amidst the tumults, the din of the court, the clamors of the marketplace, the greatest cares, and the most turbulent storms, while being most occupied. For them, the Muses <note>The Nine Muses of Greek mythology, who presided over the arts and sciences.</note> were their ordinary and principal business; for you, they are a game and a certain relaxation from cares. For them, they were the greatest exhaustion; for you, they are leisure when you are exhausted. Finally, by relaxing your mind, you reached a point which they, perhaps, did not reach even when straining every nerve of their souls. 

But what shall I say of my paraphrase? For why should I not call it mine? Either because it is mine by right of naming; or finally, why not mine, which, even if I venerate it as yours, I nevertheless love as my own? I truly admire it, and you in it, from which I gather how far I was from true praise of your verses—in which I had not looked deeply with my "owl-eyes" <note>original: "noctuinis oculis"; a metaphor for being unable to see clearly in the light of such brilliance, or perhaps having limited vision.</note> into those things which were greatest and most illustrious. I then saw them revealed through you, who alone both could and should do so: you owe it to yourself and to us, lest you should cheat yourself of much glory and us of much pleasure. I read it (God is my witness), most excellent Lorenzo, not so much for delight as for instruction. For how many things are there from Aristotle’s *Physics* <note>original: "auditu. f. physico"; referring to the 'Physica Auscultatio'.</note>, from his books <margin>Aristotle</margin> on the soul, on ethics <note>original: "de moribus".</note>, on the heavens, and from his *Problems*? How many from Plato’s *Protagoras*, from the *Republic*, <margin>Plato</margin> from the *Laws*, and from the *Symposium*? All of these, although I have read them elsewhere in the original authors, I nonetheless read in your work as if they were new, as if they were better, and transformed by you into I know not what form, so that they seem to be yours and not theirs—and in reading, I seem to learn something. 

This is the greatest proof that you understand these things not just from a commentary, but from your own self. For many are accustomed to put more "sophistry" <note>original: "σοφιστεια" (sophisteia); meaning clever imitation or superficial wisdom rather than true knowledge.</note> into literature than actual work; when they are about to write something, they keep philosophers as if they were technical advisors <note>original: "pragmaticos".</note> suggesting certain dogmas to them, which they thrust into their little books so that they might appear to be philosophers. But you may easily catch these people. For you would see those ideas are neither rightly arranged nor coherent, and are not explained by the authors, but rather entangled. And men who are otherwise eloquent appear like speechless infants when speaking of those matters. 

But who would not see that you do not hold these things on loan, but as matters over which you have right and power to turn, act, and treat at your will? You have attained these things (O happy genius!) in the heat of the republic and in an active life—things which we, who are not the disciples of philosophers but merely their tenants <note>original: "inquilini"; suggesting one who merely lives in a place without owning it.</note> in a life of shadows and sedentary study, follow after rather than actually catch. 

But what shall I say of the most sweet style of your paraphrase? To me, it seems entirely like that of Caesar <margin>Caesar</margin> in the Roman tongue: for it is an oration not made by hand <note>meaning it feels natural, not manufactured.</note>, not gilded, not twisted, but upright by its own nature, candid and "square" <note>original: "quadrata"; in classical rhetoric, this implies a sense of stability, balance, and solid construction.</note>; neither running out rashly nor losing its footing; neither luxurious nor starved; neither playful nor ungrateful; sweetly grave, and gravely lovable. The words are chosen, not grasped at; illustrious, not fake; necessary, not sought out; not merely explaining the matter, but placing it before one's very eyes. I pass over the fact that you always remember your own person—that the very seeds of your prudence are scattered everywhere...

He highlights Lorenzo's mastery of Aristotle and Plato, noting that he integrates their wisdom naturally rather than superficially.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes a correspondence regarding the stylistic qualities of Lorenzo de’ Medici before beginning a famous exchange between the humanists Giovanni Pico della Mirandola and Ermolao Barbaro. It marks the transition from praising the "Laurentian" style to Pico’s defense of Medieval "barbarous" philosophers.</meta>

These traces I have followed, along with many others, and each person according to their ability has seen far better things. But beyond these, I have seen two particular things, which perhaps not many see, however keen-sighted they may be. The first is that she <note>Likely referring to the Muse or the specific "Laurentian" style personified</note> conceals her riches to avoid envy; she holds flowers in her lap but does not display them; she does not grow tall like a plant, but settles down naturally so as to appear smaller. I do not see what the second thing is—for I am not so skillful—but I see that there is *something*, I know not what, which I would call most distinctly **Laurentian** <note>Referring to Lorenzo de’ Medici, "The Magnificent," the de facto ruler of Florence and a great patron of the arts</note>. For if anyone were to see the gifts, the talent, and the excellence of Lorenzo, he would see the whole man vividly portrayed. But these things I have said are perhaps too many; they have drawn me out, as they say, even against my will, as my mind’s feeling led me into words. I will not neglect to urge you with the greatest effort I can to steal a little leisure time from governing the state <note>original: "amoderanda repu." (a moderanda republica)</note> to finish the paraphrase you are working on. This will bring honor to yourself and your native tongue among your fellow citizens, and be of use and pleasure to all of us.

->At Florence, on the Ides of July, 1484.<-

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to his friend Ermolao Barbaro, greetings.

[Space]

Indeed, my Ermolao, I can neither keep silent about what I feel for you, nor fail to feel those things which ought to be felt toward a man in whom everything is found in the highest degree. But I wish my mind were capable of understanding you as you deserve; I wish I had such power of speech that I might one day express what I always feel. I know that what I have conceived of you falls infinitely below the height of your learning. You should know that whatever we say is far less than what we conceive; know that words are as lacking for the soul as the soul is for the reality of things. And yet, would you believe I am so bold as to hope I can imitate your works, though I cannot even estimate their greatness? Everyone can admire you; so few can imitate you that no one can find fault. 

And I wish I had such good fortune that what I write might in some part reflect my Ermolao. For your style itself—to say nothing of the rest—which you favor so little, affects and delights me so much. It is so learned, grave, composed, erudite, and refined; it is so clever, in which nothing is exposed or trivial, whether you look at the words or the ideas. Often I and our friend Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano, a leading humanist scholar and poet</note> read whatever letters of yours we have, whether addressed to others or to us. The following parts always compete with the preceding ones, and new graces bloom fruitfully as we read, so that we have no room to breathe between our perpetual exclamations. 

But it is wonderful to say how you persuade and drive the reader's mind wherever you wish. I experienced this myself, as I always do, but especially in this most recent letter of yours to me. In it, you attack these "barbarous" philosophers <term>Barbarous philosophers: A term humanists used for Medieval Scholastic thinkers whose Latin they considered clunky and unclassical</term>, whom you say are commonly held to be filthy, rude, and uncultured—men who did not even live while they were alive, let alone live now that they are dead; and if they live now, they live for punishment and disgrace. I was so moved, so ashamed and weary of my own studies. For I have spent six years among them, and I wish I had done less than to have struggled so laboriously in a matter of such little value. I have lost, I say, my better years among Thomas <margin>Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, the 13th-century Dominican theologian</note></margin>, John Scotus <margin>John Scotus <note>Duns Scotus, known as the 'Subtle Doctor'</note></margin>, Albert <margin>Albert <note>Albertus Magnus, teacher of Aquinas</note></margin>, and Averroes <margin>Averroes <note>The 12th-century Andalusian-Arabic philosopher and commentator on Aristotle</note></margin>—so many long nights in which I might perhaps have become something in "good letters" <note>original: "bonis litteris"—referring to classical literature and the humanities</note>...

<meta>This page continues a sentence from the previous page, beginning with the second half of the word "cogitabam" (I was thinking). It is a famous passage from Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's 1485 letter to the scholar Ermolao Barbaro, where Pico defends the "barbaric" (unpolished) medieval philosophers against the stylistic criticisms of Renaissance Humanists.</meta>

...I was thinking to myself, to comfort me, whether if any of those men were to return to life now, they would have anything with which to defend their cause through some reason—men who were otherwise quite argumentative.
Finally, it occurred to me that one of them, perhaps a bit more eloquent than the rest, might defend his <term>barbarism</term> <note>original: "barbariam"; here referring to the "unpolished" or "uncivilized" Latin style for which medieval Scholastic philosophers were often mocked by Renaissance scholars</note> in a way that is as little barbaric as possible, perhaps in this manner: "We have lived in fame, O Ermolao <note>Ermolao Barbaro (1454–1493), a prominent Italian Humanist scholar and the recipient of this letter</note>, and we shall live hereafter! Not in the schools of grammarians and in the schoolrooms of children, but in the circles of philosophers and in the gatherings of the wise. There, the discussion is not about the mother of Andromache <note>In the Renaissance, asking "Who was the mother of Andromache?" was a way of mocking pedantic teachers who obsessed over useless mythological trivia</note>, nor the children of Niobe, nor light trifles of that sort. Instead, the principles of human and divine things are handled and debated. In contemplating, inquiring into, and unravelling these matters, we were so subtle, sharp, and keen that we might perhaps seem to have been sometimes too anxious and fastidious—if indeed anyone can be too fastidious or over-curious in the pursuit of truth. And indeed, if anyone should accuse us of dullness or slowness in these matters: come, I pray, whoever he is, let him step forward and engage with us; he will find that we possessed..."

<summary>In this passage, Pico della Mirandola imagines a medieval philosopher defending their "barbaric" style by arguing that substance and the pursuit of truth are more important than elegant grammar or mythological trivia.</summary>

<meta>This page continues a defense of the "barbaric" or unpolished style of scholastic philosophers, likely addressed to the humanist Hermolao Barbaro. The text contrasts the "painted" language of rhetoricians with the "marrow and blood" of true philosophical inquiry.</meta>

...we will condemn and pursue these qualities in a matron. Therefore, it is not us, but those foolish men who are inept, who celebrate the Bacchanalia <note>The wild, drunken festivals of Bacchus, god of wine.</note> at the feet of Vesta <note>The goddess of the hearth, symbolizing purity and gravity; the author implies a clash between wild behavior and a sacred, sober setting.</note>. They dishonor the gravity of philosophical matters and their purity with playfulness, as if using curling irons. Surely, what <margin>Synesius</margin> said of a youth can be aptly said of a speech: a "well-groomed" oration is always a decadent one <note>original: "comatam orationem semper cinedam." The term "cinedus" refers to a passive or effeminate dancer, suggesting that overly ornate speech lacks masculine strength.</note>. For this reason, we prefer our own style to be shaggy-haired, dense, and unready, rather than beautifully groomed with either the mark or even the suspicion of impurity.

Even if there were nothing else, this is most true: nothing is more different from the practice of a <margin>Socrates</margin> philosopher, in any matter whatsoever, than that which tastes in any part of luxury or pride. Socrates used to say that Sicyonian shoes <note>Shoes from Sicyon were famous in the ancient world for being soft, comfortable, and often associated with luxury or feminine fashion.</note> were handy and fit the foot well, but they did not suit Socrates at all. The same logic applies to the habit of a citizen and a philosopher, just as it does to their tables and their speech. The philosopher uses these things only <margin>Pythagoras</margin> out of necessity; the citizen uses them also for grace. If the citizen neglects this grace, he is not "civil"; if the philosopher affects it, he will not be a philosopher. If Pythagoras could live without food, he would even spare the vegetables. If he could explain his thoughts by a look, or at least with less effort than speech requires, he would not speak at all. He is so far from polishing and adorning his tongue; indeed, we must beware of this, lest the reader, enticed by a "medicated" skin <note>Referring to skin covered in cosmetics or ointments.</note>, lingers upon it and does not penetrate to the marrow and the blood. We have often seen a corrupted interior beneath a face painted with white lead <note>White lead (ceruse) was a common but toxic cosmetic used to whiten the skin.</note>. I say we have seen this in all those for <margin>Musonius</margin> whom this style has come into use: since there is nothing inside that is not empty and vain, they detain the reader on the surface with various modulations and harmonies. If a philosopher does this, Musonius <note>Musonius Rufus, a Stoic philosopher known for his strict ethical teachings.</note> will cry out that it is not a philosopher speaking, but a flute player piping.

Therefore, let it not be attributed to us as a fault that we have not done that which it would have been a fault to do. We seek *what* we should write; we do not seek *how*. Or rather, the "how" we seek is that it be without pomp or any flowering of oration. We do not want it to be delightful, charming, or witty, but rather useful, grave, and venerable—so that it achieves majesty through a certain ruggedness rather than grace through softness. We do not expect the applause of the theater, where an even or rhythmic closing clause might stroke the ears, or where one might say "this is clever" or "that is elegant." Instead, we expect the silence of a few, born of admiration, as they look deep within at something either unearthed from the inner sanctuaries of Nature or brought down to men from the court of Heaven. We seek something so sharp that there is no room for attack, and so well-defended that there is no room for dispute.

Furthermore, let them admire us for being sagacious in inquiry, circumspect in exploration, subtle in contemplation, grave in judgment, intricate in binding an argument, and easy in unraveling it. Let them admire in us a brevity of style pregnant with many great things. We are well-instructed to remove ambiguities, to dissolve difficulties, to unroll what is tangled, and—with soul-bending syllogisms—to both weaken the false and confirm the true. By these titles, O Hermolao, we have claimed our place until now, and we do not doubt that we shall continue to claim our memory from oblivion hereafter. For if we are held to be "sordid, rude, and uncultivated" by the common crowd, as you say, this is a matter of glory for us, not an insult. We did not write for the common crowd, but for you and those like you. Not unlike how the ancients, with their enigmas and the wrappings of fables, kept uneducated men away from the mysteries, we too have become accustomed to frightening them away from our feasts, which they could not help but pollute...

<summary>In this letter, the author (Pico della Mirandola) defends the plain, unadorned language of scholastic philosophy against the polished rhetoric of humanists. He argues that true wisdom should be "rugged" and "pregnant with meaning" rather than dressed up in "medicated" or cosmetic prose that distracts from the truth.</summary>

<meta>This page continues a defense of philosophical style, specifically arguing that the internal truth of a text is more important than its rhetorical polish. It transitions from a general discussion of "vulgar" styles to specific examples from antiquity.</meta>

Since it is not fitting for philosophers merely to be approved, but even to be understood, it cannot but be unbecoming for what they write to have anything theatrical, plausible, or popular: anything that finally seems to accommodate itself to the judgment of the multitude. But perhaps you wish for me to fashion the ideal of our speech. It is the very same as the Silenus statues of our Alcibiades. <margin>Alcibiades</margin> <note>original: "Silenos nostri alcibiadis." In Plato’s *Symposium*, Alcibiades compares Socrates to Silenus statues—rough and ugly on the outside, but containing golden images of gods within.</note> For the images of these were made with a hairy, foul, and contemptible face. But inside, they were full of gems and rare, precious contents. 

Thus, if you look from the outside, you might see a beast; if you look within, you would recognize a divinity. But you will say that the ears cannot bear a texture that is now rough and now gaping, but always in harmony. You say they cannot bear barbarian names, which are almost terrifying in their very sound. 

O delicate man! When you approach flute-players and lyre-players, leave your ears behind you. But when you call upon philosophers, return from the senses to yourself, into the inner shrines of the soul and the recesses of the mind. Assume those ears of the man of Tyana <margin>Thianeus</margin> <note>Referring to Apollonius of Tyana, a 1st-century philosopher credited with supernatural perception.</note> with which—since he was not at all focused on the body—he heard not the earthly Marsyas <note>Marsyas was a satyr who challenged Apollo to a musical contest and lost.</note>, but the celestial Apollo, as he tempered the melody of the universe in ineffable modes with a divine lyre. 

If you taste the words of philosophers with these ears, they will seem honey-sweet to you, even to the envy of Nestor. <note>Nestor was the oldest and wisest Greek commander at Troy, described by Homer as having speech sweeter than honey.</note> But let us leave these things which rise up perhaps too much. Truly, to be disgusted by a less elegant style in a philosopher who is disputing with the utmost subtlety is not the mark of a delicate stomach, but an insolent one. 

Nor is it otherwise than if someone, while Socrates was teaching about morals, were to be offended by a loose shoe or a gaping toga, or were to be annoyed by an improperly cut fingernail. Cicero <margin>Tullius</margin> <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman orator.</note> does not require eloquence in a philosopher; rather, he requires that the philosopher satisfy the requirements of the subject matter and the doctrine. As a man both prudent and learned, he knew that it is our task to compose the mind rather than the diction; to take care that reason does not stray, rather than the speech. 

He knew that the internal word <note>original: "εμ Διαθεσει λογο" (en diathesei logon) — a Stoic term for the thought existing within the mind.</note> pertains to us, but the spoken word <note>original: "τομ εμ προφορα" (ton en prophora) — the thought as it is expressed in speech.</note> does not. It is laudable for us to have the Muses in the soul and not on the lips, lest anything in the soul sound too harsh through anger or too weak through lust; finally, lest there be any discord from that genuine harmony by which the soul is tunefully tempered. 

When Plato <margin>Plato</margin> understood that the state is often corrupted by these theatrical things and by the works of poets, he eliminated all poets from his republic. He left the government to philosophers, who would certainly be condemned to exile if they were to imitate the poets through the wantonness of their discourse. 

But Lucretius <margin>Lucretius</margin> <note>The Roman poet-philosopher who wrote *On the Nature of Things* in verse.</note> will insist that even if philosophical commentaries do not need the pleasantness of speaking for their own sake, the austerity of the subjects themselves must be concealed through its use. Just as wormwood <term>wormwood: a proverbially bitter herb used as a medicine for intestinal health</term> drives away diseases by itself, yet the cups are smeared with honey so that the improvident age of children may be deceived. 

Perhaps this was for you to do, O Lucretius, if you were writing your works for children; if for the common people, it was certainly for you to do—you who would offer not only wormwood but the most unmixed poisons. But we must have a far different reasoning: we who, as we said before, do not seek to entice the common people but to frighten them away. We do not offer foul wormwood, but nectar. 

But Lactantius <margin>Lactantius</margin> <note>An early Christian author known as the "Christian Cicero" for his polished Latin style.</note> will contend that it is well established that truth flows more powerfully into the minds of listeners—even elders—when it is equipped with force and adorned with the light of speech. If you had been, O Firmianus <note>Lactantius's full name was Lucius Caelius Firmianus Lactantius.</note>, as well-versed in sacred letters as you were in feigned lawsuits, you would not have said this. Perhaps you would have confirmed our views no less well than you destroyed those of others. 

Tell me, I pray, what moves more strongly and persuades more than the reading of sacred letters? They do not merely move or persuade; they compel, they agitate, they bring force. You read words that are rude and rustic, but they are living, animated, flaming, stinging, and penetrating to the very depth of the spirit, transforming the whole man with a wonderful power. Alcibiades says <margin>Alcibiades</margin> that he was not at all moved by the elaborate and brilliant speeches of Pericles <margin>Pericles</margin>...

Spanish, or what the common people are accustomed to call Parisian. When they speak to you, it will happen that much of what they say is laughed at, and much is not understood; the same will happen to you when speaking among them. **Anacharsis commits solecisms among the Athenians, but Athenians do so among the Scythians.** <note>original: "αναχαρσισ παραθηναιοισ σολοικιζει. αθηναιοι δε παρα σκυθαισ." Anacharsis was a Scythian philosopher; a "solecism" is a grammatical error or a breach of etiquette. The author is arguing that "correct" speech is relative to one’s culture.</note> That is, Anacharsis commits a solecism among the Athenians, and the Athenians among the Scythians. If the correctness of names depends on the nature of things, should we consult the rhetoricians, or rather the philosophers, who alone have thoroughly seen and explored the nature of all things regarding this correctness? Perhaps that which the ears reject as being somewhat harsh, reason accepts as being more closely related to the truth of things.

But why was it necessary for them to innovate the language, and if they were born among the Latins, why not speak in Latin? They were not able, O Hermolaus, <note>This refers to Hermolao Barbaro (1454–1493), a famous Italian humanist scholar who criticized the "barbarous" Latin of the medieval Scholastic philosophers.</note> while they were reading the laws of the fates and the order of the universe in the heavens—while they were reading the cycles of birth and death in the elements, the powers of simple things, and the temperaments of mixtures—they were not able, I say, at that same time to annotate the properties, laws, and observances of the Roman tongue in Cicero, in Pliny, or in Apuleius. They were seeking what was repellent and what was accepted in nature; meanwhile, they did not care for what was considered "true" by the Romans. 

Indeed, I now place you in a better position: I grant to you that eloquence and wisdom have conspired together in a mutual bond. But the philosophers have unyoked wisdom from eloquence; so too have the historians, the rhetoricians, and the poets. Philostratus <margin>Philostratus</margin> <note>Flavius Philostratus, a Greek sophist who wrote about the lives of philosophers.</note> laments this separation of eloquence from wisdom. You do not doubt that those who possess both will be celebrated with famous renown; but as for those others, look at what you are doing, for you see them only in terms of punishment and insult. Cicero <margin>Cicero</margin> prefers **uneloquent wisdom** to **foolish talkativeness**. In money, we do not ask what mint struck the coin, but what material it is made of. Nor is there anyone who would not prefer to have pure gold under a German stamp <note>The author is defending the "Teutonic" or German/Northern medieval scholars (like Duns Scotus) whose Latin style was seen as "clunky" compared to the "Roman" style of the Italians.</note> rather than counterfeit gold under a Roman symbol. 

Those who create a divorce between the heart and the tongue commit a sin; but those who are all tongue and have no heart at all, are they not merely—as Cato <margin>Cato</margin> says—**mortuary glossaries**? <note>A "mortuary glossary" refers to something that has words but no life or spirit.</note> We can live without a tongue, though perhaps not comfortably; but without a heart, we cannot live in any way. He who is unacquainted with more refined literature is not human; but he who is devoid of philosophy is not a man. Uneloquent wisdom can be of benefit; but foolish eloquence is like a sword in a madman's hand—it cannot help but be extremely harmful. 

Therefore, you will say, statues are commended not for their figure but for their material. And if Choerilus <margin>Choerilus</margin> <note>An ancient poet often cited as an example of a bad writer.</note> had sung of the same things as Homer, <margin>Homer</margin> or if Maevius <margin>Maevius</margin> <note>A poet ridiculed by Virgil and Horace.</note> had sung of the same as Virgil, <margin>Virgil</margin> they would have been received among the poets as equals to those greats. Do you not see the disparity in the similarity? We also assert that a thing is estimated by its form, not merely by its subject matter. For a thing is what it is because of its form. But one kind of form is required to be received among philosophers, and another among poets. 

Let Lucretius <margin>Lucretius</margin> write about nature, about God, and about providence; and let one of our own write about the same things. Let John Scotus <margin>Scotus</margin> <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a leading medieval Scholastic philosopher often mocked by Renaissance humanists for his complex, technical language.</note> write, even in verse so that he might be more "inept." Lucretius will say that the principles of things are atoms and the void; that God is corporeal and ignorant of our affairs; and that everything is carried along blindly by the fortuitous collision of small bodies. But he will say these things in Latin and elegantly. John will say that the things that exist in nature are constituted by their own matter and form; that God is a separate mind, knowing all things and providing for all things. Nor is He moved in the least from His own peace because He sees and governs all things, even the lowest. But he says this in a way that is usually called **"descending without moving downward."** <note>original: "κατιοντα μη κατιεναι" - A Neoplatonic concept describing how the Divine can interact with the lower world without losing its higher nature.</note> But he will say it tastelessly, rudely, and not in Latin words. I ask, who can doubt which is the better poet, and which the better philosopher? It is beyond all controversy that Scotus philosophizes as much more correctly as the other speaks more ornately. But see how they differ: this one has a tasteless mouth, but that one has a senseless mind; this one is ignorant of the decrees of grammarians (not to mention poets), but the other is ignorant of the decrees of God and nature. This one, though most "infantlike" <note>The Latin "infantissimus" literally means "unable to speak," here meaning uneloquent.</note> in his speech, perceives things that deserve to be praised...

<meta>This page concludes Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's famous 1485 letter to Hermolao Barbaro regarding the "barbaric" style of the Scholastic philosophers, and begins a second letter to the poet-theologian Baptista Mantuanus concerning biblical translation and Pico's personal study habits.</meta>

...they cannot be praised enough; that most eloquent speaker utters unspeakable things. They will perhaps assert these things, my dearest Hermolao, in defense of their own **barbarism** <note>Pico refers to the "Scholastic" philosophers of the Middle Ages, whom Renaissance humanists criticized for their rough or "barbaric" Latin style</note>, or perhaps they are much better due to their logical subtlety. I do not entirely agree with their opinions, nor do I think any high-born or free-thinking person should. But I have willingly exercised my skills in this infamous subject, just as some write praises of a **quartan fever** <note>A "quartan fever" was a form of malaria. Writing a formal praise for something undesirable was a common rhetorical exercise to demonstrate wit and skill</note>. I did this so that my talent might be tested, and with this intention: just as Glaucon in Plato’s works praises injustice—not from a true judgment, but to stimulate Socrates to further praise justice—so I might hear the cause of eloquence pleaded by you. I have attacked it, moving somewhat against my own feelings and nature. If I truly thought eloquence should be neglected or held inferior to those "barbarians," I would not have almost entirely deserted them for it, as I recently did—turning to Greek literature and to your never-sufficiently-praised **Themistius** <note>Hermolao Barbaro had recently translated the works of Themistius, an ancient Greek commentator on Aristotle</note>.

Yet, I will say freely what I feel: certain grammarians turn my stomach. When they have grasped two meager origins of words, they show off so much, they sell themselves so much, they carry themselves around so boastfully that they think philosophers should be considered as nothing compared to themselves. “We do not want these philosophies of yours,” they say—and what wonder? Neither do dogs want **Falernian wine** <note>Falernian was the most prized wine of ancient Rome; Pico implies the grammarians lack the "taste" for deep philosophy</note>. But let us close this letter here. Whether those "barbarians" earned any glory or name for themselves by the mere knowledge of things is not easy to say. But what place, what praises will you claim for yourself, you who are the most eloquent among philosophers, and among the eloquent, you are (to speak in Greek) **most philosophical** <note>original: "philosophōtatos"</note>?

->Florence, June 3, 1485.<-

Greetings, most beloved father. Concerning **Apollonius of Tyana** <note>A 1st-century miracle-worker and philosopher whose life story was sometimes compared to that of Jesus in the Renaissance</note>, I feel nothing other than what you feel, about which I shall write more to you when I have leisure, which will perhaps not be unwelcome to you. Concerning the variation of our translation from the Hebrew text in the third chapter of the book of Genesis <note>Genesis 3:15</note>, where it deals with Eve and the serpent, I judge as follows: in the Hebrew, it is as you write, **"He shall crush your head"** <note>original: "ipsum conteret caput tuum"</note>, and it refers to the seed of Eve, of which it had been said, "I will put enmity between your seed and her seed." However, the **Seventy** <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> and Jerome <note>The translator of the Latin Vulgate</note> translated it as **"She shall crush your head"** <note>original: "ipsa conteret caput tuum"</note>. In both cases, however, the meaning is the same. For when it is said **"He shall crush,"** it does not refer so much to the person of Eve as to the posterity of Eve. Since it is said she will do what she is to do through her seed. But as to why they preferred to translate "she" rather than "he," I think the reason was to signify that since not only women but also males were to be propagated from Eve, that which was said of the seed should be referred to the feminine seed alone <note>Pico is likely hinting at the Christian interpretation that the "woman" who crushes the serpent is the Virgin Mary</note>. These are the things that come to mind regarding this matter for the present. I am assiduously working on the **Harmony of Plato and Aristotle** <note>Pico's major project to reconcile the two greatest Greek philosophers, aiming to show they agreed on fundamental truths</note>. I give to it a proper morning period every day; after the midday hours, I give time to friends, to health, and sometimes to poets and orators and whatever studies require lighter effort; I leave the night for itself and for sleep. Your **Poliziano** <note>The famous poet Angelo Poliziano, a close friend of Pico</note> is entirely yours. Farewell, and pray to God for me.

->Florence, March 20, 1485.<-

To the Reverend Father in Christ, Brother **Baptista Mantuanus** <note>Baptista Mantuanus (1447–1516) was a famous Neo-Latin poet and Carmelite reformer</note>, of the Order of Carmelites, distinguished poet, philosopher, and theologian, etc. 
->Your son, Giovanni of Mirandola.<-

<meta>This page continues the correspondence of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, the famous Renaissance humanist and philosopher. **Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Aldus Manutius sends greetings.**

I am sending the Homer which you desired, though later than you wished and than I ought to have sent it. I am so distracted by my occupations, my dear Aldus, that there is no room even to breathe. I have long since bound myself into the service of literature <note>original: "litteris in famulatum," implying a total devotion to study</note> (as you well know). Those studies, following their own command, so severely demand their toll of reading and dictating that I can hardly rescue my own health. As for what you write that you will do: gird yourself for philosophy. But do so on this condition: that you remember there is no philosophy that calls us away from the truth of the mysteries. 

->**Philosophy seeks the truth; Theology finds it; Religion possesses it.**<-

Farewell. Florence, the eleventh day of February, in the year of grace 1490.

***

**Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Hermolao Barbaro, Patriarch of Aquileia, sends greetings.**

I hear that you have been elected Patriarch of Aquileia. I congratulate those people on an excellent shepherd, the whole church on a most energetic soldier, and you on the opportunity given to illustrate and amplify your virtue. There are generally three ways of living: the **Civil**, the **Contemplative**, and the **Religious**. In the first, we require prudence; in the second, learning; and in the third—the very summit of life—we require holiness in addition to those other two. In the past, your city has experienced you as most diligent and prudent in managing the republic and handling great affairs; and all scholars love and admire you as a patron and protector of the <term>Liberal Arts</term> <note>The "bonarum artium," referring to the humanities and classical studies</note>. We know without a doubt that you will fulfill what remains to be done, and we rejoice so sincerely that the Church shall hereafter owe you no less than your city and literature have owed you until now.

***

**Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to his friend Hermolao sends greetings.**

What shall I say this is, my dear Hermolao, that you daily burden me with new kindnesses? It is as if you owe me something, though I have long owed everything to you. My brother Antonio came here recently while returning to our homeland. I asked what Hermolao was doing; he replied, "This is what he does: he loves you, praises you, and carries you to the heavens—to me, to others, and to the Pope himself." And he does this so constantly and so strongly as if he has nothing else to do. Others whom I have there <note>Likely referring to the papal court in Rome</note> also write to me sometimes, especially Cosimo Pazzi—a man who, to sum up his praises, is worthy of your unique love. Whenever he writes, he writes of your favors toward me, of your love, and of a certain wonderful inclination of mind, so that I feel you always speak of me in the most honorable way. 

Oh, this unheard-of kindness of yours! You think you can never do enough for a man of letters. Even if you act this way toward me to make me more yours and more obligated, you are, as they say, "acting upon what is already done" <note>original: "actum... agis," a Latin proverb meaning to do work that is already completed; Pico is saying he is already as devoted to Hermolao as possible</note>. I cannot owe more or love you more than I already do. But you are such a man: you surpass all others in prudence...

### Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Girolamo <note>Likely Girolamo Savonarola, the influential Dominican friar, or possibly the scholar Girolamo Donato.</note>, Greetings.

Unless our "Angel" <note>original: *Angelus*; a reference to Angelo Poliziano, whose first name means Angel.</note> were writing to you, I would have written more to you myself, but I do not want my "magpies" <note>original: *picas*; Pico is making a self-deprecating pun on his own name, suggesting his writing is like the chattering of birds compared to the refined "Muses" of Poliziano.</note> to drown out his muses, nor do I wish to rudely disturb your pleasure.

You will be most beautifully rewarded for this if you return the longest possible letters to me in exchange for these very short ones. For nothing is more pleasing to us than your letters; I beg you not to deprive me of them. Otherwise, if you remain silent, I shall return like for like. Indeed, I shall then especially refuse to be silent, for in that way I would retaliate against you quite beautifully.

<meta>This letter continues the correspondence between the famous humanist philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola and the scholar-poet Angelo Poliziano, likely following a delivery of manuscripts or books between their respective libraries.</meta>

**Giovanni Pico della Mirandola sends greetings to Angelo Poliziano.**

Never more politely nor more cheerfully have my "Loves" <note>Pico is personifying his own writings or poems, which he had sent to Poliziano for review</note> declared themselves received than in these past few days at your house [handwritten marginal note: 18] <margin>18</margin> and how friendlily they were "pierced through" <note>original: *confossi*; a playful metaphor suggesting Poliziano’s sharp, critical editing was like a surgical or soldierly wounding</note>; while they congratulate themselves greatly, they also owe you much. For who would not want to die by that sword of yours? Yet they grieve that it was done more indulgently than was proper, and they are at the point of doubting whether you became blind to my "Loves" out of love itself. And they doubt so much that they do not quite trust your judgment—otherwise so grave—in their own case. Yet they do trust, and even now they claim their chains; they do not know how to stay at home, but securely demand their freedom and the public eye. 

But what shall I say of the liveliness of your Epictetus? <note>Poliziano had recently translated the *Enchiridion* (Manual) of the Stoic philosopher Epictetus from Greek into Latin</note> Oh, what a humorous thing and worthy of a laugh from Cato himself! He was hardly at the threshold when, opening his cloak, he said: "Behold the critical marks! Behold the arrows!—if you do not know the Greek." <note>original: *obelos* and *sagittas*; Pico refers to the technical symbols used by scholars to mark errors or points of interest in a manuscript</note> "Behold me, prepared to strike back if any of you should be bold." Who could have restrained their laughter when a Stoic man joked so charmingly? 

We certainly held back our weapons, both because he was bound to return the injury and because his skin had grown so thick that he would not admit such light strikes. Therefore, with the veneration we owed, we received the old man. When he finally sat down among us, he began to philosophize about morals. And he did so in English <note>original: *latine* (in Latin); Pico is referring to Poliziano’s Latin translation of the Greek philosopher</note>, not so much because he was among those who speak that tongue (for there were those in the assembly who knew Greek), but because through your blessing he himself tasted more brilliantly in that language. But he did not waste his effort, since he did not stop speaking until he had made us into Stoics instead of Peripatetics <note>Peripatetics were followers of Aristotle; Pico is joking that the book was so persuasive it converted them from Aristotelianism to Stoicism</note>. We all approved of that *dispassion* <term>dispassion: a translation of the Greek *apatheia*, the Stoic ideal of being free from emotional disturbance</term>, so that now one might see men who were a little while ago quite delicate now made most tolerant of all things. We can indeed be provoked by others, but harmed only by ourselves; we shall never struggle against fate, and those things which are not our own we wish to happen just as God wills. We shall never blame nor accuse anyone; we shall grieve for nothing and demand nothing; we shall not know how to serve or be defeated. 

Let us philosophize in deeds, not in speech; and since we are novices, let us observe ourselves as if we were adversaries. Let us neglect, rather than reject, the opinion of others about us and other external things of that kind. Let us care for the day as travelers care for an inn; finally, let us possess those things, rather than be possessed by them. Let us love silence, lest anything be vomited out that is not yet digested <note>A favorite Stoic metaphor: one should fully "digest" or contemplate knowledge before speaking it</note>. Let us rarely produce laughter for ourselves, and never for others. And to embrace the whole of Epictetus in one word: we have abundantly learned both to endure adversity and to abstain from pleasures <note>original: *sustine et abstine*; the fundamental maxim of Epictetus's philosophy</note>. 

See how, point by point, we have modeled our life after your Epictetus. See how quickly we have done so, lest in this part too we should not be Stoics—for they want us to be reminded that a man fails as long as he does not make progress. Though I have admired this in others, I admire it most of all in myself: though I have always frequented the Lyceum or the Academy <note>referring to the schools of Aristotle and Plato</note> and never the Porch <note>referring to the *Stoa*, the school of the Stoics</note>, I was so conquered by the old man's speech that I moved over to his opinion not just with my feet, but with my hands and my whole body. 

I am sending to you the index of Greek books which are staying here with me, along with the letter of Manuel <note>Likely Manuel Adramyttenos, a scribe and scholar</note>, as your letter requests. I likewise desire an index of yours. Give my greetings to the younger Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo de' Medici the Younger</note> in my name; I was going to write to him, but shame deterred me, lest I seem to compel the man with letters. **Farewell.**

<summary>Pico della Mirandola writes to Poliziano, playfully describing his "conversion" to Stoicism after reading Poliziano's new translation of Epictetus. He also coordinates the exchange of scholarly book catalogs and manuscript information.</summary>

### Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Tommaso Fredi. Greetings.

The fact that you dedicated your little story <note>original: "fabellam"; here referring to a short literary work or perhaps a humanist comedy</note>—and such a festive and elegant one at that—to my name was a sign to me of both your learning and your singular goodwill toward me. Both of these are weighty reasons that urge and impel me to love you. I do not know which is greater: for as the proverb goes, in matters of love, it is a disgrace not to have returned mutual affection. Likewise, not to have loved such a highly praised man, even without being prompted, is the mark of either a rustic or a truly wicked character. 

See, therefore, how you do not merely invite me to friendship, but pull me with "double ropes" (as the saying goes) <note>original: "geminis funibus"; a classical idiom for being doubly bound or strongly compelled</note>. For there is nothing in that little story that does not smell of learning and genius. Nor could you have earned my gratitude more excellently than by so kindly and generously arranging for such an outstanding story to be dedicated to my name. I am so far from neglecting or finding fault with its subject matter that I approve of it with all my might. 

For it has always been my opinion—and I think no learned man will disagree—that it requires a sharper wit to write these jests and little stories (provided it is done, as you have most abundantly, with erudition and elegance) than to have discussed the weightiest matters, even in an ornate style. Indeed, since we judge it a far greater feat to have fashioned a beautiful statue from filings <note>original: "ex lima"; literally the metal dust or shavings from a file, a metaphor for the painstaking labor of polishing a work</note> than from a block of bronze or gold, why should it not be the same when someone says something remarkable about a humble subject versus a sublime one? 

It certainly involves more "business" <note>original: "negocii"; referring to the intellectual effort or "work" required</note> and is therefore even more praiseworthy. For those writing on grand topics, the inherent dignity of the subject matter acts as a "lure" <note>original: "lenocinatur"; meaning the topic itself provides the charm or attraction</note>; but whatever these writers of humble themes bring that is worthy is drawn entirely from the writer's own storehouse. The material itself contributes nothing, like a guest who brings no contribution to a shared feast <note>original: "a symbola"; a Greek-derived term for a potluck contribution</note>. Nature diligently assists the former, whereas the latter certainly contend against nature. 

Even if this is so, I would not deny that among these "humbler" subjects I mentioned, some are wonderfully superior to others. There are some of that genre so flat and tasteless that no force or majesty of words can sufficiently lift them up or season them skillfully. This can never be said of those faults which are repaired by the charming urbanity of jests. Truly, I believe those works should be placed in the highest seats <note>meaning the highest rank of literature</note> which contain a vivid description of different ages and character types <note>original: "personarum"; referring to social roles or stock characters</note> mixed with the wit of "salts" <note>original: "saliū"; a classical metaphor for wit or sharp humor</note>. Your story has all these qualities, which belong to the comic writers, and which you have most beautifully imitated in the work you gave to me. 

What cleverness is there! What a timely and ingenious mixture of wits! How it delights! How charming and perfect it is in every way! And if anything appeared a bit "shabby" or weak due to the humility of the subject matter, it raises itself up by the light and dignity of your speech, assuming brilliance and strength. It is, to put it briefly, a work that clearly demonstrates it was perfected by a most lettered man. But among all the rest, that exquisite and suitable observation of manners, ages, and character types is especially dear to my heart; in this alone your wisdom, and that...

<summary>In this letter, the philosopher Pico della Mirandola thanks Tommaso Fredi for a book dedication and argues that writing light, humorous literature (like Fredi's story) requires more skill than writing on "heavy" philosophical topics because the author must create beauty without the help of a grand subject.</summary>

...I ought to have asked: our friendship is mutual, which you (as befits a most excellent man) have initiated with perfect care. It remains that whenever you have need of my help—however small it may be—or my effort, you should put my goodwill toward you to the test. Nor indeed (if any opportunity is given) will I omit any kind of duty toward you, since you were the first to act toward me at the very threshold of our friendship. Farewell.

->### Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, Count of Concordia, to his dear Niccolò Leoniceno, Greetings. <margin>115.</margin><-

I would have spoken with you more often and at greater length through letters, my sweetest Niccolò, if your location had been known to me by messenger, letter, or even rumor. Indeed, I have anxiously inquired about this from many people, but received only uncertain answers from everyone. At last, in recent days, a letter from Antonio Faventino <note>Antonio degli Ordelaffi, a physician and philosopher from Forlì (Latin: Faventia).</note>, a most serious philosopher, to Tommaso Frignano came into my hands. From that letter, I learned you were in Florence, which was then most pleasing for me to hear. As soon as I understood this, I sent a letter to you in Florence by courier. It was a wasted trip, for he did not find you there. I was deeply grieved. Today, Tommaso indicated that you had departed Florence and are now in Bologna; I immediately ordered these lines to be delivered to you.

In this letter, I shall not strive to reveal my goodwill or my singular love for you at great length; for you ought not to doubt my feelings for you even the slightest bit—unless you were to think me forgetful (which is not in my nature) of both your excellent virtue and your kindnesses toward me. I could not, however, help but marvel greatly that when you rescued yourself from the turmoils of the city to seek a place where you could live both peacefully and pleasantly, you either forgot this little town of ours or certainly overlooked it. You seemed, Niccolò, to lack confidence either in my will or my resources; yet while the latter may be less than your merits deserve, the former is greater than you might think. 

It will be pleasing to me if you advise me of your plans, and most pleasing of all if you do not disdain to share my hearth with me, to live at leisure here while others are occupied with Mars <note>Pico refers to the Roman god of war, suggesting that while the rest of the world is busy with military or political strife, they could study in peace.</note>. For the rest, I am sending you <term>John the Grammarian</term> <note>John Philoponus, a 6th-century commentator on Aristotle whose works were highly sought after during the Renaissance.</note>, which was not found for many days but has now been recovered. I am yours, and I await you. Farewell. From Mirandola, July 20, 1482.

If you love me, take every care to obtain an index of all the books found in the library of Saint Dominic <note>The library of the Dominican convent in Bologna, one of the most important collections of the era.</note>; send it or bring it with you. Farewell again.

I have built a suburban villa, pleasant enough given the condition of the place and region. I have composed a long poem about it; the house will be sweet to you, and the poem will not be unpleasing. Again, farewell.

->### Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to his dear Angelo Poliziano, Greetings.<-

Regarding the fact that you praised me so much in your recent letter, I owe you exactly as much as I fall short of deserving such praise. For praise is owed to a person for what is given freely, not for what is merely paid as a debt. Therefore, I owe it entirely to you for what you write about me, since there is nothing of that kind in me. Since you owed this to me in no way at all, it was entirely a product of your kindness and your singular goodwill toward me. 

As for the rest, if you examine me, you will find nothing but what is thin, humble, and narrow. We are but novices and <term>recruits</term> <note>The original Latin "tirunculi" refers to young, inexperienced soldiers in training.</note> who have only just moved our feet out of the shadows of ignorance; we have advanced almost nowhere. It is a kindness to us if...

<meta>This page concludes a correspondence with Angelo Poliziano and begins a new letter from the philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to the humanist scholar Paolo Cortesi. The transition highlights the shift from discussing the "swan-like" eloquence of Poliziano to the philosophical value of letter-writing as a mirror of the soul.</meta>

...be counted among the ranks of students. The learned have a title—something else entirely—which is peculiar to you and those like you; such grand things do not suit me. Since those matters which are foremost in the study of literature are not only unexplored by me, but I have not yet even seen them except **through a lattice** <note>original: "pertranſennam" — an idiom meaning to see something only in passing or through a gap, rather than fully.</note>. I will indeed strive (as I am doing now) to be such a person, eventually, as you now declare me to be or judge me to be—or certainly as you would wish me to be. Meanwhile, I will imitate you, Angelo, who excuses yourself to the Greeks because you are Latin, and to the Latins because you "Grecize" <note>original: "græciſſes" — to speak or act like a Greek.</note>. I too will use a similar refuge, so that I may be approved by the poets and rhetoricians on the grounds that I am said to "philosophize," and by the philosophers because I act as a rhetorician and cultivate the Muses—although it happens quite differently for me than for you. For while I wish to sit on **two chairs** <note>original: "geminis... ſellis ſedere" — a metaphor for trying to hold two positions at once; Pico suggests he fails at both, while Poliziano succeeds in all.</note> (as they say), I am excluded from both; and it turns out (to put it briefly) that I am neither a poet, nor a rhetorician, nor a philosopher. 

You, however, fulfill both roles so well that it is hardly clear which you do more, for you embrace both the Greek and our own **Minerva** <note>A reference to the goddess of wisdom, here symbolizing the intellectual traditions of both Latin and Greek literature.</note> so beautifully, like a **swan of both languages** <note>In the Renaissance, the swan was a symbol of the perfect, eloquent poet.</note>, so that what is foreign and what is native cannot easily be discerned. For, to say nothing of the Latins (among whom you hold the first place), who would believe—as was said of Hadrian—that a Roman man could speak so purely in Greek? Our **Emanuel** <note>likely referring to the scholar Manuel Marullus or a similar contemporary.</note> used to swear, while reading your works, that Athens itself was not so **Attic** <note>original: "atticas" — referring to the dialect of Athens, considered the most refined and pure form of ancient Greek.</note>. You are the one, my Angelo (away with flattery), to whom only one or two of our men—if any at all—can be compared. If there were more such men, these centuries would have no reason to envy antiquity. Apply yourself, I pray, and rescue literature as much as you can from neglect, lest that brilliance of the Roman tongue perish utterly through the injury of time. Always strike out something new which may help and illuminate the Latin cause. And those works you have at home, let them finally come forth for the common benefit of students. Indeed, just as I love you yourself, I love and long for everything of yours; all the more so because I have set you before me as the model into which I might be molded. As all ought to follow such a man, so few are able to catch up to him. Farewell.

### Ioannes Picus Miran. to his friend Paulo Cortesi. Greetings. ###
<note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494) was a famous Italian Renaissance nobleman and philosopher.</note>

<margin>b</margin>

You think rightly, Paolo. Let us send letters frequently so that we, who are divided by the distance between places, may certainly be joined by the exchange of letters. It usually lightens the longing for those who are absent if you happen to have a statue or perhaps an image of them at home. Truly, to me, this seems to be the difference between an image and a letter: the former portrays the body, while the latter portrays the **mind**; the former sketches only the outer surfaces, while the latter clearly expresses and molds even the innermost thoughts. That represents the "cloak and clothing" of a friend, as it were, but this represents the **true friend** to us. That emulates the colors and figure of the flesh as best it can; this expresses thoughts, counsels, sorrows, joys, cares, and finally all affections. And those secrets of the soul which hardly anyone speaks to another in person, he transmits most faithfully to an absent friend. In short, this is a living and effective thing; that is a dead and mute likeness. 

Let us therefore send these images of our souls to one another—you indeed send those "golden and silver" ones you are capable of, and I shall send mine, whether they be of bronze or of clay. For in this way, we shall be beyond all injury of places and times. Just as the power of the mind itself knows neither the distances of space nor the delays of time. But truly, how great is that which I owe to you, most dutiful Paolo, because you...
